# Native Shell

> Native Shell: AI-generated UI, native in your app, on every platform. Apps on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and Linux, GPUI apps and web pages load signed, sandboxed TSX modules at run time and draw them with the platform’s own UI.

Apps are TSX modules run by QuickJS on a native Rust runtime; the toolchain is the single `nsh` binary (`nsh init my-app`, `nsh run my-app/App.tsx`). Every page below is also served as Markdown at its URL plus `.md`.

---

# Introduction

Native Shell (NSH for short) is designed for **AI-generated, dynamically delivered native UI**. A model writes a small module in TSX, and a native app loads it at run time and shows it with the platform's own UI, inside a sandbox the app controls. The same mechanism makes native apps extensible in general — plugins, features, whole screens delivered after release.

NSH runs on phones and desktops alike: iOS (UIKit), Android (Android views), macOS (AppKit), Windows (Win32 windows drawn with Direct2D) and Linux (GTK 4). Each platform has a native backend of its own, and the same module runs on all of them ([Platforms](https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms.md)).

> [!IMPORTANT]
> NSH is the layer inside an app for UI that is generated, changed or added after it ships. On a phone or a desktop, the app stays a native app, built and released the way it always was.

## Why it exists

**First: UI generated by AI.** An assistant inside your app can answer with an interface rather than with text. A model writes a small TSX module (a form, a chart, a booking card), your server checks, builds and signs it, and the app downloads it and shows it in an `NshAppView`: native UI, sandboxed, limited to what you granted, and with no app update. NSH is built around this use, so its design is AI friendly throughout:

- **A format models write well.** A module is one TSX file using signals, a handful of host elements and Tailwind classes — the vocabulary models already know from the web, with no build configuration and no NPM.
- **A precise, generated contract.** Every element, prop, style key and module has TypeScript declarations generated from the Rust sources (`.nsh/types`), so generated code can be type-checked, and a model can be given the exact API instead of guessing. These docs are also served as plain text for models ([`llms.txt`](/llms.txt), [`llms-full.txt`](/llms-full.txt)).
- **Checkable before it ships.** `nsh trace` runs a module headless, without a device, and reports errors and the views it produced; build errors come with a code frame. A generation loop can compile, run, read the result and retry. The compiler also runs in-process as a library (`nsh_bundler::compile_module`) and in the browser ([Playground](/playground)).
- **Safe to run when it is not trusted.** Generated code is untrusted code. Each module runs in its own QuickJS VM with memory, call-time and node limits, reaches only the capabilities the host grants, and arrives as a signed package the app verifies first.
- **Native without native code.** The output is the platform's own UI — UIKit, Android views, AppKit, GTK 4 or Win32 with Direct2D — with the system's text, input and accessibility, yet the model never writes Swift, Kotlin, Java or Rust, and the app never needs a new release.

![From a prompt to native UI: a model writes a TSX module; your server builds, checks and signs it; across the trust boundary, the app verifies the package, runs it in a sandbox with the limits and capabilities it set, and shows it with the platform's own UI.](https://nsh.dev/diagrams/ai-flow-light.svg)

**Second: extending native apps, and delivering UI dynamically.** The same mechanism serves any module, not only generated ones. The app embeds an `NshAppView` (iOS), `NshView` (Android) or `AppView` (macOS, Windows, Linux) wherever a module should appear, and NSH runs the module inside it:

- **Delivered after release.** A module is a signed package (`.nshpkg`) the app downloads at run time. The app checks its signature against the keys it trusts and against a revocation list before running it ([Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md)). A change needs no new binary and no store release.
- **The host stays in control.** Each module runs in its own sandboxed VM, with memory, time and node limits, and reaches only what the host grants: network hosts, web pages, the status bar ([Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)). Several modules can run side by side; there are no global singletons.
- **It looks like the rest of the app.** Modules render with the platform's own UI, so text, input, accessibility and scrolling are the system's. The host can register its own native views — a map, a player, a design-system component — for modules to use ([Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md)).

**Third: standalone apps.** The same modules can also be a whole app. `nsh package` turns them into an installable iOS, Android, macOS, Windows or Linux app with the prebuilt runtime, which is also the quickest way to try NSH: the [getting started](https://nsh.dev/docs/getting-started.md) guide does exactly that. It is a supported use, but not the one NSH is designed around.

## Why Native Shell, next to GPUI Shell

[Longbridge](https://longbridge.com) is building NSH as the plugin layer of its mobile client, and its desktop client needs the same layer. [GPUI Shell](https://gpui-kit.com/shell) makes [GPUI](https://gpui-kit.com) desktop apps extensible in JavaScript, and the first idea was to use it on phones too. It does not fit there, because its modules are drawn by GPUI itself, on the GPU, not with the platform's views:

- **System behavior would have to be rebuilt.** A self-drawn surface inside a native screen has none of the platform's text selection, nor the selection menu that comes with it (Copy, Share, Translate, Look Up, Select All), nor the system's input methods, accessibility and new visual materials each iOS release brings. Recreating them in a GPU renderer is a large, never-finished job, and the copies drift from the real thing.
- **Mobile teams would have to adopt a new UI stack.** Running a self-drawn layer at scale in an existing mobile client means its iOS and Android teams take on an unfamiliar renderer, its compatibility issues across OS versions and devices, and its bugs.

NSH therefore renders modules with each platform's own UI: UIKit on [iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md), Android views on [Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md), AppKit on [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md), Win32 windows drawn with Direct2D on [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md) and GTK 4 on [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md). One module format and one runtime run in all these hosts.

The two are positioned differently. GPUI Shell is for extending GPUI desktop applications; Native Shell is for native apps on every platform, phones and desktops alike.

## A module

A module is TypeScript and JSX:

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";

function Counter() {
  const count = signal(0);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center", gap: 12 }}>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 48, fontWeight: "700" }}>{count()}</Text>
      <View
        onPress={() => count.update((n) => n + 1)}
        activeOpacity={0.6}
        class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-5 py-3"
      >
        <Text class="text-white text-lg">Tap</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(Counter);
```

`<View>` becomes a `UIView` on iOS, a `ViewGroup` on Android, an `NSView` on macOS and a GTK widget on Linux, `<Text>` a native text view, and the button's press feedback (`activeOpacity`) runs on the main thread without a round trip to JavaScript. When you tap, `count.update` changes one signal, and only the text that reads `count()` is updated: the component function does not run again.

The host app shows it with a few lines of native code ([iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md), [Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md), [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#embedding-in-a-mac-app), [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#embedding-in-a-win32-app), [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#embedding-in-a-gtk-app)). On iOS:

```swift
let app = NshAppView()                         // a UIView: place it anywhere
try app.grantCapabilities(#"{ "network": { "hosts": ["api.example.com"] } }"#)
let info = try await app.loadPackage(at: downloadedFile, trust: trust)   // verified, then run
```

Only the module's code is JavaScript. Everything it calls into — the reactive graph, the renderer, layout, text and every module it imports — is native, written in Rust.

## How a module runs

A module (an "app" in the CLI's terms) is a set of `.tsx` / `.ts` files with an entry, usually `App.tsx`. The toolchain is a single `nsh` binary:

1. **Build.** `nsh` bundles the module's files (with rolldown and Oxc) and compiles the JSX with its own compiler. Imports of `nsh` and `nsh/*` stay imports: the runtime serves them natively, so the bundle holds only your code. The bundle is compiled to QuickJS bytecode.
2. **Run.** On the device, the engine thread runs the bytecode in [QuickJS](https://github.com/quickjs-ng/quickjs). Compiled JSX calls the native renderer directly; changes are collected during one JavaScript turn, laid out with [Taffy](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/taffy) (flexbox and CSS grid), and handed to the main thread as one batch of view operations per frame.
3. **Render.** The main thread applies the batch to native views. Text is measured and laid out once on the engine thread (CoreText on Apple platforms, `StaticLayout` on Android, DirectWrite on Windows, Pango on Linux) and only drawn on the main thread.

Because JavaScript only describes the UI and handles events, the work done in the interpreter is small. Parsing styles, resolving Tailwind classes, diffing, layout and text all happen in Rust.

> [!NOTE]
> The main thread never waits for JavaScript. Questions the system asks synchronously (may this input accept another character, may the user swipe back, may this sheet close) are answered natively from props you set beforehand, such as `maxLength`, `preventBack` or `dismissible`. Events reach your code afterwards.

## What you get

- **Embedding.** `NshAppView` (Swift), `NshView` (Java/Kotlin) and the desktops' `AppView` (AppKit, GTK, Win32) put a module in a native app, as many as you like ([iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md), [Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md), [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#embedding-in-a-mac-app), [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#embedding-in-a-gtk-app), [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#embedding-in-a-win32-app)).
- **Signed, revocable delivery.** Ed25519-signed packages, release keys certified by an offline root key, revocation lists ([Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md)).
- **A sandbox the host configures.** VM limits and capabilities granted per view, in the iOS and Android SDKs ([Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)).
- **The host's own views in modules.** Register native components from Swift, Java or Rust ([Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md)).
- **Native views.** Embedding a native map, web view or video player has no layering problems, accessibility uses the platform's own tree, and text input is the system's.
- **Fine-grained reactivity.** [Signals](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md) like Solid's, implemented natively. Components run once; only the expressions that read a changed signal run again.
- **Styles and Tailwind**, resolved natively: flexbox, CSS grid, shadows, gradients, filters, transitions ([Styling](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md), [Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md)).
- **A mobile UI set** (`nsh/ui/mobile`) whose components are written in Rust and drawn by NSH, so they look the same on every platform: [Button](https://nsh.dev/components/button.md), [Card](https://nsh.dev/components/card.md), [ListView](https://nsh.dev/components/list-view.md), [navigation](https://nsh.dev/components/navigation.md), and more. Desktop layouts are built from the primitives with `desktop={{…}}` props and `Platform.select` ([Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md)), and a desktop UI set is on the way.
- **One binary toolchain.** A single `nsh` executable builds modules, writes their type declarations, serves them with hot module replacement, packages and signs them.

## Where it runs

| Platform | Status | Backend | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| iOS | Supported (iOS 15.0+) | UIKit | Devices and the simulator; embedded with `NativeShell.xcframework` ([iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md)) |
| Android | Supported (API 28, Android 9+) | Android views | `arm64-v8a` and `x86_64`; embedded with `nsh.aar` ([Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md)) |
| macOS | Supported (macOS 14+) | AppKit | Standalone apps; embedded with `AppView` ([macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md)) |
| Windows | Supported (Windows 10 1809+) | Win32, Direct2D | Standalone apps; embedded with `AppView` ([Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md)) |
| Linux | Supported (GTK 4.14+) | GTK 4 | Standalone apps; embedded with `AppView` ([Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md)) |
| GPUI (macOS, Windows, Linux) | Supported | GPUI | Standalone apps; embedded with `AppView` in GPUI and GPUI Kit apps ([GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md)) |
| Web | Supported (modern browsers) | HTML | Static sites; embedded in a page with `createPlayer` or an iframe ([Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md)) |
| Mac Catalyst | For development | UIKit | The iPhone-sized window `nsh run` opens on a Mac, to see a module as on a phone |

![One module, many hosts: the same bundle and Rust runtime on iOS, Android, Linux, macOS with AppKit and Windows with Win32 / Direct2D, GPUI on all three desktops, and web pages drawn with HTML.](https://nsh.dev/diagrams/platforms-light.svg)

## How it compares

The usual ways to put UI into an app after release are web views, server-driven UI described in JSON, and mini-program containers; for whole apps, cross-platform frameworks such as React Native, Flutter, Electron and Tauri. An NSH module renders native UI where a web view renders a page, carries its own state and logic where a server-driven schema can only recombine built-in components, and runs in a sandbox the host configures in code. [Comparing approaches](https://nsh.dev/docs/comparison.md) goes through each.

## Next steps

- [Installation](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation.md) and [Getting started](https://nsh.dev/docs/getting-started.md): get `nsh`, write a first module and run it on each platform.
- [Platforms](https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms.md): what runs where, and how to run, package and embed on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and Linux.
- [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md) and [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md): deliver modules and decide what they may do.
- [JSX and components](https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components.md) and [Reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md): the two ideas everything else builds on.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs

# Comparing approaches

An app that wants UI it did not ship with — answers generated by a model, features from partners or other teams, screens that change without a release — has a handful of established options, on phones and desktops alike. They differ in what draws the UI, what the delivered code may do, and how much of the app has to change to host them. This page compares them with NSH, and then compares NSH with the cross-platform frameworks used to write whole apps.

## The options

| | What draws it | What it can express | Confinement | Fit for generated UI | Cost to the host app |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Web view (H5)** | A browser engine | Anything HTML, CSS and JS can | Same-origin rules; native access through a hand-written bridge | Models write HTML well; the result looks and behaves like a web page | A browser engine per view; a bridge to maintain |
| **Server-driven UI** | The app's own native views | Only the components and actions the app built in, described in JSON | Total: the schema is the limit | Easy to generate, little to express: no local state or logic beyond what the schema provides | A renderer for every component and its versions, in each app |
| **Mini-program containers** | Usually a web engine with a proprietary layer | A platform-specific framework and API | The container's permission model | Proprietary dialect, less known to models | A large container SDK |
| **Over-the-air updates of a cross-platform app** (React Native with a code-push service, for example) | That framework's renderer | The whole framework | None: updates are trusted app code | Code generated per request is not what these updates are for | The app has to be written in that framework |
| **NSH** | The platform's own UI: UIKit, Android views, AppKit, GTK 4, Win32 with Direct2D | Components with state, logic, animation and layout; host-registered native views | Signed packages, a VM per view with host-set limits, capabilities granted per view | Designed for it: one TSX module, typed API, headless checks | One view and a library in an existing native app |

## How NSH differs

- **The platform's own UI.** A module is made of the platform's views, so text selection and its menu, input methods, accessibility and scrolling are the system's own — the same reason NSH exists next to [GPUI Shell](https://nsh.dev/docs.md#why-native-shell-next-to-gpui-shell).
- **More than a schema.** Server-driven UI only recombines what the app already ships. An NSH module has its own state, logic, animations and layout, so a model can produce an interface the app's developers never anticipated.
- **Confined by the host.** Delivered code is untrusted. NSH checks signatures and revocations before running anything, gives each view its own VM with memory, call-time and node limits, and lets the host decide which network hosts, web pages and system settings a module may reach ([Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)).
- **Embedded, not adopted.** The app stays native and keeps its toolchain; NSH is a view placed where a module should appear ([Platforms](https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms.md#embed-in-a-native-app)).
- **One module, every platform.** The same bundle runs on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and Linux, each time with that platform's own UI ([Platforms](https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms.md)).

## Cross-platform frameworks

NSH is designed for modules inside native apps, but the same modules can be packaged as whole apps for every platform, so it is natural to compare it with the frameworks people write cross-platform apps in. The comparison is about how each draws and where it runs, not about maturity: these frameworks have large ecosystems that NSH does not have.

| | What draws it | Platforms | App code | Code delivered after release |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **React Native** | The platform's views on iOS and Android; desktops through separate projects | iOS, Android; Windows and macOS out of tree | JavaScript or TypeScript, with React | Over-the-air updates of trusted app code |
| **Flutter** | Its own engine draws every pixel | iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux, web | Dart | Not part of the framework |
| **Electron** | Chromium, bundled with the app | macOS, Windows, Linux | HTML, CSS, JavaScript | Web content the app loads |
| **Tauri** | The system's web view | macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, Android | HTML, CSS, JavaScript; Rust for the native side | Web content the app loads |
| **NSH** | The platform's own UI on each platform | iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux | TSX modules; the runtime and components are Rust | Signed packages, verified and sandboxed per view |

What sets NSH apart:

- **Native UI on every platform, not one renderer everywhere.** Flutter draws everything itself, and Electron and Tauri show web pages; NSH builds each platform's own views, so text selection, input methods, accessibility and the system's look come from the platform.
- **Small modules inside native apps.** The frameworks above own the whole app. NSH is designed to sit inside an app written with the platform's own tools, as one view among others, and to run modules the app did not ship with, in a sandbox.
- **A light runtime.** No browser engine per app or per view; JavaScript only runs the module's own code, and everything it calls is native Rust.

## When another option fits better

- The UI is a document or an existing web page: a web view shows it as it is.
- The set of screens is fixed and small, and only content and order change: server-driven UI needs no runtime at all.
- The whole app is written in a cross-platform framework already: its own update mechanism ships its code.
- You need a large ecosystem of third-party packages, or a desktop UI kit with desktop controls today: NSH's components are the mobile set.

## See also

- [Introduction](https://nsh.dev/docs.md): why NSH exists and what it is designed for.
- [Architecture](https://nsh.dev/docs/architecture.md): what runs where inside NSH.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/comparison

---

# Installation

Everything NSH does goes through one command, `nsh`. It bundles and compiles apps, runs the dev server, launches development hosts and packages installable apps. You can use it from a prebuilt distribution, which needs no Rust, or build it from a checkout of the repository.

On top of `nsh`, each platform needs its own tools:

| Platform | Develop and package on | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| iOS | macOS | Xcode and an iOS simulator runtime |
| Android | macOS, Windows or Linux | The Android SDK and a JDK; an emulator or a device |
| macOS | macOS | Xcode's command line tools; apps run on macOS 14+ |
| Windows | Windows | Windows 10 1809+; the WebView2 Runtime for web views |
| Linux | Linux | GTK 4.14+ (and its development packages to build the runtime) |
| [GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md) | macOS, Windows or Linux, for that OS | A GPU (Metal, DirectX or Vulkan); on Linux, Wayland or X11 |

Mac Catalyst, `nsh run`'s default on macOS, needs Xcode like iOS. Details are under [Platform tools](#platform-tools).

## Installing a release

Each [GitHub release](https://github.com/longbridge/nsh/releases) carries the prebuilt distribution (below) for macOS (Apple silicon), Linux x86_64 and Windows x86_64. Every way of installing it puts the same `nsh` command on your `PATH`.

**macOS and Linux**, with the install script:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://nsh.dev/install.sh | sh
```

It installs the distribution to `~/.nsh` and links `~/.local/bin/nsh` to it; running it again updates it. `NSH_VERSION=v0.1.0` pins a release, `NSH_INSTALL_DIR` picks another directory.

**Windows**, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://nsh.dev/install.ps1 | iex
```

It installs to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\nsh` and adds its `bin` to your user `PATH` (open a new terminal afterwards). `$env:NSH_VERSION` and `$env:NSH_INSTALL_DIR` work as above.

**Homebrew** (macOS and Linux):

```sh
brew install longbridge/tap/nsh
```

**Scoop** (Windows):

```powershell
scoop install https://github.com/longbridge/nsh/releases/latest/download/nsh.json
```

**mise** (all three):

```sh
mise use -g github:longbridge/nsh
```

The archives (`nsh-macos-arm64.tar.gz`, `nsh-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `nsh-windows-x86_64.zip`, each with a `.sha256`) carry no version in their names, so `https://github.com/longbridge/nsh/releases/latest/download/<archive>` always fetches the latest. The embedding SDKs are also released alone, for native apps that need no CLI: `nsh-embed-ios.zip` and `nsh-embed-android.zip`.

> [!NOTE]
> The binaries are not signed yet. macOS quarantines files downloaded by a browser; the install script, Homebrew and mise download with `curl` and are not affected, otherwise run `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <dir>`. The Linux runtime needs glibc 2.39 and GTK 4.14 or newer (Ubuntu 24.04 and later). There is no Intel Mac or arm64 Linux / Windows build: build those from a checkout.

## The prebuilt distribution

The distribution is a directory, `dist/nsh`, with the CLI and the prebuilt native runtimes it packages apps with:

```sh
dist/nsh/bin/nsh                                             # the CLI
dist/nsh/runtime/ios/iphoneos/nsh-ios-app                    # runs packaged apps on iOS devices
dist/nsh/runtime/ios/iphonesimulator/{nsh-ios-app,nsh-ios-host}
dist/nsh/runtime/ios/maccatalyst/nsh-ios-host                # the Mac Catalyst development host
dist/nsh/runtime/android/{release,dev}/                      # classes.dex, lib/<abi>/libnsh.so
dist/nsh/runtime/macos/{nsh-macos-host,nsh-macos-app}        # the macOS (AppKit) development host and release runner
dist/nsh/runtime/linux/{nsh-linux-host,nsh-linux-app}        # the Linux development host and release runner
dist/nsh/runtime/windows/{nsh-windows-host,nsh-windows-app}.exe  # the Windows development host and release runner
dist/nsh/runtime/gpui/{nsh-gpui-host,nsh-gpui-app}[.exe]     # the GPUI development host and release runner, for this OS
dist/nsh/runtime/web/{nsh.wasm,nsh-dev.wasm,nsh.js}          # the web runtimes (nsh package / run --target web)
dist/nsh/embed/ios/{NativeShell,NativeShellDev}.xcframework  # embedding in iOS apps
dist/nsh/embed/android/{nsh,nsh-dev}.aar                     # embedding in Android apps
```

Put `dist/nsh/bin` on your `PATH` (or call `dist/nsh/bin/nsh` directly) and keep the directory together: `nsh` finds the runtimes next to itself, in `bin/../runtime` (through a symlink to it, as the installers make, too).

```sh
export PATH="$PWD/dist/nsh/bin:$PATH"
nsh --version
```

The distribution is made with `cargo xtask dist` in a checkout (below). The `nsh` binary it contains is built for that machine. On a Mac with Xcode it includes the iOS and macOS runtimes (Apple Silicon); on Linux it includes the Linux runtime instead, built for that machine; on Windows the Windows runtime, with `bin\nsh.exe`. Each also includes the [GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md) runtime, built for that machine. All include the Android runtime (on Windows only when the Android SDK is found).

## Building from a checkout

You need Rust through [rustup](https://rustup.rs). The repository's `rust-toolchain.toml` selects the stable toolchain and installs the iOS and Android targets on first use.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/longbridge/nsh.git
cd nsh
cargo build -p nsh-cli          # ./target/debug/nsh
```

Then build the development host of each target you want to run on, once, and again after you update the checkout:

```sh
cargo build -p nsh-ios-host --target aarch64-apple-ios-macabi   # nsh run (Mac Catalyst window)
cargo build -p nsh-ios-host --target aarch64-apple-ios-sim      # nsh run --target ios
cargo xtask android --dev                                       # nsh run --target android
cargo build -p nsh-macos-host                                   # nsh run --target macos (built for you in a checkout)
cargo build -p nsh-linux-host                                   # nsh run on Linux (built for you in a checkout)
cargo build -p nsh-windows-host                                 # nsh run on Windows (built for you in a checkout)
cargo build --manifest-path crates/gpui/Cargo.toml --target-dir target -p nsh-gpui-host   # nsh run --target gpui (built for you in a checkout)
cargo build --profile web -p nsh-platform-web --target wasm32-unknown-unknown   # nsh run --target web (built for you in a checkout)
```

For `nsh package`, build the release runners as well:

```sh
cargo build -p nsh-ios-app --target aarch64-apple-ios-sim       # nsh package --target ios-simulator
cargo build -p nsh-ios-app --target aarch64-apple-ios           # nsh package --target ios
cargo xtask android                                             # nsh package --target android
cargo build -p nsh-macos-app                                    # nsh package --target macos
cargo build -p nsh-linux-app                                    # nsh package --target linux
cargo build -p nsh-windows-app                                  # nsh package --target windows
cargo build --manifest-path crates/gpui/Cargo.toml --target-dir target -p nsh-gpui-app    # nsh package --target gpui
# nsh package --target web uses the same web runtime as nsh run --target web
```

A CLI built from a checkout looks for the runtimes in `target/<triple>/<profile>` (the macOS, Linux, Windows and GPUI ones, built for this machine, in `target/<profile>`) and `target/android/<profile>[-dev]`, using its own profile: `./target/debug/nsh` uses debug runtimes, `./target/release/nsh` release ones. Build both with the same profile (add `--release` to all of them for faster apps).

> [!TIP]
> `NSH_RUNTIME=/path/to/runtime` makes `nsh` use a runtime directory laid out like the distribution's `runtime/`, wherever the CLI itself lives.

## Platform tools

### iOS and Mac Catalyst

- **Xcode** (with its command line tools). `nsh run` uses `xcrun simctl` to boot simulators and install the development host; `nsh package` uses `actool` for app icons and `codesign` for signing.
- An iOS simulator runtime. If none is installed, install one with `xcodebuild -downloadPlatform iOS`.
- Apps target iOS 15.0 and later.

### Android

- **The Android SDK**, found through `ANDROID_HOME`, `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT` or Android Studio's default place (`~/Library/Android/sdk`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Android\Sdk` on Windows), with:
  - `platforms;android-35` and a recent `build-tools` (NSH uses `aapt2`, `zipalign` and `apksigner` from it, no Gradle);
  - `platform-tools` (`adb`).
- **A JDK** (`keytool` creates the debug keystore in `~/.android/debug.keystore` the first time you package, `apksigner` needs Java).
- A running emulator or a device connected over `adb`. Apps need Android 9 (API 28) or later.

```sh
sdkmanager "platforms;android-35" "build-tools;35.0.1" "platform-tools"
```

### macOS

- **Xcode's command line tools** (`xcode-select --install`): the SDK and clang to build the runtime, `codesign` and `sips` to package apps.
- Apps need macOS 14 or later.

See [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md).

### Linux

- **GTK 4.14** or later, with their development packages and clang to build the runtime: `libgtk-4-dev clang` (Debian, Ubuntu 24.04 or later), `gtk4 clang` (Arch), `gtk4-devel clang` (Fedora).
- **WebKitGTK 6.0** (2.40 or later) for web views: `libwebkitgtk-6.0-dev` (Debian, Ubuntu), `webkitgtk-6.0` (Arch), `webkitgtk6.0-devel` (Fedora) to build the runtime; apps then need it where they run. Without it, `cargo xtask dist` builds the runtime with placeholders for web views.
- **GStreamer** plugins for the video formats apps play.

See [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md).

### Windows

- **Windows 10 1809** or later, or Windows 11. The WebView2 Runtime (part of Windows 11, installed with Edge on Windows 10) for web views.
- To build the runtime: **Visual Studio Build Tools** with the "Desktop development with C++" workload and the Windows SDK, and **LLVM** (libclang, for QuickJS' bindings; found in `C:\Program Files\LLVM`, else set `LIBCLANG_PATH`).

See [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md).

### Building the Android runtime

Building the Android runtime from a checkout (`cargo xtask android`) additionally needs an **NDK** from the SDK (`ndk;<version>`; set `ANDROID_NDK_HOME` if the newest one installed is incomplete) and `javac`.

## What works where

| Command | macOS | Linux | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nsh init`, `nsh build`, `nsh trace`, `nsh dev`, `nsh check` | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `nsh run` (Mac Catalyst, the default on macOS) | Yes | No | No |
| `nsh run --target macos`, `nsh package --target macos` | Yes | No | No |
| `nsh run --target linux` (the default on Linux), `nsh package --target linux` | No | Yes | No |
| `nsh run --target windows` (the default on Windows), `nsh package --target windows` | No | No | Yes |
| `nsh run --target gpui`, `nsh package --target gpui` (a package for the OS it is made on) | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `nsh run --target ios`, `nsh package --target ios` / `ios-simulator` | Yes, with Xcode | No | No |
| `nsh run --target android`, `nsh package --target android` | Yes | Yes, from a checkout | Yes, with the Android runtime |
| `nsh keygen`, `certify`, `publish`, `verify`, `revoke` | Yes | Yes | Yes |

On Linux, build the CLI and the Android runtime from a checkout (`cargo build -p nsh-cli` and `cargo xtask android --dev`); the NDK's Linux toolchain is used automatically. On Windows the NDK's Windows toolchain is used the same way, and `cargo xtask dist` includes the Android runtime when it finds the Android SDK.

## Editor setup

NSH needs no NPM. `nsh init` writes a `tsconfig.json` and the type declarations of everything NSH provides into `.nsh/types`, and every command that builds the app keeps them up to date. Any editor that uses the TypeScript language server (VS Code, Zed, Neovim, WebStorm) type-checks the app with them. See [Project structure](https://nsh.dev/docs/project-structure.md#tsconfigjson-and-nshtypes).

## Next steps

Continue with [Getting started](https://nsh.dev/docs/getting-started.md) to create an app and run it.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/installation

---

# Getting started

NSH's main use is hosting modules inside a native app (see [Introduction](https://nsh.dev/docs.md)). This guide follows that path: write a module, develop it with hot reload on the platforms you target, show it in your app, and ship an update as a signed package. It assumes `nsh` is installed and on your `PATH` ([Installation](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation.md)); in a checkout, use `./target/debug/nsh` instead.

> [!TIP]
> No app project at hand? The first two sections need none: `nsh run` shows the module in NSH's own development host: in a window on your computer, in the iOS simulator or on an Android device. You can stop there, or [package it as a standalone app](#or-ship-it-as-a-standalone-app).

## Create a module

```sh
nsh init my-app
```

A module is what a host app loads: one or more `.tsx` files with an entry. `nsh init` creates the directory if it is missing and writes:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `App.tsx` | The entry module: renders the app with `mount` |
| `nsh.json` | The app's name, id, version and build number ([Project structure](https://nsh.dev/docs/project-structure.md#nshjson)) |
| `tsconfig.json` | TypeScript settings that resolve `nsh` to the declarations in `.nsh/types` |
| `.gitignore` | Ignores `.nsh/` and `out/` |
| `.nsh/types/` | Generated declarations of every NSH module, for your editor |

The display name defaults to the directory's name; pass `--name "My App"` to choose another. The id becomes `com.example.<name>`: change it in `nsh.json` before you ship. Files that already exist are kept, so you can run `nsh init` in a directory that has some of them.

### Start with Rust

Use `nsh init my-app --rust` to create a Cargo project with native Rust UI:

```sh
nsh init my-app --rust
cd my-app
nsh run            # --target ios, android, web, macos, linux, windows or gpui
cargo run          # the same root, straight on the desktop backend
```

`src/lib.rs` contains the UI, state and event handlers, and `nsh.json` names its root (`"root": "App"`): `nsh run` and `nsh package` mount it on every platform, the browser included, with no QuickJS. `src/main.rs` mounts the same root directly on macOS, Windows or Linux for `cargo run`. `App.tsx` imports it from `app/native`: `nsh run App.tsx` runs that TSX entry, for screens written in TSX on top of the Rust components. Rust development requires a Rust toolchain (and, for `cargo run`, the desktop backend's development libraries); the `nsh` commands build the app's runners from an NSH source checkout, found through the CLI's checkout or `NSH_SOURCE`.

See [Building with Rust](https://nsh.dev/docs/rust.md), [the CLI reference](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md#nsh-init) and `examples/gallery-rs` in the repository.

### The entry module

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { SafeAreaView } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function App() {
  const count = signal(0);
  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center", gap: 16 }}>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 28, fontWeight: "600" }}>{count()}</Text>
      <View
        onPress={() => count.update((c) => c + 1)}
        activeOpacity={0.6}
        accessibilityRole="button"
        style={{ paddingHorizontal: 20, paddingVertical: 12, borderRadius: 10, backgroundColor: "#0969da" }}
      >
        <Text style={{ color: "white", fontSize: 17 }}>Tap</Text>
      </View>
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

Line by line:

- **`import { mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh"`**: `nsh` is the core module: [signals](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md), `mount`, the other reactive primitives, and the host elements `View` and `Text`. It is served by the native runtime, not bundled.
- **`import { SafeAreaView } from "nsh/ui/mobile"`**: the mobile UI set. [`SafeAreaView`](https://nsh.dev/components/safe-area-view.md) pads its content so it stays clear of the notch, the status bar and the home indicator; on desktops, where the safe area is 0, it adds no padding.
- **`function App()`** is a component: a function that returns JSX. It runs **once**. `signal(0)` makes a value that changes over time.
- **`{count()}`** reads the signal inside JSX. The compiler sees a call and makes this text follow the signal: when `count` changes, the runtime updates this one text, nothing else.
- **`<View onPress>`** is a native view that reacts to presses; `activeOpacity` fades it while pressed, natively. `View`, `Text`, `Image`, `Scroll`, `Input` and the other [host elements](https://nsh.dev/elements.md) are imported from NSH's modules, like any component; only `If` and `Each` need no import.
- **`style={{ … }}`** takes an object of camelCase style properties, with numbers in points. Layout is flexbox, and children stack in a column by default ([Layout](https://nsh.dev/docs/layout.md)).
- **`mount(App)`** renders the component into the app's surface.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Text must be inside `<Text>`. A bare string in a `<View>` (`<View>Hello</View>`) is not displayed.

## Develop it

### Run it

`nsh run` starts a dev server, builds the app, launches a development host that loads it, and keeps rebuilding while you edit. Logs from the app (`console.log`, errors) appear in the terminal.

Without `--target`, `nsh run` uses the machine you are on: a Win32 window on Windows, a GTK window on Linux, and on macOS a Mac Catalyst window that shows the app as an iPhone would. Pick another platform with `--target`:

| Target | Command | Runs from |
|---|---|---|
| iOS simulator | `nsh run my-app/App.tsx --target ios` | macOS with Xcode |
| Android | `nsh run my-app/App.tsx --target android` | macOS, Windows, Linux |
| macOS (AppKit) | `nsh run my-app/App.tsx --target macos` | macOS |
| Windows | `nsh run my-app/App.tsx` | Windows (the default) |
| Linux (GTK 4) | `nsh run my-app/App.tsx` | Linux (the default) |
| Mac Catalyst | `nsh run my-app/App.tsx` | macOS (the default) |

#### iOS simulator

```sh
nsh run my-app/App.tsx --target ios
nsh run my-app/App.tsx --target ios --device "iPhone 16 Pro"
```

`nsh` uses a booted simulator, or boots the newest iPhone if none is running, and installs the development host into it. `--device` picks a simulator by name or UDID.

#### Android

```sh
nsh run my-app/App.tsx --target android
```

Start an emulator or connect a device first (`adb devices` lists them; NSH uses the first one). `nsh` installs a development host APK (rebuilt only when the runtime changes) and forwards the dev server's port to the device with `adb reverse`, so it works over USB without a shared network.

#### macOS (AppKit)

```sh
nsh run my-app/App.tsx --target macos
```

The app opens as a desktop Mac app (AppKit, in a resizable window), with mouse, trackpad and keyboard input instead of
touches. It needs macOS 14 or later; see [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md).

#### Windows (default on Windows)

```sh
nsh run my-app/App.tsx
```

The app opens in a desktop window (1200×800 points), with mouse, touchpad, touch and keyboard input. It needs Windows
10 1809 or later; see [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md).

#### Linux (default on Linux)

```sh
nsh run my-app/App.tsx
```

The app opens in a GTK window (390×844 points). It needs GTK 4.14 or later; see [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md).

#### Mac Catalyst (default on macOS)

```sh
nsh run my-app/App.tsx
```

The app opens in an iPhone-sized window (390×844 points) on your Mac. This is the quickest way to see a module as a phone shows it: no simulator to boot. It uses UIKit like iOS, so what you see is what an iPhone shows, apart from Mac-specific behavior such as scrolling with a mouse wheel. For the Mac app itself, use `--target macos`.

### Edit with hot reload

Leave `nsh run` running and change the label in `App.tsx`:

```tsx
<Text style={{ color: "white", fontSize: 17 }}>Add one</Text>
```

Save. The CLI rebuilds and sends a patch; the host runs the changed module again and renders again only the components whose code changed. Here that is `App`, which owns the `count` signal, so the count starts over. State survives when you edit a component that does not own it. Move the button into a component of its own:

```tsx
function TapButton(props: { onPress: () => void }) {
  return (
    <View onPress={props.onPress} activeOpacity={0.6} style={{ padding: 12, borderRadius: 10, backgroundColor: "#0969da" }}>
      <Text style={{ color: "white", fontSize: 17 }}>Tap</Text>
    </View>
  );
}
```

Use `<TapButton onPress={() => count.update((c) => c + 1)} />` in `App`, tap a few times, then change `TapButton`'s color: the button updates and the count stays.

Hot replacement works per top-level component: a function with a capitalized name whose body contains JSX. A component renders again when its own code changes, or when the module's code outside components changes (a constant it uses, a helper). If an edit cannot be applied in place (for example, it imports an NSH module the running app did not import yet, or changes `nsh.json`'s capabilities), the host reloads the whole app.

#### Errors

A build error is printed in the terminal and shown on the device as a red overlay with the file, line and column; the app keeps running the last good build. The overlay disappears with the next successful build (tap it to dismiss it earlier). An exception thrown at run time is shown the same way, with its stack mapped back to your `.tsx` source.

## Host it in your app

Your app shows a module in a view of its own: `NshAppView` (a `UIView`) on iOS, `NshView` (an Android `View`) on Android, `AppView` on macOS, Windows and Linux. Place it like any other view, on any screen, as many times as you need. During development, point it at the dev server; in a release, load a built bundle or a downloaded package.

### iOS

Link `NativeShellDev.xcframework` in Debug and `NativeShell.xcframework` in Release ([Embedding in iOS apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md)), then:

```swift
import NativeShell

let app = NshAppView()
app.onError = { message in print("nsh error: \(message)") }
view.addSubview(app)   // and constrain it like any view

#if DEBUG
try app.connectDevServer(URL(string: "ws://127.0.0.1:8790/ws")!)   // `nsh dev my-app` on your Mac
#else
try app.loadBundle(at: Bundle.main.url(forResource: "bundle", withExtension: "qbc", subdirectory: "nsh")!)
#endif
```

`nsh dev my-app/App.tsx` serves the module to the app and pushes every save, as `nsh run` does with its own host. For the release build, `nsh build my-app/App.tsx --release --out MyApp/nsh` writes the bundle into a folder you add to the app's resources.

### Android

Add `nsh-dev.aar` for debug builds and `nsh.aar` for release builds ([Embedding in Android apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md)), then:

```kotlin
val nsh = NshView(this)
nsh.setErrorListener { message -> Log.e("nsh", message) }
setContentView(nsh)   // or add it to any layout

if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
    nsh.connectDevServer("ws://127.0.0.1:8790/ws")   // with `adb reverse tcp:8790 tcp:8790`
} else {
    nsh.loadAssetBundle("nsh")   // assets/nsh, from `nsh build my-app/App.tsx --release --out app/src/main/assets/nsh`
}
```

### macOS, Windows and Linux

Desktop apps written in Rust embed modules with `AppView`, from the `nsh-platform-macos`, `nsh-platform-windows`, `nsh-platform-linux` and `nsh-platform-gpui` crates: an `NSView`, a child window, a GTK widget or a GPUI view that loads a built bundle. See [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#embedding-in-a-mac-app), [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#embedding-in-a-win32-app), [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#embedding-in-a-gtk-app) and [GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md), and [Platforms](https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms.md#embed-in-a-native-app) for every host side by side.

### What the module may do

On iOS and Android, the host decides before loading what the module may do: `grantCapabilities` sets the network hosts and other capabilities it may reach, and limits cap its memory, call time and node count ([Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)). To give modules your own native views (a map, a chart, a design-system component), register them as [native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md).

## Ship updates as signed packages

A module the app downloads after release comes as a signed package. Create a root key once and keep it offline, certify a release key with it, and publish:

```sh
nsh keygen keys/root && nsh keygen keys/release
nsh certify --root keys/root.secret --key keys/release.pub --apps 'com.example.*' -o keys/release.cert
nsh publish my-app/App.tsx --key keys/release.secret --cert keys/release.cert --build 2
```

The app trusts the root's public key and loads what it downloads; NSH verifies the signature, the certificate and the revocation list before running anything:

```swift
let support = FileManager.default.urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
let trust = try NshTrust(stateDirectory: support.appendingPathComponent("nsh"))
try trust.addRoot(rootPublicKey)   // the contents of keys/root.pub
let info = try await app.loadPackage(at: downloadedFile, trust: trust)
```

Android has the same flow with `NshTrust` and `NshPackage`. Hosting, delivery and revocation in detail: [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md).

## Or ship it as a standalone app

The same module can also be a whole app. `nsh package` builds an installable app around it from the prebuilt runtime, with no Xcode project or Gradle build of your own:

```sh
nsh package my-app --target ios-simulator --run
nsh package my-app --target android
nsh package my-app --target macos
nsh package my-app --target linux
nsh package my-app --target windows
```

This is a supported use on every platform, and the quickest way to put a module on a device or a desktop, but NSH is designed around hosting modules in native apps. Options, signing and icons: [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md).

## Try it in the terminal

`nsh trace` runs an app headless (no device) and prints the native view operations it produces and their timings, then taps the first pressable view twice:

```sh
nsh trace my-app/App.tsx
```

It is a quick way to check that an app starts without errors, and to see how much work an interaction causes ([Testing and trace](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md)).

## Next steps

- [Platforms](https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms.md): what each platform supports, and its own page ([iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md), [Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md), [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md), [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md), [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md)).
- [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md) and [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md): delivery and what modules may do.
- [JSX and components](https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components.md) and [Reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md): writing modules.
- [Project structure](https://nsh.dev/docs/project-structure.md): what goes in `nsh.json`, assets, files.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/getting-started

# Project structure

An NSH app is a directory with an entry module and an optional `nsh.json`. Everything else (more modules, images, fonts, JSON files) is found by following the entry's imports, so there is no file list to maintain.

```text
my-app/
├── App.tsx            the entry module: calls mount()
├── nsh.json           name, id, version, icon, Tailwind theme, capabilities
├── tsconfig.json      TypeScript settings for editors
├── .gitignore         .nsh/ and out/
├── components/        your own modules (any layout you like)
│   └── Header.tsx
├── assets/
│   ├── logo@2x.png    imported images
│   └── Inter.ttf      imported fonts
├── .nsh/              generated: type declarations, development host builds
└── out/               generated: nsh build / nsh package output
```

Every command takes the entry as its argument (`nsh run my-app/App.tsx`). The directory that contains the entry is the app's root: `nsh.json` is read from there, asset paths are relative to it, and `.nsh/` is written there.

## The entry module

The entry is a normal module that ends by rendering the root component:

```tsx
import { mount } from "nsh";
import { Home } from "./components/Home";

function App() {
  return <Home />;
}

mount(App);
```

`mount(component, props?)` renders the component into the app's surface and returns a function that removes it again. An app calls it once. Code at the top level of the entry runs when the bundle loads, before the first frame.

## nsh.json

`nsh.json` sits next to the entry. Every key is optional; `nsh init` writes the first four.

```json
{
  "name": "Gallery",
  "id": "com.example.gallery",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "build": 1,
  "icon": "icon.png",
  "tailwind": {
    "colors": { "brand": { "500": "#7c3aed", "600": "#6d28d9" } },
    "radius": { "card": 14 }
  },
  "capabilities": {
    "network": { "hosts": ["api.example.com", "*.cdn.example.com"] }
  }
}
```

| Key | Type | Used by | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | `package` | The display name under the app icon. Default: the entry directory's name. |
| `id` | string | `package`, `publish` | Bundle identifier / application id, e.g. `com.example.app`. Default: `com.example.<name>`. |
| `version` | string | `package`, `publish` | The user-visible version, e.g. `1.2.0` (`CFBundleShortVersionString`, Android `versionName`). |
| `build` | number | `package`, `publish` | The build number (`CFBundleVersion`, Android `versionCode`). Signed packages require it to grow with every release. |
| `icon` | string | `package` | A square PNG, ideally 1024×1024, relative to `nsh.json`. |
| `tailwind` | object | every build | Extends the Tailwind theme your `class` strings resolve against ([Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md#theme)). |
| `appearance` | string | every build, `package` | `"light"`, `"dark"` or `"system"` (the default): an app that is always light or dark says so here. `colorScheme()`, `dark:` classes, the components' theme and the platform's controls follow it from the start ([Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md#dark-mode)). |
| `theme` | string or object | every build | The theme of the `nsh/ui/mobile` components: a theme file's path relative to `nsh.json`, or the theme inline ([Components](https://nsh.dev/components.md)). |
| `capabilities` | object | every build | What the app may reach outside its VM: network hosts, web view hosts, the status bar ([Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)). |
| `rust` | string or string[] | every command | The app's Rust crate, or a list of them, relative to `nsh.json`: their components and modules, which TSX imports by each crate's `#[native_module]` specifier ([Building with Rust](https://nsh.dev/docs/rust.md#several-crates)). |
| `root` | string | `run`, `package` | A Rust app's root component, its path in the `rust` crate, the first one of a list (`App`, `shell::Gallery`): `nsh run` and `nsh package` of the app's directory mount it with no QuickJS, on every platform; `nsh run App.tsx` still runs the TSX entry ([Building with Rust](https://nsh.dev/docs/rust.md)). |

The flags of `nsh package` and `nsh publish` (`--name`, `--id`, `--app-version`, `--build`, `--icon`) override the file's values ([CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md)).

`tailwind`, `theme`, `appearance` and `capabilities` are checked when the app is built. A typo is a build error rather than a setting that silently does nothing:

```text
error building App.tsx failed
nsh.json: tailwind: unknown theme key `colours`
```

> [!WARNING]
> `nsh package` and `nsh publish` read `nsh.json` strictly and currently reject keys they do not know, including `theme`. If you set a component theme, package from a copy of the app without it until this is fixed.

### capabilities

Without a `capabilities` key, an app may use the network, web views and the status bar freely: a standalone app is its developer's own. With the key, everything not listed is denied, both in development and in packaged apps:

```json
"capabilities": {
  "network": {
    "hosts": ["api.example.com", "*.cdn.example.com"],
    "http": [{ "host": "quotes.example.com", "methods": ["GET"], "pathPrefix": "/v1/" }]
  },
  "webview": { "hosts": ["*.example.com"] },
  "statusBar": true
}
```

`network` covers `fetch`, remote images and video sources; local assets are always allowed. An app that embeds NSH may grant less than an app declares. The details are in [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

## tsconfig.json and .nsh/types

NSH does not need `node_modules`. Instead, every command that builds the app (`init`, `build`, `trace`, `dev`, `run`, `package`, `publish`) writes the TypeScript declarations of everything NSH provides into `.nsh/types`, and `tsconfig.json` points the `nsh` imports there:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2023",
    "lib": ["ES2023"],
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "Bundler",
    "jsx": "preserve",
    "jsxImportSource": "nsh",
    "strict": true,
    "noEmit": true,
    "isolatedModules": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": [],
    "paths": {
      "nsh": ["./.nsh/types/nsh/index.d.ts"],
      "nsh/*": ["./.nsh/types/nsh/*.d.ts"]
    }
  },
  "include": ["**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx", ".nsh/types/nsh/globals.d.ts", ".nsh/types/nsh/assets.d.ts"]
}
```

| File in `.nsh/types/nsh/` | Declares |
|---|---|
| `index.d.ts` | `nsh`: `signal`, `computed`, `effect`, `mount`, `View`, `Text`, ... and re-exports the types below |
| `types.d.ts` | Styles (`ViewStyle`, `TextStyle`, ...), every element's props and events, `YNode` (what a `ref` receives) |
| `jsx-runtime.d.ts` | The JSX runtime TypeScript resolves through `jsxImportSource` (the `JSX` namespace) |
| `globals.d.ts` | `If` and `Each`; `console`, timers, `requestAnimationFrame`, `fetch` and the other [global APIs](https://nsh.dev/modules/globals.md) |
| `assets.d.ts` | What importing an image or font gives |
| `list.d.ts`, `animated.d.ts`, `device.d.ts`, ... | One file per module (`nsh/list`, `nsh/animated`, `nsh/device`, ...) |
| `ui/mobile.d.ts` | `nsh/ui/mobile` |

`lib` is `ES2023` without `DOM`: there is no `document` or `window`. The files are regenerated (only when their contents change), so do not edit them and do not commit them; `.gitignore` already excludes `.nsh/`. If your editor shows `nsh` as missing after cloning a project, run any build command once, e.g. `nsh trace App.tsx`.

`jsxImportSource: "nsh"` and `jsx: "preserve"` only matter to the editor: NSH compiles JSX with its own compiler, whatever the `tsconfig.json` says. TypeScript is checked by your editor or by `nsh check`; the other commands strip types without checking them.

## Modules

Split the app into as many `.ts` and `.tsx` modules as you like and import them with relative paths; the extension may be left out:

```tsx
import { Header } from "./components/Header";
import { formatPrice } from "./lib/format";
import strings from "./strings.json";
```

All of them are bundled into one script. JSON files import as their parsed value.

### Loading code on demand

`import()` of one of the app's modules returns a promise of its exports, as in a browser:

```tsx
const open = async () => {
  const { Settings } = await import("./screens/Settings");
  screen.set(() => Settings);
};
```

Apps on devices ship one bundle, so the module is already there and the promise resolves at once. A web app published split (`nsh build --split`) gets the module, and what only it uses, as a separate file that is downloaded the first time `import()` asks for it ([Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md#split-bundles)). The specifier must be a literal relative path: the bundler has to see which module is meant.

### NSH's modules

Imports of `nsh` and `nsh/...` are not bundled: the runtime provides them natively.

| Module | What it has |
|---|---|
| `nsh` | Reactivity (`signal`, `computed`, `effect`, ...), `mount`, `split`, `context`; `View`, `Text`, `Scroll`, `Input` ([reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh.md)) |
| `nsh/ui/mobile` | The mobile UI set: components, navigation, alerts, safe area ([Components](https://nsh.dev/components.md)) |
| `nsh/list` | `List`: virtualized, recycling lists |
| `nsh/animated` | Native animations |
| `nsh/canvas` | 2D drawing |
| `nsh/gesture` | `PanResponder` |
| `nsh/device` | `Platform`, `windowSize`, `colorScheme`, `fontScale`, `PixelRatio`, `I18nManager` |
| `nsh/accessibility` | Screen reader and reduce motion state, announcements |
| `nsh/image` | `Image` (the element), `Image.getSize`, `Image.prefetch` |
| `nsh/webview`, `nsh/video` | `WebView`, `Video` |
| `nsh/native` | Components the embedding app registers |
| `nsh/ios`, `nsh/android` | Platform-only APIs |

The [modules reference](https://nsh.dev/modules.md) documents each one. Importing a module NSH does not have (`nsh/foo`) is a build error.

### npm packages

NSH needs nothing from npm, but the bundler resolves bare imports from a `node_modules` directory if you install packages with a package manager. Packages resolve their browser builds, because the runtime provides web APIs (`fetch`, streams, `URL`, `TextEncoder`, ...) and not Node's (`fs`, `Buffer`, `process`). Packages that touch the DOM do not work: there is none.

`solid-js` cannot be imported: the bundler refuses it and points to `nsh`'s own `signal`, `computed` and `effect`, which replace it.

## Assets

Images and fonts are imported like modules. The bundler records each imported file and ships it with the app: `nsh build` copies them to `out/assets/`, `nsh package` puts them in the app, and during development the dev server serves them.

```tsx
import { Text } from "nsh";
import { Image } from "nsh/image";
import logo from "./assets/logo@2x.png";   // { uri: "asset:/assets/logo@2x.png", width: 64, height: 64 }
import Inter from "./assets/Inter.ttf";     // "Inter"

<Image src={logo} />
<Text style={{ fontFamily: Inter }}>Hello</Text>
```

| Extension | Import gives |
|---|---|
| `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.gif`, `.webp`, `.heic` | An `ImageAsset`: `{ uri, width, height }`, sized in points. An `@2x` / `@3x` suffix divides the pixel size by 2 / 3. |
| `.ttf`, `.otf` | The font's family name, a string. The font is registered before the first frame. |
| `.json` | The parsed JSON |

See [Images and assets](https://nsh.dev/docs/images-and-assets.md) and [Fonts](https://nsh.dev/docs/fonts.md).

## Generated directories

- **`.nsh/`**: the type declarations (`.nsh/types`) and what `nsh run` installs on simulators and devices (the Catalyst host app, the Android development APK). Safe to delete; it is recreated.
- **`out/`**: the default output of `nsh build` (`bundle.js`, `bundle.js.map`, `bundle.nshc`, `capabilities.json`, `assets/`) and `nsh package` (`.app`, `.ipa`, `.apk`). Change it with `-o`.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/project-structure

---

# Building with Rust

Native Shell apps are written in TSX, in Rust, or in both. All three run on the same engine: the reactive graph, the
renderer, Taffy layout and the `nsh/ui/mobile` components are Rust in every case, and every platform renders with its
own UI. What differs is the language of your own code, and with it whether the app carries a JavaScript VM.

| | TSX | Rust | Rust with TSX |
|---|---|---|---|
| Your UI, state and handlers | TSX on QuickJS | Rust | Rust components and modules, TSX screens that use them |
| The app runs | QuickJS and the engine | the engine and your crate only, on every platform and in the browser | QuickJS and the engine, with your crate |
| Suits | Apps and modules delivered at run time, quick iteration | Medium and large apps with demanding business logic | A Rust core with parts that change often |
| Edits | Hot updates | Rebuild and restart | Hot updates for TSX, rebuild and restart for Rust |
| Start | `nsh init my-app` | `nsh init my-app --rust` | `nsh init my-app --rust`, then `nsh run App.tsx` |

## Choosing

**Rust** suits apps whose business logic is large and demanding: trading, editors, data-heavy tools. You get Rust's
type system and compile-time checks across the whole app, the crates.io ecosystem, native performance for your own
code (not only for NSH's), and headless tests of the real UI with `cargo test`. The app is Rust and native code from
start to end: no JavaScript VM ships with it or runs in it, on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux, GPUI and the web.
Components are functions that run once and bind signals to what they show, as in TSX ([Reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md)),
written with typed styles instead of class strings.

**Rust with TSX** keeps that core and adds TSX where it pays off: screens, settings, onboarding, experiments,
anything you iterate on with hot updates or deliver at run time as a [signed package](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md). TSX
imports your Rust components and modules like any NSH module, so the two halves meet at typed interfaces. The TSX
runs on QuickJS, which the app then carries.

## An app written in Rust

```sh
nsh init my-app --rust
cd my-app
nsh run                        # this machine's backend; --target ios, android, web, macos, linux, windows or gpui
nsh package --target web       # or ios, ios-simulator, android, macos, linux, windows, gpui
```

`src/lib.rs` holds the app: components, state, handlers, tasks.

```rust
use nsh_core::ui::prelude::*;
use nsh_ui_mobile::{Button, ButtonEvent, ButtonProps};

/// The components available to TSX through `app/native`.
#[native_module("app/native")]
fn native(registry: &mut Registry) {
    registry.register::<App>();
}

#[component]
pub fn App() -> impl IntoElement {
    let count = signal(0_u32);
    let quote = signal(SharedString::from("…"));
    // Async work runs in tasks; requests go through NSH's network stack.
    spawn(async move {
        if let Ok(response) = fetch("https://api.example.com/quote").await {
            quote.set(response.text().into());
        }
    });
    view()
        .flex_1()
        .items_center()
        .justify_center()
        .gap_4()
        .child(text(move || format!("Count: {}", count.get())))
        .child(text(quote))
        .child(
            Button::element(ButtonProps { title: "Tap".into(), ..ButtonProps::default() })
                .on_event(move |_: &ButtonEvent| count.update(|c| *c += 1)),
        )
}
```

`nsh.json` names the root, and `nsh` mounts it:

```json
{
  "name": "My App",
  "rust": ".",
  "root": "App",
  "theme": "theme.json",
  "appearance": "system"
}
```

`"root"` is the component's path in the crate (`App`, `shell::Gallery`; in the first one with
[several crates](#several-crates)); `"theme"` and `"appearance"` apply to it as they do to a TSX app. With it,
`nsh run` and `nsh package` of the app's directory build the app's own runner for the target, with the root mounted
and no QuickJS linked in:

| Target | What runs |
|---|---|
| macOS, Windows, Linux, GPUI | The release runner with your crate, in a window; `nsh run` runs a debug build and shows the app's logs in the terminal |
| iOS, the iOS simulator, Mac Catalyst | The iOS runner with your crate, in an app |
| Android | The app's `libnsh.so` with your crate, started by the runtime's activity |
| Web | `nsh.wasm` with the engine and your crate (3.3 MB for the whole Rust gallery, 0.75 MB with brotli); the page mounts the root |

During `nsh run`, a change to the crate's Rust code builds the runner again and restarts the app; in the browser,
the open page loads the new runtime by itself. `cargo run` starts the same root directly on the desktop backend
(`src/main.rs`), and native apps that embed NSH mount a Rust root with `AppSource::Rust` on the `AppView` of macOS,
Windows, Linux, GPUI and iOS.

Code for every platform, the web included, uses NSH's services: `fetch` for HTTP
([Networking](https://nsh.dev/docs/networking.md#from-rust-components)), `timer`, `set_timeout` and `set_interval` for waiting,
`nsh_core::time::Instant` and `nsh_core::time::unix_ms()` for the clock. `background` and `blocking` run work on the
native targets' threads.

## Desktop title bars

Rust apps draw their own title bars with `nsh_core::ui::desktop`. Call
`set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Hidden, Some(height))`, mark the bar's background
with `.window_drag(true)`, and reserve the native window controls' space with
`title_bar()`. Its `top` is the bar's height, and `left` and `right` are the widths
occupied by the system controls. Reading it subscribes to changes, including full
screen. The platform handles window dragging and the user's title-bar double-click
behavior; `.window_drag(false)` keeps a child out of its parent's drag region.

```rust
use nsh_core::{
    desktop::TitleBarStyle,
    ui::{desktop::{close_window, set_title_bar, title_bar}, prelude::*},
};

#[component]
fn TitleBar() -> impl IntoElement {
    set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Hidden, Some(42.0));
    view()
        .h(px(42.0))
        .flex_row()
        .items_center()
        .window_drag(true)
        .pl(move || px(title_bar().left + 12.0))
        .pr(move || px(title_bar().right + 12.0))
        .child(text("My app").flex_1())
        .child(text("Close").window_drag(false).on_press(|_: &()| close_window()))
}
```

`set_title_bar(TitleBarStyle::Default, None)` restores the system title bar.
`close_window()` follows the embedding host's normal window-close behavior.

## Extending a Rust app with TSX

The crate's `#[native_module("app/native")]` function names what TSX may import: components
(`registry.register::<Chart>()`), modules of functions (`registry.module::<Portfolio>()`, a `#[module]` `impl`),
classes (`registry.class::<Ledger>()`, `#[class]` on a struct and its `impl`) and assets. Their TypeScript
declarations, doc comments included, are generated from the Rust types into `.nsh/types`, so TSX is checked against
them by `nsh check` and your editor:

```rust
/// A ledger kept in Rust.
#[class]
pub struct Ledger {
    entries: Vec<f64>,
}

#[class]
impl Ledger {
    /// An empty ledger.
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Ledger { entries: Vec::new() }
    }

    /// Adds `amount`; the new balance.
    pub fn add(&mut self, amount: f64) -> f64 {
        self.entries.push(amount);
        self.balance()
    }

    /// The balance.
    #[getter]
    pub fn balance(&self) -> f64 {
        self.entries.iter().sum()
    }

    /// Uploads the entries; resolves when the server has them.
    pub async fn upload(this: Instance<Ledger>, url: String) -> Result<(), String> {
        let body = this.with(|l| format!("{:?}", l.entries));
        fetch(HttpRequest::post(url, body)).await.map(|_| ())
    }
}

pub struct Portfolio;

#[module]
impl Portfolio {
    /// The value of the holdings.
    pub fn total() -> f64 {
        1250.0
    }
}
```

```tsx
import { mount, signal, View, Text } from "nsh";
import { Button } from "nsh/ui/mobile";
import { Chart, Ledger, Portfolio } from "app/native";   // Rust

const ledger = new Ledger();   // its state lives in Rust

function Overview() {
  const balance = signal(ledger.add(Portfolio.total()));   // Rust, called at once
  return (
    <View className="p-4 gap-2">
      <Text>Balance: {balance()}</Text>
      <Chart symbol="NSH" range="1M" onSelect={(e) => balance.set(ledger.add(e.price))} />
      <Button title="Upload" onPress={() => ledger.upload("https://example.com/ledger")} />
    </View>
  );
}

mount(() => <Overview />);
```

Props are the fields of the component's `Props` struct and events the variants of its `Event` enum (`onSelect`),
both in camel case. A Rust component's own content, events and state stay in Rust; TSX passes props in and hears
events. A prop of the wrong type (`level={1.5}` for a `u32` prop) is a warning, as on a built-in element: the
prop keeps its value and the rest of the component renders.

A function or a member runs the way its Rust signature says. One that is not `async` runs inside the TSX call and
returns its value (`Portfolio.total()` is a number, `ledger.balance` a property): it computes and keeps state. An
`async fn` returns a Promise and runs as a task with NSH's services (`fetch`, `timer`, dialogs); a module function
taking `cx: &mut ModuleCx` reaches the platform in order with the UI (a toast, the status bar) and returns a Promise
of its value. Arguments and results are typed from the signature: numbers, strings, `Option`, `Vec`, your
`#[derive(JsObject)]` structs and `#[derive(PropEnum)]` enums, instances of your classes, and TSX functions
(`Callback<A, R>`, which Rust calls at once inside a call, or later with `post` and `call_async`). An argument of
the wrong type throws a `TypeError` in the call, or rejects the Promise of one that returns a Promise; an `Err`
throws (or rejects) with its message. A class's object owns its Rust value: it is freed when the object is collected, or at
once with `ledger.dispose()` (also `using ledger = new Ledger()`). Name the TSX entry to run it, `nsh run App.tsx` or `nsh package App.tsx --target …`: TSX edits are hot
updates, Rust edits rebuild and restart the app.

`examples/gallery-rs` in the repository is a complete Rust app with both entries: every demo is Rust,
`nsh run examples/gallery-rs --target web` (or `ios`, `android`, …) runs its root, `cargo run -p gallery-native`
starts it on the desktop backend, and `nsh run examples/gallery-rs/App.tsx` runs it under its TSX entry.

## Several crates

An app's Rust code can be split into crates, each imported by its own specifier: `"rust"` takes a list of crate
paths, and each crate in it has its own `#[native_module]` function.

```json
{
  "rust": ["native/charts", "native/storage"],
  "root": "App"
}
```

```tsx
import { Chart } from "app/charts";        // native/charts: #[native_module("app/charts")]
import { Store } from "app/storage";       // native/storage: #[native_module("app/storage")]
```

Every runner and host links all of them, and `.nsh/types` declares each specifier. Crates share code through Cargo
path dependencies (`shared = { path = "../shared" }`): a crate of company components can be used by several crates
and listed by several apps, and only the crates listed in `"rust"` export to TSX. Each listed crate has a package
name and a specifier of its own; `nsh` reports a repeated one with the two paths that share it. A Rust app's
`"root"` is a component of the first crate listed. During `nsh run` and `nsh dev`, a change to any of them, or to a
crate they depend on by path, rebuilds the app and restarts it.

## See also

- [Project structure](https://nsh.dev/docs/project-structure.md): every key of `nsh.json`.
- [Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md#apps-with-rust-components): Rust apps in the browser.
- [Networking](https://nsh.dev/docs/networking.md#from-rust-components): `fetch` from Rust.
- [CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md#nsh-init): `nsh init --rust`.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/rust

---

# CLI

`nsh` is the only tool an NSH app needs. Every subcommand that builds an app takes `[ENTRY]`: the entry module, or the app's directory, whose `App.tsx` is the entry (default: the current directory, so `cd my-app && nsh run` works). It reads `nsh.json` next to the entry and refreshes the type declarations in `.nsh/types`.

```text
nsh <COMMAND>

  init     Create an app
  build    Bundle an app and compile it to QuickJS bytecode
  trace    Run an app headless and print the mount instructions and timings
  check    Type check an app with TypeScript's native compiler
  dev      Serve an app to dev hosts (simulators, devices) and push rebuilds
  run      Like dev, and also run the app in a development host
  package  Package an installable app from the prebuilt runtime
  keygen   Create a signing key
  certify  Certify a release key with a root key
  publish  Build an app in release mode and sign it into a package (.nshpkg)
  verify   Verify a package
  revoke   Sign a revocation list
```

`nsh <command> --help` prints the flags of a command; `nsh --version` prints the version.

## Output

Every command prints one line per step, and the details only when something fails:

```text
✓ built the Rust crate gallery-native (5.0s)
✓ built App.tsx (500 B js, 809 B bytecode, 21ms)
✓ built the development host for the iOS simulator (12.7s)
• iOS Simulator (iPhone 16 Plus) connected, build 1
warn iOS Simulator: image failed: An SSL error has occurred and a secure connection to the server cannot be made.
✓ rebuilt App.tsx (18ms), 1 device
```

`✓` is a finished step, `→` where to connect, `•` what a device did; `warn` and `error` lines are problems, and
plain lines are your app's own output (`console.log`). On a terminal a spinner shows the step that is running, and
lines are colored (unless `NO_COLOR` is set); redirected to a file, only the result lines are written, without colors.
The output of the tools NSH runs (cargo for an app's Rust crate, the development hosts) is printed below an `error`
line when one of them fails.

`-v, --verbose` (any command; also `NSH_VERBOSE=1`) prints everything as it comes: every log line with its level and
source, cargo's output and the hosts' own.

## nsh init

```sh
nsh init [DIR] [--name <NAME>] [--rust]
```

By default, creates a TSX app in `DIR` (default: the current directory, created if missing): `App.tsx`, `nsh.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `.gitignore` and `.nsh/types`. Files that exist are kept; it fails only if all of them exist already.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--name <NAME>` | Display name written to `nsh.json`. Default: the directory's name. The id becomes `com.example.<name>` (letters and digits only, lower case). |
| `--rust` | Creates a Cargo project with a native Rust entry (`cargo run`) and a TSX entry sharing its Rust components. Requires Rust and the native desktop backend's development libraries. |

With `--rust`, the project also contains `Cargo.toml`, `src/main.rs`, `src/lib.rs` and a README; `nsh.json` sets `"rust": "."` and `"root": "App"`. `nsh run` and `nsh package` then mount the Rust root with no QuickJS on every target, the browser included ([Building with Rust](https://nsh.dev/docs/rust.md)); `cargo run` starts it on macOS, Windows or Linux directly; `nsh run App.tsx` runs the TSX entry. The `nsh` commands build the app's runners from an NSH source checkout (the CLI's checkout or `NSH_SOURCE`). Create Rust projects in a new app directory. Existing Cargo manifests, Rust entry files, `App.tsx` or `nsh.json` are reported as conflicts before app files are written.

## nsh run

```sh
nsh run [ENTRY] [--target catalyst|ios|android|macos|linux|windows|gpui|web] [--device <DEVICE>] [--port <PORT>] [--release] [--trace] [--fps]
```

Starts the dev server (as `nsh dev`), launches a development host that loads the app from it, and rebuilds on every save. Hot module replacement patches the running app in place; logs and errors from the app are printed in the terminal. Stop it with Ctrl-C (or by closing the Catalyst, macOS, Linux, Windows or GPUI window). However it ends (Ctrl-C, `kill` / `pkill`, an error), it stops the host it started: the Catalyst app, the macOS, Linux, Windows or GPUI host, the development host in the simulator, or on the Android device.

A Rust app (`nsh.json` `"root"`, [Building with Rust](https://nsh.dev/docs/rust.md)) runs with no dev server and no QuickJS: `nsh run` builds the app's runner for the target with its root mounted, starts it (on the desktops a debug build, its logs in the terminal; in the simulator and on Android, the app installed), and on a change to the crate's Rust code builds it again and restarts it. With `--target web` it prints the page's address, and the open page loads the new runtime by itself. Name the TSX entry (`nsh run App.tsx`) to run that instead.

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--target <TARGET>` | `catalyst` on macOS, `linux` on Linux, `windows` on Windows | `catalyst`: the Mac Catalyst host, an iPhone-sized window (390×844). `ios`: the host in an iOS simulator. `android`: the host on an Android device or emulator. `macos`: the AppKit host, a 1200×800 window ([macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md)). `linux`: the GTK host, a 390×844 window ([Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md)). `windows`: the Win32 host, a 1200×800 window ([Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md)). `gpui`: the GPUI host, a 1200×800 window, on macOS, Windows or Linux ([GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md)). `web`: the dev server's page, at the address it prints ([Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md#develop-in-the-browser)). |
| `--device <DEVICE>` | | iOS simulator to use, by name (`"iPhone 16 Pro"`) or UDID. Default: a booted one, else the newest iPhone, which is booted. |
| `--port <PORT>` | `8790` | Dev server port. If it is taken, the next free one is used. |
| `--release` | | Minify and strip debug info. Release bundles have no hot module replacement: every save reloads the app. |
| `--trace` | | The host logs the timing of every commit (JS, layout, mount items) to the terminal. |
| `--fps` | | Shows the performance monitor over the app: frame rate, what frames and commits cost, CPU, GPU and memory ([macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#performance-monitor); `--target macos` only for now). |

With `--target android`, the first device `adb devices` lists is used; the dev server's port is forwarded to it with `adb reverse`. See [Getting started](https://nsh.dev/docs/getting-started.md#run-it) and [Dev server and debugging](https://nsh.dev/docs/dev-server-and-debugging.md).

## nsh dev

```sh
nsh dev [ENTRY] [--port <PORT>] [--release]
```

Runs only the dev server: it builds the app, watches the entry's directory, and pushes every rebuild to the hosts connected to it. It prints the URL for hosts on this machine and one per LAN address for devices, and, when the web runtime is there, the page browsers open to run the app ([Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md#develop-in-the-browser)):

```text
✓ built App.tsx (3.2 KB js, 9.8 KB bytecode, 21ms)
→ dev server ws://127.0.0.1:8790/ws
  browsers: http://127.0.0.1:8790/
  devices on this network: ws://192.168.1.20:8790/ws
  browsers on this network: http://192.168.1.20:8790/
```
