Use it with hosts you start yourself, for example an app that embeds the development SDK (`NativeShellDev.xcframework`, `nsh-dev.aar`). Flags as for `nsh run`.

## nsh trace

```sh
nsh trace [ENTRY] [--tap <SELECTOR>]... [--taps <N>] [--idle-ms <MS>] [--wait <MS>] [--duration <MS>]
          [--scroll <POINTS>] [--width <W>] [--height <H>] [--safe-area <INSETS>]
```

Runs the app headless, in the CLI's own process with the same core and runtime as a device but no views, and prints every mount instruction (create, insert, style, frame, text) and the time of each commit. Then it taps views (the ones `--tap` names, or the first pressable one) and prints what each tap changed. Use it to check that an app starts without errors, to count the work an interaction causes, and in CI ([Testing and trace](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md)).

```text
✓ bundled App.tsx (3255 B in 12.6 ms)
perf commit: 56 ops, 412µs (list js 6µs), 49 mount items, 21 nodes
── initial render: 49 items
   Create { id: 2, kind: View }
   ...
── tap #1 on view 20: 3 items
   Text { id: 14, text: "1", content: 71x77 @ 0,0 }
```

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--tap <SELECTOR>` | | Tap a view; repeat it for several taps, in order. `id:<testID>`, `label:<accessibilityLabel>`, `text:<text>`, `view:<id>` (a view id from the output), or a bare string, matched as a `testID`, then a label, then a text. The first match on screen is tapped, or its nearest pressable ancestor (the button around a text). No match is an error. |
| `--taps <N>` | `2` | Without `--tap`: taps sent to the first pressable view. A tap that changes nothing is an error (exit code 1). |
| `--idle-ms <MS>` | `1200` | Before tapping, wait until the app renders nothing for this long (at most 10 s, for apps with timers or animations). The default lets the engine's idle garbage collection run first, so retention bugs show up. |
| `--wait <MS>` | | Run timers and animations exactly this long before the first tap and after each one, printing what they render, instead of waiting until the app is idle. |
| `--duration <MS>` | `0` | Keep running this long after the last tap. |
| `--safe-area <INSETS>` | `0` | Safe area insets in points, `top,right,bottom,left` (or one value for all four), e.g. `47,0,34,0` for a phone with a notch. |
| `--scroll <POINTS>` | | Scrolls the first scroll view or list by this many points, 10 points per frame, and prints each frame's batch. |
| `--width <W>` | `390` | Viewport width in points. |
| `--height <H>` | `844` | Viewport height in points. |

`nsh trace` behaves as iOS: `Platform.OS` is `"ios"`, and `ios:` classes and `ios={{…}}` props apply.

## nsh check

```sh
nsh check [ENTRY] [--tsc <TSC>] [-- <TSC ARGS>...]
```

Type checks the app: refreshes `.nsh/types`, then runs `tsc -p <app directory> --noEmit` with the app's `tsconfig.json`. It uses TypeScript 7, the native compiler, which needs no Node: the first run downloads it from the npm registry (about 9 MB), checks it against the checksum NSH records, and keeps it in NSH's cache (`~/Library/Caches/nsh` on macOS, `~/.cache/nsh` on Linux, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\nsh` on Windows, or `NSH_CACHE`). Type errors make it exit with a non-zero code.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--tsc <TSC>` | Run this `tsc` instead (also `NSH_TSC`), for example one from `node_modules` or a copy for machines without network. |
| `-- <TSC ARGS>` | Passed on to `tsc`, e.g. `nsh check -- --pretty false`. |

## nsh build

```sh
nsh build [ENTRY] [-o <OUT>] [--release] [--split]
```

Bundles the app and compiles it to QuickJS bytecode, for apps that embed NSH and ship the bundle themselves.

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `-o, --out <OUT>` | `out` | Output directory. |
| `--release` | | Minify and strip debug info. |
| `--split` | | Put what `import()` loads into chunk files of its own, downloaded when first imported (web apps, see [Split bundles](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md#split-bundles)). Without it, the bundle holds the whole app. |

It writes:

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `bundle.js` | The bundle as JavaScript |
| `bundle.js.map` | Its source map (stack traces are mapped back to your sources) |
| `bundle.nshc` | The bundle as compiled bytecode: what apps load |
| `<Chunk>.js`, `<Chunk>.js.map`, `<Chunk>.nshc` | With `--split`: each chunk, its source map and its bytecode (`Screen.js` for `import("./Screen")`) |
| `capabilities.json` | The `capabilities` of `nsh.json`, if declared (removed otherwise) |
| `assets/` | Every imported image and font, at its path relative to the app root |

## nsh package

```sh
nsh package [ENTRY] --target ios|ios-simulator|android|macos|linux|windows|gpui|web [-o <OUT>] [flags]
```

Builds an installable app from the prebuilt runtime, in release mode. No Rust and no Xcode project or Gradle build are involved: NSH assembles the app bundle itself and uses Xcode's `actool` and `codesign` (iOS) or the SDK's `aapt2`, `zipalign` and `apksigner` (Android); for macOS it assembles an ad hoc signed `.app` with `codesign` (and `sips` for the icon); for Linux it copies the runner and writes a `.tar.gz` with `tar`; for Windows it copies the runner, embeds the icon and writes a `.zip`, with no tools; for GPUI it does what it does for this machine's OS, with the GPUI runner; for the web it writes a static site, with no tools. Metadata comes from `nsh.json`, overridden by the flags. A Rust app (`nsh.json` `"root"`) is packaged with its own runner, built with Rust from an NSH source checkout: no bundle and no QuickJS, its root mounted ([Building with Rust](https://nsh.dev/docs/rust.md)).

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--target <TARGET>` | Required. `ios`: iOS devices, a signed `.ipa` (or an unsigned `.app` without `--sign`). `ios-simulator`: an ad hoc signed `.app`. `android`: a signed `.apk`. `macos`: an ad hoc signed `.app` ([macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#packaging)). `linux`: a directory `<Name>/` (the executable, `nsh/`, a `.desktop` file) and `<Name>.tar.gz` ([Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#packaging)). `windows`: a directory `<Name>\` (`<Name>.exe`, `nsh\`) and `<Name>.zip` ([Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#packaging)). `gpui`: what `macos`, `windows` or `linux` makes on this machine, with the GPUI runner ([GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md#packaging)). `web`: a directory `<Name>/`, a static site (`index.html` and files named by their content) ([Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md#publish-an-app)). |
| `-o, --out <OUT>` | Output directory (default `out`). |
| `--name <NAME>` | Display name. |
| `--id <ID>` | Bundle identifier, e.g. `com.example.app`. |
| `--app-version <VERSION>` | Version, e.g. `1.2.0`. |
| `--build <BUILD>` | Build number. |
| `--icon <ICON>` | App icon: a square PNG, ideally 1024×1024. |
| `--sign <IDENTITY>` | iOS devices: code signing identity, e.g. `"Apple Development: …"`. |
| `--profile <FILE>` | iOS devices: provisioning profile (`.mobileprovision`). Entitlements come from it. |
| `--keystore <FILE>` | Android: release keystore. Default: the debug key in `~/.android/debug.keystore` (created if missing). |
| `--key-alias <ALIAS>` | Android: key alias in the keystore. |
| `--keystore-password <PASSWORD>` | Android: keystore password. Also read from `NSH_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD`. |
| `--run` | Install and launch the app afterwards: in the simulator (`ios-simulator`) or on the connected Android device; `macos`, `linux`, `windows` and `gpui` launch it; `web` serves the site on this machine at the address it prints. |

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target ios-simulator --run
nsh package App.tsx --target ios --sign "Apple Development: Jane Doe (ABCDE12345)" --profile dev.mobileprovision
nsh package App.tsx --target android --keystore release.jks --key-alias upload
nsh package App.tsx --target macos
nsh package App.tsx --target linux
nsh package App.tsx --target windows
nsh package App.tsx --target gpui
nsh package App.tsx --target web
```

See [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md).

## Signing commands

These commands make and check signed packages (`.nshpkg`): app bundles that apps embedding NSH download and verify before running them. [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md) explains the model (an offline root key certifies release keys for some app ids).

### nsh keygen

```sh
nsh keygen <NAME>
```

Creates an Ed25519 key pair: `<NAME>.secret` and `<NAME>.pub` (e.g. `nsh keygen keys/root`). Keep a root's `.secret` offline; apps trust its `.pub`.

### nsh certify

```sh
nsh certify --root <ROOT.secret> --key <KEY.pub> --apps <PATTERN>... [--days <DAYS>] -o <OUT>
```

Certifies a release key with a root key for some app ids and a time window; packages carry the certificate.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--root <ROOT>` | The root's secret key. |
| `--key <KEY>` | The release key's public key. |
| `--apps <APPS>` | App ids it may sign for: `*`, `com.example.*` or an id. Repeatable. |
| `--days <DAYS>` | How long it may sign, from now (default 365). |
| `-o, --out <OUT>` | The certificate to write. |

### nsh publish

```sh
nsh publish [ENTRY] --key <KEY.secret> --cert <CERT> [-o <OUT>] [--id <ID>] [--app-version <V>] [--build <N>]
```

Builds the app in release mode and signs it into a package. Metadata comes from `nsh.json`, overridden by the flags.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--key <KEY>` | The release key's secret key. |
| `--cert <CERT>` | Its certificate (`nsh certify`). |
| `-o, --out <OUT>` | The package to write. Default: `out/<id>-<build>.nshpkg`. |
| `--id <ID>` | App id. |
| `--app-version <VERSION>` | Version. |
| `--build <BUILD>` | Build number: must grow with every release. |

### nsh verify

```sh
nsh verify <PACKAGE> [--root <ROOT.pub>]... [--revocations <LIST>]
```

Verifies a package as an app trusting the given roots would. Without `--root`, only the package's own signature is checked. It prints the package's SHA-256, which `nsh revoke --package` takes.

### nsh revoke

```sh
nsh revoke --root <ROOT.secret> [--extend <LIST>] [--sequence <N>] [--key <ID>]... [--package <SHA256>]... -o <OUT>
```

Signs a revocation list: release keys and packages that must not load any more.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--root <ROOT>` | The root's secret key. |
| `--extend <EXTEND>` | Keep the entries of this list (the last one published). |
| `--sequence <N>` | The list's number, higher than any published before. Default with `--extend`: that list's plus one. |
| `--key <ID>` | A release key id to revoke. Repeatable. |
| `--package <SHA256>` | A package SHA-256 to revoke. Repeatable. |
| `-o, --out <OUT>` | The list to write. |

## Environment variables

| Variable | Used by | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ANDROID_HOME`, `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT` | Android targets | The Android SDK. Fallback: `~/Library/Android/sdk`. |
| `NSH_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD` | `package --target android` | The keystore password. |
| `NSH_RUNTIME` | `run`, `package` | A runtime directory to use instead of the one next to the CLI. |
| `NSH_VERBOSE` | every command | `1`: as `--verbose`. |
| `NO_COLOR` | every command | Set: no colors on terminals. |

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/cli

---

# Platform overview

NSH runs on phones, desktops and the web: iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux, GPUI and web pages. Each has a backend of its own that draws with the platform's own UI, so a module is UIKit views on an iPhone, AppKit views on a Mac, GTK 4 widgets on Linux, GPUI elements in a GPUI app and HTML in a browser, with the platform's text, input, accessibility and dark mode. Everything above the backend is shared: QuickJS, the reactive graph, the renderer, Taffy layout and the components are the same Rust code everywhere, so one bundle runs on all of them.

On every platform, NSH's main use is the same: modules embedded in a native app of your own, which loads them at run time. You develop them with hot reload (`nsh run`), and the same modules can also be packaged as an installable app (`nsh package`), a supported second use.

## At a glance

| Platform | Backend; text | Runs on | Develop | Package |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md) | UIKit; CoreText | iOS 15.0+, devices and the simulator | `nsh run --target ios` | `.app` (simulator), signed `.ipa` |
| [Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md) | Android views; `StaticLayout` | Android 9 (API 28)+, `arm64-v8a` and `x86_64` | `nsh run --target android` | signed `.apk` |
| [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md) | AppKit and Core Animation; CoreText | macOS 14+ | `nsh run --target macos` | ad hoc signed `.app` |
| [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md) | Win32 windows drawn with Direct2D; DirectWrite | Windows 10 1809+, Windows 11 | `nsh run` (the default on Windows) | a directory and a `.zip` |
| [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md) | GTK 4 widgets; Pango | GTK 4.14+ | `nsh run` (the default on Linux) | a directory and a `.tar.gz` |
| [GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md) | GPUI; GPUI's text system | macOS, Windows, Linux (Vulkan) | `nsh run --target gpui` | as the desktop it runs on |
| [Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md) | HTML and CSS; the browser's fonts | modern browsers, desktop and phone | `nsh run --target web` | a static site |

- **[GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md)** draws modules with [GPUI](https://gpui-kit.com), the framework of the sibling project GPUI Kit, on macOS, Windows and Linux alike: one renderer for all three desktops, and an `AppView` that GPUI and GPUI Kit apps place in their own element tree.
- **[Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md)** renders apps as HTML in a browser page: `nsh package --target web` publishes a static site for any web server or CDN, and a page of your own embeds an app with `createPlayer` or an iframe. It also runs the live demos and the [playground](/playground) on this site.
- **Mac Catalyst** runs the iOS backend in an iPhone-sized window (390×844) on a Mac, for development. It is `nsh run`'s default target on macOS: the quickest way to see how a module looks on a phone.

## Develop and package

`nsh run` picks the machine's own platform when you give no `--target`: Mac Catalyst on macOS, the GTK window on Linux and the Win32 window on Windows. Phones are reached from a computer: iOS from a Mac with Xcode, Android from macOS, Linux or Windows with the Android SDK ([Installation](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation.md#what-works-where)).

```sh
nsh run my-app --target macos      # or ios, android, windows, linux, gpui, web, catalyst
nsh package my-app --target macos  # or ios, ios-simulator, android, windows, linux, gpui, web
```

Desktop backends build for the machine they run on: package a Mac app on a Mac, a Windows app on Windows and a Linux app on Linux. [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md) covers every target's output, signing and icons.

## Embed in a native app

| Platform | Host view | Ships as | Host language |
|---|---|---|---|
| iOS | `NshAppView` (a `UIView`) | `NativeShell.xcframework` | Swift |
| Android | `NshView` (a `FrameLayout`) | `nsh.aar` | Java or Kotlin |
| macOS | `AppView` (an `NSView`) | the `nsh-platform-macos` crate | Rust |
| Windows | `AppView` (a child window) | the `nsh-platform-windows` crate | Rust |
| Linux | `AppView` (a GTK widget) | the `nsh-platform-linux` crate | Rust |
| GPUI (macOS, Windows, Linux) | `AppView` (a GPUI view) | the `nsh-platform-gpui` crate | Rust |
| Web | `createPlayer` (a page element) or an iframe | the runtime files from `nsh package --target web` | JavaScript or HTML |

Each view is one engine with its own VM, and an app can show several. The host registers its own native views for modules to use on every platform ([Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md)).

> [!NOTE]
> Desktop hosts embed NSH with Rust crates from the NSH repository; their `AppView` loads bundles from the app's own files (or source code), with the default limits. The iOS and Android SDKs also load [signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md) with `NshTrust` and set limits and capabilities per view ([Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)).

## Writing for every platform

Most of an app needs no platform checks: elements, styles, layout and modules behave the same everywhere. Where platforms differ, NSH gives the difference one place ([Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md)):

- **Platform-only props** go in `ios={{…}}`, `android={{…}}`, `web={{…}}` or `desktop={{…}}` (macOS, Windows, Linux and desktop browsers).
- **`Platform.select`** takes a value per OS, or for `mobile` and `desktop` as a whole; `Platform.OS` is `"ios"`, `"android"`, `"macos"`, `"windows"`, `"linux"` or `"web"`.
- **Input follows the platform.** Phones get touches and the software keyboard; desktops get the mouse, the trackpad and the keyboard.

The components of [`nsh/ui/mobile`](https://nsh.dev/components.md) are drawn by NSH, so they also run on desktops, looking as they do on phones. A desktop layout is built from the primitives (`View`, `Text`, `Scroll`, `List`, …) and `Platform.select({ desktop: … })`, as the gallery's desktop layout is; a desktop UI set is on the way.

Each backend lists what it does not support yet: [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#what-differs-on-macos), [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#what-differs-on-windows), [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#what-differs-on-linux), [GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md#differences).

## See also

- [Getting started](https://nsh.dev/docs/getting-started.md): a first module, run on each platform.
- [Installation](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation.md): the tools each platform needs.
- [Architecture](https://nsh.dev/docs/architecture.md): what is shared and what each backend does.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms

---

# iOS

NSH apps run on iOS with UIKit views and CoreText text, on devices and in the simulator, from iOS 15.0. The main use is
embedding: an existing app shows modules in an `NshAppView` and loads signed packages it downloads, under limits and
capabilities it sets. Running and packaging whole apps work too, as on the other platforms. On iOS,
`Platform.OS` is `"ios"` and the `ios={{…}}` props apply.

## Requirements

- **Xcode** on a Mac, with an iOS simulator runtime (`xcodebuild -downloadPlatform iOS` installs one). See
  [Installation](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation.md#ios-and-mac-catalyst).
- Apps need **iOS 15.0** or later, on iPhone and iPad.

## Running an app

```sh
nsh run my-app --target ios
nsh run my-app --target ios --device "iPhone 16 Pro"
```

`nsh` uses a booted simulator, or boots the newest iPhone, installs the development host into it and keeps the app up
to date as you save, with logs in the terminal. `--device` picks a simulator by name or UDID. For a quicker loop
without a simulator, plain `nsh run` on a Mac opens the same UIKit backend in an iPhone-sized
[Mac Catalyst](https://nsh.dev/docs/getting-started.md#mac-catalyst-default-on-macos) window.

## Packaging

```sh
nsh package my-app --target ios-simulator --run      # out/<Name>.app, installed and launched in the simulator
nsh package my-app --target ios --sign "Apple Distribution: Example Inc (ABCDE12345)" --profile AppStore.mobileprovision
```

`--target ios` writes a signed `.ipa` for devices, TestFlight or the App Store. Signing identities, provisioning
profiles and icons: [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md#ios-devices).

## Embedding in an iOS app

An existing iOS app can show NSH apps inside its own UI. The runtime ships as `NativeShell.xcframework`, a static
framework with a Swift module: you create an `NshAppView` (a `UIView`), add it anywhere in your view hierarchy and load
an app into it. Your native screens, navigation and the NSH app live side by side in one UIKit hierarchy.

Each `NshAppView` is one independent engine with its own JS VM; there are no global singletons, so an app can show
several NSH apps at once, for example one per tab.

![One host app with two NshAppView regions: each is its own engine with its own thread, VM, limits and capabilities; the host grants capabilities, sets limits and registers native components such as a map.](https://nsh.dev/diagrams/host-app-light.svg)

## Get the framework

The distribution contains both variants:

```text
dist/nsh/embed/ios/NativeShell.xcframework      release: bundles and signed packages
dist/nsh/embed/ios/NativeShellDev.xcframework   also connects to a `nsh dev` server
```

From a checkout of NSH you can build just the frameworks:

```sh
cargo xtask ios-embed    # writes dist/nsh/embed/ios/{NativeShell,NativeShellDev}.xcframework
```

Each XCFramework has three arm64 slices: iOS devices, the iOS simulator (Apple silicon) and Mac Catalyst. The minimum
deployment target is iOS 15.0. The Swift module is compiled with library evolution, so apps built with other Swift
compiler versions can import it, and the framework links everything it needs: you add nothing else.

## Add it to an Xcode project

1. Drag `NativeShell.xcframework` (or `NativeShellDev.xcframework` for development builds) into the app target's
   **Frameworks, Libraries, and Embedded Content**. It is a static framework, so choose **Do Not Embed**.
2. In Swift, `import NativeShell`.

> [!TIP]
> Link `NativeShellDev.xcframework` in the Debug configuration and `NativeShell.xcframework` in Release, so only
> development builds can connect to a dev server.

## Ship a bundle with the app

Build the NSH app into a folder and add that folder to the app's resources as a folder reference named `nsh`:

```sh
nsh build App.tsx --release --out MyApp/nsh
```

`nsh build` writes:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `bundle.nshc` | The app compiled to bytecode: the fastest to load. |
| `bundle.js` | The same app as JS source. |
| `bundle.js.map` | Its source map (stack traces point at your `.tsx` files). |
| `capabilities.json` | The [capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md) the app declares, when `nsh.json` has any. |
| `assets/` | Images and fonts the app imports, at their paths relative to the entry. |

## Show the app

```swift
import NativeShell
import UIKit

final class EmbedController: UIViewController {
    private let app = NshAppView()

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()
        app.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false
        app.onError = { message in print("nsh error: \(message)") }
        view.addSubview(app)
        NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
            app.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.topAnchor),
            app.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.leadingAnchor),
            app.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.trailingAnchor),
            app.bottomAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.bottomAnchor),
        ])

        guard let url = Bundle.main.url(forResource: "bundle", withExtension: "qbc", subdirectory: "nsh") else { return }
        do {
            try app.loadBundle(at: url)
        } catch {
            print("cannot load: \(error)")
        }
    }

    // Let the embedded app's StatusBar decide the status bar.
    override var preferredStatusBarStyle: UIStatusBarStyle { NshAppView.preferredStatusBarStyle }
    override var prefersStatusBarHidden: Bool { NshAppView.prefersStatusBarHidden }
    override var preferredStatusBarUpdateAnimation: UIStatusBarAnimation {
        NshAppView.preferredStatusBarUpdateAnimation
    }
}
```

The view's size is the app's window: NSH lays the app out at the view's bounds and again whenever they change. Loading
again replaces the running app; the app stops when the view is deallocated.

The complete sample, a UIKit app that shows an NSH app below its own native header, is `examples/embed-ios/main.swift`.

## `NshAppView`

`NshAppView` is a `UIView` subclass isolated to the main actor.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `init(frame: CGRect = .zero, trace: Bool = false)` | Creates the view. `trace` logs the time of every commit. `init?(coder:)` supports storyboards and nibs. |
| `onError: ((String) -> Void)?` | Receives fatal app errors (a bundle that fails to load, uncaught JS exceptions, a VM stopped by a limit) on the main thread. Errors are always logged; development builds also show them over the app. |
| `limits: NshLimits` | The VM limits of the apps loaded from now on. |
| `grantCapabilities(_ json: String?) throws` | The most the apps loaded from now on may do, as JSON in the form of `nsh.json`'s `capabilities`; `nil` grants what each app declares. Throws `NshError` for invalid JSON. |
| `loadBundle(at url: URL) throws` | Runs a bundle written by `nsh build`. Assets come from `assets/` next to it; `bundle.js.map` and `capabilities.json` next to it are read too. |
| `run(_ package: NshPackage)` | Runs a verified signed package (see below). A package runs once. |
| `loadPackage(at:trust:) async throws -> NshPackage.Info` | Verifies the package at a URL off the main thread, then runs it. Throws why it was refused; the running app stays. |
| `connectDevServer(_ url: URL) throws` | Development: loads from a `nsh dev` server and reloads on every change. Throws with `NativeShell.xcframework`, which has no development support. |
| `register(component:_:)` | Registers a [native component](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md). |
| `static preferredStatusBarStyle`, `prefersStatusBarHidden`, `preferredStatusBarUpdateAnimation` | What the running apps asked for with `StatusBar`: return them from the hosting view controller's overrides. |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `bundle.nshc` (bytecode) loads only from inside the app bundle. QuickJS does not validate bytecode, so bytecode from
> anywhere else could corrupt memory: for a file outside the app bundle, load `bundle.js` (JS source), or better, a
> [signed package](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md).

`limits` and `grantCapabilities` apply from the next load: set them before `loadBundle` / `run`.

## Limits

```swift
app.limits = NshLimits(memoryMB: 128, callBudget: 1, maxNodes: 50_000)
```

| `NshLimits` field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `memoryMB: UInt32?` | 256 | JS heap in MB. Running out stops the app. |
| `stackKB: UInt32?` | 4096 (also the maximum) | Interpreter stack in KB. Deeper recursion throws a `RangeError`. |
| `loadBudget: TimeInterval?` | 10 s | Time to evaluate the bundle. |
| `callBudget: TimeInterval?` | 2 s | Time of any other call into JS (one event, one timer, one frame). An overrun call is cut off. |
| `maxNodes: UInt32?` | 200 000 | Nodes the app may keep. |

`nil` keeps the default. What each limit does when it is hit: [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

## Capabilities

An app declares what it may reach in its `nsh.json`; the embedding app can grant less. A request must be allowed by
both:

```swift
try app.grantCapabilities("""
{
  "network": { "hosts": ["api.example.com", "*.cdn.example.com"] },
  "webview": { "hosts": ["help.example.com"] }
}
""")
try app.loadBundle(at: url)
```

Here the app may not set the status bar (no `statusBar`), even if its `nsh.json` asks for it. Details:
[Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

## Signed packages

To run code the app downloads (updates, third-party mini apps), use [signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md):
`nsh publish` writes a `.nshpkg` signed by a release key that your root key certified, and the app verifies it before
running it.

```swift
let support = FileManager.default.urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)[0]
let trust = try NshTrust(stateDirectory: support.appendingPathComponent("nsh"))
try trust.addRoot(rootPublicKey)   // the contents of root.pub from `nsh keygen`

Task {
    do {
        let info = try await app.loadPackage(at: downloadedFile, trust: trust)
        print("running \(info.id) \(info.version) (build \(info.build))")
    } catch {
        print("refused: \(error)")   // the running app stays
    }
}
```

To verify first and run later, split the two steps:

```swift
let package = try await trust.openPackage(at: downloadedFile)   // verifies off the main thread
// ... decide, ask the user, ...
app.run(package)
```

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `NshTrust(stateDirectory: URL) throws` | Opens or creates the trust store. Its state (newest revocation list, highest build accepted per app) persists there, and packages' assets are extracted under it. Trusts no key until `addRoot`. Thread-safe. |
| `addRoot(_ publicKey: String) throws` | Trusts a root public key (base64, the contents of a `.pub` file). Several roots may be trusted. |
| `updateRevocations(_ json: String) throws` | Applies a revocation list written by `nsh revoke`, signed by a trusted root and newer than the one the store has. |
| `openPackage(at: URL) async throws -> NshPackage` | Verifies, extracts assets and accepts the package (older builds of that app are refused from then on). |
| `NshPackage.info` | `id`, `name`, `version`, `build` of the app inside. |
| `NshError` | The error every throwing call throws; `message` says why. |

## Development

With `NativeShellDev.xcframework`, point the view at a dev server instead of a bundle:

```swift
#if DEBUG
try app.connectDevServer(URL(string: "ws://127.0.0.1:8790/ws")!)
#else
try app.loadBundle(at: bundledURL)
#endif
```

Run `nsh dev App.tsx` on your Mac. The simulator shares the Mac's network, so `127.0.0.1` reaches the server; a
device uses the LAN address `nsh dev` prints (`devices on this network: ws://192.168.1.20:8790/ws`). Every save
updates the app in place, logs appear in the `nsh dev` terminal, and errors show over the app. See
[Dev server and debugging](https://nsh.dev/docs/dev-server-and-debugging.md).

> [!NOTE]
> On a device, the connection to your Mac is ordinary local network traffic over plain `ws://` and `http://` (assets).
> iOS may ask the user for local network access, and the app's App Transport Security settings must allow it.

## Notes

- **Threads.** `NshAppView` is main-actor isolated. `NshTrust`, `NshPackage` and `NshComponentContext` are thread-safe.
  The JS engine runs on its own thread; the main thread never waits for it.
- **Status bar.** The embedded app's `StatusBar` changes what `NshAppView.preferredStatusBarStyle` and friends return;
  the hosting view controller must forward them, as in the example above.
- **Safe area.** Apps use `SafeAreaView` or `useSafeAreaInsets()` from [`nsh/ui/mobile`](https://nsh.dev/components/safe-area-view.md)
  as usual. An `NshAppView` placed below your own header gets the insets that apply to it, not the window's.
- **Mac Catalyst.** The same framework works in Catalyst apps.

## See also

- [Embedding in Android apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md)
- [Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md)
- [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md)
- [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios

---

# Android

NSH apps run on Android with ordinary Android views and `StaticLayout` text, from Android 9 (API 28), on `arm64-v8a`
and `x86_64`. An existing app embeds modules in an `NshView` and loads signed packages it downloads, under limits and
capabilities it sets: that is the main use. Running and packaging whole apps work too, as on the other platforms. On Android, `Platform.OS` is
`"android"` and the `android={{…}}` props apply.

## Requirements

- **The Android SDK** (with `platforms;android-35`, build tools and `platform-tools`) and **a JDK**, on macOS, Windows
  or Linux. See [Installation](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation.md#android).
- An emulator, or a device connected over `adb`.

## Running an app

```sh
nsh run my-app --target android
```

Start an emulator or connect a device first (`adb devices` lists them; NSH uses the first one). `nsh` installs a
development host APK (rebuilt only when the runtime changes) and forwards the dev server's port with `adb reverse`, so
it works over USB without a shared network; the app updates as you save, with logs in the terminal.

## Packaging

```sh
nsh package my-app --target android --run     # out/<Name>.apk, installed and launched
```

The APK is built with the SDK's build tools, without Gradle, and signed with the debug key unless you pass a release
keystore. Signing for release and icons: [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md#android).

## Embedding in an Android app

An existing Android app can show NSH apps inside its own UI. The runtime ships as an Android library, `nsh.aar`: you
create a `com.longbridge.nsh.NshView` (a `FrameLayout`), add it to any layout and load an app into it. The NSH app
renders with ordinary Android views next to your own.

Each `NshView` is one independent engine with its own JS VM; there are no global singletons, so several can run at
once.

![One host app with two nsh views (NshAppView on iOS, NshView on Android): each is its own engine with its own thread, VM, limits and capabilities; the host grants capabilities, sets limits and registers native components such as a map.](https://nsh.dev/diagrams/host-app-light.svg)

## Get the library

The distribution contains both variants:

```text
dist/nsh/embed/android/nsh.aar       release: bundles and signed packages
dist/nsh/embed/android/nsh-dev.aar   also connects to a `nsh dev` server
```

The AAR holds the Java runtime and `libnsh.so` for `arm64-v8a` and `x86_64` (64-bit only). It declares the `INTERNET`
permission and needs **API 28** (Android 9) or newer.

Add it to the app module, for example from a `libs` folder:

```kotlin
// app/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    debugImplementation(files("libs/nsh-dev.aar"))
    releaseImplementation(files("libs/nsh.aar"))
}
```

## Ship a bundle with the app

Build the NSH app into the app's assets:

```sh
nsh build App.tsx --release --out app/src/main/assets/nsh
```

This writes `bundle.nshc` (bytecode), `bundle.js` (source), `bundle.js.map`, `capabilities.json` (when `nsh.json`
declares [capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)) and `assets/` (the images and fonts the app imports).

## Show the app

```java
import android.app.Activity;
import android.os.Bundle;
import android.util.Log;
import com.longbridge.nsh.NshView;

public final class MainActivity extends Activity {
    private NshView nsh;

    @Override
    protected void onCreate(Bundle state) {
        super.onCreate(state);
        nsh = new NshView(this);
        nsh.setErrorListener(message -> Log.e("nsh", message));
        setContentView(nsh);
        nsh.loadAssetBundle("nsh");   // runs assets/nsh/bundle.nshc
    }

    @Override
    protected void onDestroy() {
        nsh.destroy();
        super.onDestroy();
    }
}
```

In Kotlin:

```kotlin
class MainActivity : Activity() {
    private lateinit var nsh: NshView

    override fun onCreate(state: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(state)
        nsh = NshView(this)
        nsh.setErrorListener { message -> Log.e("nsh", message) }
        setContentView(nsh)
        nsh.loadAssetBundle("nsh")
    }

    override fun onDestroy() {
        nsh.destroy()
        super.onDestroy()
    }
}
```

`NshView` can also sit inside any layout, below your own toolbar for example:

```java
LinearLayout column = new LinearLayout(this);
column.setOrientation(LinearLayout.VERTICAL);
column.addView(toolbar);
column.addView(nsh, new LinearLayout.LayoutParams(ViewGroup.LayoutParams.MATCH_PARENT, 0, 1));
setContentView(column);
```

The view's size is the app's window: NSH lays the app out at the view's size and again whenever it changes. Loading
again replaces the running app. The complete sample is
`examples/embed-android/src/com/longbridge/nsh/embeddemo/MainActivity.java`.

## `NshView`

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `NshView(Context context)`, `NshView(Context context, boolean trace)` | Creates an empty view. `trace` logs the time of every commit. |
| `setErrorListener(ErrorListener listener)` | Receives fatal app errors (load failures, uncaught JS exceptions, a VM stopped by a limit) on the UI thread. They are always logged. |
| `setLimits(int memoryMb, int stackKb, int loadMs, int callMs, int maxNodes)` | VM limits of the apps loaded next; 0 keeps a default. |
| `setGrantedCapabilities(String json)` | The most the apps loaded next may do, as JSON in the form of `nsh.json`'s `capabilities`; `null` grants what each app declares. Returns `false` (and is ignored) for an invalid grant. |
| `loadAssetBundle(String dir)` | Runs `dir/bundle.nshc` from the APK's assets; app assets come from `dir/assets/`. Returns `false` if it cannot be read (also reported to the error listener). |
| `loadBundleFile(File file)` | Runs a `bundle.js` file; assets come from `assets/` next to it. Refuses `.nshc` files. |
| `runPackage(NshPackage pkg)` | Runs a verified signed package, replacing the running app. A package runs once. |
| `registerComponent(String name, NshComponent.Factory factory)` | Registers a [native component](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md). |
| `connectDevServer(String url)` | Development: loads from a `nsh dev` server and reloads on every change. Returns `false` with the release AAR. |
| `handleBack()` | Lets the app handle a back press (closes modals, pops screens, runs `BackHandler` listeners); returns whether it did. |
| `destroy()` | Stops the app. The view can no longer be used. |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Compiled bytecode (`.nshc`) only loads from the APK's own assets or from a signed package. Files on storage can be replaced,
> and QuickJS does not validate bytecode, so `loadBundleFile` takes JS source only. Code the app downloads should come
> as a [signed package](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md).

`setLimits` and `setGrantedCapabilities` apply from the next load: call them before `loadAssetBundle` and friends.

## Limits

```java
// 128 MB heap, default stack, 10 s to load, 1 s per call, 50 000 nodes
nsh.setLimits(128, 0, 10_000, 1_000, 50_000);
```

The defaults are a 256 MB heap, a 4096 KB stack, 10 s to load, 2 s per call and 200 000 nodes. What each limit does
when it is hit: [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

## Capabilities

```java
nsh.setGrantedCapabilities(
    "{\"network\": {\"hosts\": [\"api.example.com\"]}, \"webview\": {\"hosts\": [\"help.example.com\"]}}");
nsh.loadAssetBundle("nsh");
```

A request must be allowed both by what the app declares in its `nsh.json` and by the grant. See
[Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

## Signed packages

Verify downloaded packages off the UI thread, then run them on it:

```java
NshTrust trust = new NshTrust(new File(getFilesDir(), "nsh"));
trust.addRoot(rootPublicKey);   // the contents of root.pub from `nsh keygen`

executor.execute(() -> {
    try {
        NshPackage pkg = trust.openPackage(downloadedFile);
        runOnUiThread(() -> nsh.runPackage(pkg));
    } catch (NshPackage.RefusedException e) {
        Log.w("nsh", "refused: " + e.getMessage());   // the running app stays
    }
});
```

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `new NshTrust(File stateDir)` | Opens or creates the trust store. Its state (newest revocation list, highest build accepted per app) persists there and packages' assets are extracted under it. Trusts no key until `addRoot`. Usable from any thread; `close()` when done. |
| `boolean addRoot(String publicKey)` | Trusts a root public key (base64, the contents of a `.pub` file). `false` for an invalid key. |
| `boolean updateRevocations(String json)` | Applies a revocation list from `nsh revoke`, signed by a trusted root and newer than the store's. |
| `NshPackage openPackage(File file) throws NshPackage.RefusedException` | Verifies, extracts the assets and accepts the package (older builds of the app are refused from then on). Slow for large packages: call it off the UI thread. |
| `NshPackage` | `appId`, `appName`, `version`, `build`; `close()` if it will not run. |

How keys, certificates and revocation work: [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md).

## Development

With `nsh-dev.aar`:

```java
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
    nsh.connectDevServer("ws://127.0.0.1:8790/ws");
} else {
    nsh.loadAssetBundle("nsh");
}
```

Run `nsh dev App.tsx` on your computer. For an emulator or a USB device, forward the port so the device's own
`127.0.0.1` reaches the server:

```sh
adb reverse tcp:8790 tcp:8790
```

Otherwise use the LAN address `nsh dev` prints. Assets come from the dev server over plain HTTP, so `nsh-dev.aar`
declares `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"`, which the manifest merger applies to the app (a network security
config of the app may override it). The release `nsh.aar` does not.

## Activity setup

- **Back button.** On Android 13 and newer, `NshView` registers its own back callback while the app wants back presses
  (an open modal, a pushed screen, a `BackHandler` listener). On Android 12 and older, forward the press:

  ```java
  @Override
  public void onBackPressed() {
      if (!nsh.handleBack()) super.onBackPressed();
  }
  ```

  For predictive back on Android 13+, set `android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true"` on the `<application>`, as
  packaged NSH apps do.
- **Keyboard.** `NshView` scrolls focused inputs clear of the keyboard itself. Leave `android:windowSoftInputMode` unset
  or use `adjustResize`; with `adjustPan` the system moves the whole window instead.
- **Safe area.** The view reports as insets only the parts of the system bars and the keyboard that overlap it, so an
  `NshView` below a toolbar gets no top inset. For edge-to-edge content, draw behind the system bars and let the app use
  `SafeAreaView` / `useSafeAreaInsets()`.
- **Configuration changes.** An activity recreated on rotation or a theme change destroys the view, and the app starts
  again from scratch. To keep it running, declare the changes the activity handles itself; packaged NSH apps use:

  ```xml
  <activity android:name=".MainActivity"
      android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize|screenLayout|smallestScreenSize|keyboard|keyboardHidden|navigation|uiMode|density|fontScale|locale|layoutDirection"
      android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize" />
  ```

  `NshView` follows the new size, color scheme, font scale and layout direction itself.
- **Lifecycle.** Call `destroy()` when the hosting activity or fragment goes away.

## See also

- [Embedding in iOS apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md)
- [Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md)
- [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md)
- [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md): a standalone APK without writing any Java

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android

---

# macOS

NSH apps also run as native Mac apps. The macOS backend renders them with AppKit views and Core Animation and lays out
text with CoreText; the core, the reactive graph, the renderer, Taffy layout and the `nsh/ui/mobile` components are the
same as on iOS and Android, so one bundle runs everywhere. On macOS, `Platform.OS` is `"macos"` and the
`desktop={{…}}` props apply. The window's title, a title bar of the app's own, the menu bar and context menus come from
[`nsh/desktop`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-desktop.md).

The macOS backend behaves like a desktop app: mouse, trackpad and keyboard input, resizable windows, centered sheets
and a menu bar.

## Requirements

- **macOS 14** or later, where the app runs.
- Xcode's command line tools (`xcode-select --install`), to build NSH's macOS runtime from a checkout and to package
  apps (`codesign`, `sips`). The distribution made with `cargo xtask dist` on a Mac ships the runtime in
  `runtime/macos/`.

## Running an app

```sh
nsh run my-app --target macos
```

The app opens in an AppKit window (1200×800 by default), with hot reload, logs in the terminal and the error overlay as
on the other targets; Cmd+R reloads the latest build. The menu bar and the window show the app's name (nsh.json
`"name"`, else its directory's). In a checkout, `nsh run` builds the development host
(`nsh-macos-host`) first. Stopping `nsh run` closes the window, and closing the window ends `nsh run`. The host also
runs a built bundle on its own:

```sh
nsh build my-app --release -o build
dist/nsh/runtime/macos/nsh-macos-host --bundle build/bundle.nshc --size 1200x800   # in a checkout: target/debug/nsh-macos-host
```

`--size` is the window's initial size; the window can be resized.

### Performance monitor

`--fps` (`nsh run my-app --target macos --fps`, the host's `--fps`, a packaged app's `open -a MyApp --args --fps`, or
`AppOptions { fps: true, .. }` / `AppView::set_fps_monitor(true)` when embedding) shows a panel at the top right of the
app that updates twice a second:

| Row | Measures |
|---|---|
| `FPS` | Frames shown over the last second: display refreshes in which the app changed (an idle app reads low; that is not slowness). `max` is what the main thread could keep up with, then the display's rate (120 Hz on ProMotion screens). |
| `TICK` | The gaps between display refreshes as they arrived (mean, p95) and `gap`, the p95 gap between shown frames: one refresh (8.3 ms at 120 Hz) when nothing is late. |
| `MAIN` | Main-thread time per frame (applying the engine's changes, drawing text and canvases, animations, input), its 95th percentile, and `drop`: the share of frames that took longer than one refresh. |
| `JS` / `CORE` | Per commit: your code (handlers, timers, list rows) and NSH's core (layout, text, diffing); commits per second, native view changes per commit. |
| `HOP` | How long changes wait between the engine thread and the main thread; how busy the engine thread is. |
| `CPU` / `GPU` / `MEM` | The process: CPU (100% is one core), its GPU share, its memory footprint (Activity Monitor's figure). |

The bars below are the last 120 frames' main-thread time against one refresh (the line): green within half of it, amber
within it, red over. With `--trace` too, the host also logs the readings once a second (milliseconds as
mean/p50/p95/max). Measure release builds; the monitor costs nothing while it is off.

## Packaging

```sh
nsh package my-app --target macos [--run]
```

Writes an app bundle:

```text
out/<Name>.app/Contents/
  Info.plist
  MacOS/<Name>               the executable (nsh's release runner)
  Resources/nsh/bundle.nshc  your app, compiled
  Resources/nsh/assets/…     the assets it imports
  Resources/nsh/app.json     the window title and the app's appearance
  Resources/AppIcon.icns     the icon, when nsh.json names one (converted with sips)
```

The `.app` is signed ad hoc, so it runs on the Mac that built it. To distribute it, sign it with a Developer ID and
notarize it. `--run` opens the app after packaging it.

## Embedding in a Mac app

The `nsh-platform-macos` crate (from the NSH repository) gives a Rust Mac app `AppView`: one NSH engine as an `NSView`.
Each `AppView` is independent; several can run at once.

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use nsh_platform_macos::{
    objc2::MainThreadMarker, objc2_app_kit::NSWindow, AppOptions, AppView, AssetBase, Bundle,
};

fn show(window: &NSWindow) -> Rc<AppView> {
    let mtm = MainThreadMarker::new().expect("main thread");
    let view = AppView::new(mtm, AppOptions {
        asset_base: Some(AssetBase::Directory("app/assets".into())),
        ..AppOptions::default()
    });
    // register native components here, before loading
    let code = std::fs::read_to_string("app/bundle.js").expect("bundle");
    view.load(Bundle::source(code).into());
    window.setContentView(Some(&view.view()));
    // Keep the view while the window shows it; `stop` it when the window closes.
    view
}
```

`AppView::load` replaces whatever ran; `stop` ends the app. `asset_base` tells it where `asset:/` URIs resolve
(`AssetBase::Directory` or `AssetBase::Http`). Bytecode bundles (`bundle.nshc`) load with
`unsafe { Bundle::bytecode(bytes) }`: bytecode is trusted input, so only load it from your own app's files.
For an app that is only an NSH app, `run_app(source, options)` opens one `AppView` in a window with a standard menu
(About, Hide, Quit, Edit, Minimize, Zoom, Enter Full Screen, Close), which the app can replace with
`Menu.setApplicationMenu` ([`nsh/desktop`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-desktop.md)), and runs until the window closes.
By default, closing the window or choosing Quit stops the engine and returns from `run_app`;
the caller can then finish cleanup or relaunch its executable.

Set `AppOptions { keep_alive_on_close: true, ..Default::default() }` to keep the
standalone session alive when its window closes. Closing hides the window;
reopening from the Dock shows that same window and engine. For an explicit Exit
or update relaunch, call `nsh_platform_macos::quit_app()` from any thread. It
closes the retained window, stops the engine and returns from `run_app`.
`nsh_core::ui::desktop::close_window()` follows the chosen window-close policy.


Native components are registered with `AppView::register_component`; see
[Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md#registering-on-macos-rust).

## What differs on macOS

The environment is a desktop's: the safe area and the keyboard height are 0, `Platform.constants.interfaceIdiom` is
`"desktop"`, `Platform.Version` is the macOS version, and dark mode follows the system's appearance live. See
[Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md).

Input is a desktop's: the mouse, the trackpad (scrolling with momentum, pinch and rotation) and the keyboard.
`selectable` text is selected by dragging, double- and triple-clicking, and copied with Cmd+C. Escape, Option+Left,
Cmd+[ and the mouse's back button go back in a stack or ask a modal to close (Escape in a focused field or web page
only leaves it; a page gets these keys first, and keeps those it uses); page and form sheets are cards centered
in the window over a dimmed backdrop. A click anywhere in an `Input`, its padding too, puts the caret at the nearest
point. `Alert` and `ActionSheet` show an `NSAlert` sheet on the window: up to two alert buttons in a row (the cancel
button leftmost, the last regular one the default for Return), more buttons and an action sheet's options stacked in
their order with the cancel button last and no default; Escape presses the cancel button.

### Keyboard

| Keys | Do |
|---|---|
| Return | In an `Input`, what `submitBehavior` says: submit (`onSubmitEditing`), submit and leave the field, or a new line (multiline inputs) |
| Shift+Return, Option+Return, Ctrl+Return | A new line in a multiline input whose return submits |
| Tab, Shift+Tab (Ctrl too) | The next / previous field in screen order, within the newest modal; Option+Tab types a tab in a multiline input |
| Escape | Leaves the focused field; else clears a text selection, then goes back or asks the newest modal to close |
| Option+Left, Cmd+[, mouse back button | Go back (not while a field has the focus: there Option+Left moves the caret) |
| Option / Cmd + arrows, with Shift; Option+Delete, Cmd+Delete; Ctrl+A / E / K | Move, select and delete by word and line in a field, as in every Mac app |
| Cmd+Z, Shift+Cmd+Z, Cmd+X / C / V / A | Undo, redo, cut, copy, paste, select all (a secure field refuses cut and copy); Cmd+A / Cmd+C select and copy `selectable` text |
| Arrows; Page Up / Down, Space, Shift+Space, Option+Up / Down; Home / End, Cmd+Up / Down | Scroll the scroll view around the focused view or under the mouse by a line, a page, to the start / end (not while a field has the focus) |
| Cmd+W, Cmd+M, Ctrl+Cmd+F, Cmd+H, Option+Cmd+H, Cmd+Q | Close, minimize, full screen, hide, hide others, quit (`nsh package` and `nsh run` apps' menus) |
| Cmd+R | Reloads the latest build (`nsh run`) |

The app's own shortcuts ([`nsh/keymap`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-keymap.md)) come before all of these, except Quit, Hide,
Minimize and Full Screen, which cannot be bound.

Shortcuts work with any keyboard layout (on a Cyrillic or Greek one, Cmd+C is the key that types C on a US layout).
A return that commits an input method's composition (Chinese, Japanese, ...) never submits. `onKeyPress` reports
what React Native reports: the typed text, `"Enter"`, `"Backspace"`, and `"Escape"`.

Not supported, or different:

- **Zooming scroll views** (`zoomTo`, the zoom props).
- **`mixBlendMode`**, and `brightness()` above 1.
- **Inputs**: content types and autofill, keyboard types, autocapitalization, letter spacing; input accessory views
  are never shown (there is no software keyboard) and `keyboardShouldPersistTaps` is ignored.
- **`WebView`'s `scrollEnabled={false}`** keeps the mouse wheel and the trackpad from scrolling the page: they scroll
  the app's scroll views around it, as on iOS. The page still scrolls with its keyboard (Space, the arrows) and its own
  scripts, and trackpad swipes between its pages (`allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures`) stop as well.
- **Accessibility**: custom `accessibilityActions`.
- **The status bar** and **haptics** (no desktop equivalent).

## See also

- [CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md): `nsh run --target macos`, `nsh package --target macos`
- [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md)
- [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/macos

---

# Windows

NSH apps also run on Windows. The Windows backend draws them in Win32 windows with Direct2D and lays out text with
DirectWrite; the core, the reactive graph, the renderer, Taffy layout and the `nsh/ui/mobile` components are the same
as on iOS and Android, so one bundle runs everywhere. On Windows, `Platform.OS` is `"windows"` and the
`desktop={{…}}` props apply. The window's title, a title bar of the app's own, the menu bar and context menus come from
[`nsh/desktop`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-desktop.md).

## Requirements

- **Windows 10 1809** or later, or Windows 11.
- The **WebView2 Runtime** for web views. It comes with Windows 11 and with Microsoft Edge on Windows 10; without it a
  `WebView` shows a placeholder.
- **Media Foundation codecs** for the video formats your app plays (videos play through Windows' own media stack).
- To build NSH's Windows runtime (from a checkout, or `cargo xtask dist` on Windows): Visual Studio Build Tools with
  the C++ workload, the Windows SDK and LLVM (for QuickJS' bindings).

## Running an app

On Windows, `nsh run` opens the app in a window (1200×800 by default), with hot reload, logs in the terminal and the
error overlay as on the other targets:

```sh
nsh run my-app                 # --target windows is the default on Windows
```

In a checkout, `nsh run` builds the development host (`nsh-windows-host.exe`) first; the distribution made on Windows
ships it in `runtime\windows\`. Ctrl-C closes the window, and closing the window ends `nsh run`; the host never
outlives `nsh`, however it ends. The host also runs a built bundle on its own:

```sh
nsh build my-app --release -o build
dist\nsh\runtime\windows\nsh-windows-host --bundle build\bundle.nshc --size 390x844   # in a checkout: target\debug\nsh-windows-host
```

`--size` is the window's size in points (`<width>x<height>`).

## Packaging

```sh
nsh package my-app --target windows [--run]
```

Writes a directory and the same as an archive:

```text
out\<Name>\
  <Name>.exe             the executable (nsh's release runner), with the app's icon
  nsh\bundle.nshc         your app, compiled
  nsh\assets\…           the assets it imports
  nsh\app.json           the window title, the app id, the version and the appearance
out\<Name>.zip
```

The executable finds `nsh\` next to itself; copy the whole directory (or unpack the `.zip`) wherever the app should
live: nothing is installed. The icon from `nsh.json` is embedded in the executable (Explorer and the taskbar show it)
without any extra tools; packaging on another system keeps the default icon. The app id groups the app's windows in
the taskbar. `--run` launches the app after packaging it. The executable is not signed: sign it with your own
certificate (`signtool`) to distribute it.

## Embedding in a Win32 app

The `nsh-platform-windows` crate (from the NSH repository) gives a Rust Win32 app `AppView`: one NSH engine in a child
window of a window of yours. Each `AppView` is independent; several can run at once.

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use nsh_platform_windows::{
    windows::{self, Win32::{Foundation::HWND, System::Ole::OleInitialize, UI::WindowsAndMessaging::MoveWindow}},
    AppOptions, AppView, AssetBase, Bundle,
};

/// Called on the thread that runs your message loop, with your window.
fn embed(parent: HWND) -> windows::core::Result<Rc<AppView>> {
    // Once per thread: COM and OLE (the clipboard, image decoding).
    unsafe { OleInitialize(None)? };
    let view = AppView::new(
        Some(parent),
        AppOptions {
            asset_base: Some(AssetBase::Directory("app/assets".into())),
            app_id: "com.example.host".into(),
            ..AppOptions::default()
        },
    )?;
    // register native components here, before loading
    let code = std::fs::read_to_string("app/bundle.js").expect("bundle");
    view.load(Bundle::source(code).into());
    Ok(view)
}

// On WM_SIZE of `parent`:
// unsafe { MoveWindow(view.hwnd(), 0, 0, width, height, true) };
```

The view is a child window: your message loop runs it, and you place it with `MoveWindow` on its `hwnd()` when the
parent resizes. `AppView::load` replaces whatever ran; `stop` (or destroying the window) ends the app. `asset_base`
tells it where `asset:/` URIs resolve (`AssetBase::Directory` or `AssetBase::Http`). Bytecode bundles (`bundle.nshc`)
load with `unsafe { Bundle::bytecode(bytes) }` (or `Bundle::read_trusted(path)`, unsafe too): QuickJS bytecode is trusted input, so
only load it from your own app's files. A standalone window is `nsh_platform_windows::run_app(source, options)`.

Native components are registered with `AppView::register_component`; see
[Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md#registering-on-windows-rust).

## What differs on Windows

The environment is a desktop's: the safe area and the keyboard height are 0, `Platform.constants.interfaceIdiom` is
`"desktop"` and `Platform.Version` is `"10.0"` (on Windows 11 too: Windows kept the version number). Dark mode
follows Settings > Personalization > Colors live, `fontScale()` the Text size setting, reduce motion the animation
effects setting and the locale the user's regional format. See [Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md).

### Keyboard

| Keys | Do |
|---|---|
| Return | In an `Input`, what `submitBehavior` says: submit (`onSubmitEditing`), submit and leave the field, or a new line (multiline inputs) |
| Shift+Return, Alt+Return | A new line in a multiline input whose return submits (Ctrl+Return submits) |
| Tab, Shift+Tab | The next / previous text field, within the newest modal; the field's text is selected, as in Windows' dialogs |
| Escape | Leaves the focused field; else clears a text selection, then goes back or asks the newest modal to close |
| Alt+Left, Browser Back key, mouse back button | Go back (also from a field) |
| Ctrl+arrows, Home / End, Ctrl+Home / End, with Shift; Ctrl+Backspace / Delete | Move, select and delete by word and line in a field, as in every Windows app |
| Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y, Ctrl+X / C / V / A; Shift+Delete, Ctrl+Insert, Shift+Insert | Undo, redo, cut, copy, paste, select all (a secure field refuses cut and copy); Ctrl+A / Ctrl+C select and copy `selectable` text |
| Arrows; Page Up / Down, Space, Shift+Space; Home / End, Ctrl+Home / End | Scroll the scroll view around the focused view or under the mouse by a line, a page, to the start / end (not while a field has the focus) |
| F11, Alt+F4 | Full screen, close the window (`nsh package` and `nsh run` apps) |
| Ctrl+R, F5 | Reload the latest build (`nsh run`) |

Shortcuts work with any keyboard layout (on a Cyrillic or Greek one, Ctrl+C is the key that types C on a US layout).
A return that commits an input method's composition (Chinese, Japanese, ...) never submits. `onKeyPress` reports
what React Native reports: the typed text, `"Enter"`, `"Backspace"`, and `"Escape"`; pasted text is not reported.

The app's own shortcuts ([`nsh/keymap`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-keymap.md)) come before a focused field's keys, navigation
and scrolling; Alt+F4, F11 and Ctrl+Q cannot be bound.

Different, or not supported:

- **`WebView`**: a page inside a view with a 3D transform (perspective) is not shown, and a `backdropFilter` over a
  page does not blur it. `source.baseUrl` takes `http(s)` URLs. A native component that brings a window of its own
  stays above everything NSH draws.
- **Video**: the formats the installed codecs decode; no poster; the control bar always shows with `controls`.
- **Zooming scroll views** (`zoomTo`, the zoom props); the scroll indicator cannot be dragged.
- **`mixBlendMode` and `backdropFilter`** are drawn, but not inside a view that has a `filter` or a 3D transform;
  `borderCurve: "continuous"` draws circular corners.
- **Text**: head and middle ellipses on a single line only (more lines get a tail ellipsis); color emoji from COLR
  fonts only; small caps only where the font has them.
- **Text inputs**: keyboard types and autofill do not apply (there is no software keyboard); Tab moves between text
  fields. A right click opens the edit menu (Undo, Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, Select All), as on selectable text (Copy,
  Select All).
- **Accessibility** (UI Automation): headers' titles and buttons, dialogs and toasts are not exposed; headings report
  level 1.
- **Input accessory views** and the **status bar** (no desktop equivalent).

## See also

- [CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md): `nsh run --target windows`, `nsh package --target windows`
- [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md)
- [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/windows

---

# Linux

NSH apps also run on Linux. The Linux backend renders them with GTK 4 widgets and lays out text with Pango; the core,
the reactive graph, the renderer, Taffy layout and the `nsh/ui/mobile` components are the same as on iOS and Android,
so one bundle runs everywhere. On Linux, `Platform.OS` is `"linux"` and the `desktop={{…}}` props apply. The window's title, a title bar of the app's own, the menu bar and context menus come from
[`nsh/desktop`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-desktop.md).

## Requirements

- **GTK 4.14** or later. To build NSH's Linux runtime (from a checkout, or `cargo xtask
  dist` on Linux) you need their development packages and clang: `libgtk-4-dev clang` on Debian and Ubuntu (24.04 or
  later), `gtk4 clang` on Arch, `gtk4-devel clang` on Fedora.
- **WebKitGTK 6.0** (2.40 or later) for web views: `libwebkitgtk-6.0-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu, `webkitgtk-6.0` on
  Arch, `webkitgtk6.0-devel` on Fedora to build the runtime. The development host and the release runner use it by
  default, so packaged apps need WebKitGTK 6.0 where they run (`libwebkitgtk-6.0-4` on Debian and Ubuntu; GNOME
  desktops have it). `cargo xtask dist` on a machine without its development files builds a runtime whose web views
  are placeholders, and whose apps need only GTK.
- **GStreamer** plugins for the video formats your app plays (GTK plays video through GStreamer).

## Running an app

On Linux, `nsh run` opens the app in a GTK window (390×844 by default), with hot reload, logs in the terminal and the
error overlay as on the other targets:

```sh
nsh run my-app                 # --target linux is the default on Linux
```

In a checkout, `nsh run` builds the development host (`nsh-linux-host`) first; the distribution made on Linux ships
it in `runtime/linux/`. Ctrl-C closes the window, and closing the window ends `nsh run`. The host also runs a built
bundle on its own:

```sh
nsh build my-app --release -o build
dist/nsh/runtime/linux/nsh-linux-host --bundle build/bundle.nshc --size 1024x768   # in a checkout: target/debug/nsh-linux-host
```

`--size` is the window's default size; tiling window managers may give the window another one.

## Packaging

```sh
nsh package my-app --target linux [--run]
```

Writes a directory and the same as an archive:

```text
out/<Name>/
  <Name>                 the executable (nsh's release runner)
  nsh/bundle.nshc        your app, compiled
  nsh/assets/…           the assets it imports
  nsh/app.json           the window title and the application id
  <id>.desktop           a desktop entry (StartupWMClass is the id)
  <id>.png               the icon, when nsh.json names one
out/<Name>.tar.gz
```

The executable finds `nsh/` next to itself (a symbolic link to it, in `~/.local/bin` say, works too). GTK 4, Pango and
WebKitGTK 6.0 must be installed where the app runs. To show the app in a desktop's launcher, put the executable (or a link) on the
`PATH`, the `.desktop` file in `~/.local/share/applications` and the icon in an icon theme directory. `--run` launches
the app after packaging it.

## Embedding in a GTK app

The `nsh-platform-linux` crate (from the NSH repository) gives a Rust GTK app `AppView`: one NSH engine as a GTK widget.
Each `AppView` is independent; several can run at once.

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use nsh_platform_linux::{gtk4 as gtk, AppOptions, AppView, AssetBase, Bundle};
use gtk::prelude::*;

fn main() -> gtk::glib::ExitCode {
    let app = gtk::Application::builder().application_id("com.example.host").build();
    app.connect_activate(|app| {
        let window = gtk::ApplicationWindow::builder().application(app).default_width(390).default_height(844).build();
        let view = AppView::new(AppOptions {
            asset_base: Some(AssetBase::Directory("app/assets".into())),
            ..AppOptions::default()
        });
        // register native components here, before loading
        let code = std::fs::read_to_string("app/bundle.js").expect("bundle");
        view.load(Bundle::source(code).into());
        window.set_child(Some(&view.widget()));
        // The window keeps the view; closing it stops the app.
        let keep = std::cell::RefCell::new(Some(Rc::clone(&view)));
        window.connect_destroy(move |_| if let Some(view) = keep.take() { view.stop() });
        window.present();
    });
    app.run()
}
```

`AppView::load` replaces whatever ran; `stop` ends the app. `asset_base` tells it where `asset:/` URIs resolve
(`AssetBase::Directory` or `AssetBase::Http`). Bytecode bundles (`bundle.nshc`) load with `unsafe { Bundle::bytecode(bytes) }`:
QuickJS bytecode is trusted input, so only load it from your own app's files.

Native components are registered with `AppView::register_component`; see [Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md#registering-on-linux-rust).

## What differs on Linux

The environment is a desktop's: the safe area and the keyboard height are 0, `Platform.constants.interfaceIdiom` is
`"desktop"`, `Platform.Version` is the kernel's major and minor version, and dark mode follows the desktop's setting
(through the XDG settings portal) live. See [Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md).

### Keyboard

| Keys | Do |
|---|---|
| Return | In an `Input`, what `submitBehavior` says: submit (`onSubmitEditing`), submit and leave the field, or a new line (multiline inputs) |
| Shift+Return, Alt+Return | A new line in a multiline input whose return submits (Ctrl+Return submits) |
| Tab, Shift+Tab | The next / previous field in screen order, within the newest modal |
| Escape | Leaves the focused field; else clears a text selection, then goes back or asks the newest modal to close |
| Alt+Left, Back key, mouse back button | Go back (also from a field) |
| Ctrl+arrows, Home / End, with Shift; Ctrl+Backspace / Delete | Move, select and delete by word and line in a field, as in every GTK app |
| Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z, Ctrl+X / C / V / A | Undo, redo, cut, copy, paste, select all (a secure field refuses cut and copy); Ctrl+A / Ctrl+C select and copy `selectable` text |
| Arrows; Page Up / Down, Space, Shift+Space; Home / End | Scroll the scroll view around the focused view or under the mouse by a line, a page, to the start / end (not while a field has the focus) |
| Ctrl+W, F11, Ctrl+Q | Close the window, full screen, quit (`nsh package` and `nsh run` apps) |
| Ctrl+R | Reloads the latest build (`nsh run`) |

The app's own shortcuts ([`nsh/keymap`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-keymap.md)) are a window-wide shortcut controller; Ctrl+Q and
F11 cannot be bound.

Shortcuts work with any keyboard layout (on a Cyrillic or Greek one, Ctrl+C is the key that types C on a US layout).
A return that commits an input method's composition (Chinese, Japanese, ...) never submits. `onKeyPress` reports
what React Native reports: the typed text, `"Enter"`, `"Backspace"`, and `"Escape"`; pasted text is not reported.

Web views are WebKitGTK pages, drawn inside NSH's views: sheets, dialogs, toasts and views after them draw over a page,
and parents clip it and fade it. Their website data (cookies, storage, the cache) is kept per app, under
`~/.local/share/<app id>/webkit` and `~/.cache/<app id>/webkit`. The `webview` capability also applies to the pages of
frames: an `iframe` of a host your app was not granted stays empty. Escape in a page leaves it, as in a text field
(unless the page uses it); Alt+Left and the mouse's back button go back in the page while it has a history.

Not supported:

- **Video `rate`**: GTK plays at normal speed only. `onEnd` only comes for videos that do not loop.
- **Zooming scroll views** (`zoomTo`, the zoom props).
- **`mixBlendMode` and `backdropFilter`** (the background color still draws); `borderCurve: "continuous"` draws
  circular corners.
- **Input accessory views** and the **status bar** (no desktop equivalent).
- **Accessibility**: `accessible` grouping, custom `accessibilityActions`; live regions are announced instead.

## See also

- [CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md): `nsh run --target linux`, `nsh package --target linux`
- [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md)
- [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/linux

---

# GPUI

The GPUI backend draws NSH apps with [GPUI](https://gpui-kit.com) (GPUI Fast), the GPU-accelerated UI framework that
GPUI Kit is built on, on macOS, Windows and Linux alike. Its main use is embedding: an `AppView` is a GPUI view, so a
GPUI or GPUI Kit app shows NSH modules anywhere in its own element tree. The core, the reactive graph, the renderer,
Taffy layout and the `nsh/ui/mobile` components are the same as on every other platform, so one bundle runs
everywhere. `Platform.OS` is the OS it runs on (`"macos"`, `"windows"` or `"linux"`) and the `desktop={{…}}` props
apply.

Every element and module of the [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md) (AppKit), [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md) (Win32) and
[Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md) (GTK) backends is there; where GPUI draws something its own way, [Differences](#differences)
says how.

## How it works

- **One element per surface.** A surface is one GPUI element that fills the space its parent gives it and paints the
  whole view tree with GPUI's primitives: quads, shadows, paths, glyphs and images. NSH keeps one retained view per
  node, as on Windows, and redraws only when a commit changed something.
- **Text is shaped on the engine thread** with GPUI's text system (the app's own fonts), broken into lines by NSH;
  the main thread only paints the glyphs.
- **One hop per commit.** The engine runs on its own thread; each commit is one closure sent to GPUI's main thread,
  which notifies the view.
- **Input** comes from GPUI's mouse, scroll, key and input method events; hit testing, presses, the responder system,
  scrolling and text editing are the same logic as the Windows backend's.

## Requirements

- macOS, Windows or Linux, with a GPU GPUI can draw with (Metal on macOS, DirectX on Windows, Vulkan on Linux).
- On Linux: a Vulkan driver, Wayland or X11 with `libxkbcommon`, GTK 3 and WebKitGTK 4.1 (web views) and GStreamer
  1.20 or later with its base and good plug-ins (videos). Web views need X11: on a Wayland desktop run the app under
  Xwayland (`WAYLAND_DISPLAY=` empty), else they show a placeholder. Building the runtime from a checkout also needs
  the development packages; on Debian and Ubuntu:

  ```sh
  sudo apt-get install clang libclang-dev pkg-config libfontconfig-dev libfreetype-dev libwayland-dev libx11-xcb-dev \
    libxcb1-dev libxkbcommon-dev libxkbcommon-x11-dev libzstd-dev libvulkan1 libgtk-3-dev libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev \
    libgstreamer1.0-dev libgstreamer-plugins-base1.0-dev gstreamer1.0-plugins-good
  ```

## Running an app

```sh
nsh run my-app --target gpui
```

Opens the app in a GPUI window (1200×800 by default), with hot reload, logs in the terminal and the error overlay as
on the other targets. The development host (`nsh-gpui-host`) runs in place on every OS, with no app bundle around it.
In a checkout, `nsh run` builds it first; the distribution ships it in `runtime/gpui/`. The host also runs a built
bundle on its own:

```sh
nsh build my-app --release -o build
dist/nsh/runtime/gpui/nsh-gpui-host --bundle build/bundle.nshc --size 390x844   # in a checkout: target/debug/nsh-gpui-host
```

`--size` is the window's size in points (`<width>x<height>`).

## Packaging

```sh
nsh package my-app --target gpui [--run]
```

The package is laid out as the native backend's of the machine it is made on, with GPUI's release runner
(`nsh-gpui-app`) as the executable:

| Packaged on | Output |
|---|---|
| macOS | an ad hoc signed `<Name>.app`, as [`--target macos`](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#packaging) makes |
| Windows | a directory `<Name>\` with `<Name>.exe` and `nsh\`, and `<Name>.zip`, as [`--target windows`](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#packaging) makes |
| Linux | a directory `<Name>/` with the executable, `nsh/` and a `.desktop` file, and `<Name>.tar.gz`, as [`--target linux`](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#packaging) makes |

As with the native backends, the runner is built for the machine it is built on: package a Mac app on a Mac, a
Windows app on Windows and a Linux app on Linux. `--run` launches the app after packaging it.

A Linux package links WebKitGTK 4.1 (web views) and GStreamer (videos) dynamically, so the machines it runs on need them installed, with GTK 3 and GStreamer's base and good plug-ins (Debian / Ubuntu: `libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0`, `libgstreamer1.0-0`, `libgstreamer-plugins-base1.0-0`, `gstreamer1.0-plugins-good`), besides a Vulkan driver and `libxkbcommon`.

## Embedding in a GPUI app

The `nsh-platform-gpui` crate (from the NSH repository) gives a Rust GPUI app `AppView`: one NSH engine as a GPUI
view (`Entity<AppView>`), which fills the space its parent element gives it. Each `AppView` is independent; several
can run at once.

```rust
use gpui::{AppContext, Application, WindowOptions};
use nsh_platform_gpui::{App, AppOptions, AppView, Bundle};

gpui_platform::application().run(|cx| {
    cx.open_window(WindowOptions::default(), |window, cx| {
        cx.new(|cx| {
            let view = AppView::new(AppOptions::default(), window, cx);
            let code = std::fs::read_to_string("app/bundle.js").expect("bundle");
            view.load(App::Js(Bundle::source(code)));
            view
        })
    })
    .unwrap();
});
```

Put the entity in your element tree like any other view (a GPUI Kit `Root`, a panel, a dock). `AppView::load`
replaces whatever ran; `stop` (or dropping the view) ends the app. `AppOptions::asset_base` tells it where `asset:/`
URIs resolve (`AssetBase::Directory` or `AssetBase::Http`). Bytecode bundles (`bundle.nshc`) load with
`unsafe { Bundle::bytecode(bytes) }` (or `Bundle::read_trusted(path)`, unsafe too): QuickJS bytecode is trusted input,
so only load it from your own app's files.

- `open_app_window(source, options, cx)` opens a window with one `AppView` in a running GPUI app.
- `run_app(source, options)` starts GPUI and runs one app in a window until it closes (what the release runner does).
- `AppView::register_component(name, factory)` registers a native component of yours before loading
  ([Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md)).
- `set_ui_sets(sets)` replaces the default `nsh/ui/mobile` set, for apps with Rust components of their own.

## Differences

What draws or behaves differently from the native desktop backends:

- **Transforms**: rotated, skewed and projected views turn their backgrounds, borders and shadows, but text stays
  upright, and images, videos and canvases draw at their bounds.
- **Opacity** applies to each color rather than to a group, so overlapping children of a translucent view show
  through each other; an image's opacity (a fade-in, a translucent view) changes in sixteenths.
- **Rounded clips** (`overflow: "hidden"` with a radius) round the backgrounds and images of the children, but text,
  borders, videos and native components are cut by the rectangle.
- **Not drawn**: `filter: blur()`, `backdropFilter` and `mixBlendMode`; shadows show through translucent fills;
  `borderCurve: "continuous"` draws circular corners.
- **Canvas text** is approximated: upright under rotations, made smaller rather than narrower for `maxWidth`,
  gradients paint it in one color, `strokeText` fills, its shadows are not blurred, and composite operations and
  `clearRect` do not apply to it.
- **Scroll views** do not zoom (`zoomTo` and the zoom props are ignored).
- **Video** plays on Linux (GStreamer); on macOS and Windows a video shows a placeholder and reports `onError`.
- **Web views** are native views above everything NSH draws at their place. On Linux they need X11 (see
  [Requirements](#requirements)); where pages stay black under Xwayland ("Failed to create GBM buffer" in the log),
  run the app with `WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1`. On macOS and Windows clipping ancestors do not cut them and
  failed loads report no `onError`. `source.baseUrl`, `scrollEnabled` and `allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures` are
  not supported.
- **Accessibility** goes through AccessKit: screen readers can activate, focus, set values and scroll elements into
  view everywhere; custom actions and the context-menu action are not passed on yet.

For comparison, each native backend's own list: [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#what-differs-on-macos),
[Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#what-differs-on-windows), [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#what-differs-on-linux).

## See also

- [CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md): `nsh run --target gpui`, `nsh package --target gpui`
- [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md)
- [Platform overview](https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui

---

# Web

Build web apps with Native Shell using the same components, styles and application logic as on native platforms. NSH renders the interface as HTML elements and CSS: text, images, inputs, scrolling, visual styles and interactions use the browser's DOM and web APIs.

`nsh package --target web` publishes the app as a static site for any web server or CDN ([Publish an app](#publish-an-app)), and `nsh run --target web` runs it in the browser while you edit it ([Develop in the browser](#develop-in-the-browser)). Every live demo on this site uses this web backend.

## What runs where
