The page is built from HTML elements styled with CSS. NSH turns component updates into batches of DOM changes, while the browser displays the interface and handles scrolling, text selection and input. WebAssembly hosts the shared Rust engine for component state, layout and updates.

On every native platform the engine has its own thread and hands one `MountBatch` per commit to the main thread. A browser page has one thread, so the web build drives the same engine step by step from the page's event loop (`nsh_engine::LocalEngine`):

```text
pointer / keyboard / scroll events ─┐
setTimeout (the engine's deadline) ─┼─▶ nsh.wasm: engine turn (JS, core, layout) ─▶ one JSON batch ─▶ nsh.js: DOM
requestAnimationFrame ──────────────┘                                                 ▲
                                                          native animation outputs ───┘
```

- **Layout is the core's.** Every view is an absolutely positioned element at the frame Taffy computed, so flexbox, grid, `aspectRatio` and percentages behave exactly as on devices. The browser's own layout is not involved.
- **Styles are turned into CSS in Rust.** Background, borders, radii, shadows (`shadow*` and `boxShadow`), gradients, filters, `backdropFilter`, transforms, `transformOrigin`, `outline`, `mixBlendMode`, transitions and the built-in keyframe animations become CSS properties. Tailwind classes, `active:`, `hover:` and `focus:` states and `dark:` all resolve natively, as they do on devices.
- **Text is laid out in Rust** with font measurements from the browser (`CanvasRenderingContext2D.measureText`) and drawn run by run at the positions the layout chose, so what was measured is what is drawn. Lines break after spaces, around CJK characters and at `\n`; `numberOfLines` truncates with an ellipsis.
- **Native animations run in Rust** on `requestAnimationFrame`: `Animated` timing, spring and decay, `interpolate`, native values bound to `opacity`, `transform` and `backgroundColor`, drags bound with `pan`, scroll-linked values and canvas arguments. JS is not involved per frame, as on devices. `LayoutAnimation`, style transitions, the `animate-*` keyframes and screen transitions move as on the desktop backends, and `prefers-reduced-motion` turns them off (screens fade).
- **Input:** presses with `activeOpacity` and long presses, the responder system (`onTouch*`, `PanResponder`), native drags and two-finger pinch and rotation, scroll views (the browser's scrolling), pull to refresh, zooming scroll views (pinch, ctrl+wheel and touchpad pinches, `zoomTo`), `<Input>` with controlled values, focus and submit, `Canvas`, `Stack` and `Screen` with a header, `Modal`.
- **System UI is drawn in the page:** `Alert` and `ActionSheet` look like the desktop backends' dialogs on desktop browsers and like iOS's on phones (with the `desktop` idiom, see below), and `Toast.show` shows a toast at the bottom. Custom fonts are measured again once the browser has loaded them, and an app waits for the fonts it imports before its first frame shows.
- **Modals** are presented as on the platform the browser is like: `pageSheet` and `formSheet` (`desktop={{ presentationStyle }}` or `web={{ presentationStyle }}`) are cards centered over the dimmed page in desktop and tablet browsers, the sizes the desktop backends use, closed by Escape, the browser's back button or a click outside (each asks through `onRequestClose`); in phone browsers they rise from the bottom to just below the top, as iPhone sheets do. `fullScreen` and transparent modals cover the app; `animationType`, `onShow` and `onDismiss` work as on devices.

## Keyboard, mouse and touch

Published apps behave as desktop apps in desktop browsers and as phone apps in phone browsers:

- **Wheels and touchpads** scroll the innermost scroll view along their axis that can still move (a vertical wheel scrolls a horizontal list when nothing vertical can), and stay on it until the scroll ends; wheel notches glide, paging and snapping views move one page per scroll. Ctrl + wheel and touchpad pinches pinch views with native pinch values instead of zooming the page. Dragging with the mouse does not scroll, as on the desktop platforms: mouse drags go to pans, the responder system and text selection. Scroll views report `onScrollBeginDrag` / `onScrollEndDrag`, `onMomentumScrollBegin` / `End` and `onScrollEnd` as on the desktop platforms.
- **Keyboard**: Tab and Shift+Tab move between pressables and inputs (a focus ring and `focus:` styles show the keyboard focus); Return presses the focused pressable, Space presses it when released; arrows, Page Up / Page Down, Space, Home and End scroll the scroll view around the focus or under the mouse; Escape leaves a field, closes the dialog, then goes back. `nsh/keymap` shortcuts work in the browser, matched on the spot (`mod` is Command in Safari and Chrome on a Mac, Control elsewhere).
- **Going back**: Escape, Alt+Left (Cmd+[ on a Mac) and the mouse's back button pop the innermost stack, or ask the newest modal to close, as the Android back button does; `preventBack` and `onBackPress` work as there. When the app is the whole page, every pushed screen and presented modal is a browser history entry, so the browser's back button goes back in the app.
- **Touch**: only scroll views pan; the page itself never scrolls, zooms or pulls to refresh under the app, and taps have no delay. In an iframe, swipes the app does not take scroll the embedding page. Drags on views with native pans, pinches and the responder system are the app's.
- **Accessibility**: `accessibilityRole`, `accessibilityLabel`, `accessibilityHint`, `accessibilityState`, `accessibilityValue`, `accessibilityLiveRegion` and `accessibilityElementsHidden` become ARIA; `AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility` speaks through a live region and `setAccessibilityFocus` moves the focus. Views under a modal or alert are inert.
- **Selection and menus**: in desktop browsers text is selectable by default, as on a web page, except inside interactive elements (views with press or touch handlers: buttons, pressable rows, tabs) and text with `selectable={false}` or `select-none`; dragging the mouse over it selects it, Ctrl/Cmd+C copies it line by line and Ctrl/Cmd+A selects all of the text the selection is in. In phone and tablet browsers only `selectable` text is selectable, as in native apps. The browser's context menu appears only in selectable text and inputs.


## Publish an app

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target web           # out/<Name>/: a static site
nsh package App.tsx --target web --run     # and serve it on this machine (open the address it prints)
```

`nsh package --target web` writes `out/<Name>/` (`--out` for another directory), laid out like a frontend build: one
page and files named after their content.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `index.html` | The app's page: its name as the title, the icons, the colors of its `appearance`, a loading indicator, and a message when the app cannot load or start |
| `manifest.webmanifest` | The name, id, icons and colors browsers install the app with |
| `nsh.<digest>.js` | The DOM runtime, minified (79 KB, 22.5 KB with brotli) |
| `nsh.<digest>.wasm` | The engine, the core, the mobile components and QuickJS without its compiler (about 3.5 MB, 1.2 MB gzipped, 0.93 MB with brotli) |
| `app.<digest>.nshc` | The app, built as `nsh build --release --split` builds it, compiled to QuickJS bytecode: nothing is compiled in the browser, so it starts sooner |
| `harden.<digest>.nshc` | The [sandbox's](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md) hardening, compiled likewise (1.4 KB) |
| `chunks/<name>.<digest>.nshc` | What `import()` loads, compiled likewise, downloaded the first time it is imported ([split bundles](#split-bundles)) |
| `assets/<path>.<digest>.<ext>` | Every asset the app imports, loaded from its URL when it is used (fonts before the code that registers them runs, as text is measured with them: before the app starts, or with the chunk that imports them) |
| `icons/<size>.<digest>.png` | The icon of `nsh.json` at 32 (favicon), 180 (`apple-touch-icon`), 192 and 512 pixels |

`<digest>` is the start of the SHA-256 of the file's content: a file's name changes exactly when its content does, so a
new release changes only `index.html` and the files that really changed. Everything uses relative URLs, so the site
works from any directory of any host (`https://example.com/apps/counter/`).

### Deploy it

Upload the directory to any static host: an object store behind a CDN, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, GitHub Pages,
nginx. Two rules make it load fast and update reliably:

| Files | `Cache-Control` |
|---|---|
| `index.html`, `manifest.webmanifest` | `no-cache` (revalidated on every load, so a release shows at once) |
| everything else | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` |

Serve `.wasm` as `application/wasm` (browsers then compile it while it downloads) and let the host or CDN compress
text and WebAssembly (gzip or brotli). `nsh package --target web --run` serves the site this way on
`http://127.0.0.1:4173/`.

An app published for the web runs like a packaged native app: as a release, [hardened](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)
(no `eval`), with the capabilities its `nsh.json` declares. When they restrict `network`, the page also carries a
Content-Security-Policy `connect-src` with the declared hosts (and the page's own origin), so the browser itself
refuses requests and redirect hops to any other host. An error that keeps it from starting is shown on the page;
later errors go to the browser's console.

### Embed it with an iframe

There is no embedding API on the web: embed the published app with an `<iframe>`. Its size is the app's window:

```html
<iframe src="https://apps.example.com/counter/" title="Counter"
        style="width: 390px; height: 844px; border: 0"></iframe>
```

## Develop in the browser

```sh
nsh run App.tsx --target web
```

starts the dev server and prints its page's address, `http://127.0.0.1:8790/`: open it in any browser. The page is a development host
like the others: it runs each build of the app, applies edits in place (hot updates), shows build errors and runtime
errors over the app, and sends the app's `console` output to the terminal. Phones on the same network open the
address `nsh run` prints under it (`on this network: http://192.168.…:8790/`). `nsh dev` serves the same page once the
web runtime is there (in the distribution, always).

## Apps with Rust components

An app written in Rust ([Building with Rust](https://nsh.dev/docs/rust.md)) publishes and runs in the browser with the same commands:

```sh
nsh package --target web           # out/<Name>/: the app's own nsh.wasm, with its crate
nsh run --target web               # the dev server's page; editing the Rust code builds it again
```

When `nsh.json` names the app's root component (`"root"`), the page is the app's Rust and NSH's page script, and
nothing else: `nsh.wasm` holds the engine, the components and the app's crate with no QuickJS, the site has no
`app.nshc` or `harden.nshc`, and the page mounts the root as soon as the runtime and the fonts are in. The whole Rust
gallery is 3.3 MB (1.06 MB gzipped, 0.75 MB with brotli), less than the runtime of TSX apps. Under its TSX entry
(`nsh package App.tsx --target web`), the same app runs as TSX apps do, with QuickJS, and imports the crate's
components and modules.

Either way the crate's assets (`assets!()`) are published with the app's, and its fonts load before the first frame.
During `nsh run --target web`, a change to the crate's Rust code builds the runtime again and the open page loads it by
itself; TSX edits stay hot updates.

Rust code that runs on every platform, the web included, uses the engine's services: `fetch(url).await` makes
HTTP requests through the same network stack as JS's `fetch` (the browser's here, with its CORS rules); `timer`,
`set_timeout` and `set_interval` wait; and `nsh_core::time::Instant` and `nsh_core::time::unix_ms()` read the clock.
`background` and `blocking` run work on the native targets' threads.

The build needs the Rust target and a clang that compiles to WebAssembly, as the runtime's own build does:
`rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown`, plus `clang` and `llvm-ar` (on macOS, an LLVM toolchain such as
Homebrew's `llvm`, through `CC_wasm32_unknown_unknown` and `AR_wasm32_unknown_unknown`).

## Build the website's player

```sh
cargo xtask web                       # nsh.wasm, nsh.js, the player and website/demos/*.tsx
cargo xtask web --out target/play     # somewhere else
```

The output directory holds:

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `gallery/nsh.<digest>.wasm` | The runtime of published apps (about 3.5 MB, 1.2 MB gzipped, 0.93 MB with brotli; built with the `web` profile), shared by the player and the gallery |
| `nsh-playground.wasm` | The same plus NSH's TSX compiler, for the [playground](#the-playground) (about 8 MB, 2.4 MB gzipped) |
| `gallery/nsh.<digest>.js` | The DOM runtime (minified): loads the wasm, applies batches, turns input into events |
| `index.html` | A player page: runs `demos/<name>.nshc` for `#<name>` |
| `demos/<name>.nshc` | Each demo compiled by `nsh build --release` |
| `gallery/` | The gallery app published with `nsh package --target web`, shown on the [Gallery](/gallery) page |

Serve the directory with any static server (it needs the `application/wasm` MIME type for streaming compilation) and open `index.html#counter`.

## The playground

The [Playground](/playground) edits and runs an app in the browser: the page compiles the TSX with NSH's own JSX compiler (built into `nsh-playground.wasm`, without rolldown) and runs it on every pause in typing. Every demo on this site has an **Edit in Playground** link, and **Share** puts the code in the link itself, so nothing is stored on a server.

A playground app is one module: it imports NSH's modules (`nsh`, `nsh/*`, `nsh/ui/mobile`) but no other files or packages. `console.log` output and errors appear below the phone.

The compiler is also a Rust function, `nsh_bundler::compile_module(name, source, ui_sets)`, available without the crate's `bundle` feature.

## Embed it in a page

`nsh.js` is an ES module. `createPlayer` loads the runtime into a container; `run` starts a bundle that `nsh build` writes: `bundle.nshc`, its bytecode, as bytes, or `bundle.js` as a string. The runtime `nsh package --target web` ships (`nsh.wasm`) has no JavaScript compiler and runs bytecode only; the development runtime (`nsh-dev.wasm` in the distribution) runs both:

```js
import { createPlayer } from "./nsh.js";

const player = await createPlayer(document.querySelector("#phone"), {
  wasm: "./nsh.wasm",
  assetBase: "./assets/",   // where `asset:/…` URIs (image imports) are served from
  // dark: true,            // force an appearance; otherwise it follows the system
  // idiom: "phone",        // force "phone", "pad" or "desktop"; otherwise the pointer and the size decide
  // history: false,        // screens and modals as browser history entries; by default only when the app is the page, not in an iframe
});
player.run(await (await fetch("./bundle.nshc")).arrayBuffer());
```

`assets` (a map from `asset:/` paths to URLs) replaces `assetBase`, and `readAsset(uri)` returns the bytes of an asset the engine needs at once (a font) or `null`; `player.run(code, { release: true, capabilities })` runs a bundle as a release under the capabilities it declares (the default is development settings); with bytecode, a release also takes the hardening's bytecode (`harden`, the bytes of `harden.<digest>.nshc`). The page `nsh package --target web` writes uses all of them.

`run(code, { chunks, chunkBase })` also takes where the chunks of a [split bundle](#split-bundles) are.

With `nsh-playground.wasm`, `player.runSource(tsx)` compiles TSX first and returns the compile error, or `null`; `player.compile(tsx)` returns `{ code }` or `{ error }`.

The container's size is the app's window (`windowSize()`); resizing the container resizes the app. `player.setDark(true)` switches the appearance at run time, which apps observe through `colorScheme()` and `dark:` classes.

## The browser as a platform

`Platform.OS` is `"web"`. What kind of device the browser is on decides how the app behaves, as `Platform.constants.interfaceIdiom`:

- `"desktop"`: a mouse (a fine pointer that hovers) and a container at least 600 points wide. `Platform.isDesktop` is `true`, `Platform.select` picks `desktop`, `desktop={{…}}` props apply and headers are as tall as on the desktop backends.
- `"pad"`: a touch screen whose short side is at least 600 points; `"phone"` otherwise. These are mobile: `Platform.select` picks `mobile`.

The idiom is decided when the app starts and stays the same while it runs, as on every platform; a narrow desktop window is still a desktop, laid out for its `windowSize()`. `web={{…}}` props, `Platform.select({ web })` and `web:` classes apply in browsers only; `ios={{…}}`, `native` and `ios:` do not apply there.

The page reports the rest of the environment, and keeps it current:

| Value | From the browser |
|---|---|
| Locale (`Intl`'s default) | `navigator.languages[0]` |
| `I18nManager.isRTL` | `<html dir>` when set, else the locale's script |
| `reduceMotion()` | `prefers-reduced-motion` |
| `fontScale()` | the root element's font size / 16 px (the browser's text size setting) |
| `PixelRatio.get()` | `devicePixelRatio` (it changes with zoom and screens) |
| `colorScheme()` | `prefers-color-scheme` |
| `safeArea()` | `env(safe-area-inset-*)` where it overlaps the container (`viewport-fit=cover` pages on phones) |
| `keyboard()` | how much of the container the on-screen keyboard covers (`visualViewport`) |

`Platform.Version` is `"0.0"`, and `screenReaderEnabled()` stays `false` (browsers do not tell). [`StatusBar`](https://nsh.dev/components/status-bar.md)'s `web={{ themeColor }}` sets the page's `<meta name="theme-color">`, the color browsers give their bars around the page.

## Networking

`fetch` (with streams, `AbortController` and `FormData`) and `<Image>` URLs go through the browser's own network stack, after NSH has checked the app's [capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md). Since the requests are the browser's, the browser's rules apply:

- **Relative URLs** resolve against the page's URL, as in the browser: a published app reaches its own API with `fetch("/api/items")`, and `<Image src="/photos/a.jpg" />` loads from its own server. (Native platforms have no page, so they need absolute URLs.)
- **CORS.** A request to another origin than the page's only succeeds if that server allows the page's origin (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`); otherwise `fetch` rejects with a network error. Only the response headers the server exposes are visible.
- **Cookies** (and HTTP authentication) are sent to the page's own origin only (`credentials: "same-origin"`), and headers browsers forbid (`Cookie`, `User-Agent`, `Host`, ...) are dropped.
- **Redirects** are followed by the browser. A redirected request that must not follow it fails: `redirect: "manual"` and `"error"`, and requests of an app whose capabilities restrict `network` (NSH checks every hop, and browsers do not reveal a redirect before following it).
- **Request bodies** that are a `ReadableStream` are collected first and sent in one piece; response bodies stream as they arrive.

## Split bundles

A web app does not need to download all of its code before the first screen shows. `nsh package --target web` publishes apps split, with each chunk as `chunks/<name>.<digest>.nshc` and the page mapping chunks to those files (a bundle run as bytecode loads its chunks as bytecode: `Screen.nshc` next to `Screen.js`). To split a bundle yourself, `nsh build --split` puts the modules that `import()` loads into chunks of their own, next to `bundle.js`:

```sh
nsh build --release --split -o site/app
# bundle.js        the app up to its first screen
# Screen.js        import("./Screen") and what only it uses
# detail.js        what two chunks share, when they do (made by the bundler)
```

The first `import("./Screen")` downloads `Screen.js` and the chunks it imports, all at once, then evaluates them; later imports of it resolve at once. The page says where the chunks are: by default next to the page (`chunkBase`), or one URL per chunk, for files renamed with a content digest so a CDN can cache them forever:

```js
player.run(code, {
  chunks: { "Screen.js": "/app.3f2a9c.js", "detail.js": "/app.81bb07.js" },
});
```

A chunk that cannot be downloaded rejects the `import()` with a `TypeError` naming it; the next `import()` tries again. Chunk names are fixed file names from the bundle: the app cannot make the page download anything else.

The [gallery](/gallery) loads each demo this way: `lazy` (in `examples/gallery/ui.tsx`) makes a component that starts the import the first time it renders, shows a placeholder until it resolves, then renders what it loaded. Its first load is the index and the demo shown first; a font a demo imports comes with that demo's chunk. Native builds hold every module, so there the import resolves at once:

```tsx
const Stocks = lazy(() => import("./demos/Stocks").then((m) => m.Stocks));
```

## Limits

The web runtime is for demos and documentation. It does not have:

- **Web views of other sites**: `WebView` is an `<iframe>`. Inline HTML (`source={{ html }}`) gets everything: `onMessage`, `postMessage`, `injectJavaScript`, the injected scripts and load events (it runs with an origin of its own, apart from the page). A page of another site only gets `postMessage` and load events with the URL it was given: browsers hide its navigations, title, history and errors from the page around it, and `userAgent` cannot be set.
- **Videos with sound that start on their own**: `Video` is a `<video>` with every prop and event, but browsers only start a video with sound after a user gesture (muted videos play).
- **Native components**: registered native components belong to the native apps that embed NSH; on the web their view stays empty, with a warning in the console.
- **Platform services**: reading the clipboard (`Clipboard.getString`, also `hasString`) needs a secure context (HTTPS) and may ask the user. Images do not report `onProgress`.
- **Text shaping details**: line breaking is a subset of UAX #14 (spaces, CJK, hyphens), with no hyphenation and no bidirectional reordering beyond the paragraph direction.

The player and the dev server run apps with development settings (no hardening); published apps run hardened. Both use the default [limits](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

## See also

- [Packaging](https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging.md): the other targets of `nsh package`.
- [Architecture](https://nsh.dev/docs/architecture.md): the engine, the core and the mount batches the web build reuses.
- [Testing and trace](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md): `nsh trace` runs the same engine headless, with an approximate text engine.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/web

# Platform-specific code

One NSH bundle runs on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and Linux (and in Mac Catalyst), and in browsers through the [web runtime](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md). Most of an app needs no platform checks at all: elements, styles, layout, components and modules behave the same everywhere, and the components of `nsh/ui/mobile` are drawn by NSH rather than borrowed from each platform, so they look the same everywhere. When something really is specific to one platform, NSH gives it a clear place, so platform code stays visible and contained:

| Where | For |
|---|---|
| [`ios={{…}}`, `android={{…}}`, `desktop={{…}}`, `web={{…}}`](#platform-only-props) | Props only one platform has. |
| [`nsh/ios`, `nsh/android`](#platform-modules) | APIs only one platform has. |
| [`Platform.OS`, `Platform.select`](#platformos-and-platformselect) | Choosing values or code per platform. |
| [`ios:` / `android:` / `web:` classes](#platform-variants-in-tailwind) | Styles per platform. |

## Platform-only props

Props that exist on one platform only are grouped in an object named after it. Each element accepts `ios`, `android`, `desktop` (macOS, Windows, Linux, and browsers in the desktop idiom) and `web` (browsers); on other platforms the object is ignored, and on its own platform only its keys are applied. A desktop browser applies both `desktop` and `web`.

```tsx
<View
  onPress={open}
  activeOpacity={0.6}
  android={{ ripple: { color: "rgba(0,0,0,0.12)" }, elevation: 4 }}
  style={{ padding: 16, borderRadius: 12, backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}
>
  <Text>Open</Text>
</View>

<Input
  placeholder="Code"
  ios={{ textContentType: "oneTimeCode" }}
/>

<Modal visible={open()} ios={{ presentationStyle: "pageSheet" }} android={{ statusBarTranslucent: true }}>
  …
</Modal>
```

The objects are reactive like any prop; a key removed from the object is cleared.

What exists today:

| Prop | On | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `android={{ ripple }}` | every element | The material ripple while pressed: `{ color?, borderless?, radius?, foreground? }`. |
| `android={{ elevation }}` | every element | The material shadow, in points, from the view's shape. |
| `android={{ accessibilityLiveRegion }}` | every element | `"none"`, `"polite"` or `"assertive"`: TalkBack announces the view's changes. |
| `android={{ statusBarTranslucent }}` | `Modal` | The modal's content reaches under the status bar. |
| `android={{ backgroundColor }}` | `StatusBar` | The status bar's color (before Android 15's edge-to-edge). |
| `ios={{ inputAccessoryViewID }}` | `<Input>` | The `InputAccessoryView` shown over the keyboard. |
| `ios={{ textContentType }}` | `<Input>` | iOS's names for autofill types. |
| `ios={{ headerLargeTitle }}`, `ios={{ headerBackTitle }}` | `Screen` | A large title; the back button's label. |
| `ios={{ presentationStyle }}`, `ios={{ supportedOrientations }}` | `Modal` | `"pageSheet"` / `"formSheet"` sheets; allowed orientations. |
| `ios={{ allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures }}` | `WebView` | Swipe back and forward in the page history. |
| `desktop={{ headerLargeTitle }}`, `desktop={{ headerBackTitle }}` | `Screen` | A large title; the back button's label. |
| `desktop={{ presentationStyle }}` | `Modal` | `"pageSheet"` / `"formSheet"`: a card centered in the window. |
| `web={{ presentationStyle }}` | `Modal` | `"pageSheet"` / `"formSheet"` in every browser: a centered card in desktop and tablet browsers, a sheet from just below the top in phone browsers. |
| `desktop={{ allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures }}` | `WebView` | macOS: two-finger trackpad swipes go back and forward in the page history; Windows: touchscreen swipes; Linux: touchpad swipes. |
| `desktop={{ windowDrag }}` | every element | Pressing it drags the window, as the system's title bar would (see [nsh/desktop](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-desktop.md#a-title-bar-of-your-own)). |

`desktop={{…}}` is accepted everywhere; the props above are the desktop-only ones so far. `web={{…}}` is accepted everywhere too; `Modal`'s `presentationStyle` is its only element prop so far ([`StatusBar`](https://nsh.dev/components/status-bar.md) takes `web={{ themeColor }}`). The types (`IOSProps`, `AndroidProps`, `DesktopProps` and their per-element forms) tell your editor what each element takes.

Cross-platform props whose effect differs slightly are not grouped: `Alert.alert`'s `cancelable` option exists on both (iOS alerts are simply never dismissed by a tap outside), and `pagingEnabled`, `refreshing`, `hitSlop` and the rest work on every platform.

## Platform modules

`nsh/ios` and `nsh/android` hold the APIs only one platform has, `nsh/desktop` those only desktops have. All can be imported on every platform, so one bundle runs everywhere: elsewhere their functions do nothing and their components render nothing. Each exports `isAvailable`, which is `true` only on its own platforms.

### nsh/android

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `Toast.show(message, duration?)` | A toast at the bottom of the screen; `"short"` (default) or `"long"`. |
| `BackHandler.addEventListener("hardwareBackPress", listener)` | Listens to the back button after modals, before stacks; return `true` when handled. Returns `{ remove() }`. |
| `BackHandler.exitApp()` | Leaves the app. |
| `setStatusBarBackgroundColor(color, animated?)` | The status bar's color under what `StatusBar` components set (before edge-to-edge, API 35). |
| `isAvailable` | `true` on Android. |

```tsx
import { cleanup } from "nsh";
import { BackHandler, Toast } from "nsh/android";
import { Platform } from "nsh/device";
import { Alert } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function saved() {
  if (Platform.OS === "android") Toast.show("Saved");
  else Alert.alert("Saved");
}

function Player() {
  // Back leaves full screen before it leaves the screen.
  const sub = BackHandler.addEventListener("hardwareBackPress", () => {
    if (!fullScreen()) return false;
    fullScreen.set(false);
    return true;
  });
  cleanup(() => sub.remove());
  // …
}
```

The back button is handled by the top modal first, then `BackHandler` listeners (most recent first), then the top navigation stack, and the app exits when nothing handled it. See [Navigation](https://nsh.dev/docs/navigation.md#the-android-back-button).

### nsh/ios

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `InputAccessoryView` | A bar over the keyboard of the inputs naming its `nativeID` in `ios={{ inputAccessoryViewID }}`. |
| `isAvailable` | `true` on iOS and Mac Catalyst. |

See [Forms and the keyboard](https://nsh.dev/docs/forms-and-keyboard.md#a-bar-over-the-keyboard-ios-inputaccessoryview).

### nsh/desktop

| Export | Description |
|---|---|
| `Window` | The window: `setTitle`, `setTitleBar("hidden")` for a title bar of the app's own, `minimize`, `toggleMaximize`, `toggleFullScreen`, `close`. |
| `titleBar` | The hidden title bar's height and the room the system's window controls take (reactive). |
| `Menu` | `setApplicationMenu(items)` (the menu bar, with shortcuts) and `popup(items, at?)` (context menus). |
| `isAvailable` | `true` on macOS, Windows and Linux. |

See [nsh/desktop](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-desktop.md).

### The status bar

The status bar is set with [`StatusBar`](https://nsh.dev/components/status-bar.md) from `nsh/ui/mobile`, on both platforms: `barStyle` (`"default"`, `"light-content"`, `"dark-content"`), `hidden` and `animated`, with Android's color in `android={{ backgroundColor }}`. The most recently mounted `StatusBar` wins, prop by prop, so a screen can render one for itself and the previous settings come back when it goes away. `StatusBar.setBarStyle()` and `StatusBar.setHidden()` set the base values imperatively.

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { StatusBar } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function PhotoViewer() {
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: "#000000" }}>
      <StatusBar barStyle="light-content" animated />
      …
    </View>
  );
}
```

In an app embedded in a native one, the host app's view controller decides the status bar on iOS. An app that declares `"capabilities"` in `nsh.json` needs `"statusBar": true` to change it.

## Platform.OS and Platform.select

`Platform` from `nsh/device` tells you where the app runs: `Platform.OS` is `"ios"`, `"android"`, `"macos"`, `"windows"`, `"linux"` or `"web"` (Mac Catalyst is `"ios"`, with `Platform.isMacCatalyst`; the [macOS backend](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md) is `"macos"`, the [Linux backend](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md) `"linux"` and the [Windows backend](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md) `"windows"`, and their elements apply their `desktop` props; [browsers](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md) are `"web"`, and apply `desktop` props too when the idiom is `"desktop"`). See [Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md#the-platform) for `Version`, `isPad` and the rest.

```tsx
import { Platform } from "nsh/device";

if (Platform.OS === "android") {
  // …
}
```

### Platform.select

`Platform.select(spec)` returns the value for this platform. It looks for the OS's own key, then `mobile` (iOS, Android, phone and tablet browsers) or `desktop` (macOS, Windows, Linux, desktop browsers), then `native` (every platform but the web, as in React Native), then `default`:

```tsx
const styles = {
  card: {
    borderRadius: 12,
    backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
    ...Platform.select({
      ios: { shadowColor: "#000000", shadowOpacity: 0.12, shadowRadius: 8, shadowOffset: { width: 0, height: 2 } },
      android: { borderWidth: 1, borderColor: "#e5e7eb" },
    }),
  },
};

const hint = Platform.select({ ios: "Swipe down to close", android: "Press back to close", default: "Close" });
```

It returns `undefined` when nothing matches and there is no `default`.

### Rendering different components

Choose components the same way, at module level when the choice never changes:

```tsx
const Spinner = Platform.select({ ios: IosSpinner, default: MaterialSpinner })!;
```

or inline with [`<If>`](https://nsh.dev/elements/control-flow.md):

```tsx
<If when={Platform.OS === "ios"} else={<Text>Android has no input accessories.</Text>}>
  <InputAccessoryView nativeID="bar">…</InputAccessoryView>
</If>
```

## Platform variants in Tailwind

The `ios:`, `android:` and `web:` variants apply classes on one platform:

```tsx
<View class="rounded-xl bg-white p-4 ios:shadow-md android:border android:border-zinc-200">…</View>
<Text class="text-base android:font-medium">Title</Text>
```

## Prefer shared behavior

Before reaching for a platform check, consider whether the difference matters to your users. Elements and styles already map to each platform's native behavior where it should differ (scroll physics, text rendering, keyboards, accessibility), while staying the same where users expect consistency (your app's own look). Platform checks are best kept for platform conventions users rely on: Android's back button and toasts, iOS's sheets and large titles, autofill names, ripple versus opacity feedback.

## Related

- [`nsh/ios`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-ios.md) and [`nsh/android`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-android.md): the references.
- [`nsh/device`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-device.md): `Platform`.
- [Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md): using views your host app provides on each platform.
- [Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md): every variant.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific

---

# Native Components

A native component is a view the **embedding app** registers by name: a map, a camera preview, a chart library, any
`UIView` on iOS, `android.view.View` on Android, `NSView` on macOS, `gtk::Widget` on Linux, or Direct2D drawing or a
child `HWND` on Windows. The NSH app declares it with `nativeComponent()` from
[`nsh/native`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-native.md) and uses it like any other component. NSH lays it out with the rest of the
app, sends it props, delivers its events to handlers and forwards commands from a `ref`.

Because NSH renders with the system's own views, a native component is just one more subview in the same hierarchy:
there is no layering problem, it clips, scrolls and receives touches like a `<View>`.

> [!NOTE]
> Native components exist only where an app embeds NSH ([iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md), [Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md),
> [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#embedding-in-a-mac-app), [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#embedding-in-a-gtk-app),
> [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#embedding-in-a-win32-app)).
> A packaged standalone app (`nsh package`) or a development host registers none, so the element renders an empty
> view there (the name is logged once as unknown).

## How it fits together

1. The host app registers a factory under a name, such as `"embed.badge"`, on its `NshAppView` (iOS) or `NshView`
   (Android). Each view has its own registry; there is nothing global.
2. The NSH app declares a component for that name with the props and events it uses.
3. When the element is created, NSH creates a container view (decorated, framed and hit-tested like any view), then
   asks the factory for a component and puts the component's view inside the container, filling it.
4. The component receives every prop right after it is made, then each prop again when it changes.
5. The component emits events and may report its own size; JS calls its commands through a `ref`.

## Declaring the component in JS

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { nativeComponent } from "nsh/native";
import { SafeAreaView } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

/** The host app's badge: a label it draws, sized to its text. */
const Badge = nativeComponent<{ text: string; color?: string }, { tap: { count: number } }>("embed.badge", {
  props: ["text", "color"],
  events: ["tap"],
});

const colors = ["#8250df", "#0969da", "#1a7f37", "#cf222e"];

function App() {
  const taps = signal(0);
  let badge: YNode | undefined;
  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={{ flex: 1, padding: 20, gap: 16, backgroundColor: "#f6f8fa" }}>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 22, fontWeight: "700" }}>Rendered by nsh</Text>
      <Badge
        ref={(node) => (badge = node)}
        text={taps() === 0 ? "Tap the native badge" : `Tapped ${taps()}×`}
        color={colors[taps() % colors.length]}
        onTap={(e) => {
          taps.set(e.count);
          badge?.command("pulse");
        }}
        style={{ alignSelf: "flex-start", borderRadius: 8, overflow: "hidden" }}
      />
      <Text>{`JS saw ${taps()} taps`}</Text>
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

This is `examples/embedded/App.tsx`, which both embedding samples in the repository run.

### `nativeComponent(name, spec)`

```ts
function nativeComponent<P extends object = {}, E extends object = {}>(
  name: string,
  spec: NativeComponentSpec<P, E>,
): (props: NativeComponentProps<P, E>) => YNode;
```

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `string` | The name the host app registered. Use a prefix of your own (`"maps.view"`, `"acme.chart"`) so names stay unique. |
| `spec.props` | `readonly (keyof P & string)[]` | The component's own props. Only the props listed here are sent to the native side. |
| `spec.events` | `readonly (keyof E & string)[]` | The events it emits. Optional. |

The type parameters describe the props (`P`) and the payload of each event (`E`). The returned component accepts:

- the component's own props `P`;
- a handler per event: event `tap` is handled by `onTap`, `regionChange` by `onRegionChange` (the first letter is
  capitalized and `on` prepended);
- everything a `<View>` takes except children: `style`, `class` / `classList` ([Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md)), layout,
  accessibility props, `testID`, `onLayout`, `ref`. These belong to the container NSH draws, not to the component.

A native component is a leaf: it takes no children.

## Props

Each own prop is sent as JSON, so its value can be any JSON value: strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, arrays and
plain objects. Props are reactive like any other: when `text={label()}` reads a signal, the new value is sent when the
signal changes, and only then.

| What happens in JS | What the component receives |
|---|---|
| The element is created | Every own prop that is set, right after the component is made |
| A prop's value changes | That prop with its new value |
| A prop becomes `undefined` | That prop with no value (`nil` in Swift, `null` in Java) |

Values that are not JSON (functions, class instances, `NativeValue`s) cannot cross; keep the interface to data.

## Events

The component emits an event by name with an optional JSON payload. NSH delivers it to the engine thread and calls the
matching handler with the payload:

```tsx
const MapView = nativeComponent<
  { latitude: number; longitude: number; zoom?: number },
  { regionChange: { latitude: number; longitude: number }; markerPress: { id: string } }
>("acme.map", {
  props: ["latitude", "longitude", "zoom"],
  events: ["regionChange", "markerPress"],
});

<MapView
  latitude={52.52}
  longitude={13.405}
  onRegionChange={(region) => center.set(region)}
  onMarkerPress={({ id }) => open(id)}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
/>;
```

Events are asynchronous: the main thread never waits for JS. A component that must decide something on the spot (may
this gesture start, may this region change) has to decide it natively, from props it received earlier.

## Commands

Imperative calls (zoom to a point, start playback, pulse an animation) go through the element's `ref`:

```tsx
let map: YNode | undefined;

<MapView ref={(node) => (map = node)} latitude={52.52} longitude={13.405} style={{ flex: 1 }} />;

map?.command("zoomTo", { level: 3 });
```

`command(name, args?)` sends the name and the arguments (any JSON value) to the component's `command` method. Commands
are applied in order with the changes made before them, so a command issued right after a prop change sees the new prop.

## Sizing

The container is laid out like a `<View>`:

- Where the style gives a dimension (`width`, `height`, `flex: 1`, `alignSelf: "stretch"`, ...), that dimension wins.
- Where the style leaves a dimension open, the container takes the size the component reported with `setSize`, like an
  image takes its natural size. A component that never reports a size measures 0 along open dimensions.

Report the size in points (iOS) or dp (Android) whenever the content changes. The badge above measures its label each
time `text` changes and reports the label's size plus padding, so `alignSelf: "flex-start"` makes the badge exactly as
wide as its text.

## Registering on iOS (Swift)

Implement `NshComponent` and register a factory on the `NshAppView`:

```swift
import NativeShell
import UIKit

/// `embed.badge`: props `text` and `color`; emits `tap`; command `pulse`.
final class Badge: NshComponent {
    let view = UIView()
    private let label = UILabel()
    private let context: NshComponentContext
    private var taps = 0

    init(_ context: NshComponentContext) {
        self.context = context
        label.textColor = .white
        label.font = .boldSystemFont(ofSize: 17)
        label.textAlignment = .center
        label.frame = view.bounds
        label.autoresizingMask = [.flexibleWidth, .flexibleHeight]
        view.addSubview(label)
        view.addGestureRecognizer(UITapGestureRecognizer(target: self, action: #selector(tapped)))
    }

    func setProp(_ name: String, _ value: Any?) {
        switch name {
        case "text":
            label.text = value as? String
            let size = label.intrinsicContentSize
            context.setSize(CGSize(width: size.width + 32, height: size.height + 20))
        case "color":
            view.backgroundColor = (value as? String).flatMap(UIColor.init(hex:)) ?? .systemPurple
        default:
            break
        }
    }

    func command(_ name: String, _ args: Any?) {
        guard name == "pulse" else { return }
        view.alpha = 0.3
        UIView.animate(withDuration: 0.6) { self.view.alpha = 1 }
    }

    @objc private func tapped() {
        taps += 1
        context.emit("tap", ["count": taps])
    }
}

// Before loading the bundle:
app.register(component: "embed.badge") { context in Badge(context) }
```

(`UIColor(hex:)` is a small helper of the sample, not part of NativeShell.)

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `NshAppView.register(component:_:)` | Registers a factory `(NshComponentContext) -> NshComponent` under a name. It makes one component per element created from then on. Registering a name again replaces the factory. |
| `protocol NshComponent` | `var view: UIView` (fills the container), `setProp(_:_:)`, `command(_:_:)` (optional: the default ignores commands). Main-actor isolated. |
| `setProp(_ name: String, _ value: Any?)` | Values are Foundation JSON objects: `String`, `NSNumber`, `[Any]`, `[String: Any]`, `NSNull`; `nil` when the prop was removed. |
| `NshComponentContext.emit(_:_:)` | Emits an event; the data must be something `JSONSerialization` accepts (or `nil`). Thread-safe. |
| `NshComponentContext.setSize(_:)` | Reports the component's own size in points. Thread-safe. |

## Registering on Android (Java / Kotlin)

Implement `com.longbridge.nsh.NshComponent` and register a factory on the `NshView`:

```java
import com.longbridge.nsh.NshComponent;
import com.longbridge.nsh.NshComponentContext;

final class Badge implements NshComponent {
    private final TextView label;
    private final NshComponentContext context;
    private final float density;
    private int taps;

    Badge(Context app, NshComponentContext context) {
        this.context = context;
        density = app.getResources().getDisplayMetrics().density;
        label = new TextView(app);
        label.setTextColor(Color.WHITE);
        label.setTextSize(17);
        label.setGravity(Gravity.CENTER);
        label.setOnClickListener(v -> context.emit("tap", Collections.singletonMap("count", ++taps)));
    }

    @Override
    public View view() {
        return label;
    }

    @Override
    public void setProp(String name, Object value) {
        if (name.equals("text")) {
            label.setText(value instanceof String ? (String) value : "");
            label.measure(0, 0);
            // Sizes are in dp.
            context.setSize(label.getMeasuredWidth() / density + 32, label.getMeasuredHeight() / density + 12);
        } else if (name.equals("color")) {
            label.setBackgroundColor(value instanceof String ? Color.parseColor((String) value) : 0xff8250df);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void command(String name, Object args) {
        if (!name.equals("pulse")) return;
        label.setAlpha(0.3f);
        label.animate().alpha(1).setDuration(600).start();
    }
}

// Before loading the bundle:
nsh.registerComponent("embed.badge", context -> new Badge(this, context));
```

The same in Kotlin:

```kotlin
nsh.registerComponent("embed.badge") { context -> Badge(this, context) }
```

| API | Description |
|---|---|
| `NshView.registerComponent(String name, NshComponent.Factory factory)` | Registers a factory under a name; it makes one component per element created from then on (UI thread). |
| `interface NshComponent` | `View view()`, `void setProp(String, Object)`, `default void command(String, Object)`, `default void destroy()` (the element is gone). Called on the UI thread. |
| `setProp` values | `String`, `Number`, `Boolean`, `java.util.List`, `java.util.Map`, or `null` when removed (or JSON `null`). |
| `NshComponentContext.emit(String event, Object data)` | Emits an event; `data` as the same Java types, or `null`. Any thread. |
| `NshComponentContext.setSize(float width, float height)` | Reports the component's own size in dp. Any thread. |

## Registering from Rust

Apps that embed the iOS runtime from Rust (`nsh-platform-ios`) register a `NativeComponent` on an `AppView`:

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use nsh_core::JsonValue;
use nsh_platform_ios::{AppView, ComponentContext, NativeComponent};
use objc2_ui_kit::UIView;

struct Badge {
    view: objc2::rc::Retained<UIView>,
    context: ComponentContext,
}

impl NativeComponent for Badge {
    fn view(&self) -> &UIView {
        &self.view
    }

    fn set_prop(&mut self, name: &str, value: Option<&JsonValue>) {
        // ... update the view, then report its size in points:
        self.context.set_size(120.0, 40.0);
    }

    fn command(&mut self, name: &str, args: &JsonValue) {
        // optional
    }
}

fn register(app: &AppView, make_view: impl Fn() -> objc2::rc::Retained<UIView> + 'static) {
    app.register_component(
        "embed.badge",
        Rc::new(move |context: ComponentContext| -> Box<dyn NativeComponent> {
            Box::new(Badge { view: make_view(), context })
        }),
    );
}
```

`ComponentContext::emit(name, data)` sends an event (`data` is a `serde_json::Value`) and `set_size(width, height)`
reports the size; both work from any thread.

## Registering on macOS (Rust)

On macOS the component is an `NSView`, registered on the [`AppView`](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#embedding-in-a-mac-app) of
`nsh-platform-macos`:

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use nsh_core::JsonValue;
use nsh_platform_macos::{
    objc2::{rc::Retained, MainThreadMarker},
    objc2_app_kit::{NSTextField, NSView},
    objc2_foundation::NSString,
    AppView, ComponentContext, NativeComponent,
};

struct Badge {
    label: Retained<NSTextField>,
    context: ComponentContext,
}

impl NativeComponent for Badge {
    fn view(&self) -> Retained<NSView> {
        Retained::into_super(Retained::into_super(self.label.clone()))
    }

    fn set_prop(&mut self, name: &str, value: Option<&JsonValue>) {
        if name == "text" {
            let text = value.and_then(|v| v.as_str()).unwrap_or("");
            self.label.setStringValue(&NSString::from_str(text));
            self.context.set_size(120.0, 40.0);
        }
    }

    fn command(&mut self, name: &str, args: &JsonValue) {
        // optional
    }
}

fn register(app: &AppView, mtm: MainThreadMarker) {
    app.register_component(
        "embed.badge",
        Rc::new(move |context: ComponentContext| -> Box<dyn NativeComponent> {
            Box::new(Badge { label: NSTextField::labelWithString(&NSString::new(), mtm), context })
        }),
    );
}
```

The view fills the container NSH lays out; `ComponentContext::emit` and `set_size` (points) work from any thread, as
on iOS. Register before `AppView::load`; a registry belongs to one `AppView` (and the views made from the same
`AppOptions`).

## Registering on Linux (Rust)

On Linux the component is a GTK widget, registered on the [`AppView`](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#embedding-in-a-gtk-app) of
`nsh-platform-linux`:

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use nsh_core::JsonValue;
use nsh_platform_linux::{gtk4 as gtk, AppView, ComponentContext, NativeComponent};
use gtk::prelude::*;

struct Badge {
    label: gtk::Label,
    context: ComponentContext,
}

impl NativeComponent for Badge {
    fn widget(&self) -> gtk::Widget {
        self.label.clone().upcast()
    }

    fn set_prop(&mut self, name: &str, value: Option<&JsonValue>) {
        if name == "text" {
            self.label.set_text(value.and_then(|v| v.as_str()).unwrap_or(""));
            self.context.set_size(120.0, 40.0);
        }
    }

    fn command(&mut self, name: &str, args: &JsonValue) {
        // optional
    }
}

fn register(app: &AppView) {
    app.register_component(
        "embed.badge",
        Rc::new(|context: ComponentContext| -> Box<dyn NativeComponent> {
            Box::new(Badge { label: gtk::Label::new(None), context })
        }),
    );
}
```

The widget fills the container NSH lays out; `ComponentContext::emit` and `set_size` (points) work from any thread,
as on iOS. Register before `AppView::load`. A registry belongs to one `AppView` (and the views made from the same
`AppOptions`, whose `components` field it is).

## Registering on Windows (Rust)

On Windows NSH draws every view itself with Direct2D, so a component either draws into its container with Direct2D
(`draw`) or brings a window of its own (`window`: a map control, a third-party view), registered on the
[`AppView`](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#embedding-in-a-win32-app) of `nsh-platform-windows`:

```rust
use std::rc::Rc;
use nsh_core::JsonValue;
use nsh_platform_windows::{
    windows::Win32::Graphics::Direct2D::{
        Common::{D2D1_COLOR_F, D2D_RECT_F},
        ID2D1DeviceContext,
    },
    AppView, ComponentContext, NativeComponent,
};

/// A box filled with the color of its `on` prop.
struct Badge {
    on: bool,
    context: ComponentContext,
}

impl NativeComponent for Badge {
    fn draw(&self, dc: &ID2D1DeviceContext, size: (f32, f32)) {
        let color = if self.on {
            D2D1_COLOR_F { r: 0.2, g: 0.7, b: 0.3, a: 1.0 }
        } else {
            D2D1_COLOR_F { r: 0.6, g: 0.6, b: 0.6, a: 1.0 }
        };
        // SAFETY: Direct2D calls on the context nsh draws with.
        unsafe {
            if let Ok(brush) = dc.CreateSolidColorBrush(&color, None) {
                let rect = D2D_RECT_F { left: 0.0, top: 0.0, right: size.0, bottom: size.1 };
                dc.FillRectangle(&rect, &brush);
            }
        }
    }

    fn set_prop(&mut self, name: &str, value: Option<&JsonValue>) {
        if name == "on" {
            self.on = value.and_then(|v| v.as_bool()).unwrap_or(false);
            self.context.set_size(120.0, 40.0);
            self.context.redraw();
        }
    }

    fn command(&mut self, name: &str, args: &JsonValue) {
        // optional
    }
}

fn register(app: &AppView) {
    app.register_component(
        "embed.badge",
        Rc::new(|context: ComponentContext| -> Box<dyn NativeComponent> {
            Box::new(Badge { on: false, context })
        }),
    );
}
```

`draw` runs with every frame of the window, in the view's coordinates (points), clipped to its bounds; call
`ComponentContext::redraw` when what it shows changes. A drawn component is covered, clipped and transformed like any
view, and its container gets the touches. A component that returns a child window from `window` is moved, clipped and
hidden with its view, receives its own input, and sits above everything NSH draws (NSH content over it is hidden, as
with web views). `ComponentContext::emit`, `set_size` (points) and `redraw` work from any thread. Register before
`AppView::load`; a registry belongs to one `AppView` (and the views made from the same `AppOptions`).

## Rules and limits

- **Register before loading.** Factories apply to elements created after the registration. Register every name before
  `loadBundle` / `loadAssetBundle` / `run`, so the first frame finds them.
- **The container owns decoration and touches.** Background, borders, corner radius, shadows, opacity, transforms and
  `overflow: "hidden"` apply to the container NSH draws. Your view fills it and receives the touches that land inside.
- **Capabilities do not apply.** A registered component is the host app's own code; the
  [capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md) an app declares do not restrict what it does. If you embed apps you
  do not trust, only register components that are safe for them to use.
- **Keep the interface to data.** Props, event payloads and command arguments cross as JSON text; send identifiers and
  small values, not large blobs, on every change.
- **One bundle, both platforms.** Register the same names with the same props and events on iOS and Android, so one
  bundle runs on both.

## See also

- [`nsh/native` reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-native.md)
- [Embedding in iOS apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md) and [in Android apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md)
- [Architecture](https://nsh.dev/docs/architecture.md): how props and events cross threads

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components

---

# Packaging

`nsh package` turns an app into something you can install: a `.app` for the iOS simulator, a signed `.ipa` for iOS
devices, a signed `.apk` for Android, an ad hoc signed `.app` for macOS, a directory and `.tar.gz` for Linux, a directory and `.zip` for Windows, or a static site for the web; `--target gpui` makes this machine's desktop package with the GPUI runner. It combines a release build of your app with the **prebuilt runtime** that
ships with NSH, so it needs no Rust toolchain, no Xcode project and no Gradle.

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target ios-simulator --run     # build, install and launch in the simulator
nsh package App.tsx --target android --run           # build, install and launch on a device or emulator
nsh package App.tsx --target macos --run             # build and launch on this Mac
nsh package App.tsx --target linux --run             # build and launch on this machine
nsh package App.tsx --target windows --run           # build and launch on this machine
nsh package App.tsx --target web --run               # build, serve on this machine and open in the browser
nsh package App.tsx --target ios --sign "Apple Development: Jane Doe (ABCDE12345)" --profile Dev.mobileprovision
```

The app is built in release mode (minified, compiled to QuickJS bytecode) exactly as `nsh build --release` would build
it. Output goes to `out/` unless you pass `--out`.

> [!NOTE]
> To put NSH *inside* an existing native app instead, see [Platforms](https://nsh.dev/docs/platforms.md#embed-in-a-native-app). To ship updates that apps download and verify, see
> [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md).

## App metadata: `nsh.json`

`nsh package` reads `nsh.json` next to the entry file. `nsh init` writes one:

```json
{
  "name": "Gallery",
  "id": "com.example.gallery",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "build": 1,
  "icon": "icon.png"
}
```

| Key | Type | Default | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | the entry's directory name | The display name under the icon (`CFBundleDisplayName`, Android `android:label`) and the output file name. |
| `id` | string | `com.example.<name>` | The bundle identifier / Android package name. |
| `version` | string | `"1.0.0"` | The user-visible version (`CFBundleShortVersionString`, `versionName`). |
| `build` | number | `1` | The build number (`CFBundleVersion`, `versionCode`). Raise it for every release you upload. |
| `icon` | string | none | A square PNG, ideally 1024×1024, relative to `nsh.json`. |

`nsh.json` may also hold `tailwind` (see [Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md)) and `capabilities` (see
[Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)); those are read by the bundler. Unknown keys are an error.

Every key can be overridden on the command line, which is handy in CI:

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target android --app-version 1.4.0 --build 42
```

## Options

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--target <ios \| ios-simulator \| android \| macos \| linux \| windows \| gpui \| web>` | What to build for (required). |
| `-o, --out <dir>` | Output directory. Default `out`. |
| `--name <name>` | Display name. |
| `--id <id>` | Bundle identifier, such as `com.example.app`. |
| `--app-version <version>` | Version, such as `1.2.0`. |
| `--build <n>` | Build number. |
| `--icon <png>` | App icon: a square PNG, ideally 1024×1024. |
| `--sign <identity>` | iOS: the code signing identity for devices. |
| `--profile <file>` | iOS: the provisioning profile for devices (`.mobileprovision`). |
| `--keystore <file>` | Android: a release keystore (default: the debug key). |
| `--key-alias <alias>` | Android: the key alias in the keystore. |
| `--keystore-password <password>` | Android: the keystore password; also read from `NSH_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD`. |
| `--run` | Install and launch afterwards: in the iOS simulator, or on the Android device or emulator `adb` sees; macOS, Linux, Windows and GPUI apps are launched on this machine; a web site is served on this machine and opened in the browser. Not for `--target ios`. |

## iOS simulator

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target ios-simulator --run
```

Writes `out/<Name>.app`, signed ad hoc (the simulator needs a signature but no identity). With `--run` it boots a
simulator if none is running, installs the app and launches it. Requires Xcode.

## iOS devices

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target ios \
  --sign "Apple Distribution: Example Inc (ABCDE12345)" \
  --profile AppStore.mobileprovision
```

Writes `out/<Name>.ipa`, ready for TestFlight, App Store upload tools or direct installation (depending on the
profile). What happens:

- The provisioning profile is copied into the app as `embedded.mobileprovision`.
- The entitlements come from the profile. NSH checks that the profile's application identifier covers the app's `id`
  (wildcard profiles such as `TEAMID.*` or `TEAMID.com.example.*` work) and stops with an error otherwise.
- The app is signed with `codesign` using the identity, then zipped into an `.ipa` (`Payload/<Name>.app`).

Find your identities with:

```sh
security find-identity -v -p codesigning
```

Without `--sign` and `--profile`, NSH writes an unsigned `out/<Name>.app` and tells you so; it cannot be installed on a
device as it is.

The app supports iPhone and iPad, portrait and landscape (portrait upside down on iPad only), and needs iOS 15.0 or
newer.

## Android

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target android --run
```

Writes `out/<Name>.apk`. The APK is assembled directly with the SDK's build tools (`aapt2`, `zipalign`, `apksigner`),
without Gradle. Requirements:

- The Android SDK, found through `ANDROID_HOME` (or `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT`, or `~/Library/Android/sdk`), with build tools
  and the `platforms;android-35` package. NSH tells you the `sdkmanager` command when one is missing.
- A JDK, to create the debug keystore the first time.

The app targets API 35 and needs API 28 (Android 9) or newer; it contains native code for `arm64-v8a` and `x86_64`.

### Signing for release

Without `--keystore`, the APK is signed with the standard debug key (`~/.android/debug.keystore`, created if missing),
and NSH warns that it is not for store releases. For a release, create a keystore once and pass it:

```sh
keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore release.jks -alias upload -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000

NSH_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD=… nsh package App.tsx --target android \
  --keystore release.jks --key-alias upload
```

Prefer the environment variable over `--keystore-password` so the password does not end up in your shell history.

## macOS

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target macos --run
```

Writes `out/<Name>.app`: the executable in `Contents/MacOS/`, and `nsh/bundle.nshc`, `nsh/assets/…` and `nsh/app.json`
(the window title and the app's appearance) in `Contents/Resources/`. The app is signed ad hoc and needs macOS 14 or
later; to distribute it, sign it with a Developer ID and notarize it. See [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#packaging).

## Linux

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target linux --run
```

Writes `out/<Name>/` (the executable `<Name>`, `nsh/bundle.nshc`, `nsh/assets/…`, `nsh/app.json` with the window title
and the application id, `<id>.desktop` and the icon `<id>.png`) and the same as `out/<Name>.tar.gz`. Package on
Linux: the runner is built for the machine it is built on. GTK 4 (4.14 or later), Pango and WebKitGTK 6.0 (for web
views) must be installed where the app runs. Installing it and the desktop entry: [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md#packaging).

## Windows

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target windows --run
```

Writes `out\<Name>\` (the executable `<Name>.exe` with the app's icon, `nsh\bundle.nshc`, `nsh\assets\…` and
`nsh\app.json` with the window title, the app id, the version and the appearance) and the same as `out\<Name>.zip`.
No tools are needed. Package on Windows: the runner is built for the machine it is built on, and only Windows can
embed the icon. The app runs from wherever its directory is copied; nothing is installed. See
[Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md#packaging).

## GPUI

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target gpui --run
```

Writes what `--target macos`, `--target windows` or `--target linux` writes on this machine, with GPUI's release
runner (`nsh-gpui-app`) as the executable instead of the native backend's. Package on the OS the app is for: the
runner is built for the machine it is built on. See [GPUI](https://nsh.dev/docs/gpui.md#packaging).

A Linux GPUI package links WebKitGTK 4.1 (web views) and GStreamer (videos) dynamically, so the machines it runs on need them installed, with GTK 3 and GStreamer's base and good plug-ins (Debian / Ubuntu: `libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0`, `libgstreamer1.0-0`, `libgstreamer-plugins-base1.0-0`, `gstreamer1.0-plugins-good`), besides a Vulkan driver and `libxkbcommon`.

## Web

```sh
nsh package App.tsx --target web --run
```

Writes `out/<Name>/`, a static site: `index.html`, `manifest.webmanifest`, and the runtime (`nsh.<digest>.js`,
`nsh.<digest>.wasm`), the app (`app.<digest>.js`, its JS source), its assets and icons, each named after its content
so hosts can cache them for good. Deploy the directory to any web server or CDN; `--run` serves it on
`http://127.0.0.1:4173/` for you to open. Cache headers and embedding: [Web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md#publish-an-app).

## Icons

Give one square PNG, ideally 1024×1024, in `nsh.json` (`"icon": "icon.png"`) or with `--icon`:

- **iOS:** compiled by Xcode's `actool` into the app's asset catalog (`Assets.car`), which derives every size iOS
  needs.
- **Android:** resized to 192×192 and used as the launcher icon (`mipmap-xxxhdpi`).
- **macOS:** converted by `sips` to `AppIcon.icns`.
- **Linux:** copied as `<id>.png`, which the `.desktop` file names as its `Icon`.
- **Windows:** resized to 16 to 64 pixels and 256 pixels and embedded in the executable as its icon, which the window,
  Explorer and the taskbar show.
- **Web:** resized to 32 pixels (the favicon), 180 (`apple-touch-icon`), 192 and 512 (the web app manifest).

Without an icon, the system shows its default.

## What is inside

The package holds your app's bytecode, its `capabilities.json` (when it declares capabilities) and the assets it
imports, next to the prebuilt runtime:

| Target | Runtime | Your app |
|---|---|---|
| iOS | the `nsh-ios-app` executable | `<Name>.app/nsh/bundle.nshc`, `nsh/assets/…` |
| Android | `classes.dex`, `lib/<abi>/libnsh.so` (stored uncompressed, 16 KB aligned) | `assets/nsh/bundle.nshc`, `assets/nsh/assets/…` |
| macOS | the `nsh-macos-app` executable, renamed `<Name>` | `<Name>.app/Contents/Resources/nsh/bundle.nshc`, `nsh/assets/…` |
| Linux | the `nsh-linux-app` executable, renamed `<Name>` | `<Name>/nsh/bundle.nshc`, `nsh/assets/…` |
| Windows | the `nsh-windows-app.exe` executable, renamed `<Name>.exe` | `<Name>\nsh\bundle.nshc`, `nsh\assets\…` |
| GPUI | the `nsh-gpui-app` executable, renamed as on this machine's OS | as on this machine's OS |
| Web | `nsh.<digest>.wasm`, `nsh.<digest>.js` | `<Name>/app.<digest>.js` (JS source), `assets/…`, `index.html` |

A packaged app registers no [native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md); for those, embed NSH in your own app.

## Finding the runtime

`nsh package` looks for the prebuilt runtime next to the CLI (`bin/../runtime` in the distribution). In a checkout of
NSH it uses `target/<triple>/<profile>` and `target/android/<profile>`, with the CLI's own profile (a debug CLI uses
debug runtimes): build them with `cargo build -p nsh-ios-app --target aarch64-apple-ios-sim` (or `aarch64-apple-ios`
for devices) and `cargo xtask android` (add `--release` for a release CLI); `nsh-macos-app` (on macOS), `nsh-linux-app` (on Linux), `nsh-windows-app` (on Windows) and `nsh-gpui-app` (on any of them) are built for this
machine in `target/<profile>` (`cargo build -p nsh-macos-app`, `cargo build -p nsh-linux-app`, `cargo build -p nsh-windows-app`, `cargo build --manifest-path crates/gpui/Cargo.toml --target-dir target -p nsh-gpui-app`); the web runtime is built with the `web` profile whatever the CLI's, into `target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/web/`. The environment variable `NSH_RUNTIME`
points the CLI at another directory laid out like the distribution's `runtime/` (`ios/iphoneos`,
`ios/iphonesimulator`, `android/release`, `macos`, `linux`, `windows`, `gpui`, `web`, ...).

## See also

- [CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md): every command
- [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md): updates apps download
- [Project structure](https://nsh.dev/docs/project-structure.md): `nsh.json` and the files of an app

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/packaging
