# Signed Packages

A signed package (`.nshpkg`) is how a host app runs NSH code it did not ship with: an update to its own NSH screens,
or a third-party mini app. `nsh publish` builds the app and signs it; the host app verifies the signature, the
certificate chain, revocations and the build number before anything runs.

![Signed packages: an offline root key certifies a release key for app ids; nsh publish signs the package with it; on the device, NshTrust trusts only the root and the newest revocation list, checks the certificate, revocations, signature, app id, file hashes and build number, then runs the module or refuses it.](https://nsh.dev/diagrams/signed-packages-light.svg)

> [!NOTE]
> NSH verifies and runs packages; it does not deliver them. Where packages come from (your update server, a CDN, a
> store of mini apps) and when the app downloads them is up to the host app.

## Why packages are signed

The JS a host app runs can reach everything the app [grants](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md), so it must come from
someone the app trusts. There is a second reason: NSH ships apps as QuickJS bytecode, which loads faster than source,
but QuickJS does not validate bytecode, and crafted bytecode can corrupt memory. So NSH loads bytecode only from the
app's own (system-signed) resources, from the dev server the developer connected to, and from verified packages.
Anything else must be JS source.

## Keys: two levels

- A **root key** stays offline. Host apps trust its public key; they can trust several roots, which is how a root is
  rotated.
- A root **certifies release keys**: a certificate names the release key, the app ids it may sign for and a time
  window.
- **Packages are signed by a release key** and carry its certificate. Release keys can therefore be rotated (or
  revoked) without updating the host apps, which only know the root.

Every key has an id derived from its public key (the first 8 bytes of its SHA-256, in hex), printed by every command.

### Create the keys

```sh
nsh keygen keys/root
nsh keygen keys/release
```

```text
key 4e0b637f5e10f6a6: keys/root.secret (keep it secret), keys/root.pub
key 3428d7136788c9ee: keys/release.secret (keep it secret), keys/release.pub
```

Each key is two files: `<name>.secret` (readable by its owner only) and `<name>.pub`, both one line of base64. `nsh
keygen` never overwrites an existing key.

> [!CAUTION]
> Keep `root.secret` offline, for example on an encrypted drive in a safe. Whoever has it can certify keys that every
> host app trusting the root accepts. Release keys belong on the build machine or in CI secrets.

### Certify a release key

```sh
nsh certify --root keys/root.secret --key keys/release.pub --apps 'com.example.*' -o keys/release.cert
```

```text
keys/release.cert: key 3428d7136788c9ee certified by root 4e0b637f5e10f6a6 for com.example.* until 365 days from now
```

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--root <file>` | The root's secret key. |
| `--key <file>` | The release key's public key. |
| `--apps <pattern>` | App ids it may sign for: `*` (any), `com.example.*` (ids under `com.example.`) or an exact id. Repeatable. |
| `--days <n>` | How long it may sign, from now. Default 365. |
| `-o, --out <file>` | The certificate to write. |

The certificate is a small JSON file; it is not secret.

## Publish a package

```sh
nsh publish App.tsx --key keys/release.secret --cert keys/release.cert
```

```text
out/com.example.counter-2.nshpkg: com.example.counter 1.0.0 (build 2), 0 assets, 12 KB, signed by 3428d7136788c9ee
```

`nsh publish` builds the app in release mode and signs it. The app id, name, version and build come from `nsh.json`
next to the entry, overridden by the flags:

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--key <file>` | The release key's secret key. |
| `--cert <file>` | Its certificate. |
| `-o, --out <file>` | The package to write. Default `out/<id>-<build>.nshpkg`. |
| `--id <id>` | App id, such as `com.example.app`. |
| `--app-version <version>` | Version, such as `1.2.0`. |
| `--build <n>` | Build number. Required (here or in `nsh.json`); it must grow with every release. |

`nsh publish` refuses to sign what a device would refuse: the certificate must cover the app id and the current time.

```text
error the release key's certificate does not cover this package: it does not cover app `com.example.counter` (only com.other.app)
```

### What a package holds

A package is one file: a JSON header (app id, name, version, build, the declared capabilities, the bytecode version,
the signing time, the release key's certificate and a table of files with their SHA-256), then the files, then the
release key's Ed25519 signature over everything before it. The files are:

- the app's JS source (always),
- its bytecode, used only when the device's runtime has the same bytecode version (otherwise the source runs, so a
  package keeps working on newer runtimes),
- its source map,
- the assets it imports (images, fonts).

The package's identity, used for revocation, is the SHA-256 of the whole file.

## Verify a package

`nsh verify` checks a package exactly as a host app trusting the given roots would:

```sh
nsh verify out/com.example.counter-2.nshpkg --root keys/root.pub
```

```text
valid: com.example.counter 1.0.0 (build 2), release key 3428d7136788c9ee, sha256 f40565358c13fafce369792e41125fea7f93fe87dd1bc24fd575dabc09b34fd4, 0 assets, bytecode for this runtime
```

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--root <file>` | A trusted root's public key. Repeatable. Without any, only the package's own signature is checked. |
| `--revocations <file>` | A revocation list to apply first. |

A device checks, in order:

1. the certificate's signature by a trusted root;
2. that the release key is not revoked;
3. the package's signature by the release key;
4. that the certificate covers the app id and the signing time;
5. the minimum runtime the package needs;
6. that the file table covers the data exactly and each file matches its hash;
7. that the package itself is not revoked;
8. that its build is not older than the highest build of that app accepted before (rollback protection).

A refused package raises an error that says which check failed; the app that was running keeps running.

## Revoke keys and packages

A root signs **revocation lists**: release keys and packages that must not load any more.

```sh
# The first list.
nsh revoke --root keys/root.secret --sequence 1 \
  --package f40565358c13fafce369792e41125fea7f93fe87dd1bc24fd575dabc09b34fd4 -o revocations.json

# Later: keep everything in the last list and add a release key (sequence becomes 2).
nsh revoke --root keys/root.secret --extend revocations.json --key 3428d7136788c9ee -o revocations-2.json
```

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--root <file>` | The root's secret key. |
| `--extend <file>` | Keep the entries of this list (the last one published). |
| `--sequence <n>` | The list's number, higher than any published before. With `--extend`, defaults to that list's plus one. |
| `--key <id>` | A release key id to revoke. Repeatable. |
| `--package <sha256>` | A package's SHA-256 (as `nsh verify` prints it) to revoke. Repeatable. |
| `-o, --out <file>` | The list to write. |

A trust store only accepts a list with a higher sequence number than the one it has, so an old list cannot be
replayed to un-revoke something. Publish the newest list where your apps fetch it, and apply it with
`updateRevocations` before opening packages.

## Rollback protection

When a host app accepts a package, its trust store records the build number for that app id and from then on refuses
older builds. An attacker who obtained an older, signed package with a known vulnerability cannot make the app run it.
The record persists in the store's state directory (`nsh-trust.json`), so it survives restarts.

## Loading packages in a host app

Verification hashes the whole package and extracts its assets (once per package, under the trust store's directory),
so it runs off the UI thread; running the result happens on it.

**iOS (Swift)**:

```swift
let trust = try NshTrust(stateDirectory: applicationSupport.appendingPathComponent("nsh"))
try trust.addRoot(rootPublicKey)                // the contents of root.pub
try trust.updateRevocations(latestListJSON)     // when you have one

let info = try await app.loadPackage(at: downloaded, trust: trust)   // verify off the main thread, then run
```

**Android (Java)**:

```java
NshTrust trust = new NshTrust(new File(getFilesDir(), "nsh"));
trust.addRoot(rootPublicKey);
trust.updateRevocations(latestListJson);

NshPackage pkg = trust.openPackage(downloaded);   // off the UI thread; throws NshPackage.RefusedException
runOnUiThread(() -> nsh.runPackage(pkg));
```

The package's declared [capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md) travel with it: a package can do only what it
declares, and only what the host app grants on top.

Full API: [Embedding in iOS apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md#signed-packages),
[Embedding in Android apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md#signed-packages).

## Trying a package in development

The development hosts that `nsh run` installs can run a package the way an embedding app would.

On iOS, the host executable takes `--package <file>` and one or more `--root <root.pub>`. After `nsh run` has
installed the host in the simulator (`--target ios`):

```sh
xcrun simctl launch booted com.longbridge.nsh.host \
  --package "$PWD/out/com.example.counter-2.nshpkg" --root "$PWD/keys/root.pub"
```

On Android, the development host (`DevActivity`, installed by `nsh run --target android`) takes the extras `package`
(a path on the device) and `root` (base64 public keys, comma-separated):

```sh
adb push out/com.example.counter-2.nshpkg /sdcard/Android/data/com.longbridge.nsh.host/files/app.nshpkg
adb shell am start -S -n com.longbridge.nsh.host/com.longbridge.nsh.DevActivity \
  --es package /sdcard/Android/data/com.longbridge.nsh.host/files/app.nshpkg \
  --es root "$(cat keys/root.pub)"
```

Their trust state lives in the temporary (iOS) or cache (Android) directory, so builds older than one they accepted are
refused there too.

## A release checklist

1. Keep the root key offline; certify a release key per team or per app family, for a year or less.
2. Raise `build` in `nsh.json` for every release; `nsh publish` refuses a package without one.
3. Run `nsh verify --root root.pub` on the package before uploading it.
4. Ship `root.pub` inside the host app; ship revocation lists separately, so you can revoke without an app update.
5. If a release key leaks, revoke it (`nsh revoke --extend … --key <id>`), certify a new one and publish again.

## See also

- [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md)
- [Embedding in iOS apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md), [Embedding in Android apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md)
- [CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages

---

# Sandbox and Capabilities

Every NSH app runs in its own QuickJS VM, and everything an app can do outside that VM goes through NSH's native
runtime. That makes it possible to run code you did not write, such as third-party mini apps or downloaded updates,
under rules the host app controls:

- **Limits** bound the memory, time and native resources one app can use.
- **Hardening** removes the ways to turn strings into code in release builds.
- **Capabilities** list what an app may reach: which hosts it may fetch from, which pages a web view may show, whether
  it may change the status bar. The app declares them; a host app may grant less.

A bundle holds only the app's code: the reactive graph, the renderer and every module the app imports are native. So
nothing in JS is trusted, and every limit and check is enforced in Rust; there is no JS code an app could patch to get
around them.

## Limits

Each VM has these limits:

| Limit | Default | When it is hit |
|---|---|---|
| JS heap | 1 GB for an app on its own on macOS, Windows and Linux (Mac Catalyst too); 512 MB on iOS and Android; 256 MB for an app embedded in another app (the embedder may set another) | The VM stops. |
| Interpreter stack | 4096 KB (also the maximum) | Deep recursion throws a `RangeError`, which the app can catch. |
| Time to evaluate the bundle | 10 s | The evaluation is cut off. |
| Time of any other call into JS | 2 s | The call is cut off; the app goes on. |
| Nodes kept | 200 000 | The VM stops. |
| Changes at once (queued operations) | 8 000 000 values | The VM stops. |
| Operations in one canvas drawing | 1 000 000 | The VM stops. |

**Time is budgeted per call, not per app.** A "call" is one thing the runtime asks JS to do: handle one event
(including the rendering it causes), bind one list row, run one timer, run one frame's `requestAnimationFrame`
callbacks, drain the microtask queue. A long-running app never accumulates time toward a limit; only a single call
that does not return in time is interrupted. Calls nested inside another share the outer call's budget.

An interrupted call ends with an exception that no `catch` can swallow, and the error is reported with the budget it
exceeded:

```text
the script was interrupted: a call into JS exceeded its budget of 2000 ms
```

The VM keeps running: the next event, timer or frame runs normally.

**Running out of memory or going over a quota stops the VM.** The error is reported once (to the host app's error
handler, and in development builds over the app), no JS runs after that, and the views stay as they were. The node
and operation quotas exist because native views and queued changes live in native memory, which the JS heap limit does
not cover: without them, an app could exhaust the device's memory through the UI.

> [!TIP]
> These limits are generous for normal apps. If you hit the 2 s call budget, the work is too long for one event
> anyway: it would freeze the app's updates for that long. Split it with `setTimeout`, or move it out of the event
> handler.

Host apps can change the limits per view: `NshAppView.limits` on [iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md#limits),
`NshView.setLimits` on [Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md#limits). They apply from the next load.

## Hardening

Release builds (everything not loaded from a dev server) are hardened when they load:

- `eval` is removed, and the `Function`, `AsyncFunction`, `GeneratorFunction` and `AsyncGeneratorFunction`
  constructors throw. NSH runs no code made from strings:

  ```text
  TypeError: the Function constructor is disabled: nsh runs no code from strings (development builds allow it)
  ```

- The prototypes all modules share (`Object`, `Array`, `Function`, `String`, `Number`, `Promise`, `Map`, typed arrays
  and the rest) are frozen, so one module (or one library) cannot change `Array.prototype` for everyone else.
  `Error.prototype` stays writable, so error subclasses can set `this.name`.

Freezing prototypes would normally break a common pattern, the "override mistake": assigning
`Sub.prototype.constructor = Sub` or `obj.toString = …` throws when the inherited property is frozen. NSH turns the
commonly overridden members (`constructor`, `toString`, `valueOf`, `toJSON`, ...) into accessors whose setter defines
the property on the object assigned to, so such code (and libraries like axios that use it) keeps working.

Bundles served by `nsh dev` / `nsh run` (with or without `--release`) are not hardened, so you can debug with `eval`. Test the release
behavior with `nsh trace` (which hardens) or a packaged build before shipping code that relies on dynamic code.

## Capabilities

An app declares what it may reach outside its VM in `nsh.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "Quotes",
  "id": "com.example.quotes",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "build": 3,
  "capabilities": {
    "network": {
      "hosts": ["api.example.com", "*.cdn.example.com"],
      "http": [{ "host": "quotes.example.com", "methods": ["GET"], "pathPrefix": "/v1/" }]
    },
    "webview": { "hosts": ["*.example.com"] },
    "statusBar": true,
    "clipboard": true
  }
}
```

**An app without `"capabilities"` may do everything**: a standalone app is its developer's own, and nothing is
restricted. **An app with `"capabilities"` may do only what it lists**: everything else is denied. Unknown keys are
build errors, so a typo is caught when you build instead of becoming a missing permission at runtime.

### `network`

Covers `fetch` (including every redirect), remote images (`<Image>`, `defaultSource`, canvas images,
`Image.getSize` / `Image.prefetch`) and video sources.

| Key | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `hosts` | `string[]` | Hosts the app may reach with any method and scheme (`http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`). |
| `http` | `object[]` | Finer grants, one per host. |
| `http[].host` | `string` | The host (required). |
| `http[].methods` | `string[]` | Allowed methods, such as `["GET", "HEAD"]`. Empty or missing: any. |
| `http[].schemes` | `string[]` | Allowed schemes. Empty or missing: any of `http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`. |
| `http[].pathPrefix` | `string` | The URL's path must start with it. |

Host patterns are `*` (any host), `*.example.com` (any subdomain of `example.com`, not `example.com` itself) or an
exact host name. Matching ignores case and the port. The host is taken after the last `@`, so
`https://api.example.com@evil.io/` is checked as `evil.io`.

`asset:` URIs (the app's own files) are always allowed; images and videos may also use `data:` URIs and relative
paths.

### `webview`

| Key | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `hosts` | `string[]` | Hosts a [web view](https://nsh.dev/docs/web-view-and-video.md) may show and navigate to (`http` and `https`). Without `webview`, the app may not show web pages at all. |

Top-level navigations inside the web view are checked too, by the platform's navigation delegate, before they load.
The page's own subresources (its scripts, images, XHRs) are the web content's business and are not checked.
`about:blank` and inline HTML (`source={{ html }}`) need only web views to be granted at all: `"webview": { "hosts": [] }`
allows them without allowing any remote page.

### `statusBar`

`"statusBar": true` lets the app change the status bar (the `StatusBar` component and its functions in
[`nsh/ui/mobile`](https://nsh.dev/components/status-bar.md)).

### `clipboard`

`"clipboard": true` lets the app read and write the system clipboard ([`nsh/clipboard`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-clipboard.md)). Copying from a selectable text's edit menu is the user's own act and needs no capability.

### What a refusal looks like

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| `fetch` | The promise rejects; the request never reaches the network. |
| Remote image | The image fails with `onError`. |
| Video source, web view source, status bar change | Nothing is shown or changed. |
| Clipboard | `setString` does nothing; `getString` resolves `""` and `hasString` `false`. |

Each refusal is logged once, saying which key to add:

```text
fetch GET https://evil.example.org/x is not granted: add `evil.example.org` to capabilities.network in nsh.json
```

Redirects are followed by NSH, not by the platform's HTTP stack, so every hop is checked against the capabilities. (A
streamed request body is not sent twice, so a `307` / `308` redirect of a streamed upload fails.)

### Where capabilities travel

The declaration goes with the app wherever it goes:

- `nsh build` and `nsh package` write it next to the bundle as `capabilities.json`;
- `nsh publish` puts it in the [signed package](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md) header, covered by the signature;
- `nsh dev` sends it with every build, so development enforces the same rules. Changing `capabilities` reloads the app
  instead of hot-patching it.

## Grants: what a host app allows

A host app that embeds NSH can grant **at most** some capabilities, in the same JSON form:

```swift
// iOS
try app.grantCapabilities(#"{ "network": { "hosts": ["api.example.com"] } }"#)
```

```java
// Android
nsh.setGrantedCapabilities("{ \"network\": { \"hosts\": [\"api.example.com\"] } }");
```

A request must be allowed by **both** the app's declaration and the host's grant. With the grant above, an app that
declares `"hosts": ["*"]` can still only reach `api.example.com`, and cannot show web pages or change the status bar.
Without a grant (`nil` / `null`, the default), what each app declares applies.

Grants apply from the next load. A typical setup for third-party mini apps: grant each one only its own API host, run
it from a [signed package](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md) whose declaration you reviewed, and keep the default limits or lower
them.

> [!WARNING]
> [Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md) the host app registers are the host's own code: capabilities do not
> apply to them. Register only components that are safe for every app the view may run.

## Summary

| Layer | Enforced by | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| Limits (heap, stack, time, nodes) | the runtime, per VM | defaults; host app per view |
| Hardening | the runtime, on load | always on outside development |
| Capabilities | the runtime (fetch, images, video, web views, status bar) | the app (`nsh.json`) and the host app (grant) |
| Code integrity | signature verification | `nsh publish`; the host app's trusted roots |

## See also

- [Signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md)
- [Networking](https://nsh.dev/docs/networking.md)
- [Embedding in iOS apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md), [Embedding in Android apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities

---

# JSX and components

NSH apps describe their UI with JSX, but there is no React and no virtual DOM. NSH's compiler turns each JSX element into direct calls of the native renderer, and a component is a plain function that runs once to build its part of the tree. What keeps the UI up to date afterwards is [reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md): expressions in JSX that read signals are followed natively, and only they run again.

## Elements

Every tag is PascalCase and names something in scope. The **host elements**, each backed by a native view, are components you import from NSH's modules; only `If` and `Each` are globals that need no import:

| Tag | Import from | Native view | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<View>` | `nsh` | `UIView` / `ViewGroup`: a box for layout, styling and touches | [View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view.md) |
| `<Text>` | `nsh` | A native text view; nested `<Text>` elements are spans | [Text](https://nsh.dev/elements/text.md) |
| `<Image>` | `nsh/image` | An image view (local assets and URLs) | [Image](https://nsh.dev/elements/image.md) |
| `<Scroll>` | `nsh` | `UIScrollView` / `ScrollView` | [Scroll](https://nsh.dev/elements/scroll.md) |
| `<Input>` | `nsh` | `UITextField` / `UITextView` / `EditText` | [Input](https://nsh.dev/elements/input.md) |
| `<List>` | `nsh/list` | A virtualized, recycling list | [List](https://nsh.dev/elements/list.md) |
| `<Canvas>`, `<WebView>`, `<Video>`, `<Modal>` | `nsh/canvas`, `nsh/webview`, `nsh/video`, `nsh/ui/mobile` | A drawing, a web page, a video player, a presented layer | [Elements](https://nsh.dev/elements.md) |
| `<If>`, `<Each>` | nothing: globals | Control flow, no view of its own | [Control flow](https://nsh.dev/elements/control-flow.md) |

```tsx
import { mount, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { Image } from "nsh/image";
```

Tags are PascalCase so that TypeScript checks each one against the binding it names: a lowercase tag is checked against one global type per name, so a generic component such as `List` or `Each` could not infer its rows' type from `each` / `of`, and an app's own components would not be typed at all. The imports cost nothing at run time: the compiler recognizes the primitives through their imports (aliases too) and makes the native element in place, so `<View>` is a direct call of the renderer and the import is dropped from the bundle.

Props keep their camelCase names (`onPress`, `numberOfLines`, `backgroundColor`). Every element accepts `style`, `class` / `classList` ([Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md)), `ref`, touch handlers, accessibility props and `testID`; platform-only props go in `ios={{…}}` and `android={{…}}`, and only the current platform's object is sent:

```tsx
<View android={{ elevation: 4, ripple: { color: "#0001" } }} style={{ borderRadius: 12 }} />
```

A lowercase tag is a build error that says what to write:

```text
x lowercase tag <view>: tags are PascalCase components: write <View> and
| `import { View } from "nsh"`
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Text is only displayed inside `<Text>`. A string directly in a `<View>` creates no native view and is not shown.

## Components

A component is a function that takes a props object and returns JSX:

```tsx
function Badge(props: { label: string; color?: string }) {
  return (
    <View style={{ borderRadius: 999, paddingHorizontal: 10, paddingVertical: 4, backgroundColor: props.color ?? "#ddf4ff" }}>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 13, fontWeight: "600" }}>{props.label}</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

<Badge label={`${unread()} new`} color="#fff8c5" />
```

The function runs **once**, when the component is created, and does not track what it reads: there is no re-rendering. Code in its body (creating signals, starting effects, computing constants) runs one time. The JSX it returns stays connected to the props and signals it reads, so `Badge` above updates its text whenever `unread()` changes, without running `Badge` again.

A component may return an element, a string or number, an array, `null`, or a function returning any of these (which the renderer follows). The `Component<P>` type from `nsh` describes one:

```tsx
import type { Component, JSX } from "nsh";
import { Text, View } from "nsh";

const Row: Component<{ title: string; children?: JSX.Element }> = (props) => (
  <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", gap: 8 }}>
    <Text>{props.title}</Text>
    {props.children}
  </View>
);
```

### What runs again

The compiler decides for each expression in JSX whether it can change. An expression changes when it **calls a function or reads a property** (outside nested functions); everything else is set once:

```tsx
<Text>{count()}</Text>              // follows count
<Text>{props.title}</Text>          // follows the prop
<Text>{user.name}</Text>            // re-read when something it depends on changes
<Text>{label}</Text>                // a plain variable: set once
<View style={{ opacity: busy() ? 0.5 : 1 }} />   // the style object is rebuilt when busy changes
```

A changing prop or child is a small native effect that sets that one prop or replaces that one child. Style objects are diffed in Rust, so rebuilding a style only sends the properties that changed.

Event handlers are set once when they are a function or a name (`onPress={() => …}`, `onPress={save}`), and followed otherwise (`onPress={props.onPress}` follows the prop).

### Props are getters

A prop given a changing expression is passed as a getter: reading `props.title` calls it, which is what lets the JSX that reads it follow it. Static props are plain values. This is why props must be read where they are used:

```tsx
// Wrong: reads the prop once, when the component runs.
function Title(props: { text: string }) {
  const { text } = props;
  return <Text>{text}</Text>;
}

// Right: reads it in JSX, which follows it.
function Title(props: { text: string }) {
  return <Text>{props.text}</Text>;
}
```

The same applies to default values: write `props.color ?? "#ddf4ff"` in the JSX rather than destructuring with a default. To compute something from props, use a function or [`computed`](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md#computed):

```tsx
function Price(props: { cents: number }) {
  const formatted = () => `$${(props.cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
  return <Text>{formatted()}</Text>;
}
```

### Children

What you put between a component's tags arrives as `props.children`, a getter that builds those elements when read:

```tsx
function Card(props: { title: string; children?: JSX.Element }) {
  return (
    <View style={{ padding: 14, borderRadius: 12, backgroundColor: "#ffffff", gap: 8 }}>
      <Text style={{ fontWeight: "600" }}>{props.title}</Text>
      {props.children}
    </View>
  );
}

<Card title="Account">
  <Text>Signed in as {user().name}</Text>
</Card>
```

Each read of `props.children` builds the children again (new native views). Read it once, in the place where the children go. Children can also be a function, a render callback the component calls with arguments:

```tsx
function Repeat(props: { times: number; children: (i: number) => JSX.Element }) {
  return <View>{Array.from({ length: props.times }, (_, i) => props.children(i))}</View>;
}

<Repeat times={3}>{(i) => <Text>Row {i}</Text>}</Repeat>
```

Fragments (`<>…</>`) group elements without a view.

## Control flow

`<If>` and `<Each>` are built-in control flow. They render no view of their own.

```tsx
<If when={user()} else={<Text>Signed out</Text>}>
  <Text>Hello, {user()!.name}</Text>
</If>

<Each of={todos()} key={(t) => t.id}>
  {(todo, index) => (
    <Text>
      {index() + 1}. {todo().title}
    </Text>
  )}
</Each>
```

- **`<If when else>`** renders its children while `when` is truthy, else the `else` element. It renders a branch again only when the condition's truthiness changes, not every time `when` is re-evaluated.
- **`<Each of key>`** renders its only child, a function, once per item. Rows are kept by `key(item)` (default: the item itself; objects by identity, primitives by value): when the array changes, kept rows are moved rather than rebuilt, and new rows are made only for new keys. The function receives **accessors**, `todo()` and `index()`, because a kept row's item and position can change. `key="index"` (or `key={(item, i) => i}`; the key function gets the index too) keeps rows by position instead: a list of strings that changes in place, such as text streamed in, keeps its rows and only their `item()` changes.

A ternary or `&&` in JSX also works (`{busy() ? <Spinner /> : <Content />}`), but it builds its branch again every time anything it reads changes. Prefer `<If>` when a branch is more than a few elements.

For long or infinite lists, use [`List`](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md): it creates views only for the rows on screen and recycles them. See [Control flow](https://nsh.dev/elements/control-flow.md) for the details.

## Refs

`ref` gives you the native node of a host element, a `YNode`, for imperative calls: `focus()`, `blur()`, `scrollTo()`, `scrollToIndex()`, `measure()` ([where a view is](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md#where-a-view-is-measure)), ... A variable is assigned, a function is called:

```tsx
import type { YNode } from "nsh";
import { Input, Scroll, Text, View } from "nsh";

function Search() {
  let input: YNode | undefined;
  return (
    <View>
      <Input ref={input} placeholder="Search" />
      <View onPress={() => input?.focus()}>
        <Text>Focus</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

<Scroll ref={(node) => (scroller = node)} />
```

The ref is set when the element is created, before the component returns, so it is available in [effects](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md#effect) and event handlers. Calls are sent to the view in order with the changes made before them. Components from `nsh/ui/mobile` accept `ref` too.

## Spreading props

Spread an object of props onto an element or a component with `{...props}`. Getters stay getters, so spread props keep following what they read. To take some props for yourself and pass the rest on, use `split`:

```tsx
import { Input, type InputProps, split, Text, View } from "nsh";

function Field(props: InputProps & { label: string }) {
  const [own, rest] = split(props, ["label"]);
  return (
    <View style={{ gap: 4 }}>
      <Text>{own.label}</Text>
      <Input style={{ borderWidth: 1, borderRadius: 8, padding: 8 }} {...rest} />
    </View>
  );
}

<Field label="Email" value={email()} onChangeText={(t) => email.set(t)} keyboardType="email-address" />
```

`split(props, keys)` returns `[picked, rest]`, both still reading through to the original props (destructuring `{ label, ...rest } = props` would read every prop once). Element props that come later in the JSX win over earlier ones.

`<If>` and `<Each>` take no spread props, and spread children (`{...items}`) are not supported: use `<Each>` or an array expression.

## Tags and names

A tag names a binding in scope, as usual: `<Badge />`, `<Theme.Provider>`, an imported `<Button>`. A tag that names nothing in scope is a build error, except `<If>` and `<Each>`, which are globals.

```tsx
import { Button } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

<Button title="Save" onPress={save} />
```

Your bindings win over the globals: a component named `Each` in scope makes `<Each>` that component. A primitive is recognized by its import, so `import { View as Box } from "nsh"` makes `<Box>` a view, and a component of your own named `Text` is just your component. The primitives are real components too: `const Tag = inline ? Text : View;` and then `<Tag>…</Tag>` works.

Components are typed by their own declarations, like any TypeScript function: the editor checks a component's props wherever it is used, with nothing to generate.

## Mounting and the root

`mount(App)` renders the root component; `mount(App, props)` passes it props. The root view fills the surface (the window, or the view an app embeds NSH in). Give the root `flex: 1` so it fills the screen, and a background color: the surface's own background depends on the platform.

```tsx
mount(() => (
  <View style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}>
    <App />
  </View>
));
```

## Related

- [Reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md): signals, effects, context.
- [Elements](https://nsh.dev/elements.md): every host element and its props.
- [Components](https://nsh.dev/components.md): the ready-made components of `nsh/ui/mobile`.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components

---

# Reactivity

NSH updates the UI with **signals**: values that know who reads them. When a signal changes, NSH runs again exactly the computations that read it (a text, a style, an effect) and nothing else. Components do not re-render. The model is Solid's, and the reactive graph itself is native: reading a signal is a call into Rust, and the scheduling, dependency tracking and cleanup all happen outside the interpreter.

Everything on this page is imported from `nsh`:

```tsx
import { batch, cleanup, computed, context, effect, signal, untracked } from "nsh";
```

## Signals

`signal(value)` makes a signal. Call it to read the value; `set` and `update` write it:

```tsx
const count = signal(0);

count();                     // 0, and tracks the read
count.set(5);
count.update((n) => n + 1);  // 6
```

A read inside a tracking scope (JSX, `computed`, `effect`) subscribes that scope to the signal. A write notifies the subscribers when the value changed, compared with `===` by default.

```tsx
function Counter() {
  const count = signal(0);
  return (
    <View onPress={() => count.update((n) => n + 1)}>
      <Text>Tapped {count()} times</Text>
    </View>
  );
}
```

Tapping updates the one text node that reads `count()`. `Counter` itself runs once.

`signal<T>()` without a value starts as `undefined` and is typed `Signal<T | undefined>`. The second argument sets when a write counts as a change:

```tsx
const position = signal({ x: 0, y: 0 }, { equals: (a, b) => a.x === b.x && a.y === b.y });
const tick = signal(0, { equals: false });   // every write notifies
```

### Objects and arrays

Signals compare with `===`, so a value mutated in place is not a change. Write a new object or array:

```tsx
const todos = signal<Todo[]>([]);

todos.update((list) => [...list, { id: 3, title: "New" }]);                 // notifies
todos.update((list) => list.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: true } : t)));

todos().push(item);    // does not notify anyone
todos.set(todos());    // still the same array: no change
```

`<Each>` keys rows by item, so replacing one item in a new array rebuilds only that row ([JSX and components](https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components.md#control-flow)).

## computed

`computed(fn)` derives a value from other signals. It runs `fn`, remembers the result, and runs it again when a signal it read changes. Reading it is like reading a signal:

```tsx
const price = signal(12);
const quantity = signal(2);
const total = computed(() => price() * quantity());

<Text>Total: {total()}</Text>
```

Use `computed` when a derived value is read in several places or is expensive: it runs once per change however many readers it has, and readers are notified only when its result changes (`===`, or the `equals` option). For a cheap value read once, a plain function is enough:

```tsx
const label = () => `${quantity()} items`;
<Text>{label()}</Text>
```

`fn` receives the previous value (`undefined` the first time), for values that accumulate:

```tsx
const max = computed((prev: number | undefined) => Math.max(prev ?? 0, speed()));
```

## effect

`effect(fn)` runs `fn` after the current rendering, and again whenever a signal it read changes. Effects are for side effects: logging, timers, network requests, imperative calls on [refs](https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components.md#refs).

```tsx
function Search(props: { query: string }) {
  const results = signal<string[]>([]);
  effect(() => {
    const q = props.query;          // tracked: runs again when the prop changes
    if (!q) return;
    fetch(`https://api.example.com/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`)
      .then((r) => r.json())
      .then((data) => results.set(data.items));
  });
  return <Each of={results()}>{(item) => <Text>{item()}</Text>}</Each>;
}
```

An effect tracks the reads made while it runs synchronously. Reads in a `.then` callback or after an `await` are not tracked.

Effects run after the elements created in the same pass exist, so refs are set:

```tsx
let input: YNode | undefined;
effect(() => {
  if (editing()) input?.focus();
});
```

> [!TIP]
> Do not use effects to keep one signal in sync with another (`effect(() => b.set(a() * 2))`). Use `computed`: it is never out of date and does not cause a second pass. An effect that writes a signal it also reads runs itself again and again until NSH stops it with an error.

## cleanup

`cleanup(fn)` registers `fn` to run before the current effect runs again, or when the component or effect it belongs to goes away:

```tsx
function Clock() {
  const now = signal(Date.now());
  const id = setInterval(() => now.set(Date.now()), 1000);
  cleanup(() => clearInterval(id));       // when Clock is removed
  return <Text>{new Date(now()).toLocaleTimeString()}</Text>;
}

effect(() => {
  if (!running()) return;
  const id = setInterval(tick, 100);
  cleanup(() => clearInterval(id));       // before the next run, or on removal
});
```

A component goes away when it is no longer rendered: its `<If>` branch is hidden, its `<Each>` row is removed, or its screen is popped. Everything it created (effects, computed values, cleanups, nested components) is disposed with it.

## batch

Each write notifies its subscribers right away. To make several writes count as one change, wrap them in `batch`: dependants run once, after the last write.

```tsx
const save = () =>
  batch(() => {
    firstName.set(form.first);
    lastName.set(form.last);
    dirty.set(false);
  });
```

Event handlers are not batched for you: two writes in an `onPress` run an effect that reads both signals twice. `batch` returns what its function returns.

## untracked

`untracked(fn)` runs `fn` without subscribing to what it reads. Use it in a tracking scope to read a value without depending on it:

```tsx
effect(() => {
  const q = query();                     // runs again when query changes
  const filters = untracked(activeFilters); // read, but not a reason to run again
  search(q, filters);
});
```

A component body is already untracked: reading a signal there reads it once.

## context

`context(defaultValue)` makes a context, a value a component provides to everything it renders, however deep. Call the context to read the nearest provided value (or the default), and render `<Ctx.Provider value>` to provide one:

```tsx
const Theme = context<"light" | "dark">("light");

function Label(props: { children: string }) {
  const theme = Theme();
  return <Text style={{ color: theme === "dark" ? "#ffffff" : "#1f2328" }}>{props.children}</Text>;
}

mount(() => (
  <Theme.Provider value="dark">
    <Label>Hello</Label>
  </Theme.Provider>
));
```

The provider reads `value` once, when it is created. To provide something that changes, provide a signal (or an object of signals) and read it in JSX:

```tsx
const Accent = context(signal("#0969da"));

function App() {
  const accent = signal("#0969da");
  return (
    <Accent.Provider value={accent}>
      <Swatch />
    </Accent.Provider>
  );
}

function Swatch() {
  const accent = Accent();
  return <View onPress={() => accent.set("#8250df")} style={{ width: 40, height: 40, backgroundColor: accent() }} />;
}
```

Read a context in a component body (or in code that runs while components are being created), not in an event handler or a timer, where there is no component to look it up from.

## What runs, and when

| You write | Runs | Runs again when |
|---|---|---|
| Component body | Once, when it is created | Never (hot reload aside) |
| `{expr}` or `prop={expr}` that calls or reads a property | Once, when the element is created | A signal it read changes; only that prop or child is updated |
| `computed(fn)` | When created | A signal it read changes |
| `effect(fn)` | After the elements of the current pass exist | A signal it read changes |
| `<If when>` | When created | The truthiness of `when` changes |
| `<Each of>` row | When its key first appears | Never; its `item()` / `index()` accessors change instead |

The environment is reactive the same way: `windowSize()`, `colorScheme()` and `fontScale()` from [`nsh/device`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-device.md) and `safeArea()` / `keyboard()` from `nsh/ui/mobile` are accessors, so JSX that reads them follows rotation, dark mode or the keyboard.

## Common mistakes

**Destructuring props.** `const { title } = props` reads `title` once. Read `props.title` where you use it, or split props with [`split`](https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components.md#spreading-props).

**Reading a signal in the component body and expecting updates.**

```tsx
function Bad() {
  const n = count();           // read once
  return <Text>{n}</Text>;     // never changes
}

function Good() {
  return <Text>{count()}</Text>;
}
```

**Mutating instead of setting.** `list().push(x)` changes the array but notifies nobody. Write a new array.

**Deriving state with effects.** `effect(() => total.set(price() * qty()))` works, but leaves `total` stale between the write and the effect, and costs a second pass. Use `computed`.

**Creating effects outside components.** Effects and computed values belong to the component that created them and are disposed with it. Created in an event handler or a timer callback, they have no owner and live forever. Create them in a component body and let them read the signals that change.

**Expecting `async` code to be tracked.** Only reads made synchronously while an effect or computed value runs are tracked. Read the signals first, then start the asynchronous work.

## Related

- [JSX and components](https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components.md): props as getters, `<If>`, `<Each>`.
- [`nsh` module reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh.md): every function's signature.
- [Animation](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md): native values that animate on the UI thread without signals.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity

---

# Styling

Every element takes a `style` prop: an object of camelCase properties, including CSS features such as box shadows, gradients, filters, outlines, transitions and grid. Styles are decoded in Rust and only the properties that changed are sent to the native view. You can also style with [Tailwind classes](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md); both resolve to the same native styles.

```tsx
<View
  style={{
    padding: 16,
    borderRadius: 12,
    backgroundColor: "#ffffff",
    borderWidth: 1,
    borderColor: "#d0d7de",
    boxShadow: "0 4px 12px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.12)",
  }}
>
  <Text style={{ fontSize: 17, fontWeight: "600", color: "#1f2328" }}>Card</Text>
</View>
```

This page covers how styles combine and the visual properties. Layout properties (flexbox, grid, sizes, positions) are on [Layout](https://nsh.dev/docs/layout.md), text properties on [Text](https://nsh.dev/docs/text.md), and every property with its type is listed in the [style reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/style-reference.md).

## The style prop

`style` takes an object, or an array of objects merged left to right. Falsy entries (`false`, `null`, `undefined`) are skipped, which makes conditional styles short:

```tsx
const styles = {
  button: { paddingHorizontal: 16, paddingVertical: 10, borderRadius: 10, backgroundColor: "#0969da" },
  disabled: { opacity: 0.4 },
  danger: { backgroundColor: "#cf222e" },
} as const;

<View style={[styles.button, props.danger && styles.danger, busy() && styles.disabled]} />
```

Define shared styles as constants outside components (with `as const`, so TypeScript keeps literal types such as `"row"`). There is no `StyleSheet.create`: a plain object is all it takes, and styles are parsed in Rust each time they are set, from objects nobody needs to register.

A style expression that reads signals is rebuilt when they change, and NSH sends only the properties whose values differ:

```tsx
<View style={{ backgroundColor: selected() ? "#ddf4ff" : "#ffffff", padding: 12 }} />
```

When an element has both, `style` wins over `class`: classes are applied first, then the inline style on top. A key set to `undefined` sets nothing (`backgroundColor: active ? accent : undefined` keeps the class color when inactive); `null` sets the default.

## Units and values

- **Numbers are points** (density-independent pixels): `width: 100` is 100pt, which is 200 or 300 physical pixels on a 2× or 3× screen.
- **Percentages** (`"50%"`) are relative to the parent, for sizes, positions, margins and paddings ([Layout](https://nsh.dev/docs/layout.md)).
- **Angles** are degrees as numbers or strings with a unit: `45`, `"45deg"`, `"0.5rad"`.
- **Durations** are milliseconds as numbers, or strings: `"150ms"`, `"0.2s"`.

## Defaults

NSH's defaults differ from the web's:

| | Default |
|---|---|
| `flexDirection` | `"column"` |
| `flexShrink` | `0` (children do not shrink unless asked) |
| `alignContent` | `"flex-start"` |
| `position` | `"relative"` |
| `minWidth` / `minHeight` | `0` |
| `backgroundColor` | transparent |
| Text | black, 14pt, weight 400 |
| `shadowOffset` / `shadowRadius` / `shadowOpacity` | `{ width: 0, height: -3 }` / `3` / `0` |

New views carry no style at all until you give them one, so unstyled wrappers cost nothing on the native side.

## Colors

Color properties accept CSS color strings:

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| Hex | `"#09f"`, `"#09fc"`, `"#0099ff"`, `"#0099ffcc"` |
| `rgb()` / `rgba()` | `"rgb(0, 153, 255)"`, `"rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)"`, `"rgb(0 0 0 / 10%)"` |
| `hsl()` / `hsla()` | `"hsl(210 100% 50%)"` |
| `oklch()` / `oklab()` | `"oklch(62.3% 0.214 259.8)"` |
| Named | `"white"`, `"black"`, `"transparent"`, `"rebeccapurple"`, ... |

For dark mode, read [`colorScheme()`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-device.md) from `nsh/device`, an accessor that follows the system appearance, or use Tailwind's `dark:` variant:

```tsx
import { Text, View } from "nsh";
import { colorScheme } from "nsh/device";

const palette = () =>
  colorScheme() === "dark"
    ? { background: "#0d1117", text: "#e6edf3" }
    : { background: "#ffffff", text: "#1f2328" };

<View style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: palette().background }}>
  <Text style={{ color: palette().text }}>Follows the system appearance</Text>
</View>
```

The default text color is black in both appearances: set colors explicitly in apps that support dark mode.

## Borders and corners

```tsx
<View
  style={{
    borderWidth: 1,
    borderColor: "#d0d7de",
    borderStyle: "dashed",          // "solid" | "dashed" | "dotted"
    borderRadius: 12,
    borderTopLeftRadius: 24,        // per corner, overrides borderRadius
    borderBottomWidth: 3,           // per side
    borderBottomColor: "#0969da",
  }}
/>
```

- **Widths and colors** per side: `borderTopWidth`, `borderRightWidth`, ..., `borderTopColor`, ...; and the direction-aware `borderStartWidth`, `borderEndWidth`, `borderStartColor`, `borderEndColor`.
- **Radii** per corner: `borderTopLeftRadius`, `borderTopRightRadius`, `borderBottomRightRadius`, `borderBottomLeftRadius`, and `borderTopStartRadius` / `borderTopEndRadius` / `borderBottomStartRadius` / `borderBottomEndRadius`, which follow the [layout direction](https://nsh.dev/docs/layout.md#right-to-left).
- **`borderCurve: "continuous"`** draws corners whose curvature eases into the edges, like iOS app icons, on both platforms. A pill (`borderRadius` of half the height) stays a pill.
- **`overflow: "hidden"`** clips children to the rounded shape.

Radii larger than half the side are clamped, so `borderRadius: 9999` makes a circle or a pill.

## Shadows

Three ways to cast a shadow:

```tsx
// The shadow* properties
<View style={{ shadowColor: "#000", shadowOpacity: 0.2, shadowRadius: 8, shadowOffset: { width: 0, height: 4 } }} />

// CSS box-shadow: several, comma separated, with spread and inset
<View style={{ boxShadow: "0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,0.08), 0 8px 24px rgba(0,0,0,0.12)" }} />
<View style={{ boxShadow: "inset 0 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.15)" }} />

// Android's material elevation (a prop, not a style)
<View android={{ elevation: 6 }} style={{ backgroundColor: "#ffffff", borderRadius: 12 }} />
```

`boxShadow` follows CSS: `offsetX offsetY blur spread color`, `inset` for inner shadows. Shadows follow the view's rounded shape.

> [!NOTE]
> On Android, shadows need a background: a view with a transparent background (a text without one, for example) casts no shadow. `elevation` takes its color from `shadowColor`.

## Gradients

`backgroundImage` takes CSS gradients, drawn over the background color. Several gradients are separated by commas.

```tsx
<View style={{ height: 120, borderRadius: 16, backgroundImage: "linear-gradient(135deg, #54aeff, #8250df)" }} />
<View style={{ backgroundImage: "radial-gradient(circle at top left, #fff8c5, #fd8c73)" }} />
<View style={{ backgroundImage: "conic-gradient(red, yellow, lime, aqua, blue, magenta, red)" }} />
```

`experimental_backgroundImage` is accepted too, as an alias of `backgroundImage`. Text elements do not draw gradients on iOS.

## Filters and blending

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| `filter` | CSS filters of the view and its content: `brightness()`, `contrast()`, `grayscale()`, `hue-rotate()`, `invert()`, `saturate()`, `sepia()`, `opacity()`, `blur()`, `drop-shadow()`; several separated by spaces |
| `backdropFilter` | Filters of what is behind the view: `"blur(10px)"` (frosted glass) |
| `mixBlendMode` | How the view blends with what is behind it: `"multiply"`, `"screen"`, `"overlay"`, ... |

```tsx
<Image src={photo} style={{ width: 120, height: 120, filter: "grayscale(1) contrast(1.2)" }} />
<View style={{ position: "absolute", bottom: 0, left: 0, right: 0, padding: 12, backgroundColor: "rgba(255,255,255,0.4)", backdropFilter: "blur(12px)" }} />
```

Platform support differs:

| | iOS | Android |
|---|---|---|
| `filter` on views | `opacity`, `brightness` up to 1 and `drop-shadow` only | All, from Android 12 (API 31); color filters only below |
| `filter` on images | Every color filter and `blur` | As views |
| `backdropFilter` | A system blur material, approximating the radius | From Android 12 (API 31) |
| `mixBlendMode` | Yes | From Android 10 (API 29) |

## Outlines, opacity and visibility

- `outlineWidth`, `outlineColor`, `outlineStyle`, `outlineOffset`: a line outside the border that takes no space (negative offsets draw inside).
- `opacity`: 0 to 1, applied to the view and its children.
- `visibility: "hidden"`: the view is not drawn but keeps its space. `display: "none"` removes it from layout.
- `zIndex`: the order among siblings, also the native stacking order (stable for equal values).
- `cursor`: the pointer shape over the view, for pointers and desktops.

## Transforms

`transform` is a list of steps applied right to left, like CSS:

```tsx
<View style={{ transform: [{ translateX: 20 }, { rotate: "-8deg" }, { scale: 0.9 }] }} />
<View style={{ transform: [{ perspective: 600 }, { rotateY: "35deg" }], backfaceVisibility: "hidden" }} />
<View style={{ transformOrigin: "top left", transform: [{ rotate: "30deg" }] }} />
```

Steps: `translateX`, `translateY`, `scale`, `scaleX`, `scaleY`, `rotate` (`rotateZ`), `rotateX`, `rotateY`, `skewX`, `skewY`, `perspective`. `transformOrigin` takes keywords, percentages and lengths (`"top left"`, `"50% 0"`, `[10, 20]`); the default is the center. Transforms do not affect layout: siblings are placed as if the view were untransformed.

Android has no skew transforms.

## Transitions

A view animates changes of its own style when you name what to animate. The animation runs natively; no JavaScript runs per frame.

```tsx
<View
  onPress={() => open.set(!open())}
  style={{
    width: 150,
    height: 72,
    borderRadius: open() ? 36 : 12,
    backgroundColor: open() ? "#8250df" : "#54aeff",
    transform: [{ translateX: open() ? 120 : 0 }],
    transitionProperty: "all",
    transitionDuration: 300,
    transitionTimingFunction: "ease-in-out",
  }}
/>
```

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| `transitionProperty` | What animates: `"all"`, or names separated by commas: colors (`"colors"`, `"backgroundColor"`, `"borderColor"`, ...), `"opacity"`, `"transform"`, `"boxShadow"`, `"borderRadius"` / `"borderWidth"` |
| `transitionDuration` | `300`, `"300ms"`, `"0.3s"` |
| `transitionDelay` | As the duration |
| `transitionTimingFunction` | `"linear"`, `"ease"`, `"ease-in"`, `"ease-out"`, `"ease-in-out"`, `"cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)"` |

Sizes and positions are layout, not style, and do not transition; animate layout changes with `LayoutAnimation` or drive values with native animations ([Animation](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md)).

### Keyframe animations

`animationName` runs one of Tailwind's built-in keyframe animations natively: `"spin"`, `"ping"`, `"pulse"` or `"bounce"`, with `animationDuration`, `animationDelay`, `animationTimingFunction` and `animationIterationCount` (a number or `"infinite"`):

```tsx
<View style={{ width: 24, height: 24, borderRadius: 4, backgroundColor: "#0969da", animationName: "spin", animationDuration: 1000, animationIterationCount: "infinite", animationTimingFunction: "linear" }} />
```

## Press feedback

Pressed states are handled natively, without a round trip to JavaScript:

| Prop | Effect while pressed |
|---|---|
| `activeOpacity={0.6}` | The view fades to this opacity |
| `underlayColor="#eaeef2"` | The background becomes this color and the children fade to `underlayOpacity` (default 0.85) |
| `android={{ ripple: { color: "#0002" } }}` | Android's material ripple |
| `class="active:bg-zinc-100 active:scale-95"` | Any style, through Tailwind's `active:` variant |

See [Touch and gestures](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md).

## Related

- [Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md): the same styles as classes, with variants for dark mode, pressed states and breakpoints.
- [Layout](https://nsh.dev/docs/layout.md) and [Text](https://nsh.dev/docs/text.md).
- [Style reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/style-reference.md): every style property and its type.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/styling

---

# Tailwind

Every element accepts Tailwind CSS classes in `class`, resolved natively against Tailwind 4's default theme:

```tsx
<View class="flex-row items-center gap-3 rounded-2xl bg-white p-4 shadow-lg active:scale-[0.98] dark:bg-zinc-800">
  <Text class="text-base font-semibold text-zinc-900 dark:text-white">Tailwind on native views</Text>
</View>
```

No CSS is generated and nothing runs in JavaScript: the string is passed to the core, which parses each distinct class string once (and caches it), turns it into style rules, and applies them. Variants that depend on state (pressed, dark mode, window width) are re-applied by the core when that state changes, and pressed and focused states are tracked natively, so `active:` feedback has no JavaScript round trip.

Classes and the [`style` prop](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md) produce the same native styles and can be combined; this page covers what is specific to classes. The [Tailwind reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/tailwind-reference.md) lists every supported utility.

## class and classList

```tsx
<View
  class="rounded-lg px-4 py-2 transition-colors"
  classList={{ "bg-indigo-600": selected(), "bg-zinc-200": !selected(), "opacity-50": busy() }}
/>
```

- **`class`** is a string of classes. It can be dynamic: ``class={`h-6 rounded bg-${color()}-500`}`` works, because classes are resolved at run time.
- **`classList`** maps classes to conditions: a class applies while its value is truthy. It is applied after `class`.

How conflicts resolve:

1. **Later classes win** over earlier ones in the same string: `"p-2 p-4"` is `p-4`. There is no need for `tailwind-merge`: a component can append the `class` its caller passes.
2. **Variant classes apply after plain ones**, ordered by Tailwind's variant order (`hover:` before `active:`, breakpoints ascending, `dark:` last), whatever their position in the string. As in CSS, `odd:bg-a last:bg-b` gives an odd last row `bg-a`, because Tailwind sorts `odd` after `last`.
3. **`style` wins over classes.**
4. `!` makes a class important: `!p-0`.

Components from `nsh/ui/mobile` accept `class` and `classList` too; your classes are merged after the component's own styles and win at equal rank.

## Variants

| Variant | Applies when |
|---|---|
| `active:` | The view is pressed |
| `hover:` | A pointer is over the view (iPad and Mac pointers) |
| `focus:`, `focus-visible:` | An input has focus |
| `focus-within:` | The view or a descendant has focus |
| `disabled:`, `enabled:` | The element's `disabled` prop is true / false |
| `group-active:`, `group-hover:`, `group-focus:`, `group-focus-within:`, `group-disabled:` | The nearest ancestor with the `group` class is in that state |
| `group-active/name:` ... | The same, for an ancestor marked `group/name` |
| `first:`, `last:`, `odd:`, `even:`, `only:` | The element's own position among its siblings. To color a row's label by the row's position, put `last:text-*` on the row: the label inherits it |
| `placeholder:` | Styles an input's placeholder (`placeholder:text-zinc-400`) |
| `dark:` | The system appearance is dark |
| `sm:`, `md:`, `lg:`, `xl:`, `2xl:` | The window is at least 640, 768, 1024, 1280, 1536 points wide |
| `max-sm:`, `max-md:`, ... | The window is narrower than the breakpoint |
| `min-[600px]:`, `max-[600px]:` | Arbitrary breakpoints |
| `portrait:`, `landscape:` | The window's orientation |
| `ios:`, `android:`, `web:` | The platform |
| `rtl:`, `ltr:` | The [layout direction](https://nsh.dev/docs/layout.md#right-to-left) |
| `motion-safe:`, `motion-reduce:` | The user's reduce motion setting |

Variants combine: `dark:active:bg-zinc-700`, `md:landscape:flex-row`.

```tsx
<View class="group flex-row items-center gap-3 rounded-xl bg-white p-3 active:bg-zinc-50">
  <Text class="flex-1 text-zinc-900">Settings</Text>
  <Text class="text-zinc-300 transition-transform group-active:translate-x-1">›</Text>
</View>
```

`disabled` on any element applies `disabled:` classes and removes its press handlers from what is mounted, so it shows no press feedback either:

```tsx
<View disabled={saving()} onPress={save} class="rounded-lg bg-emerald-500 px-4 py-2 active:bg-emerald-600 disabled:opacity-40">
  <Text class="font-medium text-white">Save</Text>
</View>
```

Breakpoints compare against the window (the surface NSH renders into), not the device: in an iPad split view or a resizable window, they follow the window's width.

## What differs from Tailwind on the web

- **Units are points.** `p-4` is 16 points (1 spacing step = 4pt, 1rem = 16pt). Arbitrary values in `px` are points too: `p-[13px]` is 13pt.
- **`flex` is a row**, as in CSS: `class="flex"` lays out its children in a row unless a direction class says otherwise (anywhere in the string: `flex-col flex` is a column). A view without `flex` or `inline-flex` keeps NSH's default column. `block` and `flow-root` use block layout; `inline` and `inline-block` lay out as views (there is no inline formatting context).
- **Text classes on views are inherited.** `text-*`, `font-*`, `leading-*`, `tracking-*` and the other text utilities on a view pass to the `<Text>` and `<Input>` elements inside it, as CSS inheritance does: `<View class="text-white">` makes its labels white.
- **`space-x-*` / `space-y-*` are gaps** (`gap-x` / `gap-y`).
- **State backgrounds show over gradients.** In CSS a gradient covers `background-color`, so `active:bg-*` on a `bg-linear-*` surface would never be seen; in NSH a background color from `active:`, `hover:`, `focus:` or `group-*:` replaces the gradient while that state holds (unless the state sets a gradient of its own, such as `active:from-*`). So do `underlayColor` and animated background colors.
- **Classes for settings that are props in NSH**: `line-clamp-*`, `truncate`, `whitespace-nowrap`, `pointer-events-*`, `object-*` (image resize mode), `select-text`, `caret-*` and `placeholder:text-*` work, and lose to the explicit props (`numberOfLines`, `pointerEvents`, `resizeMode`, ...) when both are set.
- **Not supported**: `peer-*` variants, pseudo-elements (`before:`, `after:`), arbitrary properties (`[mask-type:luminance]`). Web-only utilities that need nothing natively (`antialiased`, `will-change-*`, `touch-*`, `scroll-*`, `snap-*`, `overscroll-*`, `box-border`, ...) are accepted and ignored.

Everything else works as documented by Tailwind 4: the color palette, opacity modifiers (`bg-black/40`), arbitrary values (`bg-[#34c759]`, `w-[72px]`, `grid-cols-[1fr_2fr]`), fractions (`w-1/2`, `translate-x-1/2`), shadows and rings, gradients (`bg-linear-to-r`, `bg-radial`, `bg-conic` with `from-` / `via-` / `to-`), filters, `backdrop-blur-*`, `mix-blend-*`, transforms, `transition-*` and `duration-*`, `animate-spin` / `ping` / `pulse` / `bounce`, and grid. The platform limits of [filters and blending](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md#filters-and-blending) apply to classes too.

## Theme

Classes resolve against Tailwind 4's default theme. Extend it in `nsh.json` under `"tailwind"`; your entries are added to the defaults (or replace the default of the same name):

```json
{
  "tailwind": {
    "colors": {
      "brand": { "50": "#f5f3ff", "500": "#7c3aed", "600": "#6d28d9", "DEFAULT": "#7c3aed" },
      "ink": "#1f2328"
    },
    "radius": { "card": 14 },
    "fontFamily": { "display": "Pacifico" },
    "breakpoints": { "tablet": 600 }
  }
}
```

With this theme, `bg-brand-500`, `text-brand` (the `DEFAULT` shade), `border-ink`, `rounded-card`, `font-display` and `tablet:flex-row` are valid classes.

| Key | Values | Makes |
|---|---|---|
| `colors` | A CSS color, or an object of shades (`"DEFAULT"` for the bare name) | `bg-*`, `text-*`, `border-*`, `from-*`, `ring-*`, ... |
| `spacing` | Points per spacing step (default 4) | `p-*`, `m-*`, `gap-*`, `w-*`, ... |
| `rem` | Points per `rem` in arbitrary values (default 16) | |
| `breakpoints` | Points | `name:` variants |
| `container` | Points | `max-w-*` sizes |
| `fontSize` | Points, or `[size, lineHeight]` with the line height a multiple of the size | `text-*` |
| `fontWeight` | 1–1000 | `font-*` |
| `fontFamily` | A family name (a system family or an [imported font's](https://nsh.dev/docs/fonts.md) name) | `font-*` |
| `tracking` | Ems | `tracking-*` |
| `leading` | Multiples of the font size | `leading-*` |
| `radius` | Points | `rounded-*` |
| `shadow`, `insetShadow`, `dropShadow` | A CSS `box-shadow` | `shadow-*`, `inset-shadow-*`, `drop-shadow-*` |
| `blur` | Points | `blur-*`, `backdrop-blur-*` |
| `perspective` | Points | `perspective-*` |
| `aspect` | A ratio (`1.5`) | `aspect-*` |
| `ease` | `[x1, y1, x2, y2]` | `ease-*` |

Unknown keys and invalid values are build errors (`nsh.json: tailwind: unknown theme key 'colours'`). The theme is compiled into the bundle and applied before the first frame.

The theme only shapes your own classes. The components of `nsh/ui/mobile` take their colors from the component theme, `"theme"` in `nsh.json` ([Components](https://nsh.dev/components.md)).

## The class check

`nsh build`, `nsh dev`, `nsh run` and `nsh trace` check the static class names in your JSX (string literals in `class` and the keys of `classList`) with the same parser and theme the runtime uses, and warn about classes that do not exist:

```text
 warn nsh::build App.tsx:12:36: unknown class `bg-brand-550`
```

Warnings do not fail the build. Classes built at run time (``bg-${color()}-500``) cannot be checked when building; the runtime logs each unknown class once when it first sees it (`unknown classes: ...`).

## Classes or styles?

Both are resolved natively and cost about the same. Classes are shorter and give you variants (pressed states, dark mode, breakpoints) without code. Inline styles take values computed in JavaScript and accept [native animated values](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md) (`opacity: fade`, `transform: [{ translateX: x }]`). Most apps use classes for the static look and `style` for what is computed or animated.

## Related

- [Styling](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md): the style prop and the platform limits of effects.
- [Tailwind reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/tailwind-reference.md): every utility and variant.
- [Layout](https://nsh.dev/docs/layout.md): flexbox and grid, also available as classes.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind

---

# Layout

NSH lays out every element with [Taffy](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/taffy), a Rust implementation of CSS flexbox, grid and block layout, configured so that children stack vertically and do not shrink by default. Layout runs in the core, after each JavaScript turn, and only the frames that changed are sent to the native views. Text is measured by the platform's text engine on the same thread, so layout never waits for the main thread.

The layout properties below are style properties. Each has a [Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md) equivalent (`flex-row`, `gap-4`, `grid-cols-3`, `absolute inset-0`, ...).

## Flexbox

A view lays out its children with flexbox. The defaults differ from the web's:

| Property | NSH default | Web default |
|---|---|---|
| `flexDirection` | `"column"` | `row` |
| `flexShrink` | `0` | `1` |
| `alignContent` | `"flex-start"` | `stretch` |
| `alignItems` | `"stretch"` | `stretch` |
| `minWidth` / `minHeight` | `0` | `auto` |
| `position` | `"relative"` | `static` |

```tsx
<View style={{ flexDirection: "row", alignItems: "center", gap: 12, padding: 16 }}>
  <Image src={avatar} style={{ width: 40, height: 40, borderRadius: 20 }} />
  <View style={{ flex: 1, gap: 2 }}>
    <Text style={{ fontWeight: "600" }}>{props.name}</Text>
    <Text style={{ color: "#6e7781" }} numberOfLines={1}>{props.message}</Text>
  </View>
  <Text style={{ color: "#6e7781" }}>{props.time}</Text>
</View>
```

| Property | Values |
|---|---|
| `flexDirection` | `"column"`, `"row"`, `"column-reverse"`, `"row-reverse"` |
| `justifyContent` | Main axis: `"flex-start"`, `"flex-end"`, `"center"`, `"space-between"`, `"space-around"`, `"space-evenly"`, `"stretch"` |
| `alignItems` | Cross axis: `"stretch"`, `"flex-start"`, `"flex-end"`, `"center"`, `"baseline"` |
| `alignSelf` | One child's cross-axis alignment; `"auto"` follows the parent's `alignItems` |
| `alignContent` | Lines of a wrapping container |
| `flexWrap` | `"nowrap"`, `"wrap"`, `"wrap-reverse"` |
| `flex` | A single-number shorthand (below) |
| `flexGrow`, `flexShrink`, `flexBasis` | As in CSS |
| `gap`, `rowGap`, `columnGap` | Space between children |

`flex` takes one number and is not the CSS shorthand: a positive number `n` means grow by `n`, shrink by 1 and start from a basis of 0, so `flex: 1` siblings share the space equally whatever their content; `flex: 0` (the default) sizes the view to its content; a negative number shrinks it by that much down to its minimum.

```tsx
<View style={{ flexDirection: "row", gap: 8 }}>
  <View style={{ flex: 1, height: 36, backgroundColor: "#c8e1ff" }} />   {/* one share */}
  <View style={{ flex: 2, height: 36, backgroundColor: "#79b8ff" }} />   {/* two shares */}
  <View style={{ width: 36, height: 36, backgroundColor: "#0366d6" }} /> {/* fixed */}
</View>
```

Because minimum sizes default to 0, a `flex: 1` text in a row shrinks and wraps instead of pushing its siblings out.

> [!NOTE]
> `display: "flex"` in a style keeps the column default. Only Tailwind's `flex` class means a row, as in CSS ([Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md#what-differs-from-tailwind-on-the-web)).

## Sizes

| Property | Values |
|---|---|
| `width`, `height` | Points, a percentage of the parent (`"50%"`), or `"auto"` |
| `minWidth`, `maxWidth`, `minHeight`, `maxHeight` | Points or percentages |
| `aspectRatio` | Width divided by height: `1`, `16 / 9` |
| `padding`, `paddingHorizontal`, `paddingVertical`, `paddingTop`, ... | Points or percentages |
| `margin`, `marginHorizontal`, `marginVertical`, `marginTop`, ... | Points, percentages, or `"auto"` |

Without a size, a view is as big as its content (plus padding), stretched across its parent's cross axis by the default `alignItems: "stretch"`. Percentages are relative to the parent's size (for padding and margin, as in CSS, to its width).

`aspectRatio` sizes the other dimension from the one that is known:

```tsx
<View style={{ width: "100%", aspectRatio: 16 / 9, backgroundColor: "#000000" }} />
```

Images imported from files have a natural size and lay out at it when no size is given ([Images and assets](https://nsh.dev/docs/images-and-assets.md)). Remote images have no size until they load: give them one.

## Grid

`display: "grid"` lays out children in CSS grid tracks:

```tsx
<View style={{ display: "grid", gridTemplateColumns: "repeat(3, 1fr)", gap: 8 }}>
  <View style={{ gridColumn: "span 2", height: 60, backgroundColor: "#d8b9ff" }} />
  <View style={{ height: 60, backgroundColor: "#b083f0" }} />
  <View style={{ gridRow: "span 2", backgroundColor: "#8250df" }} />
  <View style={{ gridColumn: "2 / 4", height: 60, backgroundColor: "#6639ba" }} />
</View>
```

| Property | Values |
|---|---|
| `gridTemplateColumns`, `gridTemplateRows` | CSS track lists: `"repeat(3, 1fr)"`, `"200px 1fr"`, `minmax()`, `auto-fill` / `auto-fit`, line names |
| `gridAutoColumns`, `gridAutoRows` | Tracks of implicitly created columns and rows |
| `gridAutoFlow` | `"row"`, `"column"`, `"dense"`, `"row dense"`, `"column dense"` |
| `gridColumn`, `gridRow` | `"1 / 3"`, `"span 2"`, a line number or name |
| `gridColumnStart`, `gridColumnEnd`, `gridRowStart`, `gridRowEnd` | Line numbers or names |
| `justifyItems`, `justifySelf` | How items sit in their areas along the row |

`display: "block"` uses CSS block layout (children stacked, each as wide as the container), and `display: "none"` removes the view from layout.

## Absolute positioning

`position: "absolute"` takes a view out of the flow and places it by `top`, `right`, `bottom` and `left`, relative to its parent:

```tsx
<View style={{ height: 200 }}>
  <Image src={cover} style={{ position: "absolute", top: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0, left: 0 }} />
  <View style={{ position: "absolute", left: 12, right: 12, bottom: 12 }}>
    <Text style={{ color: "#ffffff", fontWeight: "700" }}>Caption</Text>
  </View>
</View>
```

Offsets accept points and percentages. A view with `left` and `right` (or `top` and `bottom`) and no size stretches between them. Later siblings are drawn above earlier ones; `zIndex` changes the order.

## Measuring

`onLayout` reports a view's frame, relative to its parent, after each layout in which it changed:

```tsx
const width = signal(0);

<View onLayout={(e) => width.set(e.width)}>
  <Text>{width()} points wide</Text>
</View>
```

The event is `{ x, y, width, height }` in points. For the whole window, read `windowSize()` from [`nsh/device`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-device.md), an accessor that follows rotation and window resizing:

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { windowSize } from "nsh/device";

<View style={{ flexDirection: windowSize().width > 600 ? "row" : "column" }} />
```

Tailwind's breakpoints (`sm:`, `md:`, ...) and `portrait:` / `landscape:` give the same result without code.

## Safe areas

The root view covers the whole screen, under the status bar and the home indicator. Wrap screens in [`SafeAreaView`](https://nsh.dev/components/safe-area-view.md) from `nsh/ui/mobile`, which pads its content by the safe area insets, or read the insets with `safeArea()` / `useSafeAreaInsets()` and apply them yourself. Screens of a [navigation stack](https://nsh.dev/docs/navigation.md) already sit below their header.

## Right to left

`I18nManager` from `nsh/device` controls the layout direction of the whole app. When the app lays out right to left (the system language is right-to-left, or `I18nManager.forceRTL(true)`):

- rows run from the right;
- `left` and `right` properties (margins, paddings, positions, borders, corners) swap sides;
- `start` and `end` properties always mean the leading and trailing side: `marginStart`, `marginEnd`, `paddingStart`, `paddingEnd`, `start`, `end`, `borderStartWidth`, `borderTopStartRadius`, ...;
- text with `textAlign: "auto"` aligns right, and native controls mirror.

```tsx
import { Text, View } from "nsh";
import { I18nManager } from "nsh/device";

<View style={{ flexDirection: "row", gap: 8 }}>
  <View style={{ marginStart: 16, borderTopStartRadius: 12, width: 44, height: 44, backgroundColor: "#54aeff" }} />
</View>

<View onPress={() => I18nManager.forceRTL(!I18nManager.isRTL)}>
  <Text>{I18nManager.isRTL ? "Right to left" : "Left to right"}</Text>
</View>
```

`I18nManager.isRTL` is reactive and changes apply at once, without a restart. The `direction` style (`"inherit"`, `"ltr"`, `"rtl"`) overrides the direction for one view and its children. On Android, apps that embed NSH need `android:supportsRtl="true"` in their manifest for native controls to mirror.

## Related

- [Styling](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md): how styles combine.
- [Scrolling](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md) and [Lists](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md): content larger than the screen.
- [Style reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/style-reference.md): every layout property and its type.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/layout
