# Text

All text is shown by `<Text>`. A `<Text>` element is one paragraph, typeset by the platform's text engine (CoreText on Apple platforms, `StaticLayout` on Android) on the engine thread when it is laid out, and only drawn on the main thread. Nested `<Text>` elements are spans of the same paragraph, not separate views.

```tsx
<Text style={{ fontSize: 16, lineHeight: 24, color: "#1f2328" }}>
  By continuing you agree to the{" "}
  <Text style={{ color: "#0969da", textDecorationLine: "underline" }} onPress={openTerms}>
    Terms of service
  </Text>
  .
</Text>
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Strings are only displayed inside `<Text>`. A string placed directly in a `<View>` is not shown.

The element itself is documented on [text](https://nsh.dev/elements/text.md); this page is about using it.

## Strings and whitespace

JSX text follows the same rules as in React: each line is trimmed, lines that are only whitespace are dropped, and the remaining lines are joined with a single space. Whitespace within one line is kept, so `{first} {last}` keeps its space. Use `{" "}` for a space at the start or end of a line, and `{"\n"}` for a line break:

```tsx
<Text>
  Hello,
  {name()}!{"\n"}
  Welcome back.
</Text>
```

Expressions in text follow what they read: `<Text>{count()} items</Text>` updates its first span when `count` changes.

## Spans and inheritance

A `<Text>` inside a `<Text>` is a span. It inherits the text style of its parent and overrides what it sets:

```tsx
<Text style={{ fontSize: 17, color: "#1f2328" }}>
  <Text style={{ fontWeight: "300" }}>Light </Text>
  <Text style={{ fontWeight: "700" }}>Bold </Text>
  <Text style={{ fontStyle: "italic" }}>Italic </Text>
  <Text style={{ letterSpacing: 4 }}>Spaced</Text>
</Text>
```

Text style classes also pass down from views, as in CSS: `<View class="text-white text-sm">` styles the `<Text>` and `<Input>` elements inside it.

### Links

A span with `onPress` (or `onLongPress`) is a link: a press on its characters goes to the span, a press elsewhere to the paragraph. Links in nested spans work too.

```tsx
<Text onPress={() => log("the sentence")}>
  Read the <Text style={{ color: "#0969da" }} onPress={() => open(termsUrl)}>terms</Text> first.
</Text>
```

### Views and images inside text

Any element other than `<Text>` inside a `<Text>` is laid out inline, on the baseline, and wraps with the words. It can take presses of its own:

```tsx
<Text style={{ fontSize: 16, lineHeight: 26 }}>
  Made with <Image src={logo} style={{ width: 18, height: 18 }} /> nsh. Status{" "}
  <View style={{ backgroundColor: "#1a7f37", borderRadius: 9, paddingHorizontal: 7, height: 18, justifyContent: "center" }}>
    <Text style={{ color: "#ffffff", fontSize: 11, fontWeight: "700" }}>LIVE</Text>
  </View>
</Text>
```

Inline elements cut off by `numberOfLines` or an ellipsis are hidden; copying the text leaves them out.

## Text styles

| Property | Values |
|---|---|
| `color` | A [color](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md#colors). Default black |
| `fontSize` | Points. Default 14 |
| `fontWeight` | `"normal"` (400), `"bold"` (700), or `100`–`900` (number or string) |
| `fontStyle` | `"normal"`, `"italic"` |
| `fontFamily` | A system family, a generic family, or an [imported font](https://nsh.dev/docs/fonts.md) |
| `lineHeight` | Points |
| `letterSpacing` | Points |
| `textAlign` | `"auto"`, `"left"`, `"center"`, `"right"`, `"justify"` |
| `textAlignVertical` | `"auto"`, `"top"`, `"center"`, `"bottom"`: where text shorter than its box sits |
| `textTransform` | `"none"`, `"uppercase"`, `"lowercase"`, `"capitalize"` |
| `textDecorationLine` | `"none"`, `"underline"`, `"line-through"`, `"underline line-through"` |
| `textDecorationColor`, `textDecorationStyle` | Color; `"solid"`, `"double"`, `"dotted"`, `"dashed"`, `"wavy"` |
| `textDecorationThickness`, `textUnderlineOffset` | Points, or `"auto"` (thickness also `"from-font"`) |
| `textShadowColor`, `textShadowOffset`, `textShadowRadius` | A shadow behind the glyphs |
| `fontVariant` | OpenType features: `["tabular-nums"]`, `"small-caps"`, `"oldstyle-nums"`, `"lining-nums"`, `"proportional-nums"` |
| `writingDirection` | `"auto"`, `"ltr"`, `"rtl"`: the base direction of the paragraph |

A `<Text>` is also a view: it takes backgrounds, borders, corners, padding and the other [view styles](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md).

```tsx
<Text style={{ fontSize: 18, fontVariant: ["tabular-nums"] }}>{price().toFixed(2)}</Text>
<Text style={{ textDecorationLine: "underline", textDecorationStyle: "wavy", textDecorationColor: "#cf222e" }}>Typo</Text>
<Text style={{ fontSize: 26, fontWeight: "800", color: "#ffffff", textShadowColor: "rgba(0,0,0,0.6)", textShadowOffset: { width: 2, height: 2 }, textShadowRadius: 4 }}>
  Shadow
</Text>
```

`tabular-nums` gives every digit the same width, which keeps counters and prices from jittering as they change.

## Truncation

```tsx
<Text numberOfLines={2}>{longDescription}</Text>
<Text numberOfLines={1} ellipsizeMode="middle">{filePath}</Text>
```

| Prop | Description |
|---|---|
| `numberOfLines` | The most lines shown; `0` (default) is unlimited |
| `ellipsizeMode` | Where text that does not fit is cut: `"tail"` (default), `"head"`, `"middle"`, `"clip"` |
| `adjustsFontSizeToFit` | Shrink the font until the text fits its lines and box |
| `minimumFontScale` | How far `adjustsFontSizeToFit` may shrink (0–1) |

```tsx
<Text numberOfLines={1} adjustsFontSizeToFit minimumFontScale={0.5} style={{ fontSize: 48, width: 200 }}>
  {total()}
</Text>
```

The Tailwind classes `truncate` and `line-clamp-*` do the same and lose to the props when both are set.

## System text size

Text follows the user's text size setting (Dynamic Type on iOS, font size on Android) by default.

| Prop | Description |
|---|---|
| `allowFontScaling` | `false` keeps the size fixed. Default `true` |
| `maxFontSizeMultiplier` | The largest scale applied, e.g. `1.5`. `0` is no limit |

`fontScale()` from [`nsh/device`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-device.md) is the current scale, an accessor that changes when the user changes the setting. `<Input>` takes `allowFontScaling` and `maxFontSizeMultiplier` too.

```tsx
<Text maxFontSizeMultiplier={1.3} style={{ fontSize: 13 }}>Tab label</Text>
```

Prefer limiting the scale over turning it off: large text is an accessibility setting people rely on.

## Selection

`selectable` lets the user select and copy the text, as in the system's own text views: a long press selects the word under the finger, the handles move the selection's ends, and the edit menu offers Copy and Select All (iOS adds Look Up, Translate and Share; Android Share). A selection stays inside one text block. `selectionColor` colors the highlight and the handles. The class `select-text` does the same as `selectable`.

In desktop browsers text is selectable by default, as on a web page, except inside interactive elements (views with press or touch handlers, such as buttons and pressable rows); `selectable={false}` or the class `select-none` keeps a text unselectable there. Phone and tablet browsers follow the native rule.

```tsx
<Text selectable selectionColor="#7c3aed">{orderNumber}</Text>
```

To copy from code (a Copy button), use [`nsh/clipboard`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-clipboard.md).

## onTextLayout

`onTextLayout` reports the laid-out lines after each layout, in the text's content box:

```tsx
<Text
  onTextLayout={(e) => {
    lines.set(e.lines.length);
    console.log(e.lines.map((l) => `${l.text} (${l.width.toFixed(0)}pt)`));
  }}
>
  {body()}
</Text>
```

Each line has `text`, `x`, `y`, `width`, `height`, `ascender`, `descender`, `capHeight` and `xHeight`. Use it to show a "Read more" button only when text was cut, or to align other content with a baseline.

## Accessibility

A `<Text>` is read by screen readers as its content. Give a role to text that acts as a heading (`accessibilityRole="header"`) and to links (`accessibilityRole="link"`). See [Accessibility](https://nsh.dev/docs/accessibility.md).

## Related

- [Fonts](https://nsh.dev/docs/fonts.md): custom fonts and weights.
- [text element](https://nsh.dev/elements/text.md): every prop.
- [Forms and keyboard](https://nsh.dev/docs/forms-and-keyboard.md): text input.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/text

# Images and assets

`<Image>` shows a bitmap: a file shipped with the app, or an image downloaded from a URL. Images are read and decoded off the main thread, downsampled to the size the view shows them at, and cached; the main thread only displays the decoded result.

```tsx
import { Image } from "nsh/image";
import logo from "./assets/logo@2x.png";

<Image src={logo} />
<Image src="https://picsum.photos/seed/nsh/600/400" style={{ width: "100%", height: 200, borderRadius: 12 }} />
```

The element's props are listed on [image](https://nsh.dev/elements/image.md).

## Images in the app

Import an image file like a module. The import gives an `ImageAsset`, `{ uri, width, height }`, and the bundler ships the file with the app:

```tsx
import logo from "./assets/logo@2x.png";

logo; // { uri: "asset:/assets/logo@2x.png", width: 64, height: 64 }
```

Supported files: `.png`, `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, `.gif`, `.webp`, `.heic`.

**Sizes are in points.** An `@2x` or `@3x` suffix in the file name says the file has 2 or 3 pixels per point, so `logo@2x.png` at 128×128 pixels is a 64×64 point asset. Without a suffix, one pixel is one point. There is no automatic choice between `logo@2x.png` and `logo@3x.png`: the file you import is the one that ships. Export at the highest density you need (`@3x` for the sharpest result on every phone); images are downsampled to the screen when decoded.

**Natural size.** An image from an asset lays out at its natural size when its style leaves the width or height open, so `<Image src={logo} />` needs no style. Set one dimension and `aspectRatio`, or both, to size it differently.

Assets are resolved relative to the importing module, and their `uri` is relative to the app's root (the entry's directory). `nsh build` copies them to `out/assets/`, `nsh package` puts them in the app, and during development the dev server serves them.

> [!TIP]
> `src` also accepts `asset:/path` strings, but only imported files are guaranteed to ship. A path that is never imported works with the dev server, which serves the whole app directory, and is missing from packaged apps. Import every image you use.

## Remote images

Give `src` a URL string or `{ uri }`:

```tsx
<Image src={user().avatarUrl} style={{ width: 48, height: 48, borderRadius: 24, backgroundColor: "#eaeef2" }} />
```

- **Give remote images a size.** Their size is unknown until they load, so without a width and height (or one of them and `aspectRatio`) they collapse to no height.
- **A background color** shows while the image loads, or use `defaultSource` (below).
- Downloads are shared: several views showing the same URL download it once, also when they decode it at different sizes. A download nobody waits for any more is cancelled.
- Decoded images are cached in memory (the cache is purged under memory pressure), keyed by URL, decode size and blur radius.
- When the app declares [capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md), the image's host must be allowed under `network`; a refused image fails with `onError`.

## Resize modes

`resizeMode` decides how an image fills a box of a different shape:

| Value | Result |
|---|---|
| `"cover"` (default) | Fills the box, keeping the aspect ratio, cropping what overflows |
| `"contain"` | Fits inside the box, keeping the aspect ratio, leaving empty bands |
| `"stretch"` | Fills the box exactly, distorting the image |
| `"center"` | Natural size, centered |

```tsx
<Image src={photo} resizeMode="contain" style={{ width: 140, height: 140, backgroundColor: "#eaeef2" }} />
```

The Tailwind classes `object-cover`, `object-contain`, ... do the same.

## Styling images

Images are views: they take `borderRadius` (also per corner), borders, shadows, `opacity` and transforms. Corners clip the image.

```tsx
<Image src={avatar} style={{ width: 90, height: 90, borderRadius: 45, borderWidth: 3, borderColor: "#8250df" }} />
```

- **`tintColor`** (a style) recolors the image's opaque pixels: use it for one-color icons that follow the theme.
- **`filter`** (`grayscale()`, `sepia()`, `blur()`, ...) applies to images on both platforms ([Filters](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md#filters-and-blending)).

```tsx
<Image src={icon} style={{ width: 24, height: 24, tintColor: active() ? "#0969da" : "#6e7781" }} />
```

## Placeholders, fading and blur

| Prop | Description |
|---|---|
| `defaultSource` | An image shown until `src` has loaded; best a local asset |
| `fadeDuration` | Milliseconds the loaded image fades in over. Default 0 on iOS, 300 on Android |
| `blurRadius` | Blurs the image by this radius in points, applied once when decoding |

```tsx
<Image
  src={`https://picsum.photos/seed/${id()}/300/300`}
  defaultSource={placeholder}
  fadeDuration={250}
  style={{ width: 100, height: 100, borderRadius: 12 }}
/>
<Image src={cover} blurRadius={16} style={{ position: "absolute", top: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0, left: 0 }} />
```

## Animated images

Animated GIF, WebP and APNG files play automatically, as assets or from URLs. They take the same styles and resize modes; a tinted animated image shows its first frame on iOS.

## Load events

| Event | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `onLoadStart` | | Loading starts |
| `onProgress` | `{ loaded, total }` in bytes (`total` 0 when unknown) | During a download, at most every 100 ms |
| `onLoad` | `{ width, height }` | The image is ready; the source's size in pixels |
| `onError` | `{ message }` | Loading or decoding failed |
| `onLoadEnd` | | After `onLoad` or `onError` |

```tsx
const status = signal("loading…");

<Image
  src={url}
  onLoad={(e) => status.set(`${e.width}×${e.height}`)}
  onError={(e) => status.set(e.message)}
  style={{ width: 90, height: 60 }}
/>
```

`onLoad` reports the source image's size, not the size it was decoded at.

## Image.getSize and Image.prefetch

The same `Image` that renders the element also works with images that are not on screen:

```tsx
import { Image } from "nsh/image";

const size = await Image.getSize("https://example.com/photo.jpg");   // { width, height } in pixels
const ok = await Image.prefetch("https://example.com/next.jpg");      // true once the bytes are in memory
```

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `Image.getSize(source)` | The image's size in pixels. Rejects when it cannot be loaded |
| `Image.prefetch(source)` | `true` once the image's bytes are loaded |

`source` is a URL string or `{ uri }`. Both keep the downloaded bytes for the views that show the image next, so an image prefetched before it is shown appears without a download.

A common use is sizing a remote image by its aspect ratio:

```tsx
function RemoteImage(props: { uri: string }) {
  const ratio = signal(1);
  Image.getSize(props.uri).then((s) => ratio.set(s.width / s.height));
  return <Image src={props.uri} style={{ width: "100%", aspectRatio: ratio() }} />;
}
```

## Other assets

| Import | Gives | Page |
|---|---|---|
| `.ttf`, `.otf` | The font's family name, registered before the first frame | [Fonts](https://nsh.dev/docs/fonts.md) |
| `.json` | The parsed value, bundled into the script | [Project structure](https://nsh.dev/docs/project-structure.md#modules) |

Images are also drawn on a canvas with `drawImage` ([Canvas](https://nsh.dev/docs/canvas.md)), and the gradients of `backgroundImage` replace many decorative images ([Styling](https://nsh.dev/docs/styling.md#gradients)).

## Related

- [image element](https://nsh.dev/elements/image.md): every prop.
- [`nsh/image`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-image.md): `Image`, with `getSize` and `prefetch`.
- [Lists](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md): long lists of images recycle their views.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/images-and-assets

# Fonts

Text uses the system font (San Francisco on iOS, Roboto on Android) unless a `fontFamily` says otherwise. A family can be a generic family, a font installed on the device, or a font file you ship with the app by importing it.

## System and generic families

| `fontFamily` | Font |
|---|---|
| (none), `"system-ui"`, `"sans-serif"`, `"ui-sans-serif"`, `"-apple-system"` | The system font |
| `"serif"`, `"ui-serif"` | The system serif (New York on iOS, Noto Serif on Android) |
| `"monospace"`, `"ui-monospace"` | The system monospace font (SF Mono on iOS) |
| `"ui-rounded"` | The rounded system font (SF Pro Rounded), iOS only |

The system font honors every `fontWeight` from 100 to 900. Tailwind's `font-sans`, `font-serif` and `font-mono` map to the first three rows.

A family installed on the device can be named directly (`"Georgia"`, `"Avenir Next"` on iOS). Installed fonts differ between platforms and versions, so ship the fonts your design depends on. On iOS, a family that does not exist falls back to the system font with a warning in the log (`font family 'X' is not available`).

## Shipping a font

Import a `.ttf` or `.otf` file. The import evaluates to the font's family name, and the font is registered before the first frame, so it is ready when text first renders:

```tsx
import { Text } from "nsh";
import Pacifico from "./fonts/Pacifico-Regular.ttf";

<Text style={{ fontFamily: Pacifico, fontSize: 30 }}>Custom fonts</Text>
```

`Pacifico` is the string `"Pacifico"`: the family name stored in the font file (its typographic family name, or else its family name), not the file name. Using the imported value instead of writing the name by hand keeps the two in sync and makes sure the file is bundled.

The bundler copies the file into the app like any other [asset](https://nsh.dev/docs/images-and-assets.md). Fonts are registered for the app's process only; they are not installed on the device.

> [!WARNING]
> An import whose value is never used is removed by TypeScript's import elision, and with it the font. If you only refer to a family by its name (for example in the Tailwind theme), import the file for its side effect: `import "./fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf";`.

## Weights and italics

A family usually comes as several files, one per weight and style. Import each one; they register under the same family name, and `fontWeight` and `fontStyle` choose the face:

```tsx
import { Text } from "nsh";
import Inter from "./fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf";
import "./fonts/Inter-Medium.ttf";
import "./fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf";
import "./fonts/Inter-Italic.ttf";

const body = { fontFamily: Inter, fontSize: 16 } as const;

<Text style={body}>
  Regular, <Text style={{ fontWeight: "500" }}>medium</Text>, <Text style={{ fontWeight: "bold" }}>bold</Text> and{" "}
  <Text style={{ fontStyle: "italic" }}>italic</Text>.
</Text>
```

When no registered face has the exact weight asked for, the nearest one is used. The platforms differ when a face is missing:

| | iOS | Android |
|---|---|---|
| Weight without a face | The nearest registered face | The nearest face, with Android's synthetic bold where it applies |
| Italic without an italic face | The upright face (no slanting) | A slanted version of the upright face |

Ship the faces you use to get the same result on both.

## Fonts in Tailwind classes

Name your families in the Tailwind theme in `nsh.json` to use them as `font-*` classes:

```json
{
  "tailwind": {
    "fontFamily": { "display": "Pacifico", "body": "Inter" }
  }
}
```

```tsx
import { Text } from "nsh";
import "./fonts/Pacifico-Regular.ttf";
import "./fonts/Inter-Regular.ttf";
import "./fonts/Inter-Bold.ttf";

<Text class="font-display text-3xl text-violet-600">Custom fonts</Text>
<Text class="font-body font-bold">Bold Inter</Text>
```

An arbitrary family works without a theme entry: `font-[Pacifico]`. Weight classes (`font-light`, `font-semibold`, `font-bold`, ...) select faces as `fontWeight` does. Text classes on a view pass down to the texts inside it, so `<View class="font-body">` sets the family for a whole screen.

## A default font for the app

There is no global default font setting. Set the family on a container with a class, which the texts inside inherit, or keep a shared style:

```tsx
mount(() => (
  <View class="flex-1 font-body">
    <App />
  </View>
));
```

## Font features

`fontVariant` turns on OpenType features of the font: `"tabular-nums"`, `"proportional-nums"`, `"lining-nums"`, `"oldstyle-nums"` and `"small-caps"` ([Text](https://nsh.dev/docs/text.md#text-styles)). The font has to contain them; system fonts do.

## Related

- [Text](https://nsh.dev/docs/text.md): text styles, sizes and the system text size setting.
- [Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md#theme): the theme keys.
- [Images and assets](https://nsh.dev/docs/images-and-assets.md): how imported files are shipped.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/fonts

---

# Touch and gestures

NSH has three levels of touch handling. **Presses** (`onPress` and friends) cover buttons, rows and links, with press feedback drawn natively. **Native gestures** (`pan`, `pinch`, `rotation`) move [native values](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md#native-values) on the UI thread, so a dragged card follows the finger even while JS is busy. **Raw touches and the responder system** (`onTouchStart`, `onResponderMove`, `PanResponder`) give you every finger position in JS for anything the other two cannot express, such as drawing.

Pick the highest level that does the job: the higher the level, the less work crosses from the UI thread to JS.

## Presses

Every element accepts the press handlers; there is no separate "touchable" component. Put `onPress` on a `<View>`, a `<Text>`, an `<Image>` or anything else.

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";

function App() {
  const count = signal(0);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}>
      <View
        onPress={() => count.update((n) => n + 1)}
        onLongPress={() => count.set(0)}
        activeOpacity={0.6}
        accessibilityRole="button"
        style={{ paddingHorizontal: 20, paddingVertical: 12, borderRadius: 10, backgroundColor: "#0969da" }}
      >
        <Text style={{ color: "#ffffff", fontWeight: "600" }}>Pressed {count()} times</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `onPress` | `() => void` | | The finger lifted inside the view (after a press, not a long press). |
| `onLongPress` | `() => void` | | The finger stayed down for `delayLongPress`. `onPress` does not follow. |
| `onPressIn` | `() => void` | | The press started. |
| `onPressOut` | `() => void` | | The press ended: lifted, slid off, or taken over by a scroll view. |
| `delayLongPress` | `number` | `500` | Milliseconds before a press becomes a long press. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Takes no presses and shows no feedback; applies `disabled:` classes. |

How presses behave:

- **Only the innermost pressable view responds.** A pressable row containing a pressable button gets no press when the button is pressed.
- **Inside a scroll view, the press waits about 130 ms** before it starts (and shows feedback), so a drag that begins on a button scrolls instead of pressing it.
- **Sliding off cancels.** Moving the finger out of the view ends the press with `onPressOut` and no `onPress`.
- **`disabled` removes the press listeners** from what is mounted, so the view shows no feedback at all, and `disabled:` classes apply (`class="disabled:opacity-40"`).
- **Nested `<Text>` spans with `onPress` are links.** The paragraph is one native view; the press goes to the span under the finger. See [Text](https://nsh.dev/docs/text.md).

## Press feedback

Press feedback is drawn by the platform the moment the finger touches down, with no round trip to JS. Choose one per view:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `activeOpacity` | `number` | | The view's opacity while pressed. |
| `underlayColor` | `ColorValue` | | The background while pressed; the children fade to `underlayOpacity`. |
| `underlayOpacity` | `number` | `0.85` | The children's opacity while `underlayColor` shows. |
| `android={{ ripple }}` | `{ color?, borderless?, radius?, foreground? }` | | Android's material ripple. Ignored on iOS. |

```tsx
<View onPress={open} activeOpacity={0.5}>…</View>

<View onPress={open} underlayColor="#ddf4ff" style={{ padding: 16 }}>…</View>

<View
  onPress={open}
  activeOpacity={0.6}
  android={{ ripple: { color: "rgba(9,105,218,0.3)" } }}
>
  …
</View>
```

A borderless ripple spreads outside the view, which suits icon buttons: `android={{ ripple: { borderless: true, radius: 24 } }}`. Combining `activeOpacity` with a ripple is common: iOS uses the opacity, Android the ripple. See [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md).

The `active:` Tailwind variant is the third option. It applies classes while the view is pressed, and with a `transition` class the change animates:

```tsx
<View
  onPress={save}
  class="rounded-xl bg-emerald-600 p-4 transition active:scale-95 active:bg-emerald-800"
>
  <Text class="font-semibold text-white">Save</Text>
</View>
```

## Hit areas: hitSlop

`hitSlop` extends the area that takes touches beyond the view's bounds, without changing its layout. Use it for small targets such as close buttons and toggles.

```tsx
<View hitSlop={12} onPress={close} style={{ width: 20, height: 20 }}>…</View>
<View hitSlop={{ top: 10, bottom: 10, left: 4, right: 4 }} onPress={next}>…</View>
```

| Prop | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `hitSlop` | `number \| { top?, right?, bottom?, left? }` | Points added around the bounds. A number applies to all four sides. |

Keep the extended area inside the parent's bounds (give the small view some margin or padding around it): hit testing reaches a child through its parent, so a touch outside the parent never gets to the child's slop.

## Children outside their parent

A child placed outside its parent's bounds (`position: "absolute"` with `overflow` left visible, such as a dropdown under its field) takes touches where it is drawn, like any other view: NSH hit-tests the descendants that reach outside a view natively. A parent with `overflow: "hidden"` clips them, and then they neither show nor take touches there. The area is computed from the layout, so a child moved out of its parent by a `transform` only takes touches inside the parent's bounds.

Mind the drawing order: a dropdown is drawn over the siblings of its field only if the field comes after them or has a higher `zIndex`, and touches go to what is drawn on top.

## pointerEvents

`pointerEvents` decides which views of a subtree can be the target of a touch. It is evaluated natively during hit testing, so it costs nothing per touch.

| Value | The view | Its children |
|---|---|---|
| `"auto"` (default) | Takes touches | Take touches |
| `"none"` | Never the target | Never the target: touches pass through to what is behind |
| `"box-none"` | Never the target | Take touches |
| `"box-only"` | Takes touches | Never the target |

The typical uses: an overlay that must not block what is under it (`"none"`), a full-screen container whose empty space should let touches through to the content behind while its buttons still work (`"box-none"`), and a row that should take a press even when the finger lands on a child (`"box-only"`).

```tsx
<View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  <Map />
  {/* A floating toolbar: the empty area passes touches to the map. */}
  <View pointerEvents="box-none" style={{ position: "absolute", top: 0, left: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0, justifyContent: "flex-end", padding: 16 }}>
    <View onPress={locate} style={{ alignSelf: "flex-end", padding: 12, borderRadius: 24, backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}>
      <Text>Locate</Text>
    </View>
  </View>
</View>
```

The Tailwind classes `pointer-events-none` and `pointer-events-auto` set the same thing; an explicit prop wins over the class.

## Native gestures: pan, pinch and rotation

For drags, pinches and rotations that move something on screen, bind [native values](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md#native-values) to the gesture. The platform's gesture recognizer writes the values on the UI thread and the views bound to them move in the same frame; JS is told when the gesture starts and ends.

```tsx
import { mount, View } from "nsh";
import { createNativeValue } from "nsh/animated";

function App() {
  const x = createNativeValue(0);
  const y = createNativeValue(0);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}>
      <View
        pan={{ x, y }}
        onPanEnd={(e) => {
          // Spring back, starting at the speed the finger let go with.
          x.spring(0, { velocity: e.velocityX });
          y.spring(0, { velocity: e.velocityY });
        }}
        style={{ width: 120, height: 120, borderRadius: 24, backgroundColor: "#8250df", transform: [{ translateX: x }, { translateY: y }] }}
      />
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

| Prop | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `pan` | `{ x?: NativeValue; y?: NativeValue }` | One-finger drags move these values, in points. |
| `pinch` | `{ scale?: NativeValue }` | Two-finger pinches drive `scale` (a factor). |
| `rotation` | `{ angle?: NativeValue }` | Two-finger rotations drive `angle`, in degrees. |
| `onPanStart` / `onPanEnd` | `(e: PanEvent) => void` | The drag started / ended. |
| `onPinchStart` / `onPinchEnd` | `(e: { scale; velocity }) => void` | The pinch started / ended. |
| `onRotationStart` / `onRotationEnd` | `(e: { rotation; velocity }) => void` | The rotation started / ended. |

`PanEvent` has `translationX` / `translationY` (points since the start), `velocityX` / `velocityY` (points per **second**) and `valueX` / `valueY` (the bound values at that moment).

What the native side does for you:

- **A drag continues from where the value is.** At the start the values are read, and the translation is added to them; grabbing a value that is still animating (a spring on its way home) stops the animation where it is.
- **One axis only lets the other scroll.** With only `pan={{ x }}` the drag begins only when the finger moves more horizontally than vertically, so a horizontal swipe row inside a vertical scroll view still scrolls vertically. This decision is made natively when the system asks whether the gesture may begin.
- **Pan, pinch and rotation run together** on the same view: one card can be dragged, pinched and rotated at once.
- **Release velocity for physics.** `onPanEnd`'s velocity feeds `spring({ velocity })` or `decay({ velocity })` directly; `valueX` / `valueY` let you pick a snap point.

```tsx
// A card that snaps to the left or right edge.
<View
  pan={{ x }}
  onPanEnd={(e) => {
    const projected = (e.valueX ?? 0) + e.velocityX * 0.2;
    x.spring(projected > 0 ? 140 : -140, { velocity: e.velocityX });
  }}
  style={{ transform: [{ translateX: x }] }}
/>
```

> [!TIP]
> Use `pan` rather than `PanResponder` whenever the drag only moves things. With `pan`, a busy JS thread cannot make the drag stutter; with `PanResponder`, every move is an event to JS and a re-render.

## Raw touches

The touch handlers report every finger as it goes down, moves and lifts. They are useful for logging, custom hit testing and reacting to multi-touch; they do not claim the touch (presses and scroll views keep working).

| Prop | Description |
|---|---|
| `onTouchStart` | A finger went down on the view or inside it. |
| `onTouchMove` | A finger moved. Moves are merged per engine turn. |
| `onTouchEnd` | A finger lifted. |
| `onTouchCancel` | The system took the touch (a scroll view started scrolling, a call came in). |
| `onTouchStartCapture`, `onTouchMoveCapture`, `onTouchEndCapture`, `onTouchCancelCapture` | The same, called from the outside in, before the bubbling handlers. |

Each handler gets a `GestureResponderEvent`:

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `identifier` | Identifies the finger while it is down. |
| `locationX`, `locationY` | Position in the view the finger went down on (`target`). |
| `pageX`, `pageY` | Position in the surface. |
| `target` | The id of the view the finger went down on. |
| `timestamp` | Milliseconds. |
| `touches` | Every finger that is down. |
| `changedTouches` | The fingers this event is about. |
| `nativeEvent` | The event itself, so `e.nativeEvent.locationX` works too. |
| `stopPropagation()` | Views further out do not see this touch event. |

```tsx
<View
  onTouchStart={(e) => console.log("down", e.locationX, e.locationY, e.touches.length)}
  onTouchMove={(e) => console.log("move", e.pageX, e.pageY)}
  onTouchEnd={() => console.log("up")}
/>
```

### Where a view is: measure

`locationX` / `locationY` are relative to the view the finger went down on, which may be a child of the view you care about (a slider's knob). `ref.measure()` tells you where a view is, so you can use `pageX` / `pageY` instead:

```tsx
let track!: YNode;
let origin = 0;
<View
  ref={track}
  onStartShouldSetResponder={() => true}
  onResponderGrant={async (e) => {
    const x = e.pageX;
    origin = (await track.measure())?.pageX ?? 0;
    seek(x - origin);
  }}
  onResponderMove={(e) => seek(e.pageX - origin)}
/>;
```

It resolves once the changes made so far are laid out, to `{ x, y, width, height, pageX, pageY }`: the frame in the parent (as `onLayout` reports it) and the top left corner in the surface, or in the modal the view is in, the same coordinates as touches' `pageX` / `pageY`. The offsets of the scroll views and lists around it are taken into account; transforms (animations included) are not. It resolves to `null` for a view that is not on screen.

## The responder system

When JS has to own a touch sequence (finger drawing, a custom slider, a gesture the native recognizers do not offer), use the gesture responder system. One view at a time is the **responder** and receives the moves; views negotiate who that is.

Becoming the responder:

| Prop | Return | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `onStartShouldSetResponder` | `boolean` | Asked when a finger goes down, from the target outwards. Return `true` to become the responder. |
| `onMoveShouldSetResponder` | `boolean` | Asked on every move while there is no responder (or to take it over). |

These four get a second argument, `gestureState`: the gesture since the first finger went down, with the same fields as [PanResponder's](#panresponder) (`dx`, `dy`, `vx`, `vy`, `moveX`, `moveY`, `x0`, `y0`, `numberActiveTouches`). A swipe that claims only horizontal moves: `onMoveShouldSetResponder={(e, g) => Math.abs(g.dx) > 10 && Math.abs(g.dx) > Math.abs(g.dy)}`. That decision still reaches JS a move late, so a scroll view around may start scrolling first; for drags inside scroll views use [`panActivation`](#pans-inside-scroll-views-panactivation).
| `onStartShouldSetResponderCapture` | `boolean` | As above, asked from the outside in, before the bubbling ones. A parent uses it to take a touch from its children. |
| `onMoveShouldSetResponderCapture` | `boolean` | The move version. |

While responding:

| Prop | Description |
|---|---|
| `onResponderGrant` | This view is now the responder. Return `true` to keep native scroll views from taking the touches. |
| `onResponderReject` | Another view is the responder and would not let go. |
| `onResponderStart` | Another finger went down. |
| `onResponderMove` | A finger moved. |
| `onResponderEnd` | A finger lifted. |
| `onResponderRelease` | The last finger lifted: the gesture is over. |
| `onResponderTerminationRequest` | Another view wants the touches. Return `false` to keep them (default `true`). |
| `onResponderTerminate` | Another view, or a native gesture, took the touches. |

```tsx
import { type GestureResponderEvent, mount, signal } from "nsh";
import { Canvas } from "nsh/canvas";

function Sketch() {
  const strokes = signal<[number, number][][]>([]);
  const point = (e: GestureResponderEvent): [number, number] => [e.locationX, e.locationY];
  return (
    <Canvas
      style={{ flex: 1 }}
      onStartShouldSetResponder={() => true}
      onResponderGrant={(e) => {
        strokes.set([...strokes(), [point(e)]]);
        return true; // the scroll view around must not take the touches
      }}
      onResponderTerminationRequest={() => false}
      onResponderMove={(e) => {
        const all = strokes();
        strokes.set([...all.slice(0, -1), [...all[all.length - 1], point(e)]]);
      }}
      draw={(ctx) => {
        ctx.lineWidth = 3;
        for (const s of strokes()) {
          ctx.beginPath();
          s.forEach(([x, y], i) => (i === 0 ? ctx.moveTo(x, y) : ctx.lineTo(x, y)));
          ctx.stroke();
        }
      }}
    />
  );
}

mount(Sketch);
```

How it runs: a view with any touch or responder handler listens to touches natively; the platform reports the touches on it (and inside it) with the path of listening views, and the negotiation runs in the runtime's Rust code, calling your handlers in order: the `…Capture` handlers from the outermost view inwards, then the others from the target outwards. Two consequences:

- **Native scroll views and JS responders compete.** If `onResponderGrant` returns `true`, the scroll views around the responder stop taking the touches until it ends. If a native scroll view starts dragging first, it wins: the responder gets `onResponderTerminate` and the touch handlers `onTouchCancel`.
- **Each move is an event to JS.** Responder-driven drags are as smooth as your JS is fast; for drags that only move views, prefer [`pan`](#native-gestures-pan-pinch-and-rotation).

## PanResponder

`PanResponder` from `nsh/gesture` wraps the responder system and adds the gesture state: distance from the start, velocity, the number of fingers. Spread its `panHandlers` on a view.

```tsx
import { mount, signal, View } from "nsh";
import { PanResponder } from "nsh/gesture";

function Ball() {
  const pos = signal({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  let start = { x: 0, y: 0 };
  const responder = PanResponder.create({
    onStartShouldSetPanResponder: () => true,
    onPanResponderGrant: () => {
      start = pos();
    },
    onPanResponderMove: (_, g) => pos.set({ x: start.x + g.dx, y: start.y + g.dy }),
    onPanResponderRelease: (_, g) => console.log("released at", g.vx, g.vy, "pt/ms"),
  });
  return (
    <View
      {...responder.panHandlers}
      style={{ width: 60, height: 60, borderRadius: 30, backgroundColor: "#0969da", transform: [{ translateX: pos().x }, { translateY: pos().y }] }}
    />
  );
}

mount(Ball);
```

The callbacks get `(event, gestureState)`:

| `gestureState` field | Description |
|---|---|
| `stateID` | Identifies the gesture. |
| `moveX`, `moveY` | The latest position of the touches' centroid, in surface points. |
| `x0`, `y0` | Where the centroid was when the responder was granted. |
| `dx`, `dy` | Distance moved since the grant. |
| `vx`, `vy` | Velocity, in points per **millisecond**. |
| `numberActiveTouches` | Fingers down. |

The callbacks are `onStartShouldSetPanResponder(Capture)`, `onMoveShouldSetPanResponder(Capture)`, `onPanResponderGrant`, `onPanResponderReject`, `onPanResponderStart`, `onPanResponderMove`, `onPanResponderEnd`, `onPanResponderRelease`, `onPanResponderTerminate`, `onPanResponderTerminationRequest` and `onShouldBlockNativeResponder`. The last one defaults to `true`: a granted PanResponder keeps native scroll views from taking its touches.

## Pans inside scroll views: panActivation

A chart scrubbed sideways inside a vertical scroll view has to take horizontal drags and leave vertical ones to the scroll view. Claiming the touch on start blocks scrolling from the first pixel, and deciding in `onMoveShouldSetResponder` is too late: by the time JS answers, the scroll view may have taken the touch. `panActivation` lets the platform decide on the main thread, as the finger moves:

```tsx
<View
  panActivation={{ activeOffsetX: 10, failOffsetY: 10 }}
  onResponderGrant={(e) => scrub(e.locationX)}
  onResponderMove={(e) => scrub(e.locationX)}
  onResponderRelease={() => scrub(null)}
>
  <Chart />
</View>
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `activeOffsetX`, `activeOffsetY` | The pan activates once the finger has moved further than this from where it went down, along that axis (either direction, points). |
| `failOffsetX`, `failOffsetY` | The pan fails once the finger has moved further than this first: the scroll views keep the touches. |

Without active offsets the pan activates after 10 points in any direction. Until it activates, the scroll views around wait for it (iOS) and the view is not asked to become the responder: its `…ShouldSetResponder` handlers are skipped. When it activates, the scroll views can no longer take these touches and the view becomes the responder (`onResponderGrant`, then the moves); when it fails, the scroll view scrolls as usual. `PanResponder`'s `panHandlers` work with it too: spread them next to the prop, and `onPanResponderGrant` runs at the activation.

> [!NOTE]
> Velocities differ by API: `PanResponder`'s `vx` / `vy` are points per millisecond, while `onPanEnd`'s `velocityX` / `velocityY` and the `velocity` option of `spring` / `decay` are points per second. Multiply `vx` by 1000 before passing it to a spring.

## Why some answers are props

The main thread never waits for JS. When the system needs an answer on the spot (may this pan gesture begin, does this point hit the view, should this tap dismiss the keyboard), NSH answers natively from props mounted beforehand: `pan` (its axes), `pinch`, `hitSlop`, `pointerEvents`, `keyboardShouldPersistTaps`, `panActivation`. Your JS handlers hear about what happened afterwards. That is why these are declarative props rather than callbacks, and why the responder system's negotiation, which does call JS, only decides between JS responders and never blocks a native gesture.

## Related

- [`View`](https://nsh.dev/elements/view.md): every touch prop on the basic element.
- [Animation](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md): native values, springs and decay for gesture-driven motion.
- [Scrolling](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md): `keyboardShouldPersistTaps`, scroll views and nested gestures.
- [`nsh/gesture`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-gesture.md): the `PanResponder` reference.
- [Accessibility](https://nsh.dev/docs/accessibility.md): pressable views are accessibility elements; give them a role and a label.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures

# Scrolling

`<Scroll>` is the platform's own scroll view (UIScrollView on iOS, a ScrollView on Android): flings, bounces, the scroll indicator and pull to refresh are native, and so is snapping. JS hears about scrolling through events and can bind the offset to a [native value](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md#native-values) for effects that follow the finger frame by frame.

Use `<Scroll>` for content of a known, moderate size: a settings page, a form, an article, a row of chips. For long or unbounded data use [`List`](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md), which recycles rows and accepts the same scrolling props.

## A scroll view

A `<Scroll>` is the viewport; its children are the content. The viewport needs a size from its parent (usually `flex: 1`), and the content is laid out at the viewport's width (vertical) or height (horizontal) and as long as it needs to be.

```tsx
import { mount, Scroll, Text, View } from "nsh";

function App() {
  return (
    <Scroll style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: "#f6f8fa" }}>
      <View style={{ padding: 16, gap: 12 }}>
        <Each of={Array.from({ length: 50 }, (_, i) => i + 1)}>
          {(n) => (
            <View style={{ padding: 16, borderRadius: 10, backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}>
              <Text>Row {n()}</Text>
            </View>
          )}
        </Each>
      </View>
    </Scroll>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

The child view above can also be the scroll view's own content container: `contentContainerStyle` (or `contentContainerClass`) wraps the children in a view with that style, which scrolls with them. `flexGrow: 1` makes it at least as tall as the viewport, so a short content can be centered and a long one still scrolls:

```tsx
<Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }} contentContainerStyle={{ flexGrow: 1, justifyContent: "center", padding: 16 }}>
  <If when={messages().length > 0} else={<Text>No messages yet</Text>}>
    <Each of={messages()}>{(m) => <Text>{m().text}</Text>}</Each>
  </If>
</Scroll>
```

A horizontal scroll view takes `horizontal` and a row as its child:

```tsx
<Scroll horizontal showsIndicator={false}>
  <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", gap: 8, paddingHorizontal: 16 }}>
    <Each of={["Today", "This week", "This month", "This year"]}>
      {(label) => <Text style={{ paddingHorizontal: 14, paddingVertical: 8, borderRadius: 16, overflow: "hidden", backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}>{label()}</Text>}
    </Each>
  </View>
</Scroll>
```

Right to left (see [Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md#right-to-left)), a horizontal scroll view starts at its right end and keeps its distance from it.

Fingers drag scroll views. On the desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux) and in the browser, dragging with the mouse does not scroll, as in desktop apps: the mouse scrolls with its wheel (Shift + wheel scrolls horizontally), the touchpad, the keyboard and the scroll indicator, which shows while the mouse moves over the view and drags as a scroll bar, and its drags go to the app's pans, responders and text selection. Touchscreens on desktops still drag. Horizontal views keep their indicator there even with `showsIndicator={false}`, since a mouse without a horizontal wheel has no other way to move them.

### Behavior props

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `horizontal` | `boolean` | `false` | Scrolls sideways. |
| `scrollEnabled` | `boolean` | `true` | The user can scroll it. Scrolling from code still works. |
| `bounces` | `boolean` | `true` | Overscroll past the edges. |
| `showsIndicator` | `boolean` | `true` | The scroll indicator shows. On the desktop and in desktop browsers a horizontal view keeps it: it is the mouse's scroll bar. |
| `contentInset` | `{ top?, right?, bottom?, left? }` | | Room around the content, scrollable into. |
| `contentOffset` | `{ x?, y? }` | | Where it starts. |
| `decelerationRate` | `"normal" \| "fast" \| number` | the platform's | How fast a fling slows down: `"normal"`, `"fast"`, or the velocity kept per millisecond (`0.998` is normal, `0.99` fast; `0` is the platform's default). |

## Paging and snapping

Snapping is decided natively when the finger lifts, from the release offset, the projected glide and the velocity; the scroll view then glides to the chosen stop. No JS is involved.

| Prop | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `pagingEnabled` | `boolean` | Stops at multiples of the viewport's size. |
| `snapToInterval` | `number` | Stops at multiples of this length (0: off). |
| `snapToOffsets` | `number[]` | Stops at these offsets. |
| `snapToAlignment` | `"start" \| "center" \| "end"` | With `snapToInterval`: which point of an item aligns with the viewport. |
| `disableIntervalMomentum` | `boolean` | A fling moves one stop at most. |

A pager: pages as wide as the scroll view, and an indicator updated when the glide ends.

```tsx
import { mount, Scroll, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";

const colors = ["#0969da", "#8250df", "#bf3989", "#1a7f37"];

function Pager() {
  const width = signal(0);
  const page = signal(0);
  const settle = (e: { x: number }) => page.set(Math.round(e.x / width()));
  return (
    <View style={{ gap: 8, padding: 16 }}>
      <Scroll
        horizontal
        pagingEnabled
        showsIndicator={false}
        style={{ height: 160, borderRadius: 12 }}
        onLayout={(e) => width.set(e.width)}
        onScrollEnd={settle}
      >
        <View style={{ flexDirection: "row" }}>
          <Each of={colors}>
            {(color, i) => (
              <View style={{ width: width(), height: 160, backgroundColor: color(), alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}>
                <Text style={{ color: "#ffffff", fontSize: 24, fontWeight: "700" }}>Page {i() + 1}</Text>
              </View>
            )}
          </Each>
        </View>
      </Scroll>
      <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", justifyContent: "center", gap: 6 }}>
        <Each of={colors}>
          {(_, i) => <View style={{ width: 8, height: 8, borderRadius: 4, backgroundColor: page() === i() ? "#0969da" : "#d0d7de" }} />}
        </Each>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(Pager);
```

A carousel of cards that snap to the center, one card per fling:

```tsx
<Scroll
  horizontal
  snapToInterval={232}          // card width (220) + gap (12)
  snapToAlignment="center"
  decelerationRate="fast"
  disableIntervalMomentum
  showsIndicator={false}
>
  <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", gap: 12, paddingHorizontal: 16 }}>…</View>
</Scroll>
```

`List` takes the same snapping props, which is the better choice for a long carousel.

## Scroll events

| Prop | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `onScroll` | `ScrollEvent` | The offset changed. At most once per frame; `scrollEventThrottle` spaces them further. |
| `scrollEventThrottle` | `number` | Minimum milliseconds between `onScroll` events. |
| `onScrollBeginDrag` | `{ x, y }` | The user started dragging. |
| `onScrollEndDrag` | `{ x, y }` | The user lifted the finger. |
| `onMomentumScrollBegin` | `{ x, y }` | The glide after a fling started. |
| `onMomentumScrollEnd` | `{ x, y }` | The glide ended (also when a new drag catches it). |
| `onScrollEnd` | `{ x, y }` | A user scroll came to rest: after the glide, or at the end of a drag without one. |

`ScrollEvent` carries `x`, `y` (the offset), `contentWidth`, `contentHeight` (the content's size, zoomed), `width`, `height` (the viewport) and `zoomScale`.

```tsx
const atBottom = signal(false);

<Scroll
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  scrollEventThrottle={100}
  onScroll={(e) => atBottom.set(e.y + e.height >= e.contentHeight - 20)}
>
  …
</Scroll>
```

> [!TIP]
> `onScroll` runs JS on every frame of a scroll (subject to the throttle). For something that only has to *look* scroll-linked, such as a header that fades or a parallax image, use [`scrollValue`](#scroll-linked-effects-scrollvalue) instead: it costs no JS at all.

## Scroll-linked effects: scrollValue

`scrollValue` takes a [native value](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md#native-values) and writes the scroll offset (along the main axis) into it natively, in the same frame the content moves. Bind that value, or nodes derived from it with `interpolate`, `diffClamp` or arithmetic, to styles.

```tsx
import { mount, Scroll, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { createNativeValue } from "nsh/animated";

function App() {
  const offset = createNativeValue(0);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <View
        style={{
          height: 56,
          justifyContent: "center",
          paddingHorizontal: 16,
          // Transparent at the top, white after 80 points.
          backgroundColor: offset.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 80], outputRange: ["rgba(255,255,255,0)", "#ffffff"] }),
        }}
      >
        <Text
          style={{
            fontSize: 22,
            fontWeight: "700",
            transformOrigin: "left center",
            transform: [{ scale: offset.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 80], outputRange: [1, 0.8] }) }],
          }}
        >
          Inbox
        </Text>
      </View>
      <Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }} scrollValue={offset}>
        <View style={{ padding: 16, gap: 8 }}>…</View>
      </Scroll>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

A header that slides away while the content scrolls up and comes back as soon as it scrolls down is `diffClamp` of the offset:

```tsx
const offset = createNativeValue(0);
const header = offset.diffClamp(0, 56);

<View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  <Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }} scrollValue={offset}>
    <View style={{ paddingTop: 56 }}>…</View>
  </Scroll>
  <View style={{ position: "absolute", top: 0, left: 0, right: 0, height: 56, transform: [{ translateY: header.mul(-1) }] }}>…</View>
</View>
```

Interpolations clamp outside their input range by default, so pulling past the top (a negative offset) does not overshoot the effect; pass `extrapolate: "extend"` for a stretchy header that grows as you pull.

## Pull to refresh

`refreshing` and `onRefresh` add the platform's pull-to-refresh control. The control shows while `refreshing` is true; set it in `onRefresh` and clear it when the work is done.

```tsx
const refreshing = signal(false);
const reload = async () => {
  refreshing.set(true);
  try {
    items.set(await (await fetch("https://api.example.com/items")).json());
  } finally {
    refreshing.set(false);
  }
};

<Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }} refreshing={refreshing()} onRefresh={reload}>…</Scroll>
```

On iOS the control is UIRefreshControl; in the Mac idiom of Mac Catalyst, which has no UIRefreshControl, NSH shows its own spinner with the same behavior. `List` takes the same two props. Since the mouse does not drag scroll views, on the desktop and in the browser the pull needs a touchscreen (or a macOS trackpad, which pulls past the top); offer another way to refresh there, such as a button or a keyboard shortcut.

## Zooming

A `<Scroll>` (not a `List`) zooms when `maximumZoomScale` is above `minimumZoomScale`: pinching scales the content, and while zoomed in it scrolls both ways.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `minimumZoomScale` | `number` | `1` | The smallest zoom. |
| `maximumZoomScale` | `number` | `1` | The largest zoom; above the minimum, pinching zooms. |
| `zoomScale` | `number` | | Zooms to this scale when the prop changes; the user's zoom is kept otherwise. |
| `bouncesZoom` | `boolean` | `true` | Pinching may go past the limits and springs back. |
| `pinchGestureEnabled` | `boolean` | `true` | The user can pinch to zoom. |
| `centerContent` | `boolean` | `false` | Content smaller than the viewport (zoomed out) is centered. |

`onScroll` reports `zoomScale` and the zoomed content size. From code, `ref.zoomTo({ scale, x, y, animated })` zooms so that the content point (`x`, `y`, in unzoomed points) lands in the middle of the viewport; double tap to zoom is a press handler calling it:

```tsx
import { mount, Scroll, signal, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { Image } from "nsh/image";

function Photo() {
  let scroll!: YNode;
  const scale = signal(1);
  return (
    <Scroll
      ref={scroll}
      style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: "#000000" }}
      minimumZoomScale={1}
      maximumZoomScale={4}
      centerContent
      onScroll={(e) => scale.set(e.zoomScale)}
    >
      <Image
        src="https://picsum.photos/id/1015/1200/800"
        style={{ width: 390, height: 260 }}
        onPress={() => scroll.zoomTo({ scale: scale() > 1.5 ? 1 : 3 })}
      />
    </Scroll>
  );
}

mount(Photo);
```

Text and canvases inside a zoomed scroll view are drawn again at the new resolution when the zoom ends, so they stay sharp on iOS. Android has no zooming scroll view of its own: NSH switches the scroll view to its own implementation, which scales around the pinch's focal point, pans with any number of fingers, flings and rubber-bands at the edges and zoom limits. Android only starts a pinch once the fingers are about 27 mm apart, as the system's gesture detector does.

## Scrolling from code

Give the scroll view a [`ref`](https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components.md) and call its methods. Commands run after the rest of the changes in the same update, so scrolling to content you just added works.

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `scrollTo({ x?, y?, animated? })` | Scrolls to an offset. Animated by default. |
| `zoomTo({ scale, x?, y?, animated? })` | Zoomable scroll views: zooms to `scale` (clamped to the limits), around the content point (`x`, `y`) or the middle. |

```tsx
let scroll!: YNode;

<Scroll ref={scroll} style={{ flex: 1 }}>…</Scroll>
<View onPress={() => scroll.scrollTo({ y: 0 })}>…</View>
```

Lists add `scrollToIndex`, `scrollToOffset` and `scrollToEnd`; see [Lists](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md#scrolling-from-code).

## Scroll views and the keyboard

NSH keeps a focused input visible on its own: when the keyboard shows, the scroll view around the input gets a bottom inset as tall as the keyboard and scrolls the input into view. This happens natively, with no code in your app. Use [`KeyboardAvoidingView`](https://nsh.dev/docs/forms-and-keyboard.md#content-outside-scroll-views-keyboardavoidingview) only for content outside scroll views, such as a message bar pinned to the bottom.

Two props decide how scrolling and taps interact with the keyboard:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `keyboardDismissMode` | `"none" \| "on-drag" \| "interactive"` | `"none"` | Whether dragging the content hides the keyboard. `"interactive"` lets the keyboard follow the finger down on iOS; on Android it behaves like `"on-drag"`. |
| `keyboardShouldPersistTaps` | `"never" \| "always" \| "handled"` | `"never"` | What a tap does while the keyboard is up. |

`keyboardShouldPersistTaps`:

- `"never"`: a tap outside the focused input only hides the keyboard; buttons do not get it. The user taps once to dismiss, again to press.
- `"handled"`: a tap on something that handles it (a button) goes through and the keyboard stays; a tap on empty space hides it. Usually the right choice for forms.
- `"always"`: taps never hide the keyboard.

Both are decided natively when the tap or drag happens; nothing waits for JS. To hide the keyboard from code, call `Keyboard.dismiss()` from `nsh/ui/mobile`.

## Nested scroll views

A horizontal scroll view inside a vertical one works as expected: each takes the drags along its own axis. Two scroll views on the same axis nest too (the inner one scrolls first). JS responders that need the finger, such as a drawing canvas inside a scroll view, return `true` from `onResponderGrant` to keep the scroll views around them from taking the touches; see [Touch and gestures](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md#the-responder-system).

## Related

- [`Scroll`](https://nsh.dev/elements/scroll.md): the element reference, every prop and event.
- [Lists](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md): virtualized lists with the same scrolling props.
- [Animation](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md): native values, `interpolate` and `diffClamp` for scroll-linked effects.
- [Forms and the keyboard](https://nsh.dev/docs/forms-and-keyboard.md): inputs, focus and the keyboard.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling

# Lists

`List` from `nsh/list` renders long data on a native scroll view while only creating the rows near the screen. Which rows exist, where they go, the columns, sticky headers and which items are visible are all computed natively; your JS only fills cells with content when the native side asks for one. A list of a million items costs about as much as a list of thirty.

```tsx
import { mount, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { List } from "nsh/list";

const items = Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, i) => ({ id: i, title: `Item ${i + 1}` }));

function App() {
  return (
    <List each={items} estimatedItemSize={52} style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}>
      {(item) => (
        <View style={{ paddingHorizontal: 16, paddingVertical: 16, borderBottomWidth: 1, borderBottomColor: "#eaeef2" }}>
          <Text style={{ fontSize: 16 }}>{item().title}</Text>
        </View>
      )}
    </List>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

Like a [`<Scroll>`](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md), the list is the viewport and needs a size from its parent (`flex: 1` or a height).

## How recycling works

The row function is not called once per item. It is called **once per cell**, and cells are reused: when a row scrolls far off screen, its cell is given another item, and `item()` and `index()` change. Everything in the row that reads them updates in place, like any other [signal](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md).

Two rules follow from that:

**Read `item()` where you use it.** A value copied out at the top of the row function belongs to whichever item the cell showed first.

```tsx
// Wrong: `title` stays the first item's title when the cell is reused.
{(item) => {
  const title = item().title;
  return <Text>{title}</Text>;
}}

// Right: the text follows the cell's current item.
{(item) => <Text>{item().title}</Text>}
```

**Keep per-item state in your data, not in the row.** A signal created inside the row belongs to the cell and travels with it to the next item. Store "is this row expanded / selected / liked" in the items or in a map keyed by id:

```tsx
const liked = signal<Set<number>>(new Set());
const toggle = (id: number) =>
  liked.update((s) => {
    const next = new Set(s);
    next.has(id) ? next.delete(id) : next.add(id);
    return next;
  });

<List each={posts()} estimatedItemSize={64} style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  {(post) => (
    <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", padding: 16 }}>
      <Text style={{ flex: 1 }}>{post().title}</Text>
      <Text onPress={() => toggle(post().id)}>{liked().has(post().id) ? "♥" : "♡"}</Text>
    </View>
  )}
</List>
```

Rows can have different heights. Until a row has been measured, the list assumes `estimatedItemSize` (default 50 points); pass a value close to your typical row so the scroll indicator and jumps to far items are accurate from the start.

## Changing the data

Pass a new array to change the items: `posts.set([...posts(), ...more])`. The list compares the old and the new array **by item identity** (`===`), keeps the common start and end, and treats what is between as removed and inserted. Measurements stay with their items, and when items are inserted above the rows on screen, the visible rows stay where they are instead of jumping.

- Update immutably: a new array, with the unchanged item objects reused. Mutating the array in place (`push`) is not seen.
- A changed item should be a new object (`{ ...post, title }`), so its row shows the change.
- Prepending (new messages, a refreshed feed) keeps the user's place.

`keyExtractor` names items in viewability tokens (below); by default the key is `item.key`, then `item.id`, then the index. It does not affect how changes are matched, which is always by identity.

## Props

`List` takes every scrolling prop of `<Scroll>` that makes sense for a list (`pagingEnabled`, `snapToInterval`, `snapToOffsets`, `snapToAlignment`, `decelerationRate`, `disableIntervalMomentum`, `bounces`, `scrollEnabled`, `contentInset`, `contentOffset`, `keyboardShouldPersistTaps`, `keyboardDismissMode`, `scrollEventThrottle`, `onScroll`, `onScrollBeginDrag`, `onScrollEndDrag`, `onMomentumScrollBegin`, `onMomentumScrollEnd`, `onScrollEnd`, `scrollValue`), described in [Scrolling](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md). Lists do not zoom. Its own props:

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `each` | `readonly T[]` | | The items. |
| `children` | `(item: () => T, index: () => number) => JSX.Element` | | Renders a cell; called once per cell, see [recycling](#how-recycling-works). |
| `estimatedItemSize` | `number` | `50` | The size of rows not measured yet, in points. |
| `horizontal` | `boolean` | `false` | Scrolls sideways. |
| `numColumns` | `number` | `1` | Items per row (vertical lists). |
| `inverted` | `boolean` | `false` | Item 0 at the bottom (chat); starts at the end and keeps its distance from the end. |
| `maintainVisibleContentPosition` | `{ autoscrollToBottomThreshold?: number }` | | A list that is not inverted stays at the end while it is within that many points of it, as content grows (see below). |
| `stickyHeaderIndices` | `number[]` | | Items that stick to the top while scrolled past (one column, not inverted). |
| `contentContainerStyle` | `{ padding*, gap, rowGap, columnGap }` | | Padding and gaps of the content, numbers only. |
| `ListHeaderComponent` | component or element | | Before the items. |
| `ListFooterComponent` | component or element | | After the items. |
| `ListEmptyComponent` | component or element | | Shown instead of the items while `each` is empty. |
| `ItemSeparatorComponent` | component or element | | Between items (one column). |
| `initialScrollIndex` | `number` | | Scrolls to this item before the first frame. |
| `onEndReached` | `() => void` | | The end is near (see below). |
| `onEndReachedThreshold` | `number` | `1` | How close to the end, in viewports, `onEndReached` fires. |
| `onViewableItemsChanged` | `(info) => void` | | Items became or stopped being viewable. |
| `viewabilityConfig` | `ViewabilityConfig` | | When items count as viewable. |
| `keyExtractor` | `(item, index) => string` | | The key in viewability tokens. |
| `refreshing` / `onRefresh` | `boolean` / `() => void` | | Pull to refresh. |
| `showsIndicator` | `boolean` | `true` | The scroll indicator shows. On the desktop and in desktop browsers a horizontal view keeps it: it is the mouse's scroll bar. |
| `ref` | `YNode` | | `scrollToIndex`, `scrollToOffset`, `scrollToEnd`, `scrollTo`. |

The header, footer and empty slots take a component (`ListHeaderComponent={Header}`) or an element (`ListHeaderComponent={<Header />}`). They are cells of their own, never recycled, and they are reactive like any other JSX.

## Columns and grids

`numColumns` lays items out in rows of that many columns; `contentContainerStyle` adds padding around the content and gaps between rows (`rowGap`) and columns (`columnGap`), or both (`gap`). Rows of a grid may have different heights: each row is as tall as its tallest item.

```tsx
<List
  each={photos}
  numColumns={3}
  estimatedItemSize={120}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  contentContainerStyle={{ padding: 12, gap: 8 }}
>
  {(photo) => <Image src={photo().thumb} style={{ aspectRatio: 1, borderRadius: 8 }} />}
</List>
```

## Sticky headers

`stickyHeaderIndices` lists items that stick to the top of the viewport while the content scrolls past them, until the next sticky item pushes them out. Sections are one list of header and row items; the headers' indices stick. The pinning is done natively on every scroll frame.

```tsx
type Row = { header: string } | { name: string };

const rows: Row[] = [];
const headers: number[] = [];
for (const [letter, names] of groups) {
  headers.push(rows.length);
  rows.push({ header: letter });
  for (const name of names) rows.push({ name });
}

<List each={rows} stickyHeaderIndices={headers} estimatedItemSize={44} style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  {(row) => (
    <If
      when={"header" in row()}
      else={<Text style={{ padding: 12 }}>{(row() as { name: string }).name}</Text>}
    >
      <Text style={{ padding: 6, backgroundColor: "#eaeef2", fontWeight: "700" }}>{(row() as { header: string }).header}</Text>
    </If>
  )}
</List>
```

Because a cell may show a header now and a name later, the row decides what to render with [`<If>`](https://nsh.dev/elements/control-flow.md), which switches when the item changes. Sticky headers need one column and a list that is not inverted.

## Chat: inverted lists

`inverted` lays the list out from the end: item 0 is at the bottom, the list starts scrolled to the end, and it keeps its distance from the end as items change. Keep the newest message first in the array; prepend to add one, append to load older ones with `onEndReached` (the "end" of an inverted list is the top).

```tsx
import { Input, mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { List } from "nsh/list";
import { KeyboardAvoidingView } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

type Message = { id: number; text: string; mine: boolean };

function Chat() {
  let next = 0;
  const message = (text: string, mine: boolean): Message => ({ id: next++, text, mine });
  const messages = signal(Array.from({ length: 30 }, (_, i) => message(`Message ${30 - i}`, i % 3 === 0)));
  const draft = signal("");
  const send = () => {
    if (!draft().trim()) return;
    messages.update((m) => [message(draft(), true), ...m]); // newest first
    draft.set("");
  };
  const loadOlder = () => messages.update((m) => [...m, ...Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) => message(`Older ${i}`, false))]);
  return (
    <KeyboardAvoidingView style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <List
        each={messages()}
        inverted
        estimatedItemSize={44}
        style={{ flex: 1 }}
        contentContainerStyle={{ padding: 12, gap: 6 }}
        keyboardDismissMode="interactive"
        onEndReached={loadOlder}
        onEndReachedThreshold={0.5}
      >
        {(m) => (
          <View
            style={{
              alignSelf: m().mine ? "flex-end" : "flex-start",
              maxWidth: "75%",
              paddingHorizontal: 12,
              paddingVertical: 8,
              borderRadius: 14,
              backgroundColor: m().mine ? "#0969da" : "#eaeef2",
            }}
          >
            <Text style={{ color: m().mine ? "#ffffff" : "#1f2328" }}>{m().text}</Text>
          </View>
        )}
      </List>
      <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", gap: 8, padding: 8 }}>
        <Input
          value={draft()}
          onChangeText={(t) => draft.set(t)}
          onSubmitEditing={send}
          multiline
          submitBehavior="submit"
          returnKeyType="send"
          placeholder="Message"
          style={{ flex: 1, maxHeight: 120, borderWidth: 1, borderColor: "#d0d7de", borderRadius: 18, paddingHorizontal: 12, paddingVertical: 8 }}
        />
      </View>
    </KeyboardAvoidingView>
  );
}

mount(Chat);
```

`scrollToEnd()` on an inverted list scrolls to its start: the newest message.

### Following the end of a list that is not inverted

A list in reading order (oldest first) can follow its end too: with `maintainVisibleContentPosition={{ autoscrollToBottomThreshold: 40 }}`, while the user is at the end (or within 40 points of it), the list stays at the end as the content grows: a reply streaming into the last item, a new message appended, the keyboard shrinking the list. Scrolled further up, the visible content stays where it is and the new content grows below it. Items inserted above the visible ones never move them, with or without the option.

```tsx
<List each={messages()} keyExtractor={(m) => m.id} maintainVisibleContentPosition={{ autoscrollToBottomThreshold: 40 }} style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  {(m) => <Bubble message={m()} />}
</List>
```

## Horizontal lists

`horizontal` turns the list sideways; cells are laid out at the list's height. Combined with snapping it makes a carousel of any length:

```tsx
<List
  each={cards}
  horizontal
  estimatedItemSize={232}
  snapToInterval={232}
  decelerationRate="fast"
  showsIndicator={false}
  style={{ height: 140 }}
  contentContainerStyle={{ paddingHorizontal: 16, gap: 12 }}
>
  {(card) => <View style={{ width: 220, height: 140, borderRadius: 14, backgroundColor: card().color }} />}
</List>
```

Right to left, horizontal lists start at the right and run leftwards.

## Loading more: onEndReached

`onEndReached` fires when the viewport comes within `onEndReachedThreshold` viewports of the end (1 by default: one screen ahead). Append the next page; the list fires again when the new end comes near.

```tsx
const posts = signal<Post[]>([]);
let loading = false;
let page = 0;

const loadMore = async () => {
  if (loading) return;
  loading = true;
  try {
    const next: Post[] = await (await fetch(`https://api.example.com/posts?page=${++page}`)).json();
    posts.set([...posts(), ...next]);
  } finally {
    loading = false;
  }
};
loadMore();

<List
  each={posts()}
  estimatedItemSize={72}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  onEndReached={loadMore}
  onEndReachedThreshold={0.5}
  ListFooterComponent={<Text style={{ padding: 16, textAlign: "center", color: "#8c959f" }}>Loading…</Text>}
>
  {(post) => <PostRow post={post()} />}
</List>
```

Guard against overlapping loads as above: the end may be reported again while a page is on its way.

## Viewability

`onViewableItemsChanged` reports which items are on screen, for analytics, autoplaying the visible video, or marking messages read. It gets `{ viewableItems, changed }`, arrays of tokens `{ item, key, index, isViewable }`. Viewability is computed natively; JS only hears about changes.

| `viewabilityConfig` | Description |
|---|---|
| `itemVisiblePercentThreshold` | Percent of an item that must be visible. |
| `viewAreaCoveragePercentThreshold` | Percent of the viewport an item must cover. |
| `minimumViewTime` | Milliseconds an item must stay viewable before it is reported. |

Without a threshold, any visible pixel counts.

```tsx
<List
  each={videos}
  estimatedItemSize={300}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  keyExtractor={(v) => v.slug}
  viewabilityConfig={{ itemVisiblePercentThreshold: 60, minimumViewTime: 250 }}
  onViewableItemsChanged={({ viewableItems }) => playing.set(viewableItems[0]?.key ?? null)}
>
  {(v) => <VideoCard video={v()} />}
</List>
```

## Scrolling from code

Give the list a `ref`:

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `scrollToIndex({ index, animated?, viewPosition?, viewOffset? })` | Scrolls item `index` into view. `viewPosition` places it: 0 at the start of the viewport (default), 0.5 in the middle, 1 at the end; `viewOffset` shifts it further. |
| `scrollToOffset({ offset, animated? })` | Scrolls to a content offset along the list's axis. |
| `scrollToEnd({ animated? })` | Scrolls to the end of the content (the start of an inverted list). |
| `scrollTo({ x?, y?, animated? })` | Scrolls to an offset, as on `<Scroll>`. |

```tsx
import { type YNode } from "nsh";
import { List } from "nsh/list";

let list!: YNode;

<List ref={list} each={items} estimatedItemSize={48} style={{ flex: 1 }}>…</List>

list.scrollToIndex({ index: 120, viewPosition: 0.5 });
```

`scrollToIndex` (and `scrollToEnd`) is resolved natively with the sizes known at that moment: measured rows where they have been measured, `estimatedItemSize` elsewhere. The list then follows its target while the rows around it are measured, so it lands exactly, until the user scrolls or the items change. To open a list at an item, use `initialScrollIndex` rather than scrolling after the first frame.

## ListView from nsh/ui/mobile

`ListView` from `nsh/ui/mobile` is a ready-made list built on the same machinery: you pass `each` and render a row, and it adds the padding, dividers and an `inset` grouped look. Use it for settings-style and plain lists that should look like the rest of the mobile UI set; use `List` when you control the whole look. See [ListView](https://nsh.dev/components/list-view.md).

```tsx
import { Text } from "nsh";
import { ListView } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

<ListView variant="inset" dividers each={settings} keyExtractor={(s) => s.id}>
  {(s) => <Text>{s().label}</Text>}
</ListView>
```

## Performance notes

- Each cell is laid out on its own, so scrolling only lays out the cells that changed. Keep rows shallow and avoid reading signals in rows that change on every frame.
- The native side asks for cells in batches, up to several rounds per frame, merged into one update; a fast fling binds many cells in one frame without a JS call per cell.
- Use [`nsh trace --scroll`](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md) to measure the per-frame cost of your rows.

## Related

- [`List` element](https://nsh.dev/elements/list.md) and [`nsh/list`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-list.md): the reference.
- [Scrolling](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md): the scrolling props lists share with `<Scroll>`.
- [Reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md): why `item()` is a function.
- [Performance](https://nsh.dev/docs/performance.md): measuring lists.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/lists
