# Navigation

`nsh/ui/mobile` provides a native navigation stack and native modals. A `Stack` is a UINavigationController on iOS, with its header, swipe back and large titles, and a stack with a toolbar and predictive back on Android. You keep the list of routes in a navigator; the stack renders each route as a screen and keeps it mounted, with its state, while it is in the stack.

```tsx
import { mount, Scroll, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { createNavigator, Screen, Stack } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

type Route = { name: "inbox" } | { name: "message"; id: number };

const nav = createNavigator<Route>({ name: "inbox" });

function Inbox() {
  return (
    <Screen title="Inbox">
      <Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }}>
        <Each of={[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]}>
          {(id) => (
            <View onPress={() => nav.push({ name: "message", id: id() })} underlayColor="#eaeef2" style={{ padding: 16 }}>
              <Text>Message {id()}</Text>
            </View>
          )}
        </Each>
      </Scroll>
    </Screen>
  );
}

function Message(props: { id: number }) {
  return (
    <Screen title={`Message ${props.id}`}>
      <View style={{ flex: 1, padding: 16 }}>
        <Text>The body of message {props.id}.</Text>
      </View>
    </Screen>
  );
}

function App() {
  return (
    <Stack navigator={nav} style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      {(route) => {
        switch (route.name) {
          case "inbox":
            return <Inbox />;
          case "message":
            return <Message id={route.id} />;
        }
      }}
    </Stack>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

## The navigator

`createNavigator(initial)` creates the stack of routes. A route is any value you like (a string, an object, a discriminated union as above); routes are compared by identity, so push a new object for each screen. Create the navigator once, at module level or in your root component, and import it wherever screens navigate.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `routes()` | The routes, bottom to top (reactive). |
| `push(route)` | Pushes a screen. |
| `pop(count?)` | Pops `count` screens (default 1); at least one stays. |
| `popToTop()` | Pops back to the first screen. |
| `replace(route)` | Replaces the top screen. |
| `reset(routes)` | Replaces all screens, e.g. after signing in. |
| `remove(route)` | Removes a route wherever it is. |

`createNavigator` also takes an array, to start several screens deep: `createNavigator<Route>([{ name: "inbox" }, { name: "message", id: 3 }])`.

When the user leaves a screen natively (the back button in the header, a swipe back on iOS, Android's back button or gesture), the stack removes that route from the navigator for you, so `routes()` always matches what is on screen.

A route carries what the screen needs. The gallery app pushes routes that hold the screen component itself, which keeps the route type small when there are many screens:

```ts
import { type JSX } from "nsh";
import { createNavigator } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

export type Route = { name: "home" } | { name: "page"; page: () => JSX.Element };
export const nav = createNavigator<Route>({ name: "home" });

// Elsewhere: nav.push({ name: "page", page: Settings });
```

## Stack

| Prop | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `navigator` | `Navigator<R>` | The routes to show. |
| `children` | `(route: R, index: Accessor<number>) => JSX.Element` | Renders a route; return a `<Screen>` for header options. |
| `style` | `StyleProp<ViewStyle>` | The stack's own style (usually `flex: 1`). |

The render function runs once per route, when it is pushed; `route` is the plain value, `index()` its current position. What it returns becomes the screen's content. Return a `<Screen>` to set the header; anything else is wrapped in a screen with default options.

Screens stay mounted while their route is in the stack: going back shows the previous screen exactly as it was left, with its scroll position, inputs and signals. A screen's [`cleanup`](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md) handlers run when its route leaves the stack.

## Screen and the header

`Screen` wraps a screen's content and carries its header options. All options are reactive: change a signal and the header follows.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | `string` | | The header's title. |
| `headerShown` | `boolean` | `true` | The header shows. |
| `headerTransparent` | `boolean` | `false` | The content extends under the header. |
| `headerTintColor` | `ColorValue` | | The back button and bar buttons. |
| `headerBackgroundColor` | `ColorValue` | | The header's background. |
| `headerTitleColor` | `ColorValue` | | The title. |
| `headerBackVisible` | `boolean` | `true` | The back button shows. |
| `headerLeft` | `JSX.Element` | | Views at the start of the header (replace the back button). |
| `headerRight` | `JSX.Element` | | Views at the end of the header. |
| `headerTitle` | `JSX.Element` | | Views replacing the title. |
| `animation` | `"default" \| "fade" \| "none"` | `"default"` | How the screen enters and leaves. |
| `gestureEnabled` | `boolean` | `true` | The interactive back gesture (iOS swipe back, Android predictive back). The back buttons pop either way. |
| `preventBack` | `boolean` | `false` | The user cannot leave; back calls `onBackRequest` instead. |
| `onBackRequest` | `() => void` | | The user tried to leave a screen with `preventBack`. |
| `onDismiss` | `() => void` | | The user left the screen natively; its route is already removed. |
| `ios={{ headerLargeTitle }}` | `boolean` | | iOS: a large title that shrinks into the bar as the content scrolls. |
| `ios={{ headerBackTitle }}` | `string` | | iOS: the label of the back button that leads back to this screen. |
| `style` | `StyleProp<ViewStyle>` | | The screen's content view. |

Header items are ordinary views, so they can be pressable and reactive:

```tsx
function Compose() {
  const text = signal("");
  return (
    <Screen
      title="New message"
      headerLeft={<Text onPress={() => nav.pop()} style={{ fontSize: 17, color: "#0969da" }}>Cancel</Text>}
      headerRight={
        <Text
          onPress={() => send(text())}
          style={{ fontSize: 17, fontWeight: "600", color: text() ? "#0969da" : "#8c959f" }}
        >
          Send
        </Text>
      }
    >
      <Input multiline value={text()} onChangeText={(t) => text.set(t)} style={{ flex: 1, padding: 16, fontSize: 17 }} />
    </Screen>
  );
}
```

A colored header:

```tsx
<Screen title="Profile" headerBackgroundColor="#1a7f37" headerTintColor="#ffffff" headerTitleColor="#ffffff">
  …
</Screen>
```

A screen without a header still has the system bars around it; pad its content with [`SafeAreaView`](https://nsh.dev/components/safe-area-view.md):

```tsx
<Screen headerShown={false}>
  <SafeAreaView style={{ flex: 1, padding: 16 }}>…</SafeAreaView>
</Screen>
```

### Safe areas under the header

Inside a screen, `useSafeAreaInsets()` and `SafeAreaView` report the insets below the header, not the whole surface's. With `headerTransparent`, the content starts at the top of the screen and the top inset is the header's height, so `SafeAreaView` keeps text clear of it while a background image fills the whole screen. With `ios={{ headerLargeTitle: true }}`, put a scroll view directly in the screen so the title can collapse as it scrolls.

## Keeping the user on a screen: preventBack

To ask before discarding unsaved changes, set `preventBack` while there is something to lose and handle `onBackRequest`:

```tsx
import { Input, signal } from "nsh";
import { Alert, Screen } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function EditNote() {
  const text = signal("");
  const confirm = async () => {
    const choice = await Alert.alert("Discard your changes?", undefined, [
      { text: "Keep editing", style: "cancel" },
      { text: "Discard", style: "destructive" },
    ]);
    if (choice === 1) nav.pop();
  };
  return (
    <Screen title="Edit" preventBack={text().length > 0} onBackRequest={confirm}>
      <Input value={text()} onChangeText={(t) => text.set(t)} placeholder="A note" style={{ margin: 16, fontSize: 17 }} />
    </Screen>
  );
}
```

With `preventBack` on, the swipe back is disabled and the back buttons (in the header, Android's back button and gesture) call `onBackRequest` instead of popping. `nav.pop()` from code still pops.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `preventBack` is a prop, not a callback that returns true or false, because the main thread never waits for JS. When the user starts a swipe or presses back, the system asks right away whether the screen may go, and NSH answers natively from the props it already has. Set `preventBack` as soon as there is something to lose (as above, from the text), not when the user tries to leave.

`gestureEnabled={false}` is the lighter option: it only turns off the interactive gesture (iOS swipe back, Android's predictive back animation), and the back buttons still pop.

## Modals

`Modal` presents content over everything else, in its own native window layer: a presented view controller on iOS, a dialog on Android. Render it where its state lives and control it with `visible`:

```tsx
import { signal, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { Modal, SafeAreaView } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function Settings() {
  const open = signal(false);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <View onPress={() => open.set(true)} style={{ padding: 16 }}>
        <Text>Edit profile</Text>
      </View>
      <Modal visible={open()} animationType="slide" ios={{ presentationStyle: "pageSheet" }} onRequestClose={() => open.set(false)}>
        <SafeAreaView style={{ flex: 1, padding: 20, gap: 12 }}>
          <Text style={{ fontSize: 22, fontWeight: "700" }}>Profile</Text>
          <View onPress={() => open.set(false)}>
            <Text style={{ color: "#0969da" }}>Done</Text>
          </View>
        </SafeAreaView>
      </Modal>
    </View>
  );
}
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `visible` | `boolean` | `true` | Shown while true. |
| `animationType` | `"slide" \| "fade" \| "none"` | | How it appears. |
| `transparent` | `boolean` | `false` | The background shows what is behind (dialogs, custom sheets). |
| `dismissible` | `boolean` | `false` | The user closes it natively (iOS sheet swiped down, Android back), then `onRequestClose` and `onDismiss` follow. |
| `onRequestClose` | `() => void` | | The user asked to close it: set `visible` to false. |
| `onShow` | `() => void` | | It has appeared. |
| `onDismiss` | `() => void` | | It has gone. |
| `ios={{ presentationStyle }}` | `"fullScreen" \| "pageSheet" \| "formSheet"` | `"fullScreen"` | iOS: sheets keep what is behind visible. |
| `desktop={{ presentationStyle }}`, `web={{ presentationStyle }}` | `"fullScreen" \| "pageSheet" \| "formSheet"` | `"fullScreen"` | Desktops and browsers: sheets are cards centered over the dimmed window (in phone browsers: a sheet from just below the top); Escape or a click outside asks to close. |
| `ios={{ supportedOrientations }}` | `("portrait" \| "landscape" \| …)[]` | the presenter's | iOS: the orientations it allows. |
| `android={{ statusBarTranslucent }}` | `boolean` | `false` | Android: the content reaches under the status bar. |

Modals are **controlled** by default: a swipe down on an iOS sheet or Android's back button only asks, through `onRequestClose`, and the modal stays until you set `visible` to false. That lets you confirm first. With `dismissible`, the platform closes it right away and then tells you; use it for sheets that hold nothing to lose. As with `preventBack`, the choice is a prop because the system asks whether the sheet may close on the spot.

A transparent modal makes a custom dialog:

```tsx
<Modal visible={open()} transparent animationType="fade" onRequestClose={() => open.set(false)}>
  <View style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: "rgba(0,0,0,0.4)", alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center", padding: 32 }}>
    <View style={{ alignSelf: "stretch", backgroundColor: "#ffffff", borderRadius: 14, padding: 20, gap: 12 }}>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 20, fontWeight: "700" }}>Delete the file?</Text>
      <View onPress={() => open.set(false)}><Text style={{ color: "#cf222e" }}>Delete</Text></View>
    </View>
  </View>
</Modal>
```

Inside a modal, `SafeAreaView` and `useSafeAreaInsets()` give the modal's own insets. For system dialogs (an alert with buttons, an action sheet) use [`Alert`](https://nsh.dev/components/alert.md) and [`ActionSheet`](https://nsh.dev/components/action-sheet.md); for a panel that slides up over a dimmed backdrop and follows the finger, use [`Sheet`](https://nsh.dev/components/sheet.md).

## The Android back button

On Android, the back button (or gesture) is handled in this order:

1. The top modal: `onRequestClose` (or it closes, with `dismissible`).
2. Your `BackHandler` listeners from `nsh/android`, most recently added first.
3. The top stack: it pops its top screen, or calls `onBackRequest` with `preventBack`.
4. Nothing handled it: the app exits.

A listener returns `true` when it handled the press, which keeps the stack from popping. While a listener is registered,
Android's back gesture does not preview the pop (the app answers only once the gesture ends), so add listeners only
while they may take the press:

```tsx
import { cleanup, signal } from "nsh";
import { BackHandler } from "nsh/android";

function Editor() {
  const selecting = signal(false);
  const sub = BackHandler.addEventListener("hardwareBackPress", () => {
    if (!selecting()) return false; // let the stack pop
    selecting.set(false);
    return true;
  });
  cleanup(() => sub.remove());
  // …
}
```

`BackHandler.exitApp()` leaves the app. On iOS, `nsh/android` can be imported and its calls do nothing, so the same code runs on both platforms. See [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md).

## Tabs and other layouts

`nsh/ui/mobile` has no tab bar component. A tab bar is a row of pressable views and a signal holding the selected tab; render the selected tab's content with a function child or [`<If>`](https://nsh.dev/elements/control-flow.md). To keep each tab's state while switching, give each tab its own `Stack` and navigator and keep all of them mounted, hiding the inactive ones with `display: "none"`.

## Related

- [Navigation components](https://nsh.dev/components/navigation.md): the `createNavigator`, `Stack`, `Screen` and `Modal` reference.
- [`SafeAreaView`](https://nsh.dev/components/safe-area-view.md) and [`StatusBar`](https://nsh.dev/components/status-bar.md).
- [`Alert`](https://nsh.dev/components/alert.md), [`ActionSheet`](https://nsh.dev/components/action-sheet.md) and [`Sheet`](https://nsh.dev/components/sheet.md).
- [`nsh/android`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-android.md): `BackHandler`.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/navigation

# Forms and the keyboard

Text entry is the `<Input>` element: a UITextField or UITextView on iOS, an EditText on Android. Typing, the caret, selection, autocorrection and autofill are the platform's own; your app gets the text through events and can control it. NSH also keeps focused inputs above the software keyboard on its own, and gives you the keyboard's height as a reactive value for the cases it cannot handle by itself.

For a labeled field with a clear button in the mobile UI set's look, see [`TextField`](https://nsh.dev/components/text-field.md). This page covers the underlying element.

## Controlled and uncontrolled inputs

An input is **controlled** when you pass `value`: it shows what your signal holds, and you update the signal from `onChangeText`.

```tsx
import { Input, mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";

function App() {
  const name = signal("");
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, padding: 16, paddingTop: 60, gap: 8 }}>
      <Input
        value={name()}
        onChangeText={(text) => name.set(text)}
        placeholder="Your name"
        style={{ fontSize: 17, borderWidth: 1, borderColor: "#d0d7de", borderRadius: 10, padding: 12 }}
      />
      <Text>Hello, {name() || "stranger"}</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

Because you control the value, you can transform what the user types: `onChangeText={(t) => code.set(t.replace(/[^0-9]/g, ""))}` keeps digits only, `onChangeText={(t) => tag.set(t.toUpperCase())}` uppercases.

An input is **uncontrolled** without `value`: it keeps its own text, starting at `defaultValue`, and you read it from `onChangeText` or `onSubmitEditing` when you need it. Use this for fields you only read on submit, such as a password.

> [!NOTE]
> A controlled input never loses keystrokes. Every native edit carries an edit count, and a `value` coming back from JS is applied only if it answers the latest edit. If JS is slow and the user has typed more in the meantime, the stale value is dropped instead of overwriting the newer text.

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `value` | `string` | | The text, controlled by JS. |
| `defaultValue` | `string` | | The initial text of an uncontrolled input. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | | Shown while the input is empty. |
| `placeholderTextColor` | `ColorValue` | | The placeholder's color (also `placeholder:text-*` classes). |
| `secureTextEntry` | `boolean` | `false` | Hides the text (passwords). |
| `keyboardType` | `KeyboardType` | `"default"` | The keyboard layout. |
| `returnKeyType` | `ReturnKeyType` | `"default"` | The return key's label. |
| `autoCapitalize` | `"none" \| "sentences" \| "words" \| "characters"` | `"sentences"` | Automatic capitalization. |
| `autoCorrect` | `boolean` | `true` | The system's corrections. |
| `autoComplete` | `AutoComplete` | | What the input holds, for autofill. |
| `multiline` | `boolean` | `false` | Several lines; return inserts a line break unless `submitBehavior` says otherwise. |
| `maxLength` | `number` | | The most characters the user can enter. |
| `editable` | `boolean` | `true` | The user can change the text. |
| `autoFocus` | `boolean` | `false` | Focused when it appears. |
| `submitBehavior` | `"submit" \| "blurAndSubmit" \| "newline"` | single line `"blurAndSubmit"`, multiline `"newline"` | What return does: submit and keep the focus, submit and unfocus, or insert a line break (multiline only). Wins over `blurOnSubmit`. |
| `blurOnSubmit` | `boolean` | `true` | Return unfocuses a single-line input. |
| `caretHidden` | `boolean` | `false` | No caret is drawn. |
| `selectionColor` | `ColorValue` | | The caret and the selection. |
| `ios={{ keyboardAppearance }}` | `"default" \| "light" \| "dark"` | `"default"` | The keyboard's look (iOS). |
| `selection` | `{ start: number; end?: number }` | | The controlled selection, in UTF-16 units. |
| `allowFontScaling` | `boolean` | `true` | Follow the system text size. |
| `maxFontSizeMultiplier` | `number` | | The upper bound of the system scale (0: none). |
| `ios={{ inputAccessoryViewID }}` | `string` | | iOS: the bar shown over the keyboard (see below). |
| `ios={{ textContentType }}` | `TextContentType` | | iOS's names for `autoComplete` values. |

Events:

| Event | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `onChangeText` | `text: string` | The text changed. |
| `onSubmitEditing` | `{ text }` | The return key was pressed in an input that submits (single line, or `submitBehavior` `"submit"` / `"blurAndSubmit"`). |
| `onFocus` / `onBlur` | | The input gained / lost focus. |
| `onSelectionChange` | `{ start, end }` | The caret or selection moved (UTF-16 units). |
| `onKeyPress` | `{ key }` | Before the text changes: `key` is the typed text, `"Backspace"` or `"Enter"`. |
| `onContentSizeChange` | `{ width, height }` | The text's size changed (at the input's width when multiline). |

An input is styled like text: `fontSize`, `color`, `fontFamily`, `textAlign`, `letterSpacing` and the rest of [text styles](https://nsh.dev/docs/text.md), plus borders, padding and backgrounds. The `focus:` Tailwind variant applies while the input has focus:

```tsx
<Input class="rounded-lg border border-zinc-300 px-3 py-2 text-base focus:border-blue-500" placeholder="Search" />
```

## Keyboards and autofill

`keyboardType` picks the layout:

| Value | Keyboard |
|---|---|
| `"default"` | Text. |
| `"email-address"` | Text with `@` and `.` at hand. |
| `"url"` | Text with `/` and `.com`. |
| `"number-pad"` | Digits only: no sign, no decimal separator (codes, PINs). |
| `"decimal-pad"` | Digits and a decimal separator. |
| `"numeric"` | As React Native: iOS's decimal pad; on Android digits with a sign and a decimal separator. |
| `"numbers-and-punctuation"` | Digits, a minus sign and punctuation (iOS's numbers and punctuation keyboard; on Android digits with a sign and a decimal separator). Use it for negative numbers on iOS. |
| `"phone-pad"` | A phone dial pad. |

On iOS, `ios={{ keyboardAppearance: "dark" }}` (or `"light"`, `"default"`) gives the keyboard a light or dark look regardless of the system's appearance, for a dark app in light mode. Android's keyboards always follow the system's theme.

`autoComplete` tells the system what the field holds, so it can offer saved names, addresses, passwords and one-time codes from messages. It takes these values: `"name"`, `"given-name"`, `"family-name"`, `"email"`, `"tel"`, `"username"`, `"current-password"`, `"new-password"`, `"one-time-code"`, `"street-address"`, `"postal-code"`, `"country"`, `"cc-number"`, `"cc-exp"`, `"cc-csc"`, `"url"`, `"birthdate-full"` and others, or `"off"`. iOS's own names (`"emailAddress"`, `"oneTimeCode"`, ...) are accepted too, in `autoComplete` or `ios={{ textContentType }}`.

```tsx
<Input keyboardType="email-address" autoCapitalize="none" autoCorrect={false} autoComplete="email" placeholder="E-mail" />
<Input secureTextEntry autoComplete="new-password" placeholder="Password" />
<Input keyboardType="number-pad" autoComplete="one-time-code" maxLength={6} placeholder="Code" />
```

## The return key and moving between fields

`returnKeyType` labels the return key: `"default"`, `"done"`, `"go"`, `"next"`, `"search"` or `"send"`. `submitBehavior` says what pressing it does:

| `submitBehavior` | Return | Default for |
|---|---|---|
| `"blurAndSubmit"` | fires `onSubmitEditing`, then the input loses focus | single-line inputs |
| `"submit"` | fires `onSubmitEditing`; the input keeps focus | single-line inputs with `blurOnSubmit={false}` |
| `"newline"` | inserts a line break (multiline inputs only) | multiline inputs |

A multiline input with `"submit"` or `"blurAndSubmit"` sends on return, as chat composers do, and still wraps its lines; on a hardware keyboard (desktops, a Mac, a tablet's keyboard) Shift+Return or Option / Alt+Return inserts a line break. A return that commits an input method's composition (Chinese or Japanese input, say) only commits it and never submits.

To move to the next field, keep refs to the inputs and call `focus()`:

```tsx
import { Input, mount, signal, View, type YNode } from "nsh";

function SignIn() {
  const email = signal("");
  let password!: YNode;
  const submit = () => console.log("sign in", email());
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, padding: 16, paddingTop: 60, gap: 12 }}>
      <Input
        value={email()}
        onChangeText={(t) => email.set(t)}
        keyboardType="email-address"
        autoCapitalize="none"
        returnKeyType="next"
        blurOnSubmit={false}
        onSubmitEditing={() => password.focus()}
        placeholder="E-mail"
      />
      <Input ref={password} secureTextEntry returnKeyType="go" onSubmitEditing={submit} placeholder="Password" />
    </View>
  );
}

mount(SignIn);
```

`blurOnSubmit={false}` on the first field keeps the keyboard up while focus moves, so it does not drop and rise again. A chat input that sends on return and stays focused uses `submitBehavior="submit"` (see the composer [below](#content-outside-scroll-views-keyboardavoidingview)).

Both `maxLength` and `submitBehavior` are enforced natively: the platform asks "may this character be added?" and "should return end editing?" as the user types, and NSH answers from the props without waiting for JS.

## Focus from code

An input's ref has:

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `focus()` | Focuses the input and shows the keyboard. |
| `blur()` | Unfocuses it. |
| `setSelection(start, end?)` | Selects `start..end` (UTF-16 units); a caret without `end`. |

`Keyboard.dismiss()` from `nsh/ui/mobile` unfocuses whichever input has focus:

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { Keyboard } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

<View onPress={() => Keyboard.dismiss()}>…</View>
```

## Selection

`onSelectionChange` reports the caret and selection; `selection` sets them. Positions are UTF-16 code units, as JavaScript string indices are, so `text.slice(start, end)` is the selected text.

```tsx
const text = signal("Select part of this text");
const range = signal({ start: 0, end: 0 });
const selection = signal<{ start: number; end?: number } | undefined>(undefined);

<Input
  value={text()}
  onChangeText={(t) => text.set(t)}
  selection={selection()}
  onSelectionChange={(r) => range.set(r)}
/>
<Text>Selected: "{text().slice(range().start, range().end)}"</Text>
<View onPress={() => selection.set({ start: 0, end: text().length })}><Text>Select all</Text></View>
```

## Multiline inputs that grow

A `multiline` input scrolls its text inside its own height. To grow it with its content, feed `onContentSizeChange`'s height back into its style, with a limit:

```tsx
const height = signal(0);

<Input
  multiline
  placeholder="Write a comment"
  onContentSizeChange={(e) => height.set(Math.min(e.height, 120))}
  style={{ fontSize: 16, padding: 10, borderWidth: 1, borderColor: "#d0d7de", borderRadius: 10, height: Math.max(height(), 20) + 20 }}
/>
```

The reported height is the text's (at the input's width), so add the vertical padding yourself, as above.

## Keeping inputs above the keyboard

### Inside scroll views: automatic

When the keyboard appears over a focused input that is inside a `<Scroll>` or `List`, NSH gives the scroll view a bottom inset as tall as the keyboard and scrolls the input into view. This is native and needs no code. A long form is simply a scroll view of inputs:

```tsx
<Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }} keyboardDismissMode="on-drag" keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled">
  <View style={{ padding: 16, gap: 12 }}>
    {/* inputs */}
  </View>
</Scroll>
```

`keyboardDismissMode` (`"none"`, `"on-drag"`, `"interactive"`) lets dragging the form hide the keyboard; `keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled"` lets a tap on a button go through while the keyboard is up instead of only dismissing it. See [Scrolling](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md#scroll-views-and-the-keyboard).

### Content outside scroll views: KeyboardAvoidingView

A message bar pinned to the bottom of a screen is not in a scroll view, so nothing moves it. Wrap the screen in `KeyboardAvoidingView` from `nsh/ui/mobile`: it makes room at the bottom as tall as the keyboard, animated with the keyboard.

```tsx
import { Input, Scroll, signal, View } from "nsh";
import { keyboard, KeyboardAvoidingView, useSafeAreaInsets } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function ChatScreen() {
  const insets = useSafeAreaInsets();
  const draft = signal("");
  const send = () => {
    if (draft().trim()) console.log("send", draft());
    draft.set("");
  };
  return (
    <KeyboardAvoidingView style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }} keyboardDismissMode="interactive">
        {/* messages */}
      </Scroll>
      <View
        style={{
          flexDirection: "row",
          padding: 8,
          // Above the home indicator, unless the keyboard covers it.
          paddingBottom: 8 + (keyboard().height > 0 ? 0 : insets().bottom),
        }}
      >
        <Input
          value={draft()}
          onChangeText={(t) => draft.set(t)}
          multiline
          submitBehavior="submit"
          returnKeyType="send"
          onSubmitEditing={send}
          placeholder="Message"
          style={{ flex: 1, maxHeight: 120 }}
        />
      </View>
    </KeyboardAvoidingView>
  );
}
```

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `behavior` | `"padding" \| "height" \| "position"` | `"padding"` | `padding` pads the bottom by the keyboard's height; `height` shrinks the view (its background ends at the keyboard); `position` moves an inner content view up. |
| `enabled` | `boolean` | `true` | Avoid the keyboard. |
| `keyboardVerticalOffset` | `number` | `0` | Added to the keyboard's height while it shows (a tab bar below the view, say). |
| `contentContainerStyle` | `StyleProp<ViewStyle>` | | The inner view's style with `behavior="position"`. |

It assumes it reaches the bottom of the surface, as a screen's content does. On an Android host whose window resizes for the keyboard, the window itself shrinks and `KeyboardAvoidingView` has nothing to do. See [KeyboardAvoidingView](https://nsh.dev/components/keyboard-avoiding-view.md).

### The keyboard accessor

`keyboard()` from `nsh/ui/mobile` is a reactive `{ height, duration }`: how far the keyboard reaches into the surface (0 when hidden; the bottom safe area under it included) and its animation's duration in seconds. Read it for anything custom: hide a floating button while typing, or size a panel.

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { keyboard } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

<If when={keyboard().height === 0}>
  <View style={{ position: "absolute", right: 16, bottom: 16 }}>…</View>
</If>
```

## A bar over the keyboard (iOS): InputAccessoryView

`InputAccessoryView` from `nsh/ios` shows a bar attached to the top of the keyboard while an input that names it has focus: iOS's `inputAccessoryView`. It moves with the keyboard natively, including during interactive dismissal. It renders nothing where it is placed in the tree; inputs refer to it by `nativeID`:

```tsx
import { Input, signal, Text, View, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { InputAccessoryView } from "nsh/ios";

function Note() {
  const text = signal("");
  let input!: YNode;
  return (
    <View style={{ padding: 16 }}>
      <Input
        ref={input}
        value={text()}
        onChangeText={(t) => text.set(t)}
        ios={{ inputAccessoryViewID: "note-bar" }}
        placeholder="A note"
      />
      <InputAccessoryView nativeID="note-bar" style={{ backgroundColor: "#f6f8fa" }}>
        <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", alignItems: "center", padding: 8 }}>
          <Text style={{ flex: 1, color: "#57606a" }}>{text().length} characters</Text>
          <Text onPress={() => input.blur()} style={{ color: "#0969da", fontWeight: "600" }}>Done</Text>
        </View>
      </InputAccessoryView>
    </View>
  );
}
```

The bar is as wide as the window and as tall as its content. Android has no input accessories: there `InputAccessoryView` renders nothing, and `isAvailable` from `nsh/ios` is `false`, so plan another place for those controls (for example above the input) when `Platform.OS === "android"`.

## Related

- [`Input`](https://nsh.dev/elements/input.md): the element reference.
- [`TextField`](https://nsh.dev/components/text-field.md): a labeled input with a clear button.
- [`KeyboardAvoidingView`](https://nsh.dev/components/keyboard-avoiding-view.md) and [`Keyboard`](https://nsh.dev/components/keyboard.md).
- [`nsh/ios`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-ios.md): `InputAccessoryView`.
- [Scrolling](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md#scroll-views-and-the-keyboard): keyboard dismissal and taps in scroll views.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/forms-and-keyboard

---

# Animation

Every animation in NSH runs on the UI thread. You describe it from JS, once, and the platform plays it frame by frame (Core Animation and a display link on iOS, the UI-thread animator on Android) without calling back into JS. A busy JS thread cannot make an animation stutter, and an animation costs no JS while it runs.

There are four tools, from the simplest to the most flexible:

| Tool | Use it for |
|---|---|
| [Transitions](#transitions) | A style change that should animate instead of jump: a color, an opacity, a transform. |
| [Keyframe animations](#keyframe-animations) | A spinner, a pulsing placeholder, a bouncing hint. |
| [Native values](#native-values) | Anything driven by a value over time: springs, gestures, scroll position, sequences. |
| [LayoutAnimation](#layoutanimation) | Size and position changes after a re-render: items inserted, removed, reordered, a panel expanding. |

## Transitions

Give a view `transitionProperty` and `transitionDuration`, and later changes to those properties animate natively from what is on screen to the new value.

```tsx
import { mount, signal, View } from "nsh";

function App() {
  const on = signal(false);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}>
      <View
        onPress={() => on.set(!on())}
        style={{
          width: 100,
          height: 100,
          borderRadius: on() ? 50 : 16,
          backgroundColor: on() ? "#8250df" : "#0969da",
          transform: [{ rotate: on() ? "45deg" : "0deg" }, { scale: on() ? 1.2 : 1 }],
          transitionProperty: "all",
          transitionDuration: 400,
          transitionTimingFunction: "ease-in-out",
        }}
      />
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

| Style | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `transitionProperty` | `string` | What animates, comma-separated: `"all"`, `"colors"`, `"opacity"`, `"transform"`, `"box-shadow"`, `"border-radius"`, ... |
| `transitionDuration` | `number \| "150ms" \| "0.2s"` | Milliseconds as a number, or a CSS time. |
| `transitionDelay` | `number \| "150ms" \| "0.2s"` | Before it starts. |
| `transitionTimingFunction` | `"linear" \| "ease" \| "ease-in" \| "ease-out" \| "ease-in-out" \| "cubic-bezier(…)"` | The curve. |

Properties that transition, by group: **colors** (background, border, outline, shadow and text colors, gradient stops), **opacity**, **transform**, **shadows** (`box-shadow`) and **shape** (border radius and width). CSS names and their camel-case forms both work (`background-color`, `backgroundColor`, `transform`, `scale`, ...). Layout does not transition: for size and position changes use [LayoutAnimation](#layoutanimation).

With Tailwind, the same thing is `transition` (colors, opacity, shadows and transforms), `transition-all`, `transition-colors`, `transition-opacity`, `transition-transform`, `transition-shadow`, with `duration-*`, `delay-*` and `ease-*`. Combined with the `active:` variant it gives pressed states that animate:

```tsx
<View onPress={save} class="rounded-xl bg-blue-600 px-5 py-3 transition duration-150 active:scale-95 active:bg-blue-800">
  <Text class="font-semibold text-white">Save</Text>
</View>
```

A transition starts from the value currently on screen, so changing the target again mid-way turns smoothly.

## Keyframe animations

Four built-in keyframe animations run natively, forever by default: `spin` (one turn clockwise), `ping` (scales up to 2× and fades out), `pulse` (fades to half opacity and back) and `bounce` (jumps up by a quarter of its height and lands).

```tsx
<View class="size-8 rounded-full border-4 border-zinc-300 border-t-blue-600 animate-spin" />
<View class="h-4 w-40 rounded bg-zinc-200 animate-pulse" />
```

| Style | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `animationName` | `"none" \| "spin" \| "ping" \| "pulse" \| "bounce"` | The animation. |
| `animationDuration` | `number \| "1s" \| …` | One iteration. |
| `animationDelay` | `number \| "200ms" \| …` | Before it starts. |
| `animationTimingFunction` | as `transitionTimingFunction` | The curve. |
| `animationIterationCount` | `number \| "infinite"` | Default `"infinite"`. |

Tailwind: `animate-spin`, `animate-ping`, `animate-pulse`, `animate-bounce`, `animate-none`.

## Native values

A native value is a number that lives on the UI thread. Create one with `createNativeValue` from `nsh/animated`, bind it to styles, and animate it; the bound views follow it every frame without re-rendering.

```tsx
import { mount, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { createNativeValue, Easing } from "nsh/animated";

function App() {
  const x = createNativeValue(0);
  const opacity = createNativeValue(1);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, justifyContent: "center", padding: 24, gap: 24 }}>
      <View style={{ width: 60, height: 60, borderRadius: 12, backgroundColor: "#0969da", opacity, transform: [{ translateX: x }] }} />
      <View
        onPress={async () => {
          await x.timing(240, { duration: 600, easing: Easing.out(Easing.cubic) });
          await opacity.timing(0.3, { duration: 200 });
          x.spring(0);
          opacity.timing(1);
        }}
      >
        <Text style={{ color: "#0969da" }}>Play</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

**What can be bound:** `opacity`; `backgroundColor`, `borderColor` (every side) and a `Text`'s `color` (the whole text), through an interpolation to colors; `shadowColor`, `shadowOpacity` and `shadowRadius`; and the `translateX`, `translateY`, `scale`, `scaleX`, `scaleY`, `rotate`, `rotateX`, `rotateY` and `rotateZ` steps of `transform`. A focus ring or a price that flashes green is a color interpolation bound to `borderColor` or `color`:

```tsx
const flash = createNativeValue(0);
const color = flash.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 1], outputRange: ["#1f2328", "#1a7f37"] });

<Text style={{ color }}>{price()}</Text>
// On a new price: flash.set(1); flash.timing(0, { duration: 600 });
``` Native values also drive [canvas drawings](https://nsh.dev/docs/canvas.md#animating-with-native-values), receive scroll offsets ([`scrollValue`](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md#scroll-linked-effects-scrollvalue)) and gestures ([`pan`, `pinch`, `rotation`](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md#native-gestures-pan-pinch-and-rotation)).

The value is kept alive by the views bound to it, so a binding never breaks because a JS variable went out of scope. Create native values in the component that owns them (not at module level when every instance needs its own).

### NativeValue methods

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `set(value)` | Jumps to `value`, stopping any animation. |
| `stop()` | Stops the running animation where it is; resolves with the value there. |
| `getValue()` | A promise of the current value, read on the UI thread where it moves (it settles within a frame). |
| `setOffset(offset)` | Adds `offset` to what the value shows: bindings see value + offset, while `set`, animations and drags move the value. |
| `flattenOffset()` | Adds the offset to the value and makes the offset 0. |
| `extractOffset()` | Moves the value into the offset and makes the value 0: a drag then starts from 0, on top of where the last one left it. |
| `timing(to, { duration?, easing?, delay? })` | Animates to `to` over `duration` ms (default 300, easing `"easeInOut"`). |
| `spring(to, { stiffness?, damping?, mass?, velocity? })` | Springs to `to` (defaults: stiffness 170, damping 26, mass 1). |
| `decay({ velocity?, deceleration?, clamp?, bounce? })` | Coasts from `velocity` (units per second) and slows down (deceleration 0.998 per ms by default). With `clamp: [min, max]` it stops at a bound, or bounces back from it keeping `bounce` (0..1) of its speed. |

Each animation returns a `Promise<boolean>`: `true` when it finished, `false` when something stopped it (`stop()`, `set()`, or a new animation on the same value). Starting a new animation on a moving value interrupts the old one smoothly: a `spring` or `decay` without `velocity` continues with the value's current velocity.

```tsx
// Spring settings: lower damping overshoots more, higher stiffness is faster.
x.spring(200, { stiffness: 180, damping: 8 });   // wobbly
x.spring(200, { stiffness: 400, damping: 30 });  // stiff, no overshoot

// A fling that coasts to a stop, from a pan's release velocity.
<View pan={{ x }} onPanEnd={(e) => x.decay({ velocity: e.velocityX })} />

// A fling that stays on its track and bounces softly off its ends.
x.decay({ velocity: e.velocityX, clamp: [0, 300], bounce: 0.3 });

// Where a value is now (it moves on the UI thread, so the answer is async).
const where = await x.getValue();
```

### Interpolation

`value.interpolate({ inputRange, outputRange })` maps a value through piecewise linear segments to numbers, colors or angles, and returns a new node you can bind. One value can drive many properties.

```tsx
const t = createNativeValue(0);

<View
  style={{
    backgroundColor: t.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 1, 2], outputRange: ["#54aeff", "#8250df", "#cf222e"] }),
    opacity: t.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 1], outputRange: [0.4, 1] }),
    transform: [
      { rotate: t.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 1], outputRange: ["0deg", "180deg"] }) },
      { scale: t.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 1], outputRange: [0.6, 1.2], easing: Easing.out(Easing.back()) }) },
    ],
  }}
/>
```

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `inputRange` | Increasing input stops. |
| `outputRange` | One output per stop: numbers, colors (`"#rrggbb"`, `"rgba(…)"`, named) or angles (`"45deg"`, `"1rad"`). |
| `extrapolate` | Outside the input range: `"clamp"` (default), `"extend"` (continue the end segments) or `"identity"` (pass the input through). |
| `extrapolateLeft`, `extrapolateRight` | The same, for one side. |
| `easing` | Shapes each segment. |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Interpolations **clamp** by default: outside the input range, the output stays at the nearest end. Pulling a scroll view past its top therefore does not push a scroll-linked header beyond its end state. Pass `extrapolate: "extend"` when you want the line to continue.

### Arithmetic and diffClamp

Nodes combine with arithmetic, also natively: `a.add(b)`, `a.sub(b)`, `a.mul(b)`, `a.div(b)`, `a.mod(b)` (never negative for a positive `b`, e.g. angles in 0..360), where `b` is a node or a number. `Animated.add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide` and `modulo` are the same as functions.

`node.diffClamp(min, max)` follows the node's *changes* while staying within `min..max`. Applied to a scroll offset, it makes a header that hides as the content scrolls up and comes back as soon as it scrolls down:

```tsx
const scroll = createNativeValue(0);
const header = scroll.diffClamp(0, 56);

<Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }} scrollValue={scroll}>…</Scroll>
<View style={{ position: "absolute", top: 0, left: 0, right: 0, height: 56, transform: [{ translateY: header.mul(-1) }] }}>…</View>
```

## Composite animations

`Animated` builds animations out of steps and runs the whole tree natively: each step starts on the UI thread the moment the previous one ends, with no gap and no JS in between.

```tsx
import { Animated, createNativeValue, Easing } from "nsh/animated";

const ys = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4].map(() => createNativeValue(0));
const fade = createNativeValue(1);

const hop = Animated.stagger(
  80,
  ys.map((y) =>
    Animated.sequence([
      Animated.timing(y, { toValue: -30, duration: 200, easing: Easing.out(Easing.quad) }),
      Animated.spring(y, { toValue: 0, stiffness: 300, damping: 12 }),
    ]),
  ),
);

const breathe = Animated.loop(
  Animated.sequence([
    Animated.timing(fade, { toValue: 0.3, duration: 400 }),
    Animated.timing(fade, { toValue: 1, duration: 400 }),
  ]),
);

hop.start(({ finished }) => console.log(finished ? "landed" : "stopped"));
```

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `Animated.timing(value, { toValue, duration?, easing?, delay? })` | A timing step. |
| `Animated.spring(value, { toValue, stiffness?, damping?, mass?, velocity? })` | A spring step. |
| `Animated.decay(value, { velocity?, deceleration?, clamp?, bounce? })` | A decay step. |
| `Animated.sequence(list)` | One after another. |
| `Animated.parallel(list, { stopTogether? })` | All at once. |
| `Animated.stagger(ms, list)` | All at once, each starting `ms` after the previous one. |
| `Animated.delay(ms)` | Waits. |
| `Animated.loop(animation, { iterations?, resetBeforeIteration? })` | Repeats (forever by default). |

A `CompositeAnimation` has `start(callback?)` (also a promise of `finished`; calling it again runs it again), `stop()` (stops where it is) and `reset()` (stops and puts its values back where they were when it started). The callback runs once for the whole tree.

A running animation does not keep its values alive: when the component that owns them goes (its views and variables), an endless `Animated.loop` stops with them, and its promise resolves with `false`.

## Easing

`Easing` from `nsh/animated` gives the standard easing curves. They are data, evaluated natively, not JS functions.

| Easing | Description |
|---|---|
| `Easing.linear`, `Easing.ease` | Constant speed; CSS's `ease`. |
| `Easing.quad`, `Easing.cubic`, `Easing.poly(n)` | `t²`, `t³`, `tⁿ`. |
| `Easing.sin`, `Easing.circle`, `Easing.exp` | Sinusoidal, circular, exponential. |
| `Easing.back(s?)` | Pulls back before going (overshoot `s`, 1.70158 by default). |
| `Easing.elastic(bounciness?)` | Springy overshoot. |
| `Easing.bounce` | Bounces at the end. |
| `Easing.bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)` | A cubic Bézier, as in CSS. |
| `Easing.in(e)`, `Easing.out(e)`, `Easing.inOut(e)` | The curves are "in" curves; `out` and `inOut` turn them around. |

Anywhere an easing is accepted you can also pass a name (`"linear"`, `"ease"`, `"easeIn"`, `"easeOut"`, `"easeInOut"`) or a Bézier array `[x1, y1, x2, y2]`.

```tsx
x.timing(1, { easing: Easing.out(Easing.back()) });
x.timing(1, { easing: "easeOut" });
x.timing(1, { easing: [0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1] });
```

`Easing.sample(easing, count)` returns the curve at `count` evenly spaced points from 0 to 1, and `Animated.sampleSpring(config, fps?)` / `Animated.sampleDecay(config, fps?)` the values a spring or decay moves through, one per frame (60 per second by default) from `config.from` (0) until it ends. They are computed by the same native code the animations run, so a chart of a curve shows exactly what the animation does:

```ts
const curve = Easing.sample(Easing.out(Easing.back()), 50); // 50 progress values
const spring = Animated.sampleSpring({ toValue: 1, stiffness: 180, damping: 8 });
```

## LayoutAnimation

`LayoutAnimation.configureNext(config)` animates the frame changes of the **next** update natively: views that move or resize glide to their new frames, new views fade (or scale) in, removed views fade out. Call it right before the state change.

```tsx
import { signal } from "nsh";
import { LayoutAnimation } from "nsh/animated";

const items = signal([1, 2, 3]);
let next = 4;

const add = () => {
  LayoutAnimation.configureNext(LayoutAnimation.Presets.spring);
  items.set([next++, ...items()]);
};
const remove = () => {
  LayoutAnimation.easeInEaseOut();
  items.set(items().slice(1));
};
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `configureNext(config, onEnd?)` | Animates the next commit's changes; `onEnd` runs when done. |
| `create(duration, type?, property?)` | A config with one curve for all three phases. |
| `Presets.easeInEaseOut`, `Presets.linear`, `Presets.spring` | Ready-made configs. |
| `easeInEaseOut(onEnd?)`, `linear(onEnd?)`, `spring(onEnd?)` | `configureNext` with a preset. |
| `Types`, `Properties` | The names, for building configs. |

A config is `{ duration, create?, update?, delete? }`: `create` for inserted views, `update` for moved or resized ones, `delete` for removed ones. Each phase is `{ type?, property?, duration?, delay?, springDamping? }`, where `type` is `"easeInEaseOut"`, `"spring"`, `"linear"`, `"easeIn"` or `"easeOut"`, `property` is what appearing and disappearing views animate (`"opacity"`, `"scaleXY"`, `"scale"`), and `springDamping` (0..1, 0.7 by default) sets the spring's overshoot.

```tsx
LayoutAnimation.configureNext({
  duration: 300,
  create: { type: "easeOut", property: "opacity" },
  update: { type: "spring", springDamping: 0.8 },
  delete: { type: "easeIn", property: "scaleXY" },
});
```

## What runs where

| | Runs on | JS per frame |
|---|---|---|
| Transitions, keyframe animations | UI thread | none |
| `timing` / `spring` / `decay`, composites | UI thread | none; JS hears when they end |
| `interpolate`, arithmetic, `diffClamp` | UI thread | none |
| `scrollValue`, `pan` / `pinch` / `rotation` | UI thread | none; JS hears start and end |
| LayoutAnimation | UI thread | none |
| `requestAnimationFrame` loops, `onScroll` handlers, `PanResponder` | JS, then a re-render | every frame |

Reach for `requestAnimationFrame` (a global, following the display) only for what cannot be described ahead of time, such as a physics simulation in JS. Anything that can be a native value should be one.

## Reduced motion

When the user asks for less motion (iOS "Reduce Motion", Android "Remove animations"), `reduceMotion()` from `nsh/accessibility` is `true` and the `motion-reduce:` / `motion-safe:` Tailwind variants apply. NSH does not turn your animations off by itself; use them to choose a calmer alternative:

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { reduceMotion } from "nsh/accessibility";

const open = () => (reduceMotion() ? panel.set(0) : panel.spring(0));

<View class="motion-safe:animate-bounce" />
```

See [Accessibility](https://nsh.dev/docs/accessibility.md#reduced-motion).

## Related

- [`nsh/animated`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-animated.md): the reference.
- [Touch and gestures](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md): driving native values with the finger.
- [Scrolling](https://nsh.dev/docs/scrolling.md#scroll-linked-effects-scrollvalue): `scrollValue`.
- [Canvas](https://nsh.dev/docs/canvas.md#animating-with-native-values): native values in drawings.
- [Style reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/style-reference.md): the `transition*` and `animation*` keys.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/animation

# Canvas

`Canvas` from `nsh/canvas` is a view you draw into with the HTML Canvas 2D API: charts, progress rings, gauges, signatures, custom icons, anything that is easier to draw than to build out of views. Your `draw` function records the drawing in one go; the platform replays it natively (Core Graphics on iOS, `android.graphics.Canvas` on Android) at the screen's resolution, so drawings stay sharp at any pixel density.

```tsx
import { mount, View } from "nsh";
import { Canvas } from "nsh/canvas";

function App() {
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, padding: 24, paddingTop: 60 }}>
      <Canvas
        style={{ height: 200, borderRadius: 12, backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}
        draw={(ctx, { width, height }) => {
          ctx.fillStyle = "#0969da";
          ctx.beginPath();
          ctx.arc(width / 2, height / 2, 60, 0, Math.PI * 2);
          ctx.fill();
          ctx.strokeStyle = "#1f2328";
          ctx.lineWidth = 4;
          ctx.strokeRect(20, 20, width - 40, height - 40);
        }}
      />
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

A `Canvas` takes every prop of a [`View`](https://nsh.dev/elements/view.md) (style, classes, touch handlers, accessibility, `ref`) plus `draw`. It needs a size from its style or layout; its content is the drawing. Coordinates are in points, with the origin at the top left.

## When draw runs

`draw(ctx, { width, height })` runs:

- once the canvas's size is known (after its first layout);
- again when the canvas is resized;
- again when a [signal](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md) it read changes.

Each run replaces the whole drawing. Reading signals inside `draw` is how a canvas follows your data:

```tsx
const values = signal([12, 30, 22, 48, 36, 60]);

<Canvas
  style={{ height: 160 }}
  draw={(ctx, { width, height }) => {
    const v = values();
    const x = (i: number) => (i / (v.length - 1)) * width;
    const y = (n: number) => height - (n / 100) * height;
    ctx.beginPath();
    v.forEach((n, i) => (i === 0 ? ctx.moveTo(x(i), y(n)) : ctx.lineTo(x(i), y(n))));
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#3b82f6";
    ctx.lineWidth = 2.5;
    ctx.lineJoin = "round";
    ctx.stroke();
  }}
/>
```

Context calls only record: nothing is drawn while `draw` runs, so you cannot read pixels back. The recording is sent to the platform as one operation after `draw` returns.

## The 2D context

`CanvasRenderingContext2D` is a subset of the HTML Canvas 2D API. What is supported:

**State**

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `save()`, `restore()` | Push and pop the drawing state (styles, transform, clip). |
| `fillStyle`, `strokeStyle` | A CSS color, a gradient, or a native value interpolating colors. |
| `lineWidth`, `lineCap`, `lineJoin`, `miterLimit` | Stroke shape. |
| `setLineDash(segments)`, `getLineDash()`, `lineDashOffset` | Dashes. |
| `globalAlpha` | Opacity of what is drawn next, 0..1. |
| `globalCompositeOperation` | How it combines: `"source-over"`, `"destination-out"`, `"multiply"`, `"screen"`, ... |
| `shadowColor`, `shadowBlur`, `shadowOffsetX`, `shadowOffsetY` | Shadows. |
| `font` | CSS `font` shorthand: `"600 14px Inter"` (sizes in px, pt or rem); `small-caps` and the number forms `tabular-nums`, `oldstyle-nums`, ... may come before the size. |
| `fontVariantNumeric` | `"tabular-nums"` makes every figure the same width, so changing numbers (counters, prices, axis labels) do not jitter; also `"proportional-nums"`, `"oldstyle-nums"`, `"lining-nums"`, `"normal"`. An NSH addition (CSS's `font-variant-numeric`); setting `font` keeps it. Browsers ignore it. |
| `textAlign`, `textBaseline` | Text placement. |

**Transforms**: `translate(x, y)`, `scale(x, y)`, `rotate(angle)` (radians, clockwise), `transform(a, b, c, d, e, f)`, `setTransform(a, b, c, d, e, f)`, `resetTransform()`.

**Paths**: `beginPath()`, `moveTo`, `lineTo`, `quadraticCurveTo`, `bezierCurveTo`, `arc`, `arcTo`, `ellipse`, `rect`, `roundRect(x, y, w, h, radii)`, `closePath()`; then `fill(rule?)`, `stroke()` and `clip(rule?)`, each also taking a `Path2D`. Fill rules are `"nonzero"` and `"evenodd"`.

**Rectangles**: `fillRect`, `strokeRect`, `clearRect`.

**Text**: `fillText(text, x, y, maxWidth?)`, `strokeText(...)`, `measureText(text)` (measured synchronously by the platform's text engine with the current `font`; only `width`).

**Hit testing**: `isPointInPath(path?, x, y, rule?)` and `isPointInStroke(path?, x, y)` answer synchronously, computed from the recorded geometry (the current transform, path, `lineWidth` and `lineCap`). Keep the context of the last `draw` and the `Path2D`s you drew to find the shape under a tap:

```tsx
let ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D | undefined;
const slices = [new Path2D("M50 50 L100 50 A50 50 0 0 1 50 100 Z"), /* ... */];

<Canvas
  style={{ width: 100, height: 100 }}
  onStartShouldSetResponder={() => true}
  onResponderRelease={(e) => {
    const hit = slices.findIndex((p) => ctx?.isPointInPath(p, e.locationX, e.locationY));
    if (hit >= 0) select(hit);
  }}
  draw={(c) => {
    ctx = c;
    slices.forEach((p) => c.fill(p));
  }}
/>
```

Strokes are tested with round joins and without dashes; coordinates given as native values count as 0.

**Gradients**: `createLinearGradient`, `createRadialGradient`, `createConicGradient`, each with `addColorStop(offset, color)`.

**Images**: `drawImage(image, dx, dy)`, `drawImage(image, dx, dy, dw, dh)`, `drawImage(image, sx, sy, sw, sh, dx, dy, dw, dh)`.

`ctx.canvas.width` and `ctx.canvas.height` give the canvas's size in points.

**Not supported**: `getImageData` / `putImageData` and other pixel access, `filter`, SVG images in `drawImage`. An invalid color or font drops that one operation, as in HTML Canvas.

## Paths and Path2D

`Path2D` holds a path you build once and fill, stroke or clip many times. It takes SVG path data, parsed natively, which makes icons easy:

```tsx
import { Canvas, Path2D } from "nsh/canvas";

const heart = new Path2D("M12 21s-7-4.35-9.5-8.5C.5 8.5 3 4 7 4c2 0 3.5 1 5 3 1.5-2 3-3 5-3 4 0 6.5 4.5 4.5 8.5C19 16.65 12 21 12 21z");

function Heart(props: { size: number; color: string }) {
  return (
    <Canvas
      style={{ width: props.size, height: props.size }}
      draw={(ctx) => {
        ctx.scale(props.size / 24, props.size / 24); // the path is drawn on a 24-point grid
        ctx.fillStyle = props.color;
        ctx.fill(heart);
      }}
    />
  );
}
```

A `Path2D` has the same path methods as the context (`moveTo`, `arc`, `roundRect`, ...) and `addPath(other)`. `new Path2D(other)` copies a path.

## Gradients

```tsx
<Canvas
  style={{ height: 120 }}
  draw={(ctx, { width, height }) => {
    const linear = ctx.createLinearGradient(0, 0, width, 0);
    linear.addColorStop(0, "#22d3ee");
    linear.addColorStop(1, "#6366f1");
    ctx.fillStyle = linear;
    ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height / 2);

    const radial = ctx.createRadialGradient(width / 2, height * 0.75, 4, width / 2, height * 0.75, 40);
    radial.addColorStop(0, "#fde68a");
    radial.addColorStop(1, "#f97316");
    ctx.fillStyle = radial;
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(width / 2, height * 0.75, 28, 0, Math.PI * 2);
    ctx.fill();
  }}
/>
```

`createConicGradient(startAngle, x, y)` sweeps colors around a point; its start angle is in radians, clockwise from the x axis. A conic gradient on a stroked arc makes a gradient progress ring.

## Text

```tsx
ctx.font = "600 20px system-ui";
ctx.fillStyle = "#1f2328";
ctx.textAlign = "center";
ctx.textBaseline = "middle";
ctx.fillText("72%", width / 2, height / 2);

ctx.font = "11px system-ui";
const label = "100";
ctx.fillText(label, 32 - 6 - ctx.measureText(label).width, 16);
```

Font families are the same as in styles: system families and the names of fonts your app imports (see [Fonts](https://nsh.dev/docs/fonts.md)).

## Images

`drawImage` takes a URL, an imported asset (`import logo from "./logo.png"`) or `{ uri }`. The image is loaded natively, and the canvas draws again once it has loaded, so you do not need to track loading yourself. Remote URLs are subject to the app's [network capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

```tsx
import { Canvas } from "nsh/canvas";
import logo from "./logo.png";

<Canvas
  style={{ width: 120, height: 120 }}
  draw={(ctx) => {
    ctx.save();
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(60, 60, 56, 0, Math.PI * 2);
    ctx.clip(); // a round avatar
    ctx.drawImage(logo, 4, 4, 112, 112);
    ctx.restore();
  }}
/>
```

The nine-argument form takes the source rectangle in the image's pixels.

## Animating with native values

Any number argument of a drawing call, and `fillStyle` / `strokeStyle`, can be a [native value](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md#native-values) or a node derived from it. Such arguments are read while the platform draws, and when the value animates, the platform redraws on its own, every frame, without running `draw` or any other JS.

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { createNativeValue, Easing } from "nsh/animated";
import { Canvas } from "nsh/canvas";

function Ring() {
  const progress = createNativeValue(0.3);
  const label = signal(30);
  const go = (to: number) => {
    label.set(Math.round(to * 100));
    progress.timing(to, { duration: 900, easing: Easing.inOut(Easing.cubic) });
  };
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center", gap: 16 }}>
      <Canvas
        style={{ width: 140, height: 140 }}
        draw={(ctx, { width, height }) => {
          const cx = width / 2, cy = height / 2, r = width / 2 - 10;
          ctx.lineWidth = 12;
          ctx.lineCap = "round";
          ctx.strokeStyle = "#e5e7eb";
          ctx.beginPath();
          ctx.arc(cx, cy, r, 0, Math.PI * 2);
          ctx.stroke();
          ctx.strokeStyle = "#6366f1";
          ctx.beginPath();
          // The end angle reads the native value on every frame.
          ctx.arc(cx, cy, r, -Math.PI / 2, progress.mul(Math.PI * 2).sub(Math.PI / 2));
          ctx.stroke();
          ctx.fillStyle = "#1f2328";
          ctx.font = "600 22px system-ui";
          ctx.textAlign = "center";
          ctx.textBaseline = "middle";
          ctx.fillText(`${label()}%`, cx, cy);
        }}
      />
      <View onPress={() => go(Math.random())}>
        <Text style={{ color: "#0969da" }}>Animate</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(Ring);
```

The arc's end angle is `progress.mul(2π).sub(π/2)`: a node, so the ring sweeps natively for 900 ms while `draw` ran only once (and once more for the label, which reads a signal). A clock's second hand works the same way: `ctx.rotate(seconds.mul(Math.PI / 30))` with `seconds` animated linearly.

Colors animate the same way: `ctx.fillStyle = t.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 1], outputRange: ["#54aeff", "#cf222e"] })`.

## Touch on a canvas

A canvas is a view, so it takes presses and the [responder system](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md#the-responder-system). Finger drawing records points in a signal and draws them:

```tsx
const strokes = signal<[number, number][][]>([]);

<Canvas
  style={{ height: 240 }}
  onStartShouldSetResponder={() => true}
  onResponderGrant={(e) => {
    strokes.set([...strokes(), [[e.locationX, e.locationY]]]);
    return true; // a scroll view around must not take the touches
  }}
  onResponderMove={(e) => {
    const all = strokes();
    strokes.set([...all.slice(0, -1), [...all[all.length - 1], [e.locationX, e.locationY]]]);
  }}
  draw={(ctx) => {
    ctx.lineWidth = 3;
    ctx.lineCap = "round";
    ctx.lineJoin = "round";
    for (const s of strokes()) {
      ctx.beginPath();
      s.forEach(([x, y], i) => (i === 0 ? ctx.moveTo(x, y) : ctx.lineTo(x, y)));
      ctx.stroke();
    }
  }}
/>
```

## Performance

- A drawing is recorded in Rust as JS calls the context, and travels to the platform as one operation; there is no per-call bridge crossing.
- `draw` re-records everything. Keep the work in `draw` proportional to what is shown, and keep data that changes every frame in native values rather than signals.
- Split a drawing that has a static part and a frequently changing part into two canvases stacked on top of each other, so only one redraws.
- Inside a zooming scroll view, canvases are drawn again at the zoomed resolution when the zoom ends.

- [`Canvas` element](https://nsh.dev/elements/canvas.md) and [`nsh/canvas`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-canvas.md): the reference.
- [Animation](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md): native values, `interpolate` and `Easing`.
- [Images and assets](https://nsh.dev/docs/images-and-assets.md): importing images.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/canvas

# Web view and video

`WebView` from `nsh/webview` and `Video` from `nsh/video` embed the platform's own web engine and media player as ordinary views. Because NSH renders with native views, they sit in your layout like any other element: they scroll with their parent, take rounded corners and clipping, and other views can overlap them without layering problems.

| Component | iOS | Android | macOS | Linux | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `WebView` | WKWebView | `android.webkit.WebView` | WKWebView | WebKitGTK 6.0's `WebKitWebView` | WebView2, in a child window |
| `Video` | AVPlayerLayer; AVPlayerViewController with `controls` | MediaPlayer on a TextureView; MediaController with `controls` | AVPlayerLayer; AVKit's AVPlayerView with `controls` | GTK's media stream (GStreamer) in a `GtkPicture`; `GtkVideo` with `controls` | Media Foundation's media engine, frames drawn with Direct2D; NSH's own control bar with `controls` |

The frameworks behind them (WebKit, AVFoundation) are loaded the first time an app uses one, so apps that never show a web page or a video do not pay for them at launch. Import them from `nsh/webview` and `nsh/video`.

On [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md) the web view has no scroll view of its own: with `scrollEnabled={false}` the mouse wheel and the
trackpad scroll the app's scroll views around it instead of the page, which still scrolls with its keyboard and its
own scripts.

On [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md) a web view is a WebKitGTK page drawn inside its view: NSH content over it (a dialog, a sheet)
covers it, and its parents clip it. The `webview` capability also applies to the navigations of frames there (an
`iframe` of a host that is not granted stays empty), and `scrollEnabled: false` stops the page itself from scrolling
(elements inside it still scroll). Apps need WebKitGTK 6.0 installed; a runtime built without it shows a neutral
placeholder. Videos play the formats the installed GStreamer plugins decode; `rate` is not supported (they
play at 1×), and `onEnd` only comes for videos that do not loop.

On [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md) a web view is a WebView2 control in a child window that follows its view: it is clipped to
its parents and rounded corners, but NSH content drawn over it (a dialog, a sheet) stays under it. It needs the
WebView2 Runtime (part of Windows 11; installed with Edge on Windows 10), else it shows a placeholder;
`source.baseUrl` for HTML, `scrollEnabled` and `allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures` are not supported. Videos are
ordinary content (clipped, transformed and covered like any view) and play the formats the installed Media Foundation
codecs decode; `rate` works, there is no poster, and the control bar always shows while `controls` is on.

## WebView

```tsx
import { mount } from "nsh";
import { WebView } from "nsh/webview";

function App() {
  return <WebView source="https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swift_(programming_language)" style={{ flex: 1 }} />;
}

mount(App);
```

### Sources

| `source` | Shows |
|---|---|
| `"https://…"` or `{ uri: "https://…" }` | A web page. |
| `{ html: "<!doctype html>…" }` | HTML from a string. |
| `{ html, baseUrl: "https://example.com/" }` | HTML whose relative URLs resolve against `baseUrl`. |

Changing `source` loads the new page.

### Props

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `source` | `string \| { uri } \| { html, baseUrl? }` | | What to show. |
| `injectedJavaScript` | `string` | | Runs after each page loads. |
| `injectedJavaScriptBeforeContentLoaded` | `string` | | Runs before each page's own scripts. |
| `javaScriptEnabled` | `boolean` | `true` | Pages run scripts. |
| `scrollEnabled` | `boolean` | `true` | The user can scroll the page. |
| `userAgent` | `string` | | The browser's user agent string. |
| `ios={{ allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures }}` | `boolean` | | iOS: swipe back and forward through the page history. |
| `desktop={{ allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures }}` | `boolean` | | macOS: swipe with two fingers on the trackpad to go back and forward; Windows: swipe on a touchscreen; Linux: swipe on the touchpad. |

Events:

| Event | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `onLoadStart` | `WebViewNavigation` | A page started loading. |
| `onLoad` | `WebViewNavigation` | A page finished loading. |
| `onError` | `{ message }` | Loading failed. |
| `onNavigationStateChange` | `WebViewNavigation` | The URL, title, loading state or history changed. |
| `onMessage` | `{ data: string }` | The page posted a message (below). |

`WebViewNavigation` is `{ url, title, loading, canGoBack, canGoForward }`.

### A browser with back and forward

The ref has `reload()`, `goBack()`, `goForward()`, `stopLoading()`, `injectJavaScript(script)` and `postMessage(data)`:

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { WebView, type WebViewNavigation } from "nsh/webview";

function Browser() {
  let web!: YNode;
  const nav = signal<WebViewNavigation | null>(null);
  const button = (label: string, enabled: boolean, action: () => void) => (
    <Text onPress={enabled ? action : undefined} style={{ padding: 12, color: enabled ? "#0969da" : "#8c959f" }}>
      {label}
    </Text>
  );
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, paddingTop: 50 }}>
      <Text numberOfLines={1} style={{ paddingHorizontal: 12, color: "#57606a" }}>
        {nav()?.loading ? "Loading…" : nav()?.title ?? ""}
      </Text>
      <WebView
        ref={web}
        source="https://developer.mozilla.org/"
        style={{ flex: 1 }}
        onNavigationStateChange={(n) => nav.set(n)}
        ios={{ allowsBackForwardNavigationGestures: true }}
      />
      <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", justifyContent: "space-around" }}>
        {button("Back", !!nav()?.canGoBack, () => web.goBack())}
        {button("Forward", !!nav()?.canGoForward, () => web.goForward())}
        {button("Reload", true, () => web.reload())}
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(Browser);
```

### Messaging between the page and the app

Pages talk to the app with `window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage(string)`, which arrives as `onMessage`. The app talks to the page with the ref's `postMessage(string)`, which arrives in the page as a `message` event on `window`. Messages are strings; send JSON for structured data.

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { WebView } from "nsh/webview";

const page = `<!doctype html>
<html><head><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width"></head>
<body style="font-family: -apple-system, sans-serif; margin: 16px">
  <button onclick="window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage(JSON.stringify({ type: 'hello', at: Date.now() }))">
    Post to the app
  </button>
  <p id="got">Nothing from the app yet.</p>
  <script>
    window.addEventListener("message", (e) => {
      document.getElementById("got").textContent = "The app says: " + e.data;
    });
  </script>
</body></html>`;

function App() {
  let web!: YNode;
  const last = signal("");
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, paddingTop: 50, gap: 12 }}>
      <WebView
        ref={web}
        source={{ html: page }}
        style={{ height: 240 }}
        onMessage={(e) => last.set(JSON.parse(e.data).type)}
      />
      <Text onPress={() => web.postMessage("hi from nsh")} style={{ padding: 16, color: "#0969da" }}>
        Post to the page
      </Text>
      <Text style={{ paddingHorizontal: 16 }}>Last message: {last()}</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

`injectJavaScript(script)` runs code in the current page at any time; `injectedJavaScript` and `injectedJavaScriptBeforeContentLoaded` run on every page load, before or after the page's own scripts, which is the place to install hooks:

```tsx
<WebView
  source="https://example.com"
  injectedJavaScriptBeforeContentLoaded={`window.isNativeApp = true;`}
  injectedJavaScript={`window.ReactNativeWebView.postMessage(document.title);`}
  onMessage={(e) => console.log("title", e.data)}
/>
```

### Which sites a web view may show

If your `nsh.json` declares `"capabilities"`, a web view may only show and navigate to the hosts listed under `webview`:

```json
{
  "capabilities": {
    "webview": { "hosts": ["example.com", "*.example.com"] }
  }
}
```

The check covers the web view's `source` and every top-level navigation the page makes (links, redirects, `location` changes); it is decided natively when the platform asks whether a navigation may proceed. A page's own subresources (scripts, images, frames) are the web content's business and are not checked. `*.example.com` matches subdomains only; list `example.com` as well for the bare domain. An app without a `"capabilities"` key may show any page. See [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

## Video

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { Video } from "nsh/video";

function Player() {
  let video!: YNode;
  const paused = signal(true);
  const time = signal("");
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, justifyContent: "center", padding: 16, gap: 12 }}>
      <Video
        ref={video}
        source="https://interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.mp4"
        paused={paused()}
        repeat
        resizeMode="contain"
        style={{ height: 220, borderRadius: 12, overflow: "hidden", backgroundColor: "#000000" }}
        onProgress={(e) => time.set(`${e.currentTime.toFixed(1)} / ${e.duration.toFixed(1)} s`)}
        onEnd={() => paused.set(true)}
      />
      <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", gap: 16, alignItems: "center" }}>
        <Text onPress={() => paused.set(!paused())} style={{ color: "#0969da", fontWeight: "600" }}>
          {paused() ? "Play" : "Pause"}
        </Text>
        <Text onPress={() => video.seek(0)} style={{ color: "#0969da" }}>
          Restart
        </Text>
        <Text style={{ color: "#57606a" }}>{time()}</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(Player);
```

Playback is controlled by props: set `paused`, `muted`, `volume` and `rate` from signals and the player follows. The ref has `seek(seconds)`.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `source` | `string \| { uri }` | | The video's URL. |
| `paused` | `boolean` | `false` | Playback is paused. |
| `muted` | `boolean` | `false` | No sound. |
| `volume` | `number` | `1` | 0..1. |
| `rate` | `number` | `1` | The playback speed. |
| `repeat` | `boolean` | `false` | Plays again from the start at the end. |
| `resizeMode` | `"cover" \| "contain" \| "stretch" \| "center"` | | How the picture fits the view. |
| `controls` | `boolean` | `false` | The platform's playback controls. |
| `progressUpdateInterval` | `number` | `250` | Milliseconds between `onProgress` events. |

| Event | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `onLoadStart` | | Loading started. |
| `onLoad` | `{ duration, width, height }` | The video is ready: its length in seconds and its size. |
| `onProgress` | `{ currentTime, duration }` | While playing, every `progressUpdateInterval` ms. |
| `onBuffer` | `{ isBuffering }` | Playback stalled waiting for data, or resumed. |
| `onEnd` | | Playback reached the end. |
| `onError` | `{ message }` | Loading or playback failed. |

With `controls`, the platform draws its own play button, scrubber and full-screen button. Without, draw your own with views over or below the video; since the video is a native view in your layout, overlays work naturally:

```tsx
<View style={{ height: 220 }}>
  <Video source={url} paused={paused()} style={{ flex: 1 }} />
  <View
    onPress={() => paused.set(!paused())}
    style={{ position: "absolute", top: 0, left: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}
  >
    <If when={paused()}>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 48, color: "#ffffff" }}>▶</Text>
    </If>
  </View>
</View>
```

Video sources are network requests: with declared capabilities, the video's host must be allowed under `network` in `nsh.json`, as for `fetch` and remote images. A refused source shows nothing, and the refusal is logged once with the key to add.

## Related

- [`WebView`](https://nsh.dev/elements/web-view.md) and [`Video`](https://nsh.dev/elements/video.md): the element references.
- [`nsh/webview`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-webview.md) and [`nsh/video`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-video.md).
- [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md): `webview` and `network` grants.
- [Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md): embedding other native views your host app provides.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/web-view-and-video
