# Networking

NSH apps make HTTP requests with the standard `fetch`. It runs on the platform's network stack (NSURLSession on iOS, HttpURLConnection on Android), so requests use the system's TLS, proxies and HTTP/2, and it streams both ways: a response body arrives as a stream as the stack delivers it, and a request body can be a stream sent as you produce it. The Fetch API's companions are there too: `Headers`, `Request`, `Response`, `AbortController`, `FormData`, `Blob`, `File`, `URL`, `URLSearchParams`, `TextEncoder` / `TextDecoder` and Web Streams.

## Getting JSON

```tsx
import { mount, Scroll, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";

type Post = { id: number; title: string };

function App() {
  const posts = signal<Post[]>([]);
  const status = signal("loading…");

  (async () => {
    try {
      const response = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?_limit=5");
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
      posts.set(await response.json());
      status.set("");
    } catch (e) {
      status.set(String(e));
    }
  })();

  return (
    <Scroll style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <View style={{ padding: 16, paddingTop: 60, gap: 8 }}>
        <Text style={{ color: "#57606a" }}>{status()}</Text>
        <Each of={posts()}>{(post) => <Text numberOfLines={1}>{post().title}</Text>}</Each>
      </View>
    </Scroll>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

A `Response` reads its body once, as `json()`, `text()`, `arrayBuffer()`, `bytes()`, `blob()` or `formData()`, or as the `body` stream. `response.ok` is true for 2xx statuses; like in browsers, an HTTP error status does not reject the promise.

## Sending data

```ts
// JSON
const created = await fetch("https://api.example.com/notes", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: "Groceries", items: ["milk", "eggs"] }),
});

// A form, URL-encoded
await fetch("https://api.example.com/login", {
  method: "POST",
  body: new URLSearchParams({ user: "ada", password: "…" }),
});

// Query strings
const url = new URL("https://api.example.com/search");
url.searchParams.set("q", "native shell");
url.searchParams.set("page", "2");
const results = await (await fetch(url)).json();
```

`body` accepts a string, `URLSearchParams`, `FormData`, a `Blob` or `File`, an `ArrayBuffer` or typed array, or a `ReadableStream`.

### Uploading files with FormData

A `FormData` body is sent as `multipart/form-data` with its boundary. NSH always sets that content type for a `FormData` body, even if a library sets a default `Content-Type` first, because without the boundary the server cannot parse it.

```ts
const form = new FormData();
form.append("title", "Sunset");
form.append("photo", new Blob([bytes], { type: "image/jpeg" }), "sunset.jpg");

const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/photos", { method: "POST", body: form });
```

## Streaming

### Reading a response as it arrives

`response.body` is a `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` filled as the network delivers bytes. Read it chunk by chunk to show progress or to process server-sent lines as they come:

```ts
const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/large.csv");
const total = Number(response.headers.get("Content-Length") ?? 0);
let received = 0;

for await (const chunk of response.body!) {
  received += chunk.length;
  progress.set(total ? received / total : 0);
}
```

Text streams decode with `TextDecoderStream`, and a `TransformStream` splits them into lines:

```ts
const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/events", { headers: { Accept: "text/event-stream" } });
let rest = "";
const lines = response
  .body!.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream())
  .pipeThrough(
    new TransformStream<string, string>({
      transform(chunk, controller) {
        const parts = (rest + chunk).split("\n");
        rest = parts.pop() ?? "";
        for (const line of parts) controller.enqueue(line);
      },
    }),
  );

for await (const line of lines) {
  if (line.startsWith("data: ")) messages.update((m) => [...m, line.slice(6)]);
}
```

Back pressure works end to end: while more than 1 MiB of a response waits unread, the request is paused at the network level until your code catches up.

### Streaming a request body

A `ReadableStream` body is sent chunk by chunk as the network stack asks for it (chunked transfer). Pass `duplex: "half"`, as the Fetch standard requires:

```ts
const encoder = new TextEncoder();
const body = new ReadableStream<Uint8Array>({
  async start(controller) {
    for (const line of logLines) controller.enqueue(encoder.encode(line + "\n"));
    controller.close();
  },
});

await fetch("https://api.example.com/logs", { method: "POST", body, duplex: "half" });
```

A streamed body cannot be sent twice, so a 307 or 308 redirect of a streamed request fails.

## Cancelling and timeouts

Pass an `AbortSignal` to cancel a request; the promise rejects with the signal's reason (an `AbortError` `DOMException` by default), and a body being read stops.

```ts
const controller = new AbortController();
const request = fetch("https://api.example.com/search?q=" + encodeURIComponent(query), { signal: controller.signal });

// Typing again: cancel the previous search.
controller.abort();
```

`AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` makes a signal that aborts after a delay, and `AbortSignal.any([...])` combines signals:

```ts
const response = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000) });
```

A component that loads data should cancel when it goes away, with [`cleanup`](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md):

```tsx
import { cleanup, signal, Text } from "nsh";

function Weather(props: { city: string }) {
  const data = signal<unknown>(null);
  const controller = new AbortController();
  cleanup(() => controller.abort());
  fetch(`https://api.example.com/weather?city=${encodeURIComponent(props.city)}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then((r) => r.json())
    .then((d) => data.set(d))
    .catch(() => {});
  return <Text>{JSON.stringify(data())}</Text>;
}
```

## Errors

A request that does not produce an HTTP response rejects with a `TypeError` whose message starts with `Network request failed:`: no connection, a DNS or TLS failure, an unsupported URL scheme, or a request your app's capabilities do not allow. Check `response.ok` or `response.status` for HTTP errors.

```ts
try {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Server answered ${response.status}`);
  return await response.json();
} catch (e) {
  if (e instanceof DOMException && e.name === "AbortError") return; // cancelled
  showError(String(e));
}
```

## Capabilities: which hosts an app may reach

An app may declare in `nsh.json` which hosts it talks to. Once `"capabilities"` is present, everything not listed is denied:

```json
{
  "capabilities": {
    "network": {
      "hosts": ["api.example.com", "*.cdn.example.com"],
      "http": [
        { "host": "quotes.example.com", "methods": ["GET"], "pathPrefix": "/v1/" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

| Key | Description |
|---|---|
| `network.hosts` | Hosts reachable with any method: `"*"` (any host), `"*.example.com"` (its subdomains, not `example.com` itself) or a host name. |
| `network.http` | Finer grants: a `host`, optionally limited to `methods`, `schemes` and a `pathPrefix`. |

The checks are enforced in Rust, outside your JS, before a request reaches the network:

- A refused `fetch` rejects with a `TypeError` whose message names the key to add, such as ``Network request failed: fetch GET https://evil.io/ is not granted: add `evil.io` to capabilities.network in nsh.json``.
- **Every redirect is checked again.** NSH follows redirects itself (up to 20) instead of letting the platform do it, so a granted host cannot redirect your app to one that is not.
- The same `network` grants cover remote images (also in canvases and `Image.getSize` / `prefetch`) and video sources. `asset:` URIs of your own bundle are always allowed.
- The host is taken after the last `@`, so `https://ok.com@evil.io` counts as `evil.io`.

An app without `"capabilities"` may reach every host: a standalone app is its developer's own. Apps embedded in a host app or distributed as [signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md) should declare them; the host app can grant less than an app declares, and a request must be allowed by both. Development with `nsh dev` / `nsh run` enforces the same capabilities. See [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

## Differences from browsers

NSH's `fetch` follows the Fetch standard with the differences that make sense for an app rather than a web page:

- **No CORS.** An app talks to any host its capabilities allow; there are no preflight requests and no opaque responses.
- **No forbidden headers.** An app may set `Cookie`, `User-Agent`, `Origin` and others.
- **`redirect: "manual"`** gives the 3xx response itself (with its `Location` header) rather than an opaque redirect. `redirect: "error"` rejects on a redirect.
- **`data:` and `blob:` URLs** are answered locally. `URL.createObjectURL(blob)` makes a `blob:` URL that `fetch` can read until you revoke it.
- Browser-only options (`mode`, `credentials`, `cache`, `referrer`, `integrity`, `keepalive`, `priority`) are accepted for compatibility with libraries.

Libraries built on `fetch` (and on `AbortController`, `FormData` and streams) generally work unchanged. There is no `XMLHttpRequest`, and no WebSocket API.

## From Rust components

Rust components and modules make requests with `fetch` in a task. It goes through the same network stack as JS's
`fetch` (the platform's, or the browser's [on the web](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md#apps-with-rust-components)) and the same
capability checks, and gives the whole response:

```rust
use nsh_core::ui::prelude::*;

spawn(async move {
    match fetch("https://api.example.com/items").await {
        Ok(response) if response.ok() => items.set(parse(&response.text())),
        Ok(response) => error.set(format!("HTTP {}", response.status())),
        Err(message) => error.set(message),
    }
});

// Other methods, headers and bodies:
let request = HttpRequest::post("https://api.example.com/items", body)
    .header("content-type", "application/json");
let response = fetch(request).await?;
```

The URL is absolute. A request whose task ends (the component goes, or the task is cancelled) is cancelled with it.

## Related

- [Global APIs](https://nsh.dev/modules/globals.md): every global, with its members.
- [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md): capabilities, limits and how the embedding app grants them.
- [Images and assets](https://nsh.dev/docs/images-and-assets.md): remote images.
- [Lists](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md#loading-more-onendreached): paging through an API.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/networking

# Device and environment

The environment an app runs in changes while it runs: the window resizes (rotation, split view, a Mac window), the user switches to dark mode or a larger text size, the keyboard comes and goes. NSH exposes each of these as a **reactive accessor**: call it like a signal, and whatever read it (a style, a text, a computed value) updates when it changes. There are no listeners to add or remove.

| Accessor | Module | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `windowSize()` | `nsh/device` | `{ width, height }` of the surface, in points. |
| `colorScheme()` | `nsh/device` | `"light"` or `"dark"`: the system's, or the app's own (`setColorScheme`). |
| `fontScale()` | `nsh/device` | The user's preferred text size relative to the default (1 is the default). |
| `safeArea()` | `nsh/ui/mobile` | Insets of the surface not covered by system UI: `{ top, right, bottom, left }`. |
| `useSafeAreaInsets()` | `nsh/ui/mobile` | The insets where the calling component renders (a screen, a modal). |
| `keyboard()` | `nsh/ui/mobile` | `{ height, duration }` of the software keyboard. |
| `I18nManager.isRTL` | `nsh/device` | Whether the app lays out right to left. |
| `reduceMotion()`, `screenReaderEnabled()` | `nsh/accessibility` | See [Accessibility](https://nsh.dev/docs/accessibility.md). |

```tsx
import { mount, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { colorScheme, fontScale, windowSize } from "nsh/device";
import { safeArea } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function App() {
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, paddingTop: safeArea().top + 16, paddingHorizontal: 16, backgroundColor: colorScheme() === "dark" ? "#0d1117" : "#ffffff" }}>
      <Text style={{ color: colorScheme() === "dark" ? "#e6edf3" : "#1f2328" }}>
        {Math.round(windowSize().width)} × {Math.round(windowSize().height)} pt, text at {fontScale().toFixed(2)}×
      </Text>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

## Window size and responsive layout

`windowSize()` is the size of the surface NSH renders into: the screen on a phone, the window on an iPad in split view or on a Mac, the host view when NSH is embedded. Use it to change the layout, not only sizes:

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { windowSize } from "nsh/device";
import { Image } from "nsh/image";

function Gallery() {
  const columns = () => (windowSize().width >= 700 ? 4 : windowSize().width >= 500 ? 3 : 2);
  return (
    <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", flexWrap: "wrap", gap: 8 }}>
      <Each of={photos}>
        {(p) => <Image src={p().url} style={{ width: (windowSize().width - 32 - (columns() - 1) * 8) / columns(), aspectRatio: 1 }} />}
      </Each>
    </View>
  );
}
```

Often flexbox, percentages and `aspectRatio` do the job without reading the size at all; see [Layout](https://nsh.dev/docs/layout.md). With Tailwind, the breakpoint variants (`sm:`, `md:`, `lg:`, `xl:`, `2xl:`, `max-*:`, `min-[…]:`) and `portrait:` / `landscape:` follow the window too: `class="grid grid-cols-2 md:grid-cols-4"`.

## Dark mode

`colorScheme()` follows the system appearance unless the app sets its own. The simplest way to support dark mode is the `dark:` Tailwind variant, which applies when `colorScheme()` is `"dark"`:

```tsx
<View class="flex-1 bg-white dark:bg-zinc-900 p-4">
  <Text class="text-zinc-900 dark:text-zinc-100">Follows the system appearance</Text>
</View>
```

With inline styles, read `colorScheme()` in the style; for more than a few colors, derive a palette once:

```tsx
import { computed, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { colorScheme } from "nsh/device";

const palette = computed(() =>
  colorScheme() === "dark"
    ? { background: "#0d1117", surface: "#161b22", text: "#e6edf3", muted: "#8b949e" }
    : { background: "#f6f8fa", surface: "#ffffff", text: "#1f2328", muted: "#57606a" },
);

<View style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: palette().background }}>
  <Text style={{ color: palette().text }}>Hello</Text>
</View>
```

The components of `nsh/ui/mobile` take their colors from the component theme, which has light and dark values (`nsh.json` `"theme"`), so they switch with the system as well. To match the status bar to your background, see [`StatusBar`](https://nsh.dev/components/status-bar.md).

### An app with its own appearance

An app that is always dark (or always light) says so in `nsh.json`, and `colorScheme()`, `dark:` classes, the component theme, the status bar's default style and alerts follow it from the first frame (packaged apps also launch in it):

```json
{ "appearance": "dark" }
```

`setColorScheme` from `nsh/device` changes it at run time, for an in-app appearance setting; `"system"` follows the system again:

```tsx
import { colorScheme, setColorScheme } from "nsh/device";

<Button title={colorScheme() === "dark" ? "Light" : "Dark"} onPress={() => setColorScheme(colorScheme() === "dark" ? "light" : "dark")} />
```

> [!TIP]
> Test both appearances while developing: `xcrun simctl ui booted appearance dark` switches an iOS simulator, and Android has a dark theme toggle in Quick Settings. The change reaches your app at once, without a reload.

## Text size

`fontScale()` is the user's text size setting (Dynamic Type on iOS, font size on Android) relative to the default. Text and inputs follow it by themselves: `fontSize: 16` renders larger when the user asked for larger text. Per element you can opt out or cap it:

| Prop (on `<Text>` and `<Input>`) | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `allowFontScaling` | `true` | Follow the system text size. |
| `maxFontSizeMultiplier` | `0` (none) | The largest scale applied to this text. |

```tsx
<Text style={{ fontSize: 34, fontWeight: "700" }} maxFontSizeMultiplier={1.4}>Today</Text>
```

Read `fontScale()` to adapt layout that does not follow text automatically, such as switching a row to a column when the text gets large: `flexDirection: fontScale() > 1.3 ? "column" : "row"`.

## Safe areas

Notches, the home indicator, the status bar, Android's navigation bar and the Mac Catalyst title bar cover parts of the surface. NSH apps draw edge to edge on every platform, and get the covered parts as insets.

- `safeArea()` gives the surface's insets.
- `useSafeAreaInsets()` gives the insets **where the component renders**: inside a navigation [screen](https://nsh.dev/docs/navigation.md#safe-areas-under-the-header) they are measured below its header, inside a [modal](https://nsh.dev/docs/navigation.md#modals) they are the modal's. Prefer it in components that may be shown in several places.
- `SafeAreaView` from `nsh/ui/mobile` is a view padded by those insets (all edges by default, or `edges={["top", "bottom"]}`), on top of its own padding.

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { SafeAreaView, useSafeAreaInsets } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function Screen() {
  return (
    <SafeAreaView edges={["top", "left", "right"]} style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: "#ffffff" }}>
      <Content />
      <BottomBar />
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
}

function BottomBar() {
  const insets = useSafeAreaInsets();
  return <View style={{ paddingBottom: insets().bottom + 8, paddingTop: 8, flexDirection: "row" }}>…</View>;
}
```

On Android, a view embedded below a toolbar gets only the parts of the system bars that overlap it, like UIKit's safe area: no top inset if it does not reach the status bar.

## The platform

`Platform` from `nsh/device` describes where the app runs. It is not reactive: these do not change while the app runs.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `Platform.OS` | `"ios"`, `"android"`, `"macos"`, `"windows"`, `"linux"` or `"web"`. Mac Catalyst reports `"ios"`. |
| `Platform.Version` | iOS and desktops: the version string (`"17.5"`); Android: the API level (a number). |
| `Platform.isPad` | An iPad (or the iPad idiom). |
| `Platform.isTV` | A TV. |
| `Platform.isMacCatalyst` | Mac Catalyst in the Mac idiom. |
| `Platform.isDesktop` | macOS, Windows or Linux, or a desktop browser (the `"desktop"` idiom on the web). |
| `Platform.constants` | `{ osVersion, interfaceIdiom }`, the idiom being `"phone"`, `"pad"`, `"mac"`, `"tv"` or `"desktop"`. |
| `Platform.select(spec)` | The value for this platform; see [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md#platformselect). |

```tsx
import { Platform } from "nsh/device";

const hapticsSupported = Platform.OS === "ios" || (Platform.OS === "android" && (Platform.Version as number) >= 30);
```

`nsh trace` runs headless as iOS.

On [Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md), `Platform.OS` is `"linux"`, the idiom `"desktop"` and `Platform.Version` the kernel's major
and minor version (`"6.12"`): distributions number their releases in ways that cannot be compared. There, the safe
area and the keyboard height are 0, `colorScheme()` follows the desktop's setting (the XDG settings portal) live,
`fontScale()` the desktop's text scaling and `PixelRatio.get()` the display's scale, fractional ones included.

On [macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md) (the AppKit backend), `Platform.OS` is `"macos"`, the idiom `"desktop"` and
`Platform.Version` the macOS version. The safe area and the keyboard height are 0, `colorScheme()` follows the
system's appearance live, `fontScale()` is 1 and `PixelRatio.get()` the display's backing scale.

On [Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md), `Platform.OS` is `"windows"`, the idiom `"desktop"` and `Platform.Version` `"10.0"`, on
Windows 11 too (Windows kept the version number). The safe area and the keyboard height are 0, `colorScheme()` follows
Settings > Personalization > Colors live, `fontScale()` the Text size setting (1 to 2.25), `reduceMotion()` the
animation effects setting, `PixelRatio.get()` the monitor's scale, and `Intl` formats in the user's regional format.

In a browser ([the web runtime](https://nsh.dev/docs/web.md)), `Platform.OS` is `"web"` and `Platform.Version` `"0.0"`. The idiom is
`"desktop"` with a mouse and a window at least 600 points wide (then `Platform.isDesktop` is `true`), `"pad"` on a
tablet and `"phone"` on a phone, decided when the app starts. The locale, `reduceMotion()`, `fontScale()` (the
browser's text size), `PixelRatio.get()`, the safe area and the keyboard height come from the browser and follow it
live.

## Pixel density

`PixelRatio` from `nsh/device` converts between points and device pixels.

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `PixelRatio.get()` | Device pixels per point (2 or 3 on most phones). |
| `PixelRatio.getFontScale()` | The same as `fontScale()`, not reactive. |
| `PixelRatio.getPixelSizeForLayoutSize(points)` | Points to whole device pixels. |
| `PixelRatio.roundToNearestPixel(points)` | Points rounded to the nearest device pixel. |

A hairline, one device pixel tall:

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { PixelRatio } from "nsh/device";

const hairline = 1 / PixelRatio.get();
<View style={{ height: hairline, backgroundColor: "#d0d7de" }} />
```

`PixelRatio` is not reactive. A window can move to a screen with another density (a Mac with an external display), so read it in components that also read `windowSize()`, which changes in that case.

## Right to left

When the device language is written right to left (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, ...), NSH lays the app out right to left: rows run from the right, `left` and `right` style properties swap, text aligns to the right, and native widgets mirror. `I18nManager` from `nsh/device` controls it:

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `I18nManager.isRTL` | Whether the app lays out right to left (reactive). |
| `I18nManager.allowRTL(allow)` | Follow right-to-left languages (default `true`). |
| `I18nManager.forceRTL(force)` | Lay out right to left whatever the language. |
| `I18nManager.getConstants()` | `{ isRTL, doLeftAndRightSwapInRTL }`. |

Changes apply at once, without restarting the app; the demo on this page toggles `forceRTL`.

Write layouts that work both ways with the logical properties: `marginStart` / `marginEnd`, `paddingStart` / `paddingEnd`, `start` / `end`, `borderTopStartRadius` and so on, which mean left and right in left-to-right layouts and the reverse right to left. `left` and `right` themselves also swap. The `direction` style (`"inherit"`, `"ltr"`, `"rtl"`) overrides the direction for a subtree, for example to keep a phone number or a media player's controls left to right. The `rtl:` and `ltr:` Tailwind variants apply per direction.

Horizontal scroll views and lists start at the right end in right-to-left layouts. On Android, the host app must declare `android:supportsRtl="true"` in its manifest for native widgets to mirror.

## Related

- [`nsh/device`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-device.md): the reference.
- [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md): `Platform.select`, platform props and modules.
- [Accessibility](https://nsh.dev/docs/accessibility.md): screen readers and reduced motion.
- [`SafeAreaView`](https://nsh.dev/components/safe-area-view.md) and [`StatusBar`](https://nsh.dev/components/status-bar.md).
- [Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md): `dark:`, breakpoint and orientation variants.

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment

# Accessibility

NSH renders with native views, so the platforms' assistive technologies (VoiceOver on iOS and Mac Catalyst, TalkBack on Android, Switch Control, Voice Control, ...) see your app's real view hierarchy. What you add are the descriptions those technologies cannot infer: what an element is, what it says, what state it is in and what it can do. Every element accepts the props below.

## What you get without doing anything

- **Text is read.** A `<Text>` is an accessibility element whose label is its text. A view without a label is read as the texts inside it.
- **Pressable views are elements.** A view with `onPress` or `onLongPress` is an accessibility element by default, and activating it (double tap with VoiceOver or TalkBack) presses it.
- **Inputs are text fields**, with their placeholder, value and keyboard.
- **Text follows the user's size setting.** See [Text size](#text-size).

## Labels, hints and roles

```tsx
<View
  onPress={play}
  accessibilityRole="button"
  accessibilityLabel="Play"
  accessibilityHint="Starts the song"
  style={{ width: 44, height: 44, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center" }}
>
  <Text>▶</Text>
</View>
```

| Prop | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `accessible` | `boolean` | The view is one element for assistive technologies; its children are not exposed separately. |
| `accessibilityLabel` | `string` | What screen readers read, instead of the texts inside. |
| `accessibilityHint` | `string` | What activating the element does, read after a pause. |
| `accessibilityRole` (or `role`) | `AccessibilityRole` | What the element is. |
| `accessibilityState` | `AccessibilityState` | Its state: disabled, selected, checked, busy, expanded. |
| `accessibilityValue` | `{ min?, max?, now?, text? }` | The value of a range or textual element. |
| `accessibilityActions` | `{ name, label? }[]` | Actions offered to assistive technologies. |
| `onAccessibilityAction` | `(e: { actionName }) => void` | An action was performed. |
| `accessibilityElementsHidden` | `boolean` | Hides the view and its subtree from assistive technologies. |
| `importantForAccessibility` | `"auto" \| "yes" \| "no" \| "no-hide-descendants"` | Whether the view (and its subtree) is exposed. |
| `android={{ accessibilityLiveRegion }}` | `"none" \| "polite" \| "assertive"` | Android: how changes of the view are announced to TalkBack. |
| `testID` | `string` | An identifier for UI tests (the accessibility identifier on iOS, the resource id on Android); not read aloud. |

Give every icon-only control a label: a screen reader cannot read a glyph or an image. Keep labels short and do not include the role ("Play", not "Play button"): the role is announced on its own.

### Roles

`accessibilityRole` tells the user what kind of element this is and how to operate it. The values are `"none"`, `"button"`, `"link"`, `"search"`, `"image"`, `"imagebutton"`, `"keyboardkey"`, `"text"`, `"adjustable"`, `"header"`, `"summary"`, `"alert"`, `"checkbox"`, `"combobox"`, `"menu"`, `"menubar"`, `"menuitem"`, `"progressbar"`, `"radio"`, `"radiogroup"`, `"scrollbar"`, `"spinbutton"`, `"switch"`, `"tab"`, `"tablist"`, `"timer"`, `"toolbar"`, `"list"` and `"grid"`.

The most useful ones:

- `"button"` for anything pressable that is not a link; `"link"` for navigation to content.
- `"header"` for section titles: screen reader users jump between headers to skim a screen.
- `"switch"`, `"checkbox"`, `"radio"` with `accessibilityState.checked`.
- `"adjustable"` for sliders and steppers, with `accessibilityValue` and the `increment` / `decrement` actions.
- `"image"` for meaningful images, with a label; decorative images should be hidden instead.

```tsx
<Text accessibilityRole="header" style={{ fontSize: 22, fontWeight: "700" }}>Settings</Text>
```

### States and values

```tsx
// A toggle drawn with views.
<View
  onPress={() => on.set(!on())}
  accessibilityRole="switch"
  accessibilityLabel="Wi-Fi"
  accessibilityState={{ checked: on() }}
  hitSlop={8}
  class="h-[31px] w-[51px] rounded-full p-0.5 transition-colors"
  classList={{ "bg-green-500": on(), "bg-zinc-300": !on() }}
>
  <View class="size-[27px] rounded-full bg-white transition-transform" classList={{ "translate-x-5": on() }} />
</View>
```

`accessibilityState` is `{ disabled?, selected?, checked?: boolean | "mixed", busy?, expanded? }`. `disabled` is also implied by the `disabled` prop. `accessibilityValue` with `min`, `max` and `now` is read as a percentage; with `text` it is read as given ("3 of 10", "Medium").

## Actions

A pressable view supports activation already. For anything else, declare actions and handle them:

```tsx
function Quantity() {
  const n = signal(1);
  return (
    <View
      accessible
      accessibilityRole="adjustable"
      accessibilityLabel="Quantity"
      accessibilityValue={{ text: String(n()) }}
      accessibilityActions={[{ name: "increment" }, { name: "decrement" }]}
      onAccessibilityAction={(e) => {
        if (e.actionName === "increment") n.update((v) => v + 1);
        if (e.actionName === "decrement") n.update((v) => Math.max(0, v - 1));
      }}
      style={{ flexDirection: "row", alignItems: "center", gap: 12 }}
    >
      <View onPress={() => n.update((v) => Math.max(0, v - 1))}><Text>−</Text></View>
      <Text>{n()}</Text>
      <View onPress={() => n.update((v) => v + 1)}><Text>+</Text></View>
    </View>
  );
}
```

Some action names are standard and map to the platforms' own gestures:

| Name | iOS (VoiceOver) | Android (TalkBack) |
|---|---|---|
| `activate` | Double tap | Double tap (click) |
| `increment`, `decrement` | Swipe up / down on an adjustable element | Scroll forward / backward |
| `longpress` | | Double tap and hold |
| `expand`, `collapse` | | Expand / collapse |
| `magicTap` | Two-finger double tap | |
| `escape` | Two-finger Z scrub | |

Any other name becomes a custom action, listed in VoiceOver's actions rotor and TalkBack's actions menu with its `label` (or its name). Custom actions are the accessible form of swipe-to-delete and similar gestures:

```tsx
<View
  accessibilityActions={[{ name: "archive", label: "Archive" }, { name: "delete", label: "Delete" }]}
  onAccessibilityAction={(e) => (e.actionName === "archive" ? archive(mail.id) : remove(mail.id))}
>
  …
</View>
```

## Grouping and hiding

`accessible` makes a view one element: a card with a title, a subtitle and a price is read in one go, instead of the user swiping through three texts.

```tsx
<View accessible onPress={open} accessibilityRole="button" style={{ padding: 16 }}>
  <Text>Blue jacket</Text>
  <Text>Size M</Text>
  <Text>$120</Text>
</View>
```

Hide what adds nothing: decorative images, dividers, an icon next to a text that already says the same.

```tsx
<Image src={decoration} accessibilityElementsHidden importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants" />
```

`accessibilityElementsHidden` (iOS's name) and `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"` (Android's) both hide the subtree on both platforms; setting both is harmless.

## AccessibilityInfo

`nsh/accessibility` reports the user's settings and lets you talk to the screen reader.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `screenReaderEnabled()` | Whether VoiceOver or TalkBack runs (reactive). |
| `reduceMotion()` | Whether the user asked for less motion (reactive). |
| `AccessibilityInfo.isScreenReaderEnabled()` | The same, as a promise. |
| `AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled()` | The same, as a promise. |
| `AccessibilityInfo.addEventListener(event, listener)` | `"screenReaderChanged"` or `"reduceMotionChanged"`; returns `{ remove() }`. |
| `AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility(message)` | The screen reader reads `message`. |
| `AccessibilityInfo.setAccessibilityFocus(ref)` | Moves the screen reader's focus to a view. |

Prefer the reactive accessors in components: they update what reads them, and need no cleanup.

```tsx
import { signal, Text, View, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { AccessibilityInfo, screenReaderEnabled } from "nsh/accessibility";

function Upload() {
  const done = signal(false);
  let result!: YNode;
  const finish = () => {
    done.set(true);
    AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility("Upload complete");
    AccessibilityInfo.setAccessibilityFocus(result);
  };
  return (
    <View style={{ gap: 12 }}>
      {/* Autoplaying carousels are hard to use with a screen reader: show a list instead. */}
      <If when={!screenReaderEnabled()} else={<PhotoList />}>
        <PhotoCarousel />
      </If>
      <Text ref={result}>{done() ? "Uploaded 3 photos" : "Uploading…"}</Text>
    </View>
  );
}
```

Announce changes the user would otherwise miss: a background save finishing, an error appearing away from the focus, a timer ending. On Android, `android={{ accessibilityLiveRegion: "polite" }}` on a view makes TalkBack announce its changes by itself.

## Text size

Text and inputs follow the system text size (Dynamic Type on iOS, font size on Android) unless you set `allowFontScaling={false}`. Rather than turning it off, design for it:

- Let text wrap: avoid fixed heights on views that contain text.
- Cap very large headings with `maxFontSizeMultiplier` instead of disabling scaling.
- Switch layouts when the text is large: read `fontScale()` from `nsh/device` (for example, stack a label and its value vertically above 1.3).

See [Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md#text-size).

## Reduced motion

`reduceMotion()` is `true` when the user turned on iOS's Reduce Motion or Android's remove animations setting. NSH does not disable your animations by itself. Use it, or the `motion-reduce:` and `motion-safe:` Tailwind variants, to replace large movement with a fade or an instant change:

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { reduceMotion } from "nsh/accessibility";
import { LayoutAnimation } from "nsh/animated";

const toggle = () => {
  if (!reduceMotion()) LayoutAnimation.configureNext(LayoutAnimation.Presets.spring);
  expanded.set(!expanded());
};

<View onPress={open} class="transition active:scale-95 motion-reduce:transition-none" />
<View class="motion-safe:animate-bounce" />
```

## Touch targets

Make pressable elements at least 44 × 44 points. When a control must look smaller, extend its touch area with `hitSlop` instead of its size; see [Touch and gestures](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md#hit-areas-hitslop).

## Checking your app

- Turn on VoiceOver (iOS Settings, Accessibility, or triple-click the side button if set up) or TalkBack, and use the app without looking: every control should say what it is and what it does.
- On iOS simulators, Xcode's Accessibility Inspector shows each element's label, traits and value.
- Try the largest text size and dark mode.
- `testID` gives UI tests a stable handle that does not change with the label's language.

## Related

- [`nsh/accessibility`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-accessibility.md): the reference.
- [`View`](https://nsh.dev/elements/view.md): every accessibility prop.
- [Animation](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md#reduced-motion) and [Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md).

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/accessibility

# Dev Server and Debugging

During development, NSH builds your app on every save and pushes it to every connected host, which updates in place.
Two commands do this:

- `nsh run` starts the dev server **and** launches a development host: a Mac Catalyst or AppKit window, a GTK window on
  Linux, a Win32 window on Windows, an iOS simulator or an Android device or emulator.
- `nsh dev` starts only the dev server, for hosts you start yourself: your own app with the development SDK, a device
  on the network, or several hosts at once.

```sh
nsh run App.tsx                     # Mac Catalyst window, 390×844 (macOS); GTK window (Linux); Win32 window (Windows)
nsh run App.tsx --target macos      # AppKit window (macOS)
nsh run App.tsx --target ios        # iOS simulator
nsh run App.tsx --target android    # Android device or emulator
nsh dev App.tsx                     # server only
```

## `nsh run`

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--target <catalyst \| ios \| android \| macos \| linux \| windows>` | Where to run. Default `catalyst` on macOS (an iPhone-sized, 390×844 Mac window), `linux` on Linux, `windows` on Windows. |
| `--device <name or UDID>` | The iOS simulator to use. Default: a booted one, else the newest iPhone (booted for you). |
| `--port <port>` | Dev server port. Default 8790; the next free port is used if it is taken. |
| `--release` | Serve release builds (minified, no debug info, no hot updates). |
| `--trace` | Log the time of every commit on the host. |

What each target does:

- **`catalyst`** (macOS) runs the development host as a Mac app. Stopping `nsh run` (Ctrl-C, or `kill`) closes it, and
  closing the window ends `nsh run`.
- **`macos`** (macOS) runs the AppKit development host, a desktop app in a 1200×800 window, the same way; Cmd+R
  reloads the latest build. Requires macOS 14 or later ([macOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md)).
- **`linux`** (Linux) runs the GTK development host in a 390×844 window, the same way: stopping `nsh run` closes
  it, closing the window ends `nsh run`. Requires GTK 4.14 or later ([Linux](https://nsh.dev/docs/linux.md)).
- **`windows`** (Windows) runs the Win32 development host in a 1200×800 window, the same way; the host never outlives
  `nsh run`, even when the console is closed. Requires Windows 10 1809 or later ([Windows](https://nsh.dev/docs/windows.md)).
- **`ios`** installs the development host in the simulator, launches it pointed at the dev server and keeps watching.
  The simulator shares the Mac's network, so the host reaches the server on `127.0.0.1`. Stopping `nsh run` (Ctrl-C)
  closes the host, which would otherwise join the next session. Requires Xcode.
- **`android`** installs the development host APK (again only when the runtime changed), runs
  `adb reverse tcp:<port> tcp:<port>` so the device's own `127.0.0.1` reaches the server, and starts it. Works with an
  emulator or a USB device. Requires the Android SDK (`ANDROID_HOME`). When `nsh run` ends (Ctrl-C too), it stops the
  host and removes that port forwarding, so the host does not join the next session.

When `nsh run` ends, however it ends, it stops the host it started: it quits the Catalyst app or closes the macOS, Linux or Windows host, terminates the
development host in the simulator, or force-stops it on the device.

The hosts are generic: they run any NSH app the server sends, so there is nothing to build per app.

## `nsh dev`

```sh
nsh dev App.tsx
```

```text
✓ built App.tsx (3.2 KB js, 9.8 KB bytecode, 21ms)
→ dev server ws://127.0.0.1:8790/ws
  devices on this network: ws://192.168.1.20:8790/ws
```

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--port <port>` | Dev server port. Default 8790 (the next free one if taken). |
| `--release` | Serve release builds. |

Connect hosts to the printed URL:

- **Your own iOS app**, linked with `NativeShellDev.xcframework`:
  `try app.connectDevServer(URL(string: "ws://192.168.1.20:8790/ws")!)`. See [Embedding in iOS apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md#development).
- **Your own Android app**, with `nsh-dev.aar`: `nsh.connectDevServer("ws://192.168.1.20:8790/ws")`, or
  `adb reverse tcp:8790 tcp:8790` and `ws://127.0.0.1:8790/ws`. See [Embedding in Android apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md#development).

Any number of hosts can be connected at once; every build goes to all of them. A host that connects later receives the
current build right away. A host that cannot run the app, because it lacks a UI set the app imports (a development
host built for another app), gets no build: it shows why, and the terminal prints a `warn` line with the command that
installs the app's host.

> [!NOTE]
> A device on the LAN needs to reach your computer on the dev server's port: same network, no firewall in between.
> Assets (images, fonts) are served over plain HTTP from the same port.

## Hot module replacement

Development builds keep one module per source file. When you save, NSH rebuilds, compares the modules with the last
good build and sends a **patch** with only the modules that changed. The host applies it in place in well under a
millisecond; from saving a file to seeing the change takes roughly 120 ms.

What happens to your app:

- **Only the components you edited render again.** Every top-level component (a capitalized function that returns JSX)
  is wrapped in a stable proxy. When its code changes (or the rest of its module's code, which it may use), its
  instances render again with the new code; components whose code did not change keep their instances, and with them
  their signals and state. Edit a button's style and the
  screen stays where it was, with the same input text and scroll position.
- **Modules that changed run again**, and so do the modules importing a changed module that cannot take the update
  by itself, up to the entry. Module-level code therefore runs again, except for what keeps its state:
- **Top-level signals and navigators keep their state**: a `const` made by `signal(…)` or `createNavigator(…)` at the
  top of a module keeps its value (a navigator its screens) across edits, as long as its own initializer is the same;
  change the initializer (`signal(0)` to `signal(10)`) to start afresh.
- **Top-level `context()` objects keep their identity**, taking the new default value, so providers and consumers in
  different modules keep matching.
- **Editing the entry keeps the app mounted.** `mount(App)` (or `mount(() => <App />)`) run again with the same
  component keeps what it mounted: only the components you edited render again. Edit `App` itself and it renders
  again, with what it renders (their own state starts afresh), but a navigator made at the top of the module keeps its
  routes, so a pushed screen stays pushed. A `mount` call that changed (another component, props) mounts the app
  again.
- **A component that throws** reports the error and renders nothing until you fix it; the rest of the app keeps
  running. The next good save recovers.

The host **reloads the whole app** instead of patching when:

- the change imports an NSH module the running app did not import yet (for example the first `import … from "nsh/list"`);
- the app's `capabilities` in `nsh.json` changed;
- the host is not running the build the patch is based on (it just connected, or a previous load failed);
- a patch cannot be applied.

> [!TIP]
> State a component keeps in its own signals resets when that component, or one that renders it, is edited. Keep
> state that must survive edits in top-level signals (or a store module), and make navigators at the top of a module.

`--release` serves release builds, without hot updates: every save reloads the app. Use it to check the minified build.
Anything loaded from a dev server, `--release` or not, skips the runtime's hardening (`eval` stays available); see
[Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md#hardening).

## Logs

`console.log`, `console.info`, `console.debug`, `console.warn` and `console.error` go to the native log with target
`js`. While a host is connected, its log lines are forwarded to the terminal running `nsh run` / `nsh dev`: your
`console.log` lines as they are (prefixed with the device's name when several devices are connected), warnings and
errors after the device's name:

```text
• iPhone 16 Pro connected, build 1
loading more after 1000
warn iPhone 16 Pro: deprecated option
error iPhone 16 Pro: uncaught exception: TypeError: cannot read property 'id' of undefined
          at Row (demos/Photos.tsx:18:22)
```

`console.log` formats values like a browser console: strings as they are, errors with their stack, functions by name,
objects and arrays as JSON. When the host is not connected, logs go to the platform's log (Xcode's console / the
unified log on iOS, `adb logcat` on Android).

The rest of the terminal is one line per step (`✓` done, `→` where to connect, `•` what a device did); the output of
the tools NSH runs (cargo, the hosts themselves) is only printed when one fails. `nsh run -v` (or `NSH_VERBOSE=1`)
prints everything: every log line with its level and source, cargo's output and the hosts' own.

`--trace` adds the cost of every commit:

```text
perf commit: 10 ops, 151µs (list js 2µs), 8 mount items, 27 nodes
```

See [Testing with nsh trace](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md) for what these numbers mean.

## The error overlay

These errors show a red overlay over the app on the host, with the message and stack:

- a build failure (a syntax error, an unknown element, a missing import), with a code frame pointing at the line;
- an error while the bundle is evaluated;
- an uncaught exception in an event handler, timer or effect.

Tap the overlay to dismiss it. It also disappears on the next successful reload. Build failures are printed in the
terminal too:

```text
error building App.tsx failed
App.tsx

  x <Buton> names nothing in scope
   ,-[3:11]
 2 | function App() {
 3 |   return <Buton />;
   :           ^^^^^
 4 | }
```

The bundler removes TypeScript types without checking them; run [`nsh check`](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md#nsh-check) (TypeScript's
native compiler with the `tsconfig.json` `nsh init` writes; no Node needed) or rely on your editor for type errors.

In release builds (an embedding app with the release SDK, a packaged app), errors are logged and passed to the host
app's error handler (`NshAppView.onError`, `NshView.setErrorListener`) but not shown over the app.

## Source maps and stack traces

Bundling produces a source map that composes every step (TypeScript → JSX → the bundle), and it is sent along with each
build. Before a stack trace is printed or shown, the runtime rewrites the bundle's positions to your sources, so stacks
point at `App.tsx:2:28`, not at the bundle:

```text
error Mac Catalyst: uncaught exception: Error: tap boom
          at <anonymous> (App.tsx:2:58)
```

`nsh build` writes the map as `bundle.js.map`; an embedding app that loads a bundle from a folder reads it from next to
the bundle, and [signed packages](https://nsh.dev/docs/signed-packages.md) carry it too.

## Debugging tips

- **Nothing updates after an edit**: check the terminal for a build error; the overlay shows it on the host too.
- **The app keeps old state you expected to reset**: hot replacement keeps unchanged components' state, top-level
  signals and navigators on purpose. Restart with Ctrl-C and `nsh run`, or change the state's initializer.
- **A request fails only in a packaged or embedded build**: check the app's [capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md);
  refusals are logged with the key to add.
- **Something is slow**: run with `--trace`, or reproduce it headless with [`nsh trace`](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md), which
  prints every native view operation.
- **Type errors in the editor**: `nsh run` and `nsh dev` keep `.nsh/types` up to date; see
  [Project structure](https://nsh.dev/docs/project-structure.md).

## See also

- [CLI](https://nsh.dev/docs/cli.md)
- [Testing with nsh trace](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md)
- [Embedding in iOS apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md), [Embedding in Android apps](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/dev-server-and-debugging

# Testing with nsh trace

`nsh trace` runs an app **headless**: the real runtime (the same QuickJS VM, reactive graph, renderer, components,
layout and list virtualization as on a device), but no simulator, no device and no window. Instead of drawing, it
prints every operation the runtime would send to the native views, with timings. It runs anywhere the CLI runs,
including Linux CI machines.

```sh
nsh trace App.tsx
```

Use it to:

- check that an app (or a demo) builds, evaluates and renders without errors;
- see exactly which native views a change creates, moves or updates, and how many;
- measure the cost of the first frame, of a tap and of each scrolling frame;
- catch regressions in CI.

## What it does

1. Bundles the entry (development settings, not minified) and compiles it to bytecode.
2. Starts an engine with a 390×844 viewport and renders the first frame.
3. Optionally scrolls the first scroll view or list.
4. Waits while the app is idle (by default 1.2 s, so the engine's idle garbage collection runs first and retention bugs
   show up), printing whatever the app renders meanwhile (timers, fetches, animations). An app that never stops
   rendering (a clock, a looping animation) is waited for at most 10 s; `--wait` sets the time instead.
5. Taps the views `--tap` names, or the first pressable view (the first view with `onPress`) a number of times, and
   prints what each tap changes, then what the app renders after it.

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--tap <selector>` | none | A view to tap (repeatable, in order): `id:<testID>`, `label:<accessibilityLabel>`, `text:<text>`, `view:<id>`, or a bare string matched as each of the first three. |
| `--taps <n>` | 2 | Without `--tap`: taps to send to the first pressable view. |
| `--idle-ms <ms>` | 1200 | Idle time before tapping. |
| `--wait <ms>` | none | Run exactly this long before the first tap and after each one, instead of waiting until the app is idle. |
| `--duration <ms>` | 0 | Keep running this long after the last tap. |
| `--safe-area <insets>` | 0 | Safe area insets: `top,right,bottom,left` in points, e.g. `47,0,34,0`. |
| `--scroll <points>` | none | Scroll the first scroll view or list by this many points, in 10 pt frames, printing each frame's batch. |
| `--width <points>` | 390 | Viewport width. |
| `--height <points>` | 844 | Viewport height. |

## Reading the output

Here is the counter example (`examples/counter/App.tsx`), shortened:

```text
✓ bundled App.tsx (3255 B in 14.3 ms)
perf commit: 56 ops, 395µs (list js 6µs), 49 mount items, 21 nodes
perf first frame: eval 271µs, total 1235µs
── initial render: 49 items
   LayoutDirection { rtl: false }
   Create { id: 2, kind: View }
   Create { id: 4, kind: Text }
   Insert { parent: 2, child: 4, before: None }
   ...
   Events { id: 20, events: EventMask(1) }
   Frame { id: 2, x: 0, y: 0, w: 390, h: 844 }
   Frame { id: 4, x: 24, y: 64, w: 342, h: 34 }
   ...
   Text { id: 4, text: "nsh counter", content: 342x34 @ 0,0 }
   Text { id: 14, text: "0", content: 36x77 @ 0,0 }
perf event Press on view 20
perf event js: 196µs
perf commit: 10 ops, 248µs (list js 6µs), 8 mount items, 24 nodes
── tap #1 on view 20: 8 items
   Create { id: 42, kind: Text }
   Insert { parent: 32, child: 42, before: None }
   Frame { id: 14, x: 136, y: 49, w: 71, h: 77 }
   Frame { id: 32, x: 24, y: 366, w: 342, h: 43 }
   Frame { id: 42, x: 0, y: 23, w: 342, h: 20 }
   Text { id: 14, text: "-1", content: 71x77 @ 0,0 }
   Text { id: 42, text: "• -1", content: 342x20 @ 0,0 }
   Text { id: 34, text: "Recent values: 1", content: 342x17 @ 0,0 }
```

### Batches and mount items

Each `── title: N items` block is one **mount batch**: everything the platform applies to native views for one frame,
in one hop to the main thread. The lines in it are **mount items**:

| Item | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Create { id, kind }` | Create a native view (`View`, `Text`, `Image`, `Scroll`, ...). |
| `Insert { parent, child, before }` | Put a view into its parent, before a sibling (`None`: at the end). |
| `Remove` / `Delete` | Detach a view from its parent / free it. |
| `ViewStyle { id, style }` | The view's decoration: background, borders, radius, shadow, opacity, transform, ... |
| `ViewProps { id, props }` | Touch and accessibility settings, `testID`. |
| `Events { id, events }` | Which events the view reports (`EventMask(1)` is press). |
| `Frame { id, x, y, w, h }` | Its position and size in its parent, in points. |
| `Text { id, text, content }` | Laid-out text for a text view. |
| `Image { id, source, ... }` | An image to load. |

Only what changed is sent: a tap that changes one number sends one `Text` item; views get no default style and no empty
event mask; unchanged frames are not sent. A frame of scrolling that reveals no new row produces **no batch at all**.

### The `perf` lines

| Line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `✓ bundled App.tsx (3255 B in 14.3 ms)` | Bundling time and bundle size (development settings). |
| `commit: 56 ops, 395µs (list js 6µs), 49 mount items, 21 nodes` | One commit: the operations JS queued, the time the core spent (rendering components, laying out, diffing), JS time spent binding list rows, the mount items produced, and the nodes alive. |
| `turn: 2640µs (timers and tasks 1964µs)` | A turn that committed: its whole time, and what its JS timers and Rust component tasks took before the commit (a Rust component renders in the commit). |
| `first frame: eval 271µs, total 1235µs` | Time to evaluate the bundle, and from start to the first batch. |
| `event Press on view 20` / `event js: 196µs` | An event dispatched, and the time its handler (and what it caused) took in JS. |

> [!NOTE]
> Text is measured with an approximate text engine headless, so text sizes differ a little from a device, which uses
> CoreText or Android's text layout. Layout logic, view counts and operation counts are the same.

Single-run timings depend a lot on the CPU's clock state (a machine that just woke from idle is slow). Compare runs on
the same machine, look at the minimum of several runs, and trust the op and item counts more than the microseconds.

## Scrolling

```sh
nsh trace examples/gallery/Bench.tsx --scroll 3000 --taps 0
```

Scrolls the first `<Scroll>` or `List` 10 points per frame and prints each frame's batch:

```text
perf commit: 26 ops, 297µs (list js 111µs), 22 mount items, 233 nodes
── scroll to 20: 22 items
   Create { id: 448, kind: View }
   ...
   Text { id: 456, text: "Photo #25", content: 298x20 @ 0,0 }
```

For a [list](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md), this shows the virtualization at work: which frames bind new rows, how many operations a row
costs, and that frames revealing no new row produce nothing. Use it with a release build of the CLI
(`./target/release/nsh` in a checkout) for meaningful timings.

## Taps

Name the views to tap with `--tap`, by `testID`, accessibility label or text, in the order to tap them. A match that is
not pressable itself (a `Text` inside a button) taps its nearest pressable ancestor, and the views a tap brings in (a
pushed screen, an opened menu) can be tapped next:

```sh
nsh trace --tap label:Plan --tap "text:Add stage" --tap id:save --wait 300
```

Without `--tap`, `nsh trace` taps the **first** view with `onPress` on screen. You can also write a small entry file
that renders only the screen under test:

```tsx
// trace/AddItem.tsx: renders the screen and puts the button under test first
import { mount } from "nsh";
import { Cart } from "../src/Cart";

mount(() => <Cart initialItems={[]} />);
```

```sh
nsh trace trace/AddItem.tsx --taps 5
```

If a tap produces no update, `nsh trace` stops with `error tap #1 produced no update` and a non-zero exit code: that
is how it catches handlers that stopped working, for example because the app's nodes were garbage-collected.

## In CI

`nsh trace` needs nothing but the CLI, so it runs on Linux runners. Errors in the app (a failed bundle evaluation, an
uncaught exception) are printed as `error` lines; a build failure, an app that renders nothing, or a tap that changes
nothing make it exit with a non-zero code. Check both:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -e
for entry in App.tsx trace/*.tsx; do
  out=$(nsh trace "$entry" --idle-ms 300 2>&1) || { echo "$out"; exit 1; }
  if echo "$out" | grep -E '^ *error' >/dev/null; then
    echo "$out"
    echo "errors in $entry"
    exit 1
  fi
done
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/trace.yml
jobs:
  trace:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./scripts/trace.sh
```

(Install the `nsh` CLI on the runner the way you install it locally; see [Installation](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation.md).)

To guard performance, record the item counts of a few interactions (the `── … : N items` lines and the `ops` /
`mount items` numbers) and fail when they grow. Counts are deterministic; timings on shared CI machines are not.

> [!NOTE]
> `nsh trace` runs with every capability: it does not apply the `capabilities` of `nsh.json`, and its `fetch` really
> goes to the network. Test capability rules on a device or in a packaged build.

## `testID` for UI tests

`nsh trace` checks what the runtime renders. To drive the real native UI with the platform's test tools (XCUITest,
Espresso / UI Automator, Appium, Maestro), give views a `testID`:

```tsx
<View testID="add-to-cart" onPress={add} style={{ padding: 12 }}>
  <Text testID="cart-count">{`${count()} items`}</Text>
</View>
```

| Platform | Where `testID` goes |
|---|---|
| iOS | The view's `accessibilityIdentifier` (`app.otherElements["add-to-cart"]` in XCUITest). |
| Android | The accessibility node's view id resource name (`By.res("add-to-cart")` in UI Automator). |

`testID` is a prop of every element and of the components in `nsh/ui/mobile`. It does not change what screen readers
say; use `accessibilityLabel` for that (see [Accessibility](https://nsh.dev/docs/accessibility.md)). In `nsh trace` output it appears in
the view's `ViewProps` item as `test_id: Some("add-to-cart")`.

## See also

- [Performance](https://nsh.dev/docs/performance.md): what to look for in these numbers
- [Dev server and debugging](https://nsh.dev/docs/dev-server-and-debugging.md)
- [Architecture](https://nsh.dev/docs/architecture.md): ops, commits and mount batches

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace

# Performance

Performance is NSH's first priority, and most of it is decided by the framework rather than by your app: the runtime
is native, each update crosses threads once, animations and list virtualization run without JS. This page explains the
rules NSH follows, what they mean for the code you write, and how to measure.

## The rules

### 1. JS does as little as possible

QuickJS is an interpreter: small, quick to start, and much slower than native code for heavy work. So in NSH, **only
your app's code is JS**. The reactive graph (signals, computed values, effects), the renderer your compiled JSX calls,
the layout engine, the components of `nsh/ui/mobile`, list virtualization, animation and every module you import are
Rust. Parsing, diffing, layout and string processing happen natively.

The effect is measurable. The same counter app on NSH's earlier JS runtime and on the native runtime (release builds):

| | Former JS runtime | Native runtime |
|---|---|---|
| Bundle size | 14 KB JS / 19.6 KB bytecode | 886 B JS / 1.7 KB bytecode |
| Evaluating the bundle | ~390 µs | ~95 µs |
| JS time of one tap (median) | ~14 µs | ~5 µs |
| Commit of one tap | ~22 µs | ~15 µs |
| Scrolling a 1000-row list, JS per rebinding frame | ~150 µs | ~77 µs |

The same holds for components: a `Button` from `nsh/ui/mobile` (Rust) against an equivalent TSX button, 200 of them:

| | Rust `Button`: JS / core | TSX button: JS / core |
|---|---|---|
| First frame (ops) | 1.32 ms / 0.77 ms (1015) | 2.32 ms / 0.70 ms (2415) |
| Updating all 200 titles (ops) | 0.42 ms / 0.42 ms (200) | 0.77 ms / 0.36 ms (600) |

(Measured on Apple silicon; the second table on the former runtime. Both from NSH's performance baselines.)

**For your code:** keep event handlers and computed values light. Heavy computation (parsing large payloads, sorting
thousands of items on every keystroke) costs more in QuickJS than you may be used to in V8 or JavaScriptCore with a JIT.
Do it once, cache it in a `computed`, or move it off the interaction path.

### 2. Cross threads in batches

Your app's JS runs on an engine thread, never on the main thread. One JS turn, for example one event handler with
everything it changes, becomes **one commit**: the runtime renders components, lays out, diffs and produces one batch
of native view operations, which reaches the main thread in **one hop**. There is no bridge message per view and no
serialization per prop.

**For your code:** you do not need to coalesce writes for performance; ten `set` calls in one handler still produce one
commit. Use `batch` when you want effects and computed values to see all the writes at once instead of running after
each one.

### 3. Fine-grained updates

Components run **once**. Afterwards, only the bindings that read a signal run again when it changes: a text, a style
property, a branch of `<If>`, the rows of `<Each>`. Nothing re-renders a whole subtree to find out what changed.

```tsx
import type { Accessor } from "nsh";
import { Text } from "nsh";

type Quote = { price: number; change: number };

function Price(props: { quote: Accessor<Quote> }) {
  // Runs once. When quote() changes, only the text and the color update.
  return (
    <Text style={{ color: props.quote().change < 0 ? "#cf222e" : "#1a7f37" }}>
      {props.quote().price.toFixed(2)}
    </Text>
  );
}
```

**For your code:**

- Read signals where they are used (inside JSX expressions, `computed`, `effect`), not at the top of a component, so
  the narrowest binding updates.
- Use `<Each>` (rows kept by key) or [`List`](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md) for collections; a plain `.map()` in JSX creates every row
  again on each change.
- Derive values with `computed` when several bindings use them, so they are computed once per change.

Appending a fourth item to a three-item list, as `nsh trace` shows it:

```tsx
{items().map((n) => <Text>{`row ${n}`}</Text>)}                   // 22 mount items: 3 views removed, 4 created
<Each of={items()}>{(n) => <Text>{`row ${n()}`}</Text>}</Each>      // 4 mount items: 1 view created
```

See [Reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md).

### 4. Do not send what is not needed

The core sends only what changed: new views get no default style and no empty event mask, unchanged styles and frames
are not sent, a change of text color does not lay the text out again. A tap that changes one number sends one text
item. You can see this in `nsh trace` output (below).

### 5. Animate natively

An animation driven from JS (a signal written in `requestAnimationFrame`) costs a JS call and a commit per frame, and
stutters when the engine thread is busy. [`nsh/animated`](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md) runs animations natively instead:

```tsx
import { View } from "nsh";
import { createNativeValue } from "nsh/animated";
import { List } from "nsh/list";

const scrollY = createNativeValue(0);

<View
  style={{
    opacity: scrollY.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 120], outputRange: [1, 0.35] }),
    transform: [{ translateY: scrollY.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 120], outputRange: [0, -6] }) }],
  }}
/>;
<List each={photos()} scrollValue={scrollY} estimatedItemSize={64} style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  {(photo) => <Row photo={photo()} />}
</List>;
```

- `timing`, `spring` and `decay` run on the platform's UI thread, frame by frame, with no JS per frame.
- `scrollValue` writes a scroll offset into a native value in the same frame; `pan={{ x, y }}` lets drags move a view
  directly. JS hears about the end (the promise resolves, `onPanEnd` gets the velocity).
- `Animated.sequence` / `parallel` / `stagger` / `loop` run as one native tree: each step starts the moment the
  previous one ends, with no gap waiting for JS.
- `LayoutAnimation.configureNext` animates the next commit's frames, insertions and removals natively.

### 6. Virtualize long lists

[`List`](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md) keeps only the rows near the viewport, recycles their cells, and computes positions, columns,
sticky headers and viewability natively. Scrolling frames that reveal no new row call no JS and produce no batch; a
frame that binds one new row of the gallery's photo list is 4 operations and 4 mount items.

**For your code:**

- Give `estimatedItemSize` close to the real row height.
- Keep per-item state in your data (keyed by id), not in signals created inside the row: cells are reused for other
  items, and `item()` / `index()` change when they are.
- Keep rows cheap: a row binds once per recycle, so its JS runs while the user scrolls.
- Use `scrollValue` instead of `onScroll` for effects that follow the scroll position. `onScroll` delivers at most one
  event per engine turn, but each is still a call into JS.

## Measuring

### Headless: `nsh trace`

```sh
nsh trace App.tsx                                   # first frame + 2 taps
nsh trace App.tsx --scroll 3000 --taps 0            # scrolling, 10 pt per frame
```

```text
perf commit: 56 ops, 395µs (list js 6µs), 49 mount items, 21 nodes
perf first frame: eval 271µs, total 1235µs
perf event js: 88µs
perf commit: 10 ops, 151µs (list js 2µs), 8 mount items, 27 nodes
```

What to look at:

- **ops** (operations your JS queued) and **mount items** (native view operations): these are deterministic. If a tap
  that should change one label produces 40 items, something re-creates views it should update.
- **event js**: the JS cost of a handler and what it triggered.
- **commit**: the core's cost of rendering components, layout and diffing.
- **list js**: JS spent binding list rows during that commit.

Full guide: [Testing with nsh trace](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md).

### On a device: `--trace`

```sh
nsh run App.tsx --trace
nsh run App.tsx --target android --trace --release
```

logs the same commit lines from the real host, with the platform's own text engine. `NshAppView(trace: true)` and
`new NshView(context, true)` do the same in an embedding app.

### On screen: `--fps`

```sh
nsh run App.tsx --target macos --fps --release
```

shows the frame rate and what frames and commits cost over the running app, with CPU, GPU and memory
([macOS: performance monitor](https://nsh.dev/docs/macos.md#performance-monitor)).

> [!TIP]
> Single measurements are dominated by the CPU's clock state: a thread that just slept runs slower for a while.
> Compare the minimum of several runs, on the same machine, and prefer release builds for timing.

## Reference numbers

From NSH's own baselines (Apple silicon unless noted):

| Scenario | Numbers |
|---|---|
| Counter app, headless (debug) | First frame ~0.5–0.65 ms (58 ops / 49 mount items); one tap ~0.15 ms |
| Counter app, Mac Catalyst (release) | First frame ~1.05–1.15 ms (about 0.7 ms of it lays out 10 texts with CoreText for the first time); one tap ~0.12 ms |
| Gallery photo list, headless (debug) | First frame 653 ops / 224 nodes, ~2.7 ms |
| Scrolling the photo list, Catalyst (release) | Rebinding one row while scrolling slowly ~0.4 ms; a whole screen of ~32 rows on a fast fling 0.9–1.6 ms |
| Scrolling the photo list, Android emulator (arm64, release) | Rebinding one row ~0.3–0.4 ms (JS ~60 µs) |
| Engine startup (release) | ~75–155 µs; the global APIs (`fetch`, `URL`, ...) cost nothing until first used, then ~90 µs |
| Hot reload | ~120 ms from saving a file to the new version running; applying the update 0.2–0.5 ms |

## Checklist

- Interactions: a tap changes a handful of mount items, not dozens.
- Lists: `List` for anything long, with `estimatedItemSize`; per-item state in data.
- Animations: native values, not signals written every frame.
- Scroll effects: `scrollValue`, not `onScroll`.
- Handlers: no heavy work per keystroke or per scroll event; cache in `computed`.
- Components: prefer the Rust components of `nsh/ui/mobile` where they fit; they cost less JS than equivalents written
  in TSX.

## See also

- [Architecture](https://nsh.dev/docs/architecture.md)
- [Testing with nsh trace](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md)
- [Lists](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md), [Animation](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md), [Reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/performance

# Architecture

This page is for app developers who want to know what happens between `count.set(1)` and a label changing on screen.
You do not need it to write apps, but it explains why NSH behaves the way it does: why components run once, why
animations stay smooth while JS is busy, why the main thread never waits for your code.

## The big picture

![How an nsh app runs: the nsh CLI builds App.tsx into bytecode; on the engine thread, QuickJS runs a handler, the reactive graph in nsh-js queues ops, and nsh-core commits one MountBatch; it crosses to the main thread in one hop, which applies it to UIKit or Android views; touches go back as events. Native animations run on the main thread without JavaScript.](https://nsh.dev/diagrams/architecture-light.svg)

## Building: only your code becomes JS

`nsh build`, `nsh dev` and the other commands bundle your app with a toolchain written in Rust (no Node.js):

1. **Oxc** removes the TypeScript types.
2. **NSH's JSX compiler** turns JSX into direct calls to the native renderer, in the same pass. Static props and
   children are set once; expressions that can change (they call a function or read a property) become bindings the
   renderer follows. Components become plain function calls with a props object whose changing props are getters.
3. **rolldown** bundles your modules into one ES module. Imports of NSH's modules (`nsh`, `nsh/list`,
   `nsh/ui/mobile`, ...) stay imports: those modules are native, served by the runtime. **The bundle contains only your
   app's code**; the counter example is under 1 KB of JS.
4. The bundle is compiled to **bytecode** (`bundle.nshc`), which loads faster than source, and a **source map**
   is composed across all steps so stack traces point at your `.tsx` lines.

Images and fonts you import are collected as assets, and type declarations for your editor are written to
`.nsh/types`.

## Running: two threads per app

Each running app (an `NshAppView` on iOS, an `NshView` on Android, the window of a packaged app) is one **engine** with
its own QuickJS VM and its own **engine thread**. There are no global singletons, so several apps can run side by side
in one host app.

### The engine thread

Everything about your app's logic happens here:

- **QuickJS** runs your code: components, event handlers, timers, effects.
- **The reactive graph** (signals, computed values, effects, owners, context) is native. Its nodes are QuickJS objects
  of native classes, so the garbage collector sees the references through them, but tracking dependencies and
  scheduling updates is Rust (it follows the algorithm of Solid 1.9).
- **The renderer** your compiled JSX calls is native. It creates nodes and turns every change into an **op** pushed
  straight into a native queue: no JSON, no messages per prop.
- **The core** keeps a shadow tree of all nodes. When a JS turn ends, it takes all queued ops at once and **commits**:
  renders the Rust components (`nsh/ui/mobile`), rebuilds changed texts, lays out with **Taffy** (flexbox and grid, with a
  column default and no shrinking), diffs frames and styles, and produces one **MountBatch**: the list of operations the native
  views need.

### The main thread

The platform's main (UI) thread applies each MountBatch in one hop: create views, insert them, set styles and frames,
hand over laid-out text. Besides that it only does what must happen on it:

- **drawing text** that was already laid out on the engine thread;
- **native animations**: values from `nsh/animated` are driven frame by frame (a `CADisplayLink` on iOS, a UI-thread
  animator on Android) and written to the views directly;
- **gestures and scrolling**: touches become events sent to the engine thread; `scrollValue` and `pan` feed native
  values in the same frame.

**The main thread never waits for JS.** When the system needs an answer on the spot (may this text change, may the
back button pop this screen, may this sheet close), the answer was mounted beforehand as a prop, and JS hears about it
afterwards through an event. A busy engine thread can delay updates, but it cannot freeze scrolling, animations or
the system's gestures.

## From a tap to the screen

```text
 main thread               engine thread                                              main thread
 ───────────               ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────      ───────────
 tap on a view ─ event ─▶  handler runs: count.set(count() + 1)
                           reactive graph: the bindings that read count() run again
                           renderer: one op per changed binding → native queue
                           JS turn ends → core commit: render, text, layout, diff
                           → MountBatch (e.g. 1 Text item)                 ─ hop ─▶   apply: draw the new text
```

In the counter example, a tap costs about 0.12 ms in a release build on a Mac, JS and commit together, and produces a
handful of mount items (see [Testing with nsh trace](https://nsh.dev/docs/testing-and-trace.md)).

Three properties follow from this design:

- **One JS turn is one commit.** However many signals a handler sets, the views change once, together.
- **Components run once.** Only bindings re-run; there is no re-render of a component and no virtual DOM diff. The
  diffing that remains is the core's, over frames and styles, in Rust.
- **Only changes travel.** Unchanged styles and frames are not sent; new views get no default values.

## Text: laid out once, off the main thread

Text is often the most expensive part of a UI. NSH lays it out on the engine thread with the platform's own text
engine, so it looks exactly like native text:

1. **prepare**: a `<Text>` and its nested spans become one attributed string (CoreText on Apple platforms,
   `PrecomputedText` / `StaticLayout` on Android);
2. **measure** at the widths layout asks for; measurements are cached by content and width, so a color-only change does
   not measure again;
3. **layout** at the final size.

The main thread receives the immutable result and only draws it. A text nested in a `<Text>` is a span, not a view;
strings outside `<Text>` render nothing.

## Lists

`List` is virtualized natively. The core decides which rows are near the viewport, computes positions, columns and
sticky headers, and recycles cells. When a cell needs a different item, the runtime binds it (your row function's
`item()` and `index()` accessors change); frames that reveal no new row call no JS at all. See [Lists](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md).

## Everything else the runtime does

- **Networking**: `fetch` and the other global APIs are native classes. Requests go to the platform's HTTP stack
  (`NSURLSession`, `HttpURLConnection`), streaming in both directions.
- **Images** download and decode off the main thread, at the size of the view, with a memory cache.
- **Limits and capabilities** are enforced by the runtime, in Rust: see [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).
- **Hot module replacement** is native too: patches are applied by the runtime in well under a millisecond (see
  [Dev server and debugging](https://nsh.dev/docs/dev-server-and-debugging.md)).

## The crates

NSH is a Rust workspace. You never build it to write apps (the distribution ships the CLI and prebuilt runtimes), but
the names show up in logs and docs:

| Crate | What it is |
|---|---|
| `nsh-core` | The platform-independent core: shadow tree, styles, Taffy layout, text merging, list virtualization, mount items; CSS values and Tailwind; the Rust components' framework and theme. |
| `nsh-ui-mobile` | The components and modules of `nsh/ui/mobile` (`Button`, `Card`, `SafeAreaView`, `Alert`, ...), written in Rust. |
| `nsh-animation` | The native animation graph: values, interpolation, timing / spring / decay. |
| `nsh-js` | The QuickJS host and NSH's runtime: the reactive graph, the renderer, every native module, the global APIs, hot module replacement, limits; and the TypeScript declarations of all of it. |
| `nsh-engine` | The engine thread: drives `nsh-js` and `nsh-core` and hands one batch per frame to the platform. |
| `nsh-package` | Signed packages: keys, certificates, revocation, the trust store. |
| `nsh-bundler` | The bundler: rolldown, Oxc, NSH's JSX compiler, source maps, Tailwind class checks. |
| `nsh-dev` | The dev server and its client. |
| `nsh-platform-ios` | The UIKit backend (iOS, simulator, Mac Catalyst): view mounting, the CoreText text engine, input; the embedding SDK. |
| `nsh-platform-android` | The Android backend: `libnsh.so` and the Java runtime (`NshView`, the views, images, networking). |
| `nsh-cli` | The `nsh` command. |

The dependency direction is `nsh-core` ← `nsh-js` ← `nsh-engine` ← platforms. The core depends on no platform and no JS
engine, which is what lets `nsh trace` run the real runtime headless on any machine.

## See also

- [Performance](https://nsh.dev/docs/performance.md)
- [Reactivity](https://nsh.dev/docs/reactivity.md)

Source: https://nsh.dev/docs/architecture

---

# Elements

Host elements are the primitives every screen is made of: `<View>`, `<Text>`, `<Image>` and the rest, imported from NSH's
modules. Each one is a native view (a UIView subclass on iOS and Mac Catalyst, an Android `View`), created and laid out
by the NSH runtime. Everything an app shows is
made of them: the components of [`nsh/ui/mobile`](https://nsh.dev/components.md) are drawn with the same elements.

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";

function App() {
  const count = signal(0);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "center", gap: 12 }}>
      <Text style={{ fontSize: 24 }}>Tapped {count()} times</Text>
      <View onPress={() => count.update((n) => n + 1)} activeOpacity={0.6} class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2">
        <Text class="text-white">Tap</Text>
      </View>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

Every tag is PascalCase and names a binding in scope: import each element from its module, as the table below says.
Only `<If>` and `<Each>` are globals that need no import. A lowercase tag such as `<view>` is a build error, because
TypeScript would check it against one global type per name, and generic components such as `List` and `Each` could not
infer their item types. The compiler recognizes the elements through their imports and makes the native views in place,
so importing them costs nothing at run time. See [JSX and components](https://nsh.dev/docs/jsx-and-components.md).

## All elements

| Tag | Import from | Native view (iOS / Android) | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<View>` | `nsh` | UIView / ViewGroup | [View](https://nsh.dev/elements/view.md) |
| `<Text>` | `nsh` | CoreText view / StaticLayout view | [Text](https://nsh.dev/elements/text.md) |
| `<Image>` | `nsh/image` | a view with an image layer / an image view | [Image](https://nsh.dev/elements/image.md) |
| `<Scroll>` | `nsh` | UIScrollView / ScrollView | [Scroll](https://nsh.dev/elements/scroll.md) |
| `<Input>` | `nsh` | UITextField or UITextView / EditText | [Input](https://nsh.dev/elements/input.md) |
| `<List>` | `nsh/list` | UIScrollView / ScrollView with recycled cells | [List](https://nsh.dev/elements/list.md) |
| `<Canvas>` | `nsh/canvas` | a view replaying a 2D drawing | [Canvas](https://nsh.dev/elements/canvas.md) |
| `<WebView>` | `nsh/webview` | WKWebView / android.webkit.WebView | [WebView](https://nsh.dev/elements/web-view.md) |
| `<Video>` | `nsh/video` | AVPlayerLayer / MediaPlayer on a TextureView | [Video](https://nsh.dev/elements/video.md) |
| `<Modal>` | `nsh/ui/mobile` | presented view controller / Dialog | [Modal](https://nsh.dev/elements/modal.md) |
