```ts
function split<T extends object, K extends readonly (keyof T)[]>(
  props: T,
  keys: K,
): [Pick<T, K[number]>, Omit<T, K[number]>];
```

Splits a props object into the props named in `keys` and the rest. Both halves stay reactive: props whose values change are getters, and `split` keeps them as getters. Use it in a component that handles some props itself and passes the others on. Destructuring props (`const { label } = props`) would read them once and lose updates.

```tsx
import { Input, type InputProps, split, Text, View } from "nsh";

function LabeledInput(props: InputProps & { label: string }) {
  const [own, rest] = split(props, ["label"]);
  return (
    <View style={{ gap: 4 }}>
      <Text>{own.label}</Text>
      <Input {...rest} />
    </View>
  );
}
```

## View, Text, Scroll, Input

```ts
function View(props: ViewProps): YNode;
function Text(props: TextProps): YNode;
function Scroll(props: ScrollProps): YNode;
function Input(props: InputProps): YNode;
```

The host elements `nsh` exports, written as tags: `<View>`, `<Text>`, `<Scroll>`, `<Input>`. The compiler makes the
native view in place for a tag that names one of them through its import (an alias too), so importing them costs
nothing at run time. They are components like any other, so they can also be passed around (`const Tag = inline ? Text : View`).
The other elements come from their own modules: `Image` from [`nsh/image`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-image.md), `List` from
[`nsh/list`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-list.md), `Canvas`, `WebView` and `Video` from theirs. Their props are documented under
[Elements](https://nsh.dev/elements.md).

## Types

`nsh` also exports the types of the reactive API and of the host elements. The most used ones:

| Type | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Accessor<T>` | A readable value: `() => T` |
| `Signal<T>` | An `Accessor<T>` with `set` and `update` |
| `SignalOptions<T>` | Options of `signal` and `computed` (`equals`) |
| `Context<T>` | What `context` returns |
| `Component<P>` | `(props: P) => JSX.Element` |
| `JSX` | The JSX namespace (`JSX.Element`) |
| `YNode` | What a `ref` receives: focus, scroll and other commands. See [Elements](https://nsh.dev/elements.md) |
| `ViewProps`, `TextProps`, `ImageProps`, `ScrollProps`, `InputProps`, `CommonProps`, `TouchProps` | Props of host elements |
| `ViewStyle`, `TextStyle`, `ImageStyle`, `LayoutStyle`, `StyleProp<T>` | Style objects; see the [style reference](https://nsh.dev/modules/style-reference.md) |
| `ColorValue`, `DimensionValue`, `LengthValue`, `TransformStep` | Values inside styles |
| `GestureResponderEvent`, `LayoutEvent`, `ScrollEvent`, `PanEvent`, `TouchPoint` | Event payloads |
| `ImageAsset` | What importing an image file gives (`{ uri, width, height }`) |
| `OS` | `"ios" \| "android" \| "macos" \| "windows" \| "linux" \| "web"` |
| `AccessibilityRole`, `AccessibilityState` | Accessibility props |

```tsx
import { type GestureResponderEvent, type YNode, signal } from "nsh";

let field: YNode | undefined;
const onPress = (e: GestureResponderEvent) => field?.focus();
```

`StyleProp<T>` accepts one style or a list merged left to right, skipping falsy entries:

```tsx
<View style={[styles.card, selected() && styles.selected]} />
```

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh

---

# nsh/animated

`nsh/animated` animates on the UI thread. You create a **native value**, bind it (or values derived from it) to a style property, and start an animation; from then on every frame is computed natively, without running JavaScript. A busy JS thread cannot make the animation stutter, and an animation costs no JS work per frame.

```ts
import { Animated, createNativeValue, Easing, LayoutAnimation, NativeNode, NativeValue } from "nsh/animated";
```

See [Animation](https://nsh.dev/docs/animation.md) for the guide.

## What a native value can drive

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| `opacity` | `style={{ opacity: value }}` |
| `backgroundColor` | `style={{ backgroundColor: value.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 1], outputRange: ["#fff", "#000"] }) }}` |
| `borderColor`, `color` | The same: a node of colors. `borderColor` colors every side; a `Text`'s `color` colors the whole text |
| `shadowColor`, `shadowOpacity`, `shadowRadius` | `style={{ shadowOpacity: value }}` (a node of colors for `shadowColor`) |
| `transform` | `translateX`, `translateY`, `scale`, `scaleX`, `scaleY`, `rotate`, `rotateX`, `rotateY`, `rotateZ` steps: `transform: [{ translateX: value }]` |
| Scroll position | `<Scroll scrollValue={value}>` and `<List scrollValue={value}>` write the scroll offset into it each frame |
| Gestures | `pan={{ x, y }}`, `pinch={{ scale }}`, `rotation={{ angle }}` on any element: the gesture writes the values directly (see [Touch and gestures](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md)) |
| Canvas | Any number or color argument of a [canvas](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-canvas.md) drawing call |

Other style properties take plain values; to animate the layout itself (sizes, positions in the flow), use [`LayoutAnimation`](#layoutanimation).

## createNativeValue

```ts
function createNativeValue(value?: number): NativeValue;
```

Creates a native value starting at `value` (default `0`).

```tsx
import { mount, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { createNativeValue } from "nsh/animated";

function App() {
  const x = createNativeValue(0);
  let right = false;
  const toggle = () => {
    right = !right;
    x.spring(right ? 200 : 0);
  };
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, padding: 24, paddingTop: 48, gap: 16 }}>
      <View style={{ width: 60, height: 60, borderRadius: 12, backgroundColor: "#6366f1", transform: [{ translateX: x }] }} />
      <Text onPress={toggle}>Move</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

> [!NOTE]
> A native value lives on the UI thread and changes there every frame, so JS reads it asynchronously: `await value.getValue()` (or the promise `stop()` returns) gives the value at that moment. Keep the target in a variable or a signal when your code needs it right away, as above. Gesture events report the values at their end (`PanEvent.valueX` / `valueY`).

## NativeValue

```ts
class NativeValue extends NativeNode {
  constructor(value: number);
  set(value: number): void;
  stop(): Promise<number>;
  getValue(): Promise<number>;
  setOffset(offset: number): void;
  flattenOffset(): void;
  extractOffset(): void;
  timing(to: number, options?: { duration?: number; easing?: Easing; delay?: number }): Promise<boolean>;
  spring(to: number, options?: { stiffness?: number; damping?: number; mass?: number; velocity?: number }): Promise<boolean>;
  decay(options?: { velocity?: number; deceleration?: number; clamp?: [number, number]; bounce?: number }): Promise<boolean>;
}
```

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `set(value)` | Jumps to `value`, stopping any running animation. |
| `stop()` | Stops the running animation where it is; resolves with the value there. |
| `getValue()` | Resolves with the current value (with its offset), read on the UI thread. |
| `setOffset(offset)` | An offset added to the value: bindings see value + offset; `set`, animations and drags move the value. |
| `flattenOffset()` | Adds the offset to the value and makes it 0. |
| `extractOffset()` | Moves the value into the offset and makes the value 0 (a drag then starts from where the last one ended). |
| `timing(to, options)` | Animates to `to` along an easing curve. `duration` in ms (default 300), `easing` (default `"easeInOut"`), `delay` in ms (default 0). |
| `spring(to, options)` | Springs to `to`. `stiffness` (default 170), `damping` (default 26), `mass` (default 1), `velocity` (initial velocity, units per second). |
| `decay(options)` | Coasts from `velocity` (units per second) and slows down by `deceleration` per millisecond (default 0.998). Use it after a fling, with the velocity from `onPanEnd`. With `clamp: [min, max]` it stops at a bound, or bounces back from it keeping `bounce` (0..1, default 0) of its speed. |

Each animation method returns a promise that resolves with `true` when the animation finished and `false` when it was stopped (by `stop`, `set` or another animation of the same value).

```ts
const opacity = createNativeValue(1);
const finished = await opacity.timing(0, { duration: 200 });
if (finished) visible.set(false);
```

## NativeNode

```ts
class NativeNode {
  interpolate(config: {
    inputRange: number[];
    outputRange: number[] | string[];
    extrapolate?: Extrapolation;
    extrapolateLeft?: Extrapolation;
    extrapolateRight?: Extrapolation;
    easing?: Easing;
  }): NativeNode;
  diffClamp(min: number, max: number): NativeNode;
  add(b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  sub(b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  mul(b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  div(b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  mod(b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
}

type Extrapolation = "extend" | "clamp" | "identity";
```

A node of the native animation graph: a `NativeValue`, or a value derived from others. Derived nodes are evaluated on the UI thread whenever their inputs change.

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `interpolate(config)` | Maps the input through piecewise ranges. `outputRange` holds numbers, colors (`"#ff0000"`, `"rgba(…)"`) or angles (`"45deg"`, `"1rad"`). Outside `inputRange` it clamps by default; `extrapolate` (or `extrapolateLeft` / `extrapolateRight`) can be `"extend"` (continue the line), `"clamp"` or `"identity"` (pass the input through). `easing` shapes each segment. |
| `diffClamp(min, max)` | Follows the input's changes but keeps the result within `min..max`: a header that hides while content scrolls up and comes back as soon as it scrolls down. |
| `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div` | Arithmetic with another node or a constant. |
| `mod(b)` | Modulo, never negative for a positive `b` (keeping angles in 0..360). |

```tsx
const scroll = createNativeValue(0);
const header = scroll.diffClamp(0, 44);

<Scroll scrollValue={scroll} style={{ flex: 1 }}>{/* rows */}</Scroll>
<View style={{ height: 44, transform: [{ translateY: header.mul(-1) }] }} />
```

```ts
const progress = createNativeValue(0);
const rotate = progress.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 1], outputRange: ["0deg", "360deg"] });
const color = progress.interpolate({ inputRange: [0, 0.5, 1], outputRange: ["#22c55e", "#eab308", "#ef4444"] });
```

## Animated

```ts
const Animated: {
  timing(value: NativeValue, config: { toValue: number; duration?: number; easing?: Easing; delay?: number }): CompositeAnimation;
  spring(value: NativeValue, config: { toValue: number; stiffness?: number; damping?: number; mass?: number; velocity?: number }): CompositeAnimation;
  decay(value: NativeValue, config?: { velocity?: number; deceleration?: number; clamp?: [number, number]; bounce?: number }): CompositeAnimation;
  sequence(list: CompositeAnimation[]): CompositeAnimation;
  parallel(list: CompositeAnimation[], config?: { stopTogether?: boolean }): CompositeAnimation;
  stagger(ms: number, list: CompositeAnimation[]): CompositeAnimation;
  delay(ms: number): CompositeAnimation;
  loop(animation: CompositeAnimation, config?: { iterations?: number; resetBeforeIteration?: boolean }): CompositeAnimation;
  add(a: NativeNode, b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  subtract(a: NativeNode, b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  multiply(a: NativeNode, b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  divide(a: NativeNode, b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  modulo(a: NativeNode, b: NativeNode | number): NativeNode;
  diffClamp(a: NativeNode, min: number, max: number): NativeNode;
  sampleSpring(config: SpringConfig & { from?: number }, fps?: number): number[];
  sampleDecay(config: DecayConfig & { from?: number }, fps?: number): number[];
};

interface CompositeAnimation {
  start(callback?: (result: { finished: boolean }) => void): Promise<boolean>;
  stop(): void;
  reset(): void;
}
```

`Animated` builds animations out of steps (`timing`, `spring`, `decay`, `sequence`, `parallel`, ...). Nothing runs until `start()`; then the whole tree runs natively, and each step starts on the UI thread at the exact moment the previous one ends (no frame gap, no JS round trip between steps).

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `timing`, `spring`, `decay` | One animation of one value; same options and defaults as the [`NativeValue`](#nativevalue) methods, with the target as `toValue`. |
| `sequence(list)` | Runs the animations one after another. |
| `parallel(list, { stopTogether })` | Runs them at the same time. With `stopTogether` (default `true`), stopping one stops all. |
| `stagger(ms, list)` | Runs them in parallel, each starting `ms` after the previous one. |
| `delay(ms)` | Waits; useful inside `sequence`. |
| `loop(animation, { iterations, resetBeforeIteration })` | Repeats `animation` `iterations` times (forever by default), putting its values back before each run unless `resetBeforeIteration` is `false`. |
| `add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`, `modulo`, `diffClamp` | The same as the [`NativeNode`](#nativenode) methods, as functions. |

`CompositeAnimation`:

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `start(callback?)` | Runs it (again). Resolves, and calls `callback`, once for the whole tree with whether it finished rather than being stopped. |
| `stop()` | Stops it where it is. |
| `reset()` | Stops it and puts its values back where they were when it started. |

```ts
const ys = [0, 1, 2, 3].map(() => createNativeValue(0));
const hop = Animated.stagger(
  80,
  ys.map((y) =>
    Animated.sequence([
      Animated.timing(y, { toValue: -36, duration: 220, easing: Easing.out(Easing.quad) }),
      Animated.spring(y, { toValue: 0, stiffness: 300, damping: 12 }),
    ]),
  ),
);
hop.start(({ finished }) => console.log(finished ? "done" : "stopped"));
```

## Easing

```ts
type Easing =
  | "linear" | "ease" | "easeIn" | "easeOut" | "easeInOut"
  | [number, number, number, number]   // cubic Bézier x1, y1, x2, y2
  | EasingCurve;

const Easing: {
  linear: Easing;
  ease: Easing;
  bezier(x1: number, y1: number, x2: number, y2: number): Easing;
  in(e: Easing): Easing;
  out(e: Easing): Easing;
  inOut(e: Easing): Easing;
  sample(easing: Easing, count: number): number[];
  quad: EasingCurve;
  cubic: EasingCurve;
  poly(n?: number): EasingCurve;
  sin: EasingCurve;
  circle: EasingCurve;
  exp: EasingCurve;
  elastic(bounciness?: number): EasingCurve;
  back(s?: number): EasingCurve;
  bounce: EasingCurve;
};
```

An easing is data, not a JS function: the runtime evaluates it natively. To draw one, `Easing.sample(easing, count)` gives its values at `count` evenly spaced points from 0 to 1; `Animated.sampleSpring` and `Animated.sampleDecay` give a spring's or decay's values one per frame (at `fps`, 60 by default) from `from` (0) until it ends. All three come from the native code the animations run. Wherever an `Easing` is accepted you can pass a name (`"easeOut"`), a cubic Bézier as four numbers, or a curve from the `Easing` object.

| Curve | Shape |
|---|---|
| `quad` | `t²` |
| `cubic` | `t³` |
| `poly(n)` | `tⁿ` (`n` defaults to 2) |
| `sin` | Sinusoidal |
| `circle` | Circular |
| `exp` | Exponential |
| `elastic(bounciness)` | Springy overshoot (`bounciness` defaults to 1) |
| `back(s)` | Pulls back before going; `s` is the overshoot (default 1.70158) |
| `bounce` | Bounces at the end |

The curves are in their "in" form (slow at the start). `Easing.out(curve)` reverses one, `Easing.inOut(curve)` makes it symmetric, `Easing.in(curve)` keeps it as is.

```ts
value.timing(1, { duration: 600, easing: Easing.out(Easing.back()) });
value.timing(1, { easing: Easing.bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) });
value.timing(1, { easing: "easeOut" });
```

## LayoutAnimation

```ts
const LayoutAnimation: {
  configureNext(config: LayoutAnimationConfig, onEnd?: () => void): void;
  create(duration: number, type?: LayoutAnimationType, property?: LayoutAnimationProperty): LayoutAnimationConfig;
  Types: { easeInEaseOut; spring; linear; easeIn; easeOut };
  Properties: { opacity; scaleXY };
  Presets: { easeInEaseOut: LayoutAnimationConfig; linear: LayoutAnimationConfig; spring: LayoutAnimationConfig };
  easeInEaseOut(onEnd?: () => void): void;
  linear(onEnd?: () => void): void;
  spring(onEnd?: () => void): void;
};

interface LayoutAnimationConfig {
  duration: number;                // ms
  create?: LayoutAnimationAnimation;    // views inserted
  update?: LayoutAnimationAnimation;    // views moved or resized
  delete?: LayoutAnimationAnimation;    // views removed
}

interface LayoutAnimationAnimation {
  type?: "easeInEaseOut" | "spring" | "linear" | "easeIn" | "easeOut";
  property?: "opacity" | "scaleXY" | "scale";
  duration?: number;
  delay?: number;
  springDamping?: number;          // 0..1, default 0.7
}
```

`LayoutAnimation.configureNext(config)` animates the layout changes of the next commit natively: views that move or resize glide to their new frames, new views appear (fading or scaling in, by `property`) and removed views disappear. Call it right before the state change that changes the layout.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `configureNext(config, onEnd?)` | Animates the next commit's changes; `onEnd` runs when done. |
| `create(duration, type?, property?)` | A config using the same curve for all three phases. |
| `Presets.easeInEaseOut` | 300 ms, views fading in and out. |
| `Presets.linear` | 500 ms at constant speed. |
| `Presets.spring` | 700 ms; frames spring (damping 0.4), views fade linearly. |
| `easeInEaseOut(onEnd?)`, `linear(onEnd?)`, `spring(onEnd?)` | Shorthands for `configureNext(Presets.…)`. |
| `Types`, `Properties` | The names, as constants. |

```tsx
const open = signal(false);
const toggle = () => {
  LayoutAnimation.configureNext(LayoutAnimation.Presets.spring);
  open.update((o) => !o);
};

<View>
  <Text onPress={toggle}>Details</Text>
  <If when={open()}>
    <Text>Shown with a spring.</Text>
  </If>
</View>
```

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-animated

---

# nsh/list

`nsh/list` exports `List`: a virtualized list on a native scroll view. Only the rows near the viewport exist, and their cells are reused as you scroll. Which rows exist, where they are, columns, sticky headers and viewability are all computed natively, so scrolling a list of ten thousand items runs no JS except the row bindings that change when a cell is reused.

```ts
import { List, type ListProps, type ViewToken, type ViewabilityConfig } from "nsh/list";
```

See [Lists](https://nsh.dev/docs/lists.md) for the guide and [`<List>`](https://nsh.dev/elements/list.md) for the element's props.

## List

```ts
function List<T>(props: ListProps<T>): YNode;
```

```tsx
import { mount, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { List } from "nsh/list";

const contacts = Array.from({ length: 1000 }, (_, i) => ({ id: String(i), name: `Contact ${i}` }));

function App() {
  return (
    <List each={contacts} estimatedItemSize={48} style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      {(item, index) => (
        <View style={{ height: 48, paddingHorizontal: 16, justifyContent: "center", backgroundColor: index() % 2 ? "#f8fafc" : "#fff" }}>
          <Text>{item().name}</Text>
        </View>
      )}
    </List>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

### Rows are recycled

`children` is a function that renders **one cell**. It runs once per cell, not once per item: when a cell scrolls out of view it is reused for another item, and `item()` and `index()` (both accessors) change. Read them inside JSX expressions (`{item().name}`) so the cell updates when it is reused.

> [!WARNING]
> Do not keep per-item state in signals created inside the row function: the cell is reused for other items and the signal would follow the cell, not the item. Keep it in your data, keyed by id (a signal holding a `Set` of selected ids, for example).

## Props

`ListProps<T>` combines the list's own props with the scrolling props shared with `<Scroll>`.

### Data and rendering

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `each` | `readonly T[]` | (required) | The items. Pass a signal's value (`each={items()}`) to follow changes; inserting items above the visible rows keeps those rows in place. |
| `children` | `(item: () => T, index: () => number) => JSX.Element` | (required) | Renders one row (see above). |
| `estimatedItemSize` | `number` | `50` | The size of rows not measured yet, in points, along the list's axis. Close estimates make the scroll indicator and `scrollToIndex` more accurate. |
| `numColumns` | `number` | `1` | Items per row (vertical lists): a grid. |
| `horizontal` | `boolean` | `false` | Scrolls sideways. |
| `inverted` | `boolean` | `false` | Lays out from the end, item 0 last (chat style); starts scrolled to the end and keeps its distance from the end as content changes. |
| `stickyHeaderIndices` | `number[]` | | Items that stick to the start while scrolled past (one column, not inverted). |
| `ListHeaderComponent` | `ListSlot` | | Rendered before the items. |
| `ListFooterComponent` | `ListSlot` | | Rendered after the items. |
| `ListEmptyComponent` | `ListSlot` | | Shown instead of the items while `each` is empty. |
| `ItemSeparatorComponent` | `ListSlot` | | Rendered between items (one column). |
| `keyExtractor` | `(item: T, index: number) => string` | `item.key`, `item.id`, or the index | The key of an item in viewability tokens. |
| `initialScrollIndex` | `number` | | Scrolls to this item before the first frame. |
| `contentContainerStyle` | `ListContentStyle` | | Padding and gaps of the content: `padding`, `paddingHorizontal`, `paddingVertical`, `paddingTop`, `paddingRight`, `paddingBottom`, `paddingLeft`, `gap`, `rowGap`, `columnGap` (numbers). |
| `style` | `StyleProp<ViewStyle>` | | The list's own style (give it a size: `flex: 1` or a height). |
| `ref` | `YNode \| ((node: YNode) => void)` | | See [ref methods](#ref-methods). |

`ListSlot` is a component (`Header`) or an element (`<Header />`).

### Loading, refreshing and viewability

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `onEndReached` | `() => void` | | Called when the end comes within `onEndReachedThreshold` viewports: load more. |
| `onEndReachedThreshold` | `number` | `1` | How close to the end (in viewport lengths) `onEndReached` fires. |
| `refreshing` | `boolean` | | The pull-to-refresh spinner shows. |
| `onRefresh` | `() => void` | | Enables pull to refresh; set `refreshing` while you load. |
| `onViewableItemsChanged` | `(info: { viewableItems: ViewToken<T>[]; changed: ViewToken<T>[] }) => void` | | Items that became or stopped being viewable. |
| `viewabilityConfig` | `ViewabilityConfig` | | When an item counts as viewable. |

```ts
interface ViewToken<T> {
  item: T;
  key: string;
  index: number;
  isViewable: boolean;
}

interface ViewabilityConfig {
  /** Percent of the viewport an item must cover to count as viewable. */
  viewAreaCoveragePercentThreshold?: number;
  /** Percent of an item that must be visible. Without either threshold, any visible pixel counts. */
  itemVisiblePercentThreshold?: number;
  /** Milliseconds items must stay viewable before they are reported. */
  minimumViewTime?: number;
}
```

### Scrolling

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `showsIndicator` | `boolean` | `true` | The scroll indicator shows. |
| `scrollEnabled` | `boolean` | `true` | The user can scroll it. |
| `bounces` | `boolean` | `true` | Overscroll past the edges. |
| `pagingEnabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Stops at multiples of the viewport. |
| `snapToInterval` | `number` | `0` | Stops at multiples of this length (0: off). |
| `snapToOffsets` | `number[]` | | Stops at these offsets. |
| `snapToAlignment` | `"start" \| "center" \| "end"` | `"start"` | Which point of an item aligns with the viewport with `snapToInterval`. |
| `disableIntervalMomentum` | `boolean` | `false` | A fling moves one snap point at most. |
| `decelerationRate` | `"normal" \| "fast" \| number` | platform | How fast a fling slows down (`0.998` / `0.99`, or the velocity kept per millisecond). |
| `contentInset` | `{ top?, right?, bottom?, left? }` | | Room around the content. |
| `contentOffset` | `{ x?, y? }` | | Where it starts. |
| `keyboardShouldPersistTaps` | `"never" \| "always" \| "handled" \| boolean` | `"never"` | Whether a tap dismisses the keyboard (`"never"`: the tap only dismisses it). |
| `keyboardDismissMode` | `"none" \| "on-drag" \| "interactive"` | `"none"` | Whether dragging dismisses the keyboard. |
| `scrollEventThrottle` | `number` | | Minimum milliseconds between `onScroll` events (at most one per frame anyway). |
| `scrollValue` | `NativeValue` | | A [native value](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-animated.md) fed with the scroll offset (main axis) on the UI thread, for scroll-linked effects. |

### Scroll events

| Event | Payload | When |
|---|---|---|
| `onScroll` | `ScrollEvent`: `{ x, y, contentWidth, contentHeight, width, height, zoomScale }` | While scrolling. |
| `onScrollBeginDrag` | `{ x, y }` | A drag starts. |
| `onScrollEndDrag` | `{ x, y }` | The finger lifts. |
| `onMomentumScrollBegin` | `{ x, y }` | A glide starts after the drag. |
| `onMomentumScrollEnd` | `{ x, y }` | The glide ends (also when a new drag catches it). |
| `onScrollEnd` | `{ x, y }` | Scrolling came to rest. |

Lists also take the props every element takes ([common props](https://nsh.dev/elements.md)).

## Ref methods

A list's `ref` receives a `YNode` with these methods:

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `scrollToIndex({ index, animated?, viewPosition?, viewOffset? })` | Scrolls item `index` into view. `viewPosition` places it: `0` at the start of the viewport (default), `0.5` in the middle, `1` at the end; `viewOffset` shifts it further. Resolved natively with the measured (or estimated) row sizes. |
| `scrollToOffset({ offset, animated? })` | Scrolls to a content offset along the list's axis. |
| `scrollToEnd({ animated? })` | Scrolls to the end of the content (the start of an inverted list). |
| `scrollTo({ x?, y?, animated? })` | Scrolls to an offset. |

```tsx
import { Text, View, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { List } from "nsh/list";

let list!: YNode;

<View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  <Text onPress={() => list.scrollToIndex({ index: 60, viewPosition: 0.5 })}>Jump to 60</Text>
  <List ref={list} each={items} numColumns={3} estimatedItemSize={90} style={{ flex: 1 }}
        contentContainerStyle={{ padding: 12, gap: 8 }}>
    {(item) => <View style={{ height: 90, backgroundColor: "#e0e7ff" }}><Text>{item().title}</Text></View>}
  </List>
</View>
```

## Examples

A chat: newest message at the bottom, older messages loaded as you scroll up.

```tsx
<List
  each={messages()}
  inverted
  estimatedItemSize={44}
  style={{ flex: 1 }}
  contentContainerStyle={{ padding: 12, gap: 6 }}
  keyboardDismissMode="interactive"
  onEndReached={loadOlder}
  onEndReachedThreshold={0.5}
>
  {(m) => (
    <View style={{ alignSelf: m().mine ? "flex-end" : "flex-start", maxWidth: "75%", padding: 10, borderRadius: 14, backgroundColor: m().mine ? "#6366f1" : "#e2e8f0" }}>
      <Text style={{ color: m().mine ? "#fff" : "#0f172a" }}>{m().text}</Text>
    </View>
  )}
</List>
```

Pull to refresh:

```tsx
const refreshing = signal(false);
const refresh = async () => {
  refreshing.set(true);
  items.set(await load());
  refreshing.set(false);
};

<List each={items()} refreshing={refreshing()} onRefresh={refresh} style={{ flex: 1 }}>
  {(item) => <Text style={{ padding: 16 }}>{item().title}</Text>}
</List>
```

## ListItemsProps

```ts
type ListItemsProps<T> = Pick<ListProps<T>,
  "each" | "children" | "keyExtractor" | "stickyHeaderIndices" | "initialScrollIndex"
  | "onViewableItemsChanged" | "viewabilityConfig" | "refreshing" | "onRefresh"
  | "onEndReached" | "onEndReachedThreshold"
  | "ListHeaderComponent" | "ListFooterComponent" | "ListEmptyComponent">;
```

The data-and-rows half of `ListProps`: what you pass to a component that lays out a list itself, such as [`ListView`](https://nsh.dev/components/list-view.md) from `nsh/ui/mobile`.

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-list

---

# nsh/canvas

`nsh/canvas` draws with an HTML Canvas 2D–style context. Your `draw` function **records** the drawing; the platform replays it natively (Core Graphics on iOS, `android.graphics.Canvas` on Android) at the screen's resolution. Numbers and colors in a drawing may be [native values](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-animated.md): when they animate, the platform redraws on its own, without running `draw` again.

```ts
import { Canvas, CanvasGradient, CanvasRenderingContext2D, Path2D } from "nsh/canvas";
```

See [Canvas](https://nsh.dev/docs/canvas.md) for the guide and [`<Canvas>`](https://nsh.dev/elements/canvas.md) for its props.

## Canvas

```ts
function Canvas(props: CanvasProps): YNode;

interface CanvasProps extends ViewProps {
  draw: (ctx: CanvasRenderingContext2D, size: CanvasSize) => void;
}

interface CanvasSize {
  width: number;   // points
  height: number;
}
```

A view drawn with a 2D context. It takes every [view prop](https://nsh.dev/elements/view.md) (style, classes, touch handlers, accessibility, `ref`), plus:

| Prop | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `draw` | `(ctx, { width, height }) => void` | Draws the canvas. Runs once the size is known, again when the signals it reads change, and again when the canvas resizes. Native values passed as numbers or colors animate without running it. |

Give the canvas a size through its style (`width` / `height`, `flex: 1`, `aspectRatio`, ...). Coordinates are in points, the origin at the top left.

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { Canvas } from "nsh/canvas";

function App() {
  const values = signal([12, 30, 22, 48, 36, 60, 52, 75]);
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1, padding: 24 }}>
      <Canvas
        style={{ height: 160 }}
        draw={(ctx, { width, height }) => {
          const v = values();
          const step = width / (v.length - 1);
          ctx.strokeStyle = "#6366f1";
          ctx.lineWidth = 3;
          ctx.lineJoin = "round";
          ctx.beginPath();
          v.forEach((n, i) => (i ? ctx.lineTo(i * step, height - n * 2) : ctx.moveTo(0, height - n * 2)));
          ctx.stroke();
        }}
      />
      <Text onPress={() => values.update((v) => [...v.slice(1), Math.random() * 80])}>Next</Text>
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

## Animating without redrawing

Any argument typed `CanvasNumber` and any paint (`fillStyle`, `strokeStyle`) accepts a `NativeNode`. The canvas then reads the node while it draws, and redraws natively on every frame of its animation:

```tsx
import { createNativeValue, Easing } from "nsh/animated";
import { Canvas } from "nsh/canvas";

const progress = createNativeValue(0);

<Canvas
  style={{ width: 120, height: 120 }}
  draw={(ctx, { width }) => {
    const c = width / 2;
    ctx.lineWidth = 12;
    ctx.lineCap = "round";
    ctx.strokeStyle = "#6366f1";
    ctx.beginPath();
    // The end angle is a native node: animating `progress` redraws natively.
    ctx.arc(c, c, c - 10, -Math.PI / 2, progress.mul(Math.PI * 2).sub(Math.PI / 2));
    ctx.stroke();
  }}
/>;

progress.timing(0.75, { duration: 900, easing: Easing.inOut(Easing.cubic) });
```

```ts
type CanvasNumber = number | NativeNode;
type CanvasPaint = string | CanvasGradient | NativeNode;
```

## CanvasRenderingContext2D

The context `draw` receives. Calls only record operations; the platform draws them after `draw` returns.

### State and transforms

```ts
readonly canvas: { readonly width: number; readonly height: number };
save(): void;
restore(): void;
translate(x: CanvasNumber, y: CanvasNumber): void;
scale(x: CanvasNumber, y: CanvasNumber): void;
rotate(angle: CanvasNumber): void;
transform(a: CanvasNumber, b: CanvasNumber, c: CanvasNumber, d: CanvasNumber, e: CanvasNumber, f: CanvasNumber): void;
setTransform(a: CanvasNumber, b: CanvasNumber, c: CanvasNumber, d: CanvasNumber, e: CanvasNumber, f: CanvasNumber): void;
resetTransform(): void;
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `canvas` | The canvas's size in points. |
| `save()` / `restore()` | Pushes / pops the drawing state (transform, clip, styles). |
| `translate(x, y)` | Moves the origin. |
| `scale(x, y)` | Scales the axes. |
| `rotate(angle)` | Rotates the axes; radians, clockwise. |
| `transform(a, b, c, d, e, f)` | Multiplies the transform by the matrix `[a c e; b d f]`. |
| `setTransform(a, b, c, d, e, f)` | Replaces the transform. |
| `resetTransform()` | Back to the identity. |

### Properties

| Property | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `fillStyle` | `CanvasPaint` | Color, gradient or native color node used by `fill`, `fillRect`, `fillText`. |
| `strokeStyle` | `CanvasPaint` | The same for strokes. |
| `lineWidth` | `CanvasNumber` | Stroke width in points. |
| `lineCap` | `"butt" \| "round" \| "square"` | How strokes end. |
| `lineJoin` | `"miter" \| "round" \| "bevel"` | How stroke segments join. |
| `miterLimit` | `number` | Miter joins longer than this (in line widths) are beveled. |
| `lineDashOffset` | `CanvasNumber` | Where the dash pattern starts. |
| `globalAlpha` | `CanvasNumber` | Opacity of what is drawn next, 0..1. |
| `globalCompositeOperation` | `string` | How what is drawn next combines with the canvas (`"source-over"`, `"multiply"`, ...). |
| `shadowColor` | `string` | The color of shadows (transparent: none). |
| `shadowBlur` | `number` | Shadow blur in points. |
| `shadowOffsetX`, `shadowOffsetY` | `number` | Shadow offset in points. |
| `font` | `string` | CSS `font` shorthand, e.g. `"600 14px Inter"` (sizes in `px`, `pt` or `rem`). |
| `textAlign` | `"start" \| "end" \| "left" \| "right" \| "center"` | Where text sits horizontally relative to its x. |
| `textBaseline` | `"alphabetic" \| "top" \| "hanging" \| "middle" \| "ideographic" \| "bottom"` | Where text sits vertically relative to its y. |

Dashes: `setLineDash(segments: number[])` and `getLineDash(): number[]`.

### Paths

The context has a current path, built with the same methods as [`Path2D`](#path2d):

```ts
beginPath(): void;
moveTo(x, y): void;
lineTo(x, y): void;
quadraticCurveTo(cpx, cpy, x, y): void;
bezierCurveTo(cp1x, cp1y, cp2x, cp2y, x, y): void;
arc(x, y, radius, startAngle, endAngle, counterclockwise?: boolean): void;
arcTo(x1, y1, x2, y2, radius): void;
ellipse(x, y, radiusX, radiusY, rotation, startAngle, endAngle, counterclockwise?: boolean): void;
rect(x, y, w, h): void;
roundRect(x, y, w, h, radii?: CanvasNumber | CanvasNumber[]): void;
closePath(): void;
```

All coordinates are `CanvasNumber`s. Angles are in radians, clockwise from the x axis. `roundRect`'s `radii` is one radius or 2–4 as in CSS `border-radius` (top left first).

### Drawing

```ts
fill(path?: Path2D | "nonzero" | "evenodd", rule?: "nonzero" | "evenodd"): void;
stroke(path?: Path2D): void;
clip(path?: Path2D | "nonzero" | "evenodd", rule?: "nonzero" | "evenodd"): void;
fillRect(x, y, w, h): void;
strokeRect(x, y, w, h): void;
clearRect(x, y, w, h): void;
```

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `fill(path?, rule?)` | Fills the current path (or `path`) with `fillStyle`, by the nonzero (default) or even-odd rule. |
| `stroke(path?)` | Strokes the current path (or `path`) with `strokeStyle`. |
| `clip(path?, rule?)` | Restricts what is drawn next to the path. |
| `fillRect`, `strokeRect` | A rectangle, without touching the current path. |
| `clearRect` | Makes a rectangle transparent. |

### Text

```ts
fillText(text: string, x: CanvasNumber, y: CanvasNumber, maxWidth?: number): void;
strokeText(text: string, x: CanvasNumber, y: CanvasNumber, maxWidth?: number): void;
measureText(text: string): TextMetrics; // { width: number }
```

`measureText` is synchronous: it measures with the platform's text engine and the current `font`. Only `width` is reported.

```ts
ctx.font = "11px system-ui";
const label = "100";
ctx.fillText(label, 40 - ctx.measureText(label).width, 20);
```

### Gradients

```ts
createLinearGradient(x0: number, y0: number, x1: number, y1: number): CanvasGradient;
createRadialGradient(x0: number, y0: number, r0: number, x1: number, y1: number, r1: number): CanvasGradient;
createConicGradient(startAngle: number, x: number, y: number): CanvasGradient;

class CanvasGradient {
  addColorStop(offset: number, color: string): void; // offset 0..1, any CSS color
}
```

```ts
const g = ctx.createLinearGradient(0, 0, 0, height);
g.addColorStop(0, "rgba(99, 102, 241, 0.4)");
g.addColorStop(1, "rgba(99, 102, 241, 0)");
ctx.fillStyle = g;
ctx.fillRect(0, 0, width, height);
```

### Images

```ts
drawImage(image: string | ImageAsset | { uri: string }, ...args: CanvasNumber[]): void;
```

Draws an image given as a URL, an imported asset (`import logo from "./logo.png"`) or `{ uri }`. It is loaded natively; the canvas draws again once it has loaded. Three forms, as in HTML:

- `drawImage(image, dx, dy)`: at its natural size.
- `drawImage(image, dx, dy, dw, dh)`: scaled into a rectangle.
- `drawImage(image, sx, sy, sw, sh, dx, dy, dw, dh)`: part of it (source in image pixels).

## Path2D

```ts
class Path2D {
  constructor(path?: Path2D | string);
  addPath(path: Path2D): void;
  // and every path method: moveTo, lineTo, quadraticCurveTo, bezierCurveTo,
  // arc, arcTo, ellipse, rect, roundRect, closePath
}
```

A reusable path to fill, stroke or clip. The constructor copies another `Path2D` or parses SVG path data natively:

```ts
const heart = new Path2D("M12 21s-7-4.5-9.5-9A5.5 5.5 0 0 1 12 6a5.5 5.5 0 0 1 9.5 6c-2.5 4.5-9.5 9-9.5 9z");
ctx.save();
ctx.scale(4, 4);
ctx.fillStyle = "#ef4444";
ctx.fill(heart);
ctx.restore();
```

## Not supported

Pixel access (`getImageData`, `putImageData`), `filter`, `isPointInPath` and SVG images are not available. An invalid color or font drops that one operation, as in HTML Canvas.

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-canvas

---

# nsh/device

`nsh/device` tells the app about the device and its environment. `windowSize`, `colorScheme` and `fontScale` are reactive accessors: read them in JSX, `computed` or `effect`, and what reads them updates when the platform reports a change (rotation, a window resize, switching to dark mode, changing the text size).

```ts
import { colorScheme, fontScale, I18nManager, PixelRatio, Platform, windowSize } from "nsh/device";
```

See [Device and environment](https://nsh.dev/docs/device-and-environment.md) for the guide.

## windowSize

```ts
const windowSize: Accessor<{ width: number; height: number }>;
```

The size of the surface in points: the window, or the embedded `NshAppView` / `NshView`. Reactive.

```tsx
const wide = () => windowSize().width >= 600;

<View style={{ flexDirection: wide() ? "row" : "column" }}>{/* ... */}</View>
```

## colorScheme

```ts
const colorScheme: Accessor<"light" | "dark">;
```

The system appearance. Reactive. Tailwind's `dark:` variant follows it too (see [Tailwind](https://nsh.dev/docs/tailwind.md)).

```tsx
const dark = () => colorScheme() === "dark";

<View style={{ flex: 1, backgroundColor: dark() ? "#000" : "#fff" }} />
```

## fontScale

```ts
const fontScale: Accessor<number>;
```

The user's preferred text size relative to the default (`1` is the default size; Dynamic Type on iOS, font size on Android). Reactive. Text already scales with it unless `allowFontScaling={false}`; read it when other sizes should follow, such as icons next to text.

## Platform

```ts
const Platform: {
  readonly OS: "ios" | "android" | "macos" | "windows" | "linux" | "web";
  readonly isDesktop: boolean;
  readonly Version: string | number;
  readonly isPad: boolean;
  readonly isTV: boolean;
  readonly isMacCatalyst: boolean;
  readonly constants: {
    readonly osVersion: string | number;
    readonly interfaceIdiom: "phone" | "pad" | "mac" | "tv" | "desktop";
  };
  select<T>(spec: PlatformSelectSpec<T>): T | undefined;
};
```

The platform the app runs on, constant while it runs.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `OS` | The operating system. iOS, the iOS simulator and Mac Catalyst report `"ios"`, browsers `"web"`. |
| `isDesktop` | A desktop OS (macOS, Windows, Linux), or a browser with a mouse and a wide window. |
| `Version` | iOS and desktops: the version string (`"17.5"`); Android: the API level (a number). |
| `isPad` | A tablet: an iPad, or an Android tablet. |
| `isTV` | A TV (Apple TV idiom, Android TV). |
| `isMacCatalyst` | Mac Catalyst in the Mac idiom. |
| `constants.osVersion` | The same as `Version`. |
| `constants.interfaceIdiom` | `"phone"`, `"pad"`, `"mac"`, `"tv"` or `"desktop"`. |
| `select(spec)` | The value for this platform (see below). |

### Platform.select

```ts
interface PlatformSelectSpec<T> {
  ios?: T;
  android?: T;
  macos?: T;
  windows?: T;
  linux?: T;
  mobile?: T;   // iOS and Android
  desktop?: T;  // macOS, Windows and Linux
  native?: T;   // every platform
  default?: T;
}
```

Returns the value for the current OS (`ios`, `android`, `web`, ...), else `mobile` / `desktop`, else `native` (every platform but the web), else `default`, else `undefined`. In a browser, `mobile` or `desktop` follows the idiom.

```ts
const shadow = Platform.select({
  ios: { shadowColor: "#000", shadowOpacity: 0.15, shadowRadius: 8 },
  android: { elevation: 4 },
});
```

> [!TIP]
> For props that only one platform has, prefer the `ios={{…}}` / `android={{…}}` props of elements and components to branching on `Platform` (see [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md)).

## PixelRatio

```ts
const PixelRatio: {
  get(): number;
  getFontScale(): number;
  getPixelSizeForLayoutSize(size: number): number;
  roundToNearestPixel(size: number): number;
};
```

Device pixels per point.

| Method | Description |
|---|---|
| `get()` | Device pixels per point (e.g. `3` on most iPhones). |
| `getFontScale()` | The same as `fontScale()`, without tracking. |
| `getPixelSizeForLayoutSize(size)` | `size` points in whole device pixels. |
| `roundToNearestPixel(size)` | `size` rounded to the nearest device pixel, in points. |

```ts
const hairline = 1 / PixelRatio.get();
```

`PixelRatio` is not reactive. A window can move to another screen (on Mac Catalyst, or an external display); read it in components that also read `windowSize()`, so they run again when the window changes.

## I18nManager

```ts
const I18nManager: {
  isRTL: boolean;                  // reactive
  doLeftAndRightSwapInRTL: true;
  allowRTL(allow: boolean): void;
  forceRTL(force: boolean): void;
  getConstants(): { isRTL: boolean; doLeftAndRightSwapInRTL: boolean };
};
```

Right-to-left layout. In right-to-left layout, rows run from the right, and `left` / `right` style properties (`marginLeft`, `paddingRight`, ...) mean start and end. Changes apply at once; no restart is needed.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `isRTL` | Whether the app lays out right to left. Reading it is tracked. |
| `doLeftAndRightSwapInRTL` | Always `true`: `left` and `right` swap in right-to-left layout. |
| `allowRTL(allow)` | Follow right-to-left languages (default `true`). |
| `forceRTL(force)` | Lay out right to left whatever the language. |
| `getConstants()` | `{ isRTL, doLeftAndRightSwapInRTL }`. |

```tsx
<Text onPress={() => I18nManager.forceRTL(!I18nManager.isRTL)}>
  {I18nManager.isRTL ? "Right to left" : "Left to right"}
</Text>
```

## Related

- Safe area insets and the keyboard (`safeArea()`, `keyboard()`, `useSafeAreaInsets()`) are part of [`nsh/ui/mobile`](https://nsh.dev/components.md).
- Screen reader and reduced motion settings are in [`nsh/accessibility`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-accessibility.md).

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-device

---

# nsh/gesture

`nsh/gesture` exports `PanResponder`: drag gestures on top of the gesture responder system, with `onPanResponder…` callbacks that receive the touch event and a gesture state. It tracks the touches' centroid, the distance moved and the velocity for you.

```ts
import { PanResponder, type PanResponderGestureState } from "nsh/gesture";
```

> [!TIP]
> `PanResponder` delivers every move to JS, so it suits gestures that change app state (reordering, swipe-to-delete decisions). To move a view with the finger, the `pan={{ x, y }}`, `pinch` and `rotation` props are faster: the drag writes [native values](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-animated.md) on the UI thread and JS only hears `onPanStart` / `onPanEnd`. See [Touch and gestures](https://nsh.dev/docs/touch-and-gestures.md).

## PanResponder.create

```ts
const PanResponder: { create(config: PanResponderCallbacks): PanResponderInstance };

interface PanResponderInstance {
  panHandlers: TouchProps;
}
```

Creates a pan responder. Spread its `panHandlers` on the view that should receive the gesture:

```tsx
import { mount, signal, View } from "nsh";
import { PanResponder } from "nsh/gesture";

function App() {
  const pos = signal({ x: 0, y: 0 });
  let start = { x: 0, y: 0 };
  const pan = PanResponder.create({
    onStartShouldSetPanResponder: () => true,
    onPanResponderGrant: () => (start = pos()),
    onPanResponderMove: (_, g) => pos.set({ x: start.x + g.dx, y: start.y + g.dy }),
    onPanResponderRelease: (_, g) => console.log(`released at ${g.vx.toFixed(2)} pt/ms`),
  });
  return (
    <View style={{ flex: 1 }}>
      <View
        {...pan.panHandlers}
        style={{
          width: 64,
          height: 64,
          borderRadius: 32,
          backgroundColor: "#6366f1",
          transform: [{ translateX: pos().x }, { translateY: pos().y }],
        }}
      />
    </View>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

## Callbacks

Every callback receives the touch event (`GestureResponderEvent`, from [`nsh`](https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh.md#types)) and the gesture state.

```ts
type PanHandler<R = void> = (e: GestureResponderEvent, gestureState: PanResponderGestureState) => R;
```

| Callback | Returns | Called when |
|---|---|---|
| `onStartShouldSetPanResponder` | `boolean` | A finger goes down: return `true` to become the responder. Asked from the touched view outwards. |
| `onStartShouldSetPanResponderCapture` | `boolean` | The same, asked from the outside in before the bubbling one (a parent taking the gesture from its children). |
| `onMoveShouldSetPanResponder` | `boolean` | A finger moves: return `true` to become the responder (e.g. only once `Math.abs(g.dx) > 10`). |
| `onMoveShouldSetPanResponderCapture` | `boolean` | The same, capture phase. |
| `onPanResponderGrant` | | This view is the responder now: the gesture starts. |
| `onPanResponderReject` | | Another view is the responder and would not let go. |
| `onPanResponderStart` | | A finger went down while responding. |
| `onPanResponderMove` | | The fingers moved. |
| `onPanResponderEnd` | | A finger lifted while responding. |
| `onPanResponderRelease` | | The last finger lifted: the gesture ended. |
| `onPanResponderTerminate` | | Another view (or a native gesture, like a scroll view) took the touches. |
| `onPanResponderTerminationRequest` | `boolean` | Another view wants the touches: return `false` to keep them (default `true`). |
| `onShouldBlockNativeResponder` | `boolean` | Whether to keep native scroll views from taking the touches while responding (default `true`). |

## PanResponderGestureState

```ts
interface PanResponderGestureState {
  stateID: number;
  moveX: number;               // latest centroid of the touches (surface points)
  moveY: number;
  x0: number;                  // the centroid when the responder was granted
  y0: number;
  dx: number;                  // distance moved since the grant
  dy: number;
  vx: number;                  // velocity, points per millisecond
  vy: number;
  numberActiveTouches: number;
}
```

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `stateID` | Identifies the gesture. |
| `moveX`, `moveY` | Latest position of the touches' centroid, in surface points. |
| `x0`, `y0` | Where the centroid was when the responder was granted. |
| `dx`, `dy` | Distance moved since the grant. |
| `vx`, `vy` | Velocity in points per millisecond. |
| `numberActiveTouches` | Fingers down. |

## Inside scroll views

While a pan responder is the responder, native scroll views around it do not scroll (`onShouldBlockNativeResponder` defaults to `true`). To let a horizontal swipe coexist with vertical scrolling, become the responder only on horizontal moves:

```ts
const swipe = PanResponder.create({
  onMoveShouldSetPanResponder: (_, g) => Math.abs(g.dx) > 10 && Math.abs(g.dx) > Math.abs(g.dy),
  onPanResponderMove: (_, g) => offset.set(g.dx),
  onPanResponderRelease: (_, g) => (Math.abs(g.dx) > 120 ? remove() : offset.set(0)),
  onPanResponderTerminate: () => offset.set(0),
});
```

The underlying responder props (`onStartShouldSetResponder`, `onResponderGrant`, `onTouchStart`, ...) can also be used directly on any element; see [Elements](https://nsh.dev/elements.md).

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-gesture

---

# nsh/image

`nsh/image` exports `Image`, the [`<Image>`](https://nsh.dev/elements/image.md) element that shows images. The same `Image` also asks the native image loader about images without showing them: their size, and loading them before they are shown.

```ts
import { Image, type ImageSize } from "nsh/image";
```

`Image` is a component carrying two functions: `<Image src=…>` renders the native image view (the compiler makes it in place, as it does `<View>`), and `Image.getSize` / `Image.prefetch` are called on it directly.

```ts
const Image: ((props: ImageProps) => YNode) & {
  getSize(source: string | { uri: string }): Promise<ImageSize>;
  prefetch(source: string | { uri: string }): Promise<boolean>;
};
```

See [Images and assets](https://nsh.dev/docs/images-and-assets.md) for the guide.

## Image.getSize

```ts
getSize(source: string | { uri: string }): Promise<ImageSize>;

interface ImageSize {
  width: number;   // pixels
  height: number;
}
```

Loads the image and resolves with its size in pixels (of the source image, not a downsampled copy). The loaded bytes stay in memory, so the `<Image>` that shows it next does not download it again. The promise rejects if the image cannot be loaded.

```tsx
import { signal } from "nsh";
import { Image } from "nsh/image";

const url = "https://picsum.photos/seed/nsh/1200/800";
const ratio = signal(1);

Image.getSize(url).then(({ width, height }) => ratio.set(width / height));

<Image src={url} style={{ width: "100%", aspectRatio: ratio() }} />;
```

## Image.prefetch

```ts
prefetch(source: string | { uri: string }): Promise<boolean>;
```

Loads an image ahead of showing it. Resolves with `true` once its bytes are in memory (`false` when it could not be loaded). Use it for the next page of a gallery or the image behind a tap.

```ts
const next = photos.slice(index + 1, index + 4);
next.forEach((p) => Image.prefetch(p.url));
```

## Related

- [`<Image>`](https://nsh.dev/elements/image.md): `src`, `resizeMode`, `defaultSource`, `onLoad`, `onProgress`, `onError` and the other props.
- Importing an image file (`import logo from "./logo.png"`) gives an `ImageAsset` (`{ uri, width, height }`, sized in points) that `<Image src>` and canvas `drawImage` accept.

> [!NOTE]
> When your app declares `capabilities` in `nsh.json`, `getSize` and `prefetch` of remote URLs must be allowed under `network`, like `fetch`. See [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-image

---

# nsh/clipboard

`nsh/clipboard` reads and writes the text on the system clipboard: `UIPasteboard` on iOS, `ClipboardManager` on Android, `navigator.clipboard` on the web.

```ts
import { Clipboard } from "nsh/clipboard";
```

```ts
const Clipboard: {
  setString(text: string): void;
  getString(): Promise<string>;
  hasString(): Promise<boolean>;
};
```

The user can also copy from a [selectable text](https://nsh.dev/elements/text.md) themselves; `Clipboard` is for copying from code, such as a Copy button.

## Clipboard.setString

```ts
setString(text: string): void;
```

Puts `text` on the clipboard, replacing what was there.

```tsx
import { signal, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { Clipboard } from "nsh/clipboard";

const copied = signal(false);

<View
  onPress={() => {
    Clipboard.setString(code);
    copied.set(true);
  }}
>
  <Text>{copied() ? "Copied" : "Copy"}</Text>
</View>;
```

## Clipboard.getString

```ts
getString(): Promise<string>;
```

Resolves with the clipboard's text, or `""` when it holds none. On iOS, reading the clipboard can show the system's paste notice ("App pasted from …"), and on Android 10 and later only the app in the foreground can read it. Read it when the user asks to paste, not on every screen.

```ts
const pasted = await Clipboard.getString();
if (pasted) code.set(pasted.trim());
```

## Clipboard.hasString

```ts
hasString(): Promise<boolean>;
```

Resolves with whether the clipboard holds text, without reading it: no paste notice on iOS. Use it to decide whether to show a Paste button. On the web, browsers only tell by reading, so it may ask the user for permission.

```ts
const canPaste = signal(false);
Clipboard.hasString().then((has) => canPaste.set(has));
```

> [!NOTE]
> When your app declares `capabilities` in `nsh.json`, the clipboard must be granted with `"clipboard": true`. Without it `setString` does nothing, `getString` resolves `""` and `hasString` `false`. See [Sandbox and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md).

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-clipboard

---

# nsh/keymap

`nsh/keymap` binds the app's keyboard shortcuts: a keystroke such as `"mod+k"` and the function it runs.

```ts
import { keymap } from "nsh/keymap";
```

```ts
const keymap: {
  bind(keystroke: string, handler: (keystroke: string) => void, options?: KeyBindingOptions): () => void;
  bind(bindings: Record<string, (keystroke: string) => void>, options?: KeyBindingOptions): () => void;
  label(keystroke: string): string;
};

interface KeyBindingOptions {
  when?: "always" | "notEditing";
  repeat?: boolean;
}
```

Shortcuts work on macOS, Windows, Linux and in browsers (the browser's own keys, such as Ctrl+T or Cmd+W, never reach the page). On iOS and Android, `bind` keeps the bindings but no key fires them yet, so the same code runs everywhere.

## keymap.bind

```ts
bind(keystroke: string, handler: (keystroke: string) => void, options?: KeyBindingOptions): () => void;
```

Runs `handler` when `keystroke` is pressed and returns a function that removes the binding. The handler gets the keystroke as you wrote it, in its case.

```tsx
import { mount, signal, Text } from "nsh";
import { keymap } from "nsh/keymap";

const open = signal(false);
keymap.bind("mod+k", () => open.set(true));
keymap.bind("escape", () => open.set(false));

mount(() => <Text>{open() ? "Search…" : "Press ⌘K"}</Text>);
```

Pass an object to bind several keystrokes at once; the function returned removes them all:

```ts
const unbind = keymap.bind({
  "mod+s": save,
  "mod+shift+p": openPalette,
  f5: refresh,
});
```

A binding made while a component renders is removed with the component, so a screen's shortcuts live as long as the screen:

```tsx
function Editor() {
  keymap.bind("mod+enter", send);
  return <Input multiline />;
}
```

With the dev server, editing a module removes the bindings its top-level code made before it runs again, so hot reload never leaves stale shortcuts behind.

## keymap.label

```ts
label(keystroke: string): string;
```

Returns `keystroke` as menus and hints show it where the app runs: `"⇧⌘L"` on macOS and iOS (and in a browser on a Mac, iPhone or iPad), `"Ctrl+Shift+L"` on Windows, Linux and other browsers, for `"mod+shift+l"`. Use it to show an app's shortcuts with the keys that work:

```tsx
<Text>Search {keymap.label("mod+k")}</Text>
```

It throws a `TypeError` for an invalid keystroke, as `bind` does.

## Keystrokes

A keystroke is modifiers and a key joined by `+`: `"mod+k"`, `"ctrl+shift+p"`, `"alt+enter"`, `"escape"`, `"f5"`, `"cmd+-"` (Command and minus).

| Modifier | macOS | Windows | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mod` (also `cmdorctrl`) | Command (⌘) | Ctrl | Ctrl |
| `cmd` (also `command`, `meta`, `super`, `win`) | Command (⌘) | Windows key | Super |
| `ctrl` (also `control`) | Control (⌃) | Ctrl | Ctrl |
| `alt` (also `option`, `opt`) | Option (⌥) | Alt | Alt |
| `shift` | Shift (⇧) | Shift | Shift |

In a browser, keys follow the platform the browser runs on: `mod` is Command on a Mac, iPhone or iPad and Ctrl elsewhere.

Use `mod` for an app's own shortcuts: it is the key each platform's apps use for them (⌘K on macOS, Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux), so one spelling fits everywhere. The Windows key and Super mostly belong to the system, so `cmd` is rarely right outside macOS.

The key is a letter, digit or punctuation key, written as the character it types on a US keyboard without Shift (`k`, `1`, `,`, `/`, `[`; `"shift+/"` for `?`, `"shift+k"` for Shift+K), or a name: `plus` (the `=` / `+` key, also written `=`), `minus` (also `-`), `space`, `enter` (`return`), `escape` (`esc`), `tab`, `backspace`, `delete` (`del`), `insert`, the arrows `up`, `down`, `left`, `right` (`arrowup`, …), `home`, `end`, `pageup`, `pagedown`, `f1` to `f24`. Case does not matter: `"Mod+Shift+K"` is `"mod+shift+k"`, and a capital letter is the same key, not Shift (`"mod+K"` is `"mod+k"`). Lowercase is the recommended style, which these pages use. `"mod-k"` and `"mod++"` are errors whose messages give the right spelling. Menu shortcuts in `nsh/desktop` take the same keystrokes.

Shortcuts work with any keyboard layout: on a Cyrillic or Greek layout, `mod+k` is the key that types K on a US layout, as menu shortcuts are.

`bind` throws a `TypeError` that says what is wrong with an invalid keystroke (`keymap.bind: invalid keystroke "cmd+kk": unknown key "kk"`), and refuses the keystrokes the system keeps for itself, so an app can never break them:

| Platform | Reserved |
|---|---|
| macOS, iOS | Cmd+Q (quit), Cmd+H (hide), Option+Cmd+H (hide others), Cmd+M (minimize), Ctrl+Cmd+F (full screen) |
| Linux, Windows, Android | Ctrl+Q (quit), Alt+F4 (close), F11 (full screen) |
| Web | None (the browser keeps its own keys) |

## While typing

A text input with the keyboard focus needs its keys: typing, moving the caret, deleting, and select all, cut, copy, paste, undo and redo. So by default a binding does not fire while a text input (or a web view) has the focus if its keystroke is one of these: plain keys and keys with only Shift or Option, the arrows, Home, End, Page Up / Down, Return, Tab, Escape, Backspace, Delete, and `mod+a`, `mod+c`, `mod+v`, `mod+x`, `mod+z`. Other keystrokes with Command or Control, and the function keys, fire wherever the focus is.

`when` changes that:

| `when` | Fires |
|---|---|
| (default) | As above |
| `"always"` | Also in text inputs, before the input sees the key |
| `"notEditing"` | Never while a text input has the focus |

```ts
// Sends from the message field too.
keymap.bind("mod+enter", send, { when: "always" });
// Only when the user is not typing.
keymap.bind("mod+e", archive, { when: "notEditing" });
```

## Which binding runs

A key that fires a binding is consumed: it is not typed, the system does not beep, and NSH's own keys do not see it (Escape going back, Tab moving the focus, the arrows scrolling). When several bindings have the same keystroke, the newest one that may fire runs, so a dialog can bind Escape over the screen's binding and the screen's comes back when the dialog's goes. Bindings are checked natively the moment the key is pressed; the handler runs right after, on the JS thread.

Holding a key down fires its binding once, until the key is released; with `repeat: true` it fires again on every auto-repeat (to step through a list, say):

```ts
keymap.bind("alt+down", nextItem, { repeat: true });
```

Menu shortcuts give way to a binding of the same keystroke: the application menu's ([`nsh/desktop`](./nsh-desktop)) on every desktop, and on macOS the built-in menus' too (Cmd+W, Cmd+C, ...). While you develop with `nsh run`, Cmd+R / Ctrl+R always reloads the app, even if it binds `mod+r`; a packaged app can bind it.

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-keymap

---

# nsh/native

`nsh/native` connects your app to native views that the host app provides. An iOS or Android app that embeds NSH can register its own views (a map, a chart, a camera preview) by name; `nativeComponent` gives you a typed component for one of them. Because NSH renders with real native views, such a component sits in the view hierarchy like any other view: it is laid out by NSH, clips and scrolls with its parents, and overlaps correctly.

```ts
import { nativeComponent } from "nsh/native";
```

See [Native components](https://nsh.dev/docs/native-components.md) for registering the native side, and [Embedding on iOS](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-ios.md) / [Embedding on Android](https://nsh.dev/docs/embedding-android.md).

## nativeComponent

```ts
function nativeComponent<P extends object = {}, E extends object = {}>(
  name: string,
  spec: NativeComponentSpec<P, E>,
): (props: NativeComponentProps<P, E>) => YNode;

interface NativeComponentSpec<P, E> {
  /** Its own props: sent to the component (any JSON value), each when it changes. */
  props: readonly (keyof P & string)[];
  /** The events it emits. */
  events?: readonly (keyof E & string)[];
}
```

Returns a component for the native component the embedding app registered as `name` (Swift `NshAppView.register(component:)`, Java `NshView.registerComponent`).

- `P` is the type of its own props. Each prop listed in `spec.props` is sent to the native side as JSON when it changes; setting it to `undefined` removes it.
- `E` maps event names to their payloads. An event `regionChange` becomes the handler prop `onRegionChange`.
- The component also takes every [view prop](https://nsh.dev/elements/view.md) except `children`: `style`, `class`, layout, accessibility, touch handlers and `ref`.

```ts
type NativeComponentProps<P, E> = Omit<ViewProps, "children"> & P & NativeEventHandlers<E>;
type NativeEventHandlers<E> = { [K in keyof E & string as `on${Capitalize<K>}`]?: (data: E[K]) => void };
```

### Size

The component is laid out like a view, at the size its style gives it. Where the style leaves a dimension open, it uses the size the native component reports (as an image uses its natural size).

### Commands

Its `ref` receives a `YNode`; `ref.command(name, args)` calls command `name` of the native component with `args` (any JSON value):

```ts
map.command("zoomTo", { level: 3 });
```

### When nothing is registered

Where nothing is registered under `name` (a different host app, the dev host, the browser), the component renders an empty view and a warning is logged once. Keep the app usable without it, or check for your host before using it.

## Example

The badge here is a native view of the host app, registered as `embed.badge`. NSH lays it out, sends it `text` and `color`, receives its `tap` events, and calls its `pulse` command:

```tsx
import { mount, signal, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { nativeComponent } from "nsh/native";
import { SafeAreaView } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

const Badge = nativeComponent<{ text: string; color?: string }, { tap: { count: number } }>("embed.badge", {
  props: ["text", "color"],
  events: ["tap"],
});

function App() {
  const taps = signal(0);
  let badge: YNode | undefined;
  return (
    <SafeAreaView style={{ flex: 1, padding: 20, gap: 16 }}>
      <Badge
        ref={(node) => (badge = node)}
        text={taps() === 0 ? "Tap the native badge" : `Tapped ${taps()}×`}
        color="#8250df"
        onTap={(e) => {
          taps.set(e.count);
          badge?.command("pulse");
        }}
        style={{ alignSelf: "flex-start", borderRadius: 8, overflow: "hidden" }}
      />
    </SafeAreaView>
  );
}

mount(App);
```

> [!NOTE]
> Props, events and command arguments cross to the native side as JSON. Registered components are the host app's own code: NSH's [sandbox limits and capabilities](https://nsh.dev/docs/sandbox-and-capabilities.md) do not apply to what they do.

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-native

---

# nsh/accessibility

`nsh/accessibility` reads the user's accessibility settings (is a screen reader running, did they ask for less motion) and talks to the screen reader. The accessibility props of elements (`accessibilityLabel`, `accessibilityRole`, ...) are documented under [Elements](https://nsh.dev/elements.md); the guide is [Accessibility](https://nsh.dev/docs/accessibility.md).

```ts
import { AccessibilityInfo, reduceMotion, screenReaderEnabled } from "nsh/accessibility";
```

## screenReaderEnabled

```ts
const screenReaderEnabled: Accessor<boolean>;
```

Whether a screen reader (VoiceOver, TalkBack) is running. Reactive: what reads it updates when the user turns the screen reader on or off.

```tsx
<If when={!screenReaderEnabled()} else={<Text onPress={next}>Next photo</Text>}>
  <Text>Swipe for the next photo</Text>
</If>
```

## reduceMotion

```ts
const reduceMotion: Accessor<boolean>;
```

Whether the user asked for less motion (Reduce Motion on iOS, Remove animations on Android). Reactive. Tailwind classes follow it too with the `motion-reduce:` variant.

```ts
const open = () => {
  if (reduceMotion()) panel.set(0);
  else panel.spring(0);
};
```

## AccessibilityInfo

```ts
const AccessibilityInfo: {
  announceForAccessibility(message: string): void;
  setAccessibilityFocus(node: YNode): void;
  isScreenReaderEnabled(): Promise<boolean>;
  isReduceMotionEnabled(): Promise<boolean>;
  addEventListener(
    event: "screenReaderChanged" | "reduceMotionChanged",
    listener: (enabled: boolean) => void,
  ): { remove(): void };
};
```

The system's accessibility settings, read once or followed with listeners. `screenReaderEnabled()` and `reduceMotion()` are their reactive forms; prefer them in components.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `announceForAccessibility(message)` | The screen reader reads `message` (a VoiceOver announcement, TalkBack). Use it for results that appear without focus moving, such as "Saved". |
| `setAccessibilityFocus(node)` | Moves the screen reader's focus to `node` (an element's `ref`). |
| `isScreenReaderEnabled()` | Resolves with whether a screen reader runs. |
| `isReduceMotionEnabled()` | Resolves with whether reduced motion is on. |
| `addEventListener(event, listener)` | Calls `listener` with the new value when the setting changes; returns a subscription to `remove()`. |

```tsx
import { cleanup, Text, View, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { AccessibilityInfo } from "nsh/accessibility";

function Saved() {
  let note!: YNode;
  const save = () => {
    AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility("Saved");
    AccessibilityInfo.setAccessibilityFocus(note);
  };
  const sub = AccessibilityInfo.addEventListener("screenReaderChanged", (on) => console.log("screen reader", on));
  cleanup(() => sub.remove());
  return (
    <View style={{ gap: 8 }}>
      <Text onPress={save} accessibilityRole="button">Save</Text>
      <Text ref={note}>Your changes are kept on this device.</Text>
    </View>
  );
}
```

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-accessibility

---

# nsh/ios

`nsh/ios` holds APIs that only iOS has. The module can be imported on every platform, so one bundle runs everywhere: elsewhere its components render nothing, and `isAvailable` tells you whether you are on iOS.

```ts
import { InputAccessoryView, isAvailable } from "nsh/ios";
```

iOS-only *props* of elements and components are not here: they go in the `ios={{…}}` prop (for example `<Input ios={{ textContentType: "oneTimeCode" }} />`). See [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md).

## isAvailable

```ts
const isAvailable: boolean;
```

`true` on iOS, the iOS simulator and Mac Catalyst; `false` elsewhere.

## InputAccessoryView

```ts
function InputAccessoryView(props: InputAccessoryViewProps): YNode | null;

interface InputAccessoryViewProps {
  nativeID: string;
  style?: StyleProp<ViewStyle>;
  class?: string;
  children?: JSX.Element;
}
```

A bar over the keyboard (UIKit's `inputAccessoryView`), shown while an input whose `ios={{ inputAccessoryViewID }}` matches its `nativeID` has focus. It is as wide as the window and as tall as its content, and moves with the keyboard natively.

| Prop | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `nativeID` | `string` | Inputs with this `inputAccessoryViewID` show the bar. |
| `style` | `StyleProp<ViewStyle>` | The bar's style (its background, for example). |
| `class` | `string` | Tailwind classes. |
| `children` | `JSX.Element` | The bar's content. |

It renders nothing where it is placed in the tree, and nothing at all on Android, so you can place it next to the input it belongs to.

```tsx
import { Input, signal, Text, View, type YNode } from "nsh";
import { InputAccessoryView } from "nsh/ios";

function Note() {
  const text = signal("");
  let input: YNode | undefined;
  return (
    <View>
      <Input
        ref={(n) => (input = n)}
        value={text()}
        onChangeText={(v) => text.set(v)}
        placeholder="Write a note"
        ios={{ inputAccessoryViewID: "note-bar" }}
      />
      <InputAccessoryView nativeID="note-bar" style={{ backgroundColor: "#f1f5f9" }}>
        <View style={{ flexDirection: "row", alignItems: "center", padding: 10 }}>
          <Text style={{ flex: 1, color: "#64748b" }}>{text().length} characters</Text>
          <Text onPress={() => input?.blur()} style={{ fontWeight: "600" }}>Done</Text>
        </View>
      </InputAccessoryView>
    </View>
  );
}
```

See also [Forms and keyboard](https://nsh.dev/docs/forms-and-keyboard.md).

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-ios

---

# nsh/android

`nsh/android` holds APIs that only Android has. The module can be imported on every platform, so one bundle runs everywhere: elsewhere its functions do nothing, and `isAvailable` tells you whether you are on Android.

```ts
import { BackHandler, isAvailable, setStatusBarBackgroundColor, Toast } from "nsh/android";
```

Android-only *props* of elements and components are not here: they go in the `android={{…}}` prop (for example `<View android={{ elevation: 4, ripple: … }} />`). See [Platform-specific code](https://nsh.dev/docs/platform-specific.md).

## isAvailable

```ts
const isAvailable: boolean;
```

`true` on Android; `false` elsewhere.

## Toast

```ts
const Toast: {
  show(message: string, duration?: "short" | "long" | null): void;
};
```

Shows a short message at the bottom of the screen (Android's toast). `duration` is `"short"` by default.

```ts
import { Platform } from "nsh/device";
import { Toast } from "nsh/android";
import { Alert } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

const notify = (message: string) =>
  Platform.OS === "android" ? Toast.show(message) : Alert.alert("Done", message);
```

## BackHandler

```ts
const BackHandler: {
  addEventListener(event: "hardwareBackPress", listener: () => boolean | void): { remove(): void };
  exitApp(): void;
};
```

The system back button and back gesture. Modals and navigation stacks handle the back press first (a modal closes, a stack pops); only when none of them takes it do `BackHandler`'s listeners run.

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `addEventListener("hardwareBackPress", listener)` | `listener` returns `true` when it handled the press. The most recently added listener runs first. If no listener handles it, the app exits. Returns a subscription to `remove()`. |
| `exitApp()` | Leaves the app. |

```tsx
import { cleanup, signal } from "nsh";
import { BackHandler } from "nsh/android";
import { Alert } from "nsh/ui/mobile";

function Editor() {
  const dirty = signal(false);
  const sub = BackHandler.addEventListener("hardwareBackPress", () => {
    if (!dirty()) return false; // let the app go back or exit
    Alert.alert("Discard changes?", undefined, [{ text: "Keep" }, { text: "Discard", style: "destructive" }]).then(
      (i) => i === 1 && BackHandler.exitApp(),
    );
    return true;
  });
  cleanup(() => sub.remove());
  // ...
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> The listener runs after the system has delivered the press: the main thread never waits for JS. While at least one listener is registered, NSH takes back presses that modals and stacks leave, and exits the app itself when no listener returns `true`.

## setStatusBarBackgroundColor

```ts
function setStatusBarBackgroundColor(backgroundColor: string, animated?: boolean | null): void;
```

Sets the status bar's color, below what rendered `<StatusBar android={{ backgroundColor }}>` components set (the last mounted `StatusBar` wins over this base value). It has an effect on Android versions before edge-to-edge became mandatory (API 35); from API 35 the status bar is transparent and your content draws behind it.

```ts
setStatusBarBackgroundColor("#1e293b", true);
```

See [`StatusBar`](https://nsh.dev/components/status-bar.md) for the component.

Source: https://nsh.dev/modules/nsh-android

---

# nsh/desktop

`nsh/desktop` holds what only desktops have: the window and its title bar, the application menu and context menus. It works on macOS, Windows and Linux. The module can be imported on every platform, so one bundle runs everywhere: on iOS and Android its functions do nothing, and `isAvailable` tells you whether you are on a desktop.

```ts
import { isAvailable, Menu, titleBar, Window } from "nsh/desktop";
```

## isAvailable

```ts
const isAvailable: boolean;
```

`true` on macOS, Windows and Linux; `false` elsewhere.

## Window

```ts
const Window: {
  setTitle(title: string): void;
  setTitleBar(style: "default" | "hidden", height?: number): void;
  minimize(): void;
  toggleMaximize(): void;
  toggleFullScreen(): void;
  setFrame(frame: {
    x?: number;
    y?: number;
    width?: number;
    height?: number;
    animated?: boolean;
  }): void;
  setLevel(level: "normal" | "floating" | "desktopIcon"): void;
  close(): void;
};
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `setTitle(title)` | The window's title: the title bar, the taskbar or Dock, the window switcher. |
| `setTitleBar(style, height?)` | `"hidden"` removes the system's title bar: the app fills the window up to its top edge and draws a title bar of its own. The system's window controls stay (macOS's traffic lights, Windows' minimize / maximize / close buttons, GTK's window buttons). `height` is your bar's height in points: the controls are centered in it (Windows' caption buttons fill it); without it they take the platform's height. `"default"` brings the system's title bar back. |
| `minimize()` | Minimizes the window. |
| `toggleMaximize()` | Maximizes the window, or restores it when it is maximized. |
| `toggleFullScreen()` | Enters or leaves full screen. |
| `setFrame(frame)` | Moves and sizes the window in points; omitted fields keep their values. On macOS and Windows, `width` and `height` include window decorations; on Linux they set GTK's default window size. `x` and `y` are the bottom left corner in macOS screen coordinates and the top left on Windows. `animated: true` enables macOS's resize animation (default: false). |
| `setLevel(level)` | On macOS and Windows, `"floating"` keeps the window above normal windows and `"normal"` restores the normal level. `"desktopIcon"` selects macOS's desktop icon level; on Windows it moves the window to the bottom of the current z-order, where later activation can raise it. |
| `close()` | Closes the window; the app ends with it. |

Window sizing is supported on macOS, Windows and Linux; positioning and levels on macOS and Windows. Linux's window manager controls placement and stacking. GPUI's host configures window bounds and level when opening the window.

When sizing a window from content measured with `onLayout`, allow room for window decorations on macOS and Windows. `width` and `height` accept positive finite numbers; `x` and `y` accept finite numbers. Invalid fields keep their previous values.

## A title bar of your own

With the title bar hidden, the app draws its own bar and says which parts of it move the window with `desktop={{ windowDrag: true }}`:

```tsx
import { Input, Text, View } from "nsh";
import { titleBar, Window } from "nsh/desktop";

Window.setTitleBar("hidden", 40); // a bar 40 points tall

function TitleBar() {
  return (
    <View
      desktop={{ windowDrag: true }}
      style={{
        height: titleBar().height || 40,
        paddingLeft: titleBar().left + 8, // macOS's traffic lights
        paddingRight: titleBar().right + 8, // the caption buttons on Windows, GTK's buttons
        flexDirection: "row",
        alignItems: "center",
      }}
    >
      <Text>My App</Text>
      <View style={{ flex: 1 }} />
      <Input placeholder="Search" style={{ width: 180 }} />
    </View>
  );
}
```

Pressing a view with `windowDrag` drags the window as the system's title bar would: a double click maximizes it (or does what the user set: on macOS, "Double-click a window's title bar to"), and on Windows and Linux a right click opens the window menu.

- The nearest view that sets `windowDrag` decides: `desktop={{ windowDrag: false }}` keeps a part of a draggable view clickable.
- Text fields and views with press or touch handlers (`onPress`, `onTouch*`, responders) inside a draggable view stay clickable without it: the search field and any buttons in the example above work as usual.
- `windowDrag` also works with the system's title bar: a sidebar or toolbar can move the window too.

### titleBar

```ts
const titleBar: Accessor<{ height: number; left: number; right: number }>;
```

The hidden title bar's area, in points (reactive): its `height`, and the widths the system's window controls take at its `left` and `right` ends. Lay your bar out with it so that nothing goes under the controls. All three are 0 while the system shows its title bar (and in full screen, and off desktops).

| | `height` | `left` | `right` |
|---|---|---|---|
| macOS | `height`, else the title bar's (28 or 32, by macOS version) | The traffic lights' width | 0 |
| Windows | `height`, else 32 | 0 | The three caption buttons (138) |
| Linux | `height`, else the header bar's | The window buttons at the start (the desktop's button layout) | The window buttons at the end |

On Windows the caption buttons are drawn by NSH in Windows 11's style and follow the app's appearance; hovering the maximize button shows Windows 11's snap layouts. The window keeps its resize borders, shadow and rounded corners on every platform.

## Menu

```ts
const Menu: {
  setApplicationMenu(items: MenuItem[] | null): void;
  popup(items: MenuItem[], at?: { x: number; y: number }): Promise<void>;
};
```

| Member | Description |
|---|---|
| `setApplicationMenu(items)` | Sets the application menu: one submenu per top-level item (`File`, `Edit`, ...). On macOS it is the menu bar, whose first menu is the app menu (AppKit titles it with the app's name). On Windows and Linux it is the window's menu bar, which is not shown while the title bar is hidden; its shortcuts still work, and a title bar of the app's own can open its menus with `Menu.popup`. `null` restores the platform's default menu. |
| `popup(items, at?)` | Shows a context menu with its top left corner at `at` (the window's coordinates, in points), or at the pointer. The promise resolves once the menu closes, whether an item was chosen or not: a button that opened it can stay pressed until then. |

Call `setApplicationMenu` again to change the menu. Inside an `effect` it follows the signals it reads: a check mark or an enabled state that depends on app state stays current.

### Menu items

```ts
type MenuItem =
  | { type: "separator" }
  | {
      label?: string;
      role?: MenuRole;
      shortcut?: string;
      enabled?: boolean;
```
